chunks.text: The prototypic lesion is the vegetation - a mass of platelets, fibrin, microorganisms and scant inflammatory cells - usually on heart valves but also on the low-pressure side of a ventricular septal defect, on mural endocardium injured by aberrant blood jets or foreign bodies, or on intracardiac devices. Intact endothelium resists most bacteria; endothelial injury (e.g., at sites of high-velocity jet impact or on the low-pressure side of a structural lesion) permits direct infection by virulent organisms or formation of a sterile platelet-fibrin thrombus (nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis, NBTE) that becomes a nidus for bacterial seeding during transient bacteremia. NBTE is most often associated with mitral regurgitation, aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, ventricular septal defects and complex congenital heart disease, and also arises from hypercoagulable states (marantic endocarditis of malignancy/chronic disease and the bland vegetations of SLE and antiphospholipid syndrome). Circulating organisms adhere via surface adhesins (MSCRAMMs) - fibronectin-binding proteins, S. aureus clumping factor, enterococcal Fss2/Ace/Ebp pili, streptococcal glucans/FimA; S. aureus can even invade intact endothelium via fibronectin-binding proteins and von Willebrand factor, allowing infection of previously normal valves. Adherent organisms proliferate into microcolonies, induce platelet deposition and a local procoagulant (tissue-factor) state, and become buried in fibrin; deep organisms are metabolically inactive and relatively antibiotic-resistant while surface organisms are continuously shed into the blood. Clinical manifestations arise from intracardiac structural damage, embolization of vegetation fragments causing remote infarction/infection, hematogenous seeding during bacteremia, and immune-complex deposition; constitutional symptoms reflect cytokine release.

source.page: Harrison 22e p.1036-1048 (Chapter 133, Infective Endocarditis)

chunks.text: IE spans a clinical continuum from acute to subacute, and the causative organism largely dictates the tempo: beta-hemolytic streptococci, S. aureus and pneumococci tend to produce an acute, rapidly destructive course, whereas viridans streptococci, enterococci, CoNS and HACEK organisms usually cause subacute disease (Bartonella, T. whipplei, C. burnetii and M. chimaera are exceptionally indolent).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.1036-1048 (Chapter 133, Infective Endocarditis)

chunks.text: Up to half of arterial emboli precede the diagnosis of IE; embolic risk falls rapidly once effective antibiotics begin, so emboli occurring late during or after therapy do not by themselves indicate treatment failure.

source.page: Harrison 22e p.1036-1048 (Chapter 133, Infective Endocarditis)

chunks.text: In hemodynamically stable patients with suspected subacute IE, empirical antibiotics can reasonably be withheld initially to allow uncontaminated blood cultures, but patients with sepsis or deteriorating hemodynamics should be treated immediately after the first three culture sets are drawn.

source.page: Harrison 22e p.1036-1048 (Chapter 133, Infective Endocarditis)

chunks.text: Surgery is indicated (as a knowledge concept, distinct from antibiotic regimens) for optimal outcome when there is moderate-severe CHF/shock from valve dysfunction, paravalvular extension with abscess/fistula/heart block, persistent bacteremia without an extracardiac source despite 7-10 days of therapy, lack of effective antimicrobial therapy (fungal, Brucella, multidrug-resistant gram-negative), or an unstable partially dehisced prosthetic valve; it is strongly considered for large (>10 mm) hypermobile vegetations with prior embolus and valve dysfunction, very large (>30 mm) vegetations, S. aureus PVE with intracardiac complications, and relapse after optimal therapy. Removal of all hardware is recommended for established CIED-IE.

source.page: Harrison 22e p.1036-1048 (Chapter 133, Infective Endocarditis)

chunks.text: Fever is present in 80-90% of cases and a heart murmur in 80-85%, but in subacute IE fever is typically low-grade (rarely above 39.4 C) and may be blunted altogether in elderly, severely debilitated, or renal-failure patients.

source.page: Harrison 22e p.1036-1048 (Chapter 133, Infective Endocarditis)

chunks.text: A new or worsening regurgitant murmur is heard in only 20-50% of cases; in acute IE on a previously normal valve a murmur may be absent at first but is ultimately detected in about 85%.

source.page: Harrison 22e p.1036-1048 (Chapter 133, Infective Endocarditis)

chunks.text: Classic peripheral stigmata (Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, Roth spots, subungual/splinter hemorrhages) appear in only about 2-15% of cases and have become infrequent with earlier diagnosis; their absence does not exclude IE.

source.page: Harrison 22e p.1036-1048 (Chapter 133, Infective Endocarditis)

chunks.text: Janeway lesions are nonsuppurative painless hemorrhagic macules of the palms/soles classically linked to prolonged subacute infection, whereas septic emboli (subungual hemorrhages, Osler nodes) mimicking these lesions are common in acute S. aureus IE.

chunks.text: Three independent predictors of embolization are S. aureus etiology, mobile vegetations larger than 10 mm, and involvement of the anterior mitral leaflet.

chunks.text: In people who inject drugs, 35-60% of IE is confined to the tricuspid valve and presents with fever but faint or absent murmur and no peripheral stigmata, often with septic pulmonary emboli (cough, pleuritic pain, nodular infiltrates).

chunks.text: S. aureus bacteremia carries an 8-14% prevalence of IE and high mortality, so echocardiography (high-quality TTE, preferably TEE) is recommended routinely; intracardiac device, emboli, 2 or more positive cultures, community acquisition, vertebral osteomyelitis or persistent bacteremia each raise IE risk and argue for early TEE.

chunks.text: About 12-17% of patients with E. faecalis bacteremia and about 7% with non-beta-hemolytic streptococcal bacteremia have IE, justifying echocardiographic screening when predictive features are present.

chunks.text: Overall survival in developed countries is about 80-85%, but varies markedly by subgroup. About 85-90% survive NVE caused by viridans streptococci, HACEK organisms, or synergy-susceptible enterococci. Non-injecting patients with S. aureus NVE have 55-70% survival; injecting patients have 85-90%, but 1-year mortality rises to 20-30% if substance-use disorder is not addressed. Prosthetic-valve IE arising within 2 months of surgery carries 40-50% mortality versus only 10-20% for late-onset PVE; elderly TAVR-PVE in-hospital mortality is 35-50%, rising to 60-75% at 1 year. Crude survival after successful treatment is roughly 80-90% at 1 year and 70-80% at 2 years. Death often reflects comorbidities and end-organ complications rather than antibiotic failure. Adverse outcomes are linked to older age, severe comorbidity/diabetes, delayed diagnosis, prosthetic or aortic valve involvement, virulent or resistant pathogens (S. aureus, P. aeruginosa, yeast), intracardiac and major neurologic complications, and health care-associated infection.

source.page: Harrison 22e p.1036-1048 (Chapter 133, Infective Endocarditis)

chunks.text: Diagnosis uses the 2023 Duke-International Society for Cardiovascular Infectious Diseases (Duke-ISCVID) update of the modified Duke criteria (sensitivity 80-93%). MAJOR criteria: (1) Microbiologic - a typical IE organism in 2 or more separate blood culture sets (S. aureus, S. lugdunensis, E. faecalis, all streptococci except S. pneumoniae and S. pyogenes, Granulicatella/Abiotrophia/Gemella, HACEK group; and, when intracardiac prosthetic material is present, CoNS, C. striatum, C. jeikeium, S. marcescens, P. aeruginosa, C. acnes, nontuberculous mycobacteria and Candida), OR a nontypical organism in 3 or more sets; positive PCR/single culture/serology for C. burnetii, Bartonella spp. or T. whipplei. (2) Imaging - echocardiography or cardiac CT showing vegetation, perforation/leaflet aneurysm, abscess, pseudoaneurysm or fistula, OR new valvular regurgitation, OR new prosthetic dehiscence; OR abnormal FDG-PET/CT activity on a valve/graft/lead/prosthetic material. (3) Surgical - IE seen at direct surgical inspection. MINOR criteria: predisposing condition (prior IE, injection drug use, prosthetic valve, prior valve repair, congenital heart disease such as bicuspid aortic valve, CIED, more-than-mild regurgitation/stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy); fever over 38.0 C; vascular phenomena (arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial/conjunctival hemorrhage, Janeway lesions); immunologic phenomena (glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots, positive rheumatoid factor); microbiologic evidence not meeting a major criterion; and PET/CT activity within 3 months of prosthetic implantation. CLASSIFICATION: DEFINITE IE = pathologic confirmation OR 2 major, or 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor criteria. POSSIBLE IE = 1 major + 1 minor, or 3 minor. REJECTED = firm alternative diagnosis, or resolution with under 4 days of antibiotics, or no histologic evidence at surgery/autopsy after under 4 days of therapy. IE is also classified by tempo (acute vs subacute), site (native vs prosthetic valve, right-sided/tricuspid), cause, and predisposition (injection drug use, health care-associated).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.1036-1048 (Chapter 133, Infective Endocarditis)

chunks.text: Blood cultures (≥3 sets from separate sites, before antibiotics) — The single most important diagnostic step — identifies the organism and is a major Duke criterion; false-negative cultures from premature antibiotics significantly complicate diagnosis and management.

Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE), followed by transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) if TTE inconclusive or high suspicion persists — Identifies vegetations, abscess, or valve destruction — a major Duke criterion and essential for surgical planning.
ECG — Screens for new conduction abnormalities (e.g., new heart block), which can indicate perivalvular abscess extension.
CBC, ESR/CRP, renal function — Supports overall assessment of inflammatory burden and any renal involvement (e.g., immune complex glomerulonephritis).
Infective Endocarditis (infective) — Cardiovascular

veryLikely: Viridans group streptococci (native valve, subacute presentation), Staphylococcus aureus (acute presentation, IV drug use); likely: Enterococcus species (especially post-genitourinary procedures, elderly), Coagulase-negative staphylococci (prosthetic valve, particularly early post-operative); possible: HACEK organisms and other fastidious organisms (culture-negative endocarditis)

[guideline] empiric → Vancomycin + Ceftriaxone (empiric, native valve, pending cultures) This combination provides empiric coverage of the most likely organisms (streptococci, staphylococci including MRSA, and many enterococci) while blood culture and susceptibility results are pending, balancing broad coverage against the need for prolonged targeted therapy once identified.
[guideline] alternative → Vancomycin + Gentamicin + Rifampin (suspected prosthetic valve infection)

PCR (notably real-time PCR) of blood/CSF/urine — confirms diagnosis with high accuracy during the first 5 days of illness, before serology becomes positive (p.1443)
Bilirubin, aminotransferases, alkaline phosphatase (bilirubin may be high; transaminase rises typically only moderate) (p.1443)
Chest radiograph / CT (patchy bilateral lower-lobe alveolar pattern from alveolar hemorrhage; pleura-based densities; ground-glass ARDS pattern) (p.1443)
ECG (nonspecific ST/T changes; repolarization abnormalities and arrhythmias are poor prognostic signs) (p.1443)
CSF examination when meningitis suspected (pleocytosis from a few to >1000 cells/uL, lymphocytic but may be PMN-predominant early; protein normal or slightly raised, glucose normal) (p.1443)
Co-testing for rickettsiae, dengue, and hantavirus given overlap and reported dual infections (p.1443)

Microscopic agglutination test (MAT) using live leptospiral strains — paired acute/convalescent sera seeking a fourfold rise; single high titer (1:200-1:800 depending on endemicity) supportive (p.1443)
IgM ELISA and commercial rapid lateral-flow / latex agglutination tests (useful where MAT/culture unavailable) (p.1443)
Blood/urine/CSF culture (special media; may take weeks to months) (p.1441, 1443)
C-reactive protein, procalcitonin, ESR (raised inflammatory markers) (p.1443)
Coagulation profile / DIC markers (D-dimer, antithrombin, protein C) in severe disease (p.1443)
Serum amylase (often elevated even without overt pancreatitis) (p.1443)
Serum electrolytes including magnesium (urinary magnesium loss is characteristic; hypokalemia, hyponatremia) (p.1443)
Urinalysis (leukocytes, erythrocytes, hyaline/granular casts, mild proteinuria) (p.1443)

Leptospires enter through cuts, abraded skin, or mucous membranes (especially conjunctival and oral). The highly motile organisms proliferate, cross tissue barriers, and disseminate hematogenously to all organs (leptospiremic phase), evading innate immune mechanisms such as complement-mediated killing and phagocytosis; an exaggerated proinflammatory response correlates with mortality. With the immune phase, antibodies appear and leptospires clear from blood but persist in liver, lung, kidney, heart, and brain. Renal pathology shows acute tubular damage and interstitial nephritis, progressing to interstitial edema and acute tubular necrosis, with dysregulated nephron transporters causing impaired sodium absorption, potassium wasting, and polyuria. Liver histology shows focal (not widespread) hepatocellular necrosis, inflammation, bile canaliculus plugging, and hepatocyte apoptosis, with disruption of intercellular junctions and bile leakage. Petechiae and hemorrhages occur across many organs. Hemorrhage is associated with thrombocytopenia (likely platelet consumption); a consumptive coagulopathy with elevated coagulation-activation markers, reduced anticoagulant markers, and dysregulated fibrinolysis may progress to overt DIC. Endothelial cell activation (raised soluble E-selectin and von Willebrand factor) correlates with severity, and leptospires/leptospiral proteins disrupt endothelial barrier function, increasing permeability. The LPS has unusually low endotoxic potency, yet serovar-specific anti-LPS antibodies are central to protective humoral immunity (p.1441-1442).

Classically biphasic: an acute leptospiremic phase (fever lasting ~3-10 days, organism culturable/PCR-detectable in blood) followed by an immune phase in which symptoms may resolve as antibodies appear and leptospires can be recovered from urine; the two phases are not always distinct, mild cases may lack the second phase, and severe disease can be monophasic and fulminant (p.1442).
Idea that specific serogroups cause distinct clinical syndromes has been refuted, although some serovars tend to cause more severe disease (p.1442).
Serology lacks sensitivity in the early acute phase (up to day 5) and cannot guide a timely treatment decision; PCR (notably real-time PCR) can confirm diagnosis during the first 5 days (p.1443).
MAT antibodies generally do not reach detectable levels until the second week of illness, and the antibody response may be blunted by early antibiotics (p.1443).
Incubation is usually 1-2 weeks but ranges from 2 to 30 days (p.1442).
Conjunctival suffusion (redness without exudate) is a characteristic but non-pathognomonic sign; muscle pain is intense, especially in the calves, back, and abdomen (p.1442).
Headache is intense and frontal or retro-orbital, sometimes with photophobia, resembling dengue (p.1442).
Weil's syndrome denotes the severe triad of jaundice, acute kidney injury, and hemorrhage (p.1442-1443).

Severe pulmonary hemorrhage (with or without jaundice) is increasingly recognized as an important and widespread presentation; hemoptysis may not become apparent until the patient is intubated (p.1439, 1442).
Jaundice occurs in only ~5-10% of patients, can be deep with an orange skin cast, and is usually NOT associated with fulminant hepatic necrosis (p.1442).

Aseptic meningitis is more common in children than adults; altered mental status in severe disease may reflect leptospiral meningitis, which can occur in anicteric patients lacking other hallmarks (p.1442-1443).
Autoimmune-associated uveitis is a recognized, potentially chronic late sequela (p.1443).
Absence of a travel or freshwater-exposure history does not exclude the diagnosis (p.1443).
Absence of renal involvement does not rule out leptospirosis (p.1443).
Relying on serology in the first ~5 days risks a false-negative; antibodies are often undetectable until the second week and early antibiotics blunt the response (p.1443).
Cross-reactions are frequent in MAT, so the infecting serovar/serogroup cannot be definitively identified without isolating the organism (p.1443).
Leptospiral meningitis may present without jaundice or other classic severe-disease hallmarks, making it easy to miss (p.1443).
Jaundice can be profound yet usually does not signify fulminant hepatic necrosis, so hepatic transaminase rises are only moderate (p.1442-1443).
The transient rash may be misdiagnosed as scrub typhus or a viral exanthem (p.1442).
Dual infection (e.g., with dengue, rickettsiae, or hantavirus) can occur, so a positive alternative test does not exclude leptospirosis (p.1443).

Most patients recover, with renal and hepatic function typically returning to normal in survivors (hemodialysis can be lifesaving). Overall mean case-fatality is near 10% for severe cases; severe leptospirosis carries a case-fatality of 1-50%. Mortality is highest in the elderly and those with pulmonary hemorrhage or Weil's syndrome. Untreated leptospiral meningitis has reported mortality of ~13% versus ~2% with antibiotics. Pregnancy is associated with high fetal mortality. Post-leptospirosis sequelae include prolonged fatigue, myalgia, malaise, headache, depression-like symptoms persisting for years, and chronic autoimmune uveitis (p.1443-1444).
Age >40 years
Pregnancy (high fetal mortality)
Altered mental status
Acute kidney injury / oliguria or anuria
Respiratory insufficiency, hemoptysis, or pulmonary hemorrhage
Hypotension / septic shock
Cardiac arrhythmias and repolarization abnormalities on ECG
Jaundice with bleeding (Weil's syndrome triad)
Thrombocytopenia (platelet count <=100 x10^9/L) — linked to bleeding and renal failure
Evidence of coagulation activation / DIC

Harrison distinguishes mild leptospirosis (sudden-onset flu-like febrile illness with headache, myalgia, conjunctival suffusion; usually self-limiting over 7-10 days, low mortality) from severe leptospirosis, which is often rapidly progressive with multiorgan involvement. Severe disease classically presents as Weil's syndrome (triad of jaundice, acute kidney injury, and hemorrhage) and/or severe pulmonary hemorrhage syndrome, with a case-fatality of 1-50% (p.1442-1443).

Leptospira IgM ELISA / MAT (microscopic agglutination test) — Confirms diagnosis serologically; MAT is the reference standard but often only available at referral labs, so treatment should not be delayed pending results.
Renal function tests — Assesses for acute kidney injury, a hallmark of severe leptospirosis (Weil's disease) with major prognostic significance.
Liver function tests — Jaundice with relatively modest transaminase elevation (compared to viral hepatitis) is a classic pattern in leptospirosis.
CBC, coagulation profile — Screens for thrombocytopenia and bleeding risk, relevant to hemorrhagic complications.
CPK (creatine phosphokinase) — Often elevated due to myositis, supporting the diagnosis and explaining myalgia.
Leptospirosis (infective) — Tropical Fever

[guideline] empiric → Doxycycline (mild-moderate, outpatient) / Ceftriaxone or Penicillin G (severe/hospitalized, Weil's disease) Effective for mild-moderate leptospirosis and also provides empiric coverage for scrub typhus, which can present similarly — a practical advantage when the two cannot be immediately distinguished.
[guideline] alternative → Azithromycin (alternative, mild disease)

chunks.text: Pyogenic liver abscesses arise either from haematogenous spread of bacteria or from local spread from contiguous intraperitoneal infection. The organism reaches the liver by several routes: ascending biliary infection (currently the most common associated source), portal venous seeding via suppurative thrombosis of the portal vein (pylephlebitis, classically from pelvic or other intra-abdominal infection), direct contiguous spread, or systemic bacteraemic (haematogenous) seeding. Historically, ruptured appendicitis was the leading source. Hypervirulent (hypermucoviscous) K. pneumoniae causes a distinct community-acquired monomicrobial syndrome in which the organism establishes a primary liver abscess and then disseminates metastatically; this contrasts with the polymicrobial, source-driven pattern of biliary or enteric abscesses. (p.1117, p.1289-1290)

A lung abscess is necrosis and cavitation of lung parenchyma after microbial infection, typically a single dominant cavity >2 cm. In primary disease, anaerobes and microaerophilic streptococci colonizing the gingival crevices are aspirated into a susceptible host who carries an overwhelming aspirated burden or cannot clear it. An initial pneumonitis (worsened by gastric-acid tissue damage) progresses over about 7-14 days to parenchymal necrosis and cavitation, with anaerobes driving more extensive synergistic tissue destruction in polymicrobial infection. Secondary abscesses follow the predisposing mechanism: post-obstructive (tumor/foreign body) impairment of secretion clearance, or impaired host defense in immunocompromise allowing a broad pathogen range. Abscesses may also arise hematogenously from septic emboli (e.g., tricuspid endocarditis, Lemierre's syndrome).

Roughly 80% of lung abscesses are primary, arising from aspiration in the absence of an underlying pulmonary or systemic disease; the remaining ~20% are secondary to a predisposing process such as bronchial obstruction or immunocompromise (p.1034).

A foul-smelling (putrid) breath, sputum, or empyema is considered essentially diagnostic of an anaerobic lung abscess; abscesses with no isolated pathogen (about 40%) are termed nonspecific and anaerobes are presumed (p.1035).

Primary abscesses favor the dependent segments (posterior segments of upper lobes, superior segments of lower lobes), and the right lung is involved more often than the left because the right mainstem bronchus is less angulated (p.1035).

Anaerobic abscesses often present indolently with night sweats, fatigue, and anemia, whereas non-anaerobic causes such as S. aureus can produce a fulminant course with high fevers and rapid progression (p.1035-1036).

Edentulous patients are thought very unlikely to develop a lung abscess, since teeth (especially with gingivitis/periodontal disease) provide the nidus for the anaerobic/microaerophilic colonization that seeds the lung (p.1034).

Lemierre's syndrome (oropharyngeal infection, classically Fusobacterium necrophorum, with septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein) is a recognized embolic source of lung abscess (p.1034-1035).
Metronidazole alone is inadequate because it covers anaerobes but not the microaerophilic streptococci that are commonly part of the mixed flora of primary abscesses (p.1036).

Failure to exclude an obstructing malignancy: in older patients, those with malignancy risk factors, or those lacking clear aspiration risk, early bronchoscopy/biopsy and CT are indicated rather than assuming a primary anaerobic abscess (p.1035-1036).
Treating a presumed primary abscess that does not improve without re-evaluating for a secondary cause (obstruction, unusual pathogen) (p.1036).
Sputum culture may miss the diagnosis: infection is usually polymicrobial and routine cultures often fail to reflect anaerobes (p.1035).
Using metronidazole as monotherapy, which misses microaerophilic streptococci (p.1036).
Misclassifying a peripheral abscess as a pleural infection (empyema) or vice versa, since empyema may need urgent drainage (p.1035).
Underestimating risk in immunocompromised hosts, who are fragile, infected by a wide pathogen range, and warrant early culture-directed diagnostics (p.1035).

Mortality for primary lung abscess can be as low as ~2%, but secondary abscesses carry a much higher mortality, reported as high as 75% in some series. Adverse prognostic factors include age >60, malignancy-associated abscess, presence of aerobic bacteria, sepsis at presentation, symptom duration >8 weeks, and abscess size >6 cm. Defervescence on appropriate therapy can take up to 7 days, and 10-20% of patients fail to respond. Larger cavities at presentation predispose to persistent pneumatoceles or bronchiectasis. Prevention centers on airway protection, oral hygiene, minimizing sedation, head-of-bed elevation in aspiration-prone patients, and pathogen prophylaxis in selected immunocompromised hosts (p.1036).

Failure to defervesce or radiographic progression despite appropriate therapy (10-20% of patients do not respond) (p.1036)
Abscess >6-8 cm in diameter, which is less likely to respond to antibiotics alone (p.1036)

Lung abscesses are classified as primary (~80%, aspiration-related, anaerobe-predominant, no underlying lung/systemic disease) versus secondary (underlying obstruction, systemic illness, or immunocompromise); and by chronicity as acute (<4-6 weeks) versus chronic (~40% of cases). Size >6-8 cm marks lesions less responsive to antibiotics alone (p.1034, p.1036).

Chest X-ray and CT chest — CT better characterizes cavity size, wall thickness, and surrounding parenchymal involvement, and helps distinguish abscess from other cavitary lesions (e.g., malignancy, TB).
Sputum culture (including anaerobic culture if obtainable) — May identify causative organisms, though anaerobic cultures are technically difficult to obtain without invasive sampling.
Blood cultures — May identify the organism if bacteremic spread has occurred.

chunks.text: Infection begins when a female Anopheles inoculates sporozoites, which reach the liver and undergo preerythrocytic schizogony, each sporozoite yielding 10,000 to >30,000 merozoites. Released merozoites invade red cells, becoming trophozoites that multiply roughly 6- to 20-fold each asexual cycle (every 48 h for P. falciparum/P. vivax/P. ovale, 72 h for P. malariae, 24 h for P. knowlesi); symptoms begin around densities of ~50 parasites/uL. In P. vivax and P. ovale a fraction of liver forms persist as dormant hypnozoites for weeks to a year or more, causing the relapses characteristic of these species (P. falciparum, P. malariae, and P. knowlesi do not relapse). Disease results from red-cell invasion and destruction plus the host inflammatory response: schizont rupture releases material that activates monocytes/macrophages and proinflammatory cytokines, producing fever. The central pathology of severe falciparum malaria is cytoadherence: ~12-15 h after invasion 'knobs' on the infected red cell extrude the variant adhesin PfEMP1, which binds endothelial receptors (ICAM-1 and endothelial protein C receptor in brain, VAR2CSA/chondroitin sulfate A in placenta, CD36 elsewhere). Cytoadherence, rosetting (adherence to uninfected red cells), and agglutination sequester mature parasites in vital organs, especially the brain, obstructing microcirculatory flow and metabolism while escaping splenic clearance. Uninfected red cells also become less deformable in severe disease. P. falciparum invades cells of all ages and can reach very high densities (P. knowlesi can also, owing to its 24-h cycle), whereas other species spare most red cells and rarely exceed ~2% parasitemia. The spleen augments clearance and 'pits' damaged ring forms; severe lactic acidosis arises from anaerobic glycolysis in sequestered beds, parasite lactate production, gut-derived acids, and failed hepatic/renal clearance, and hypoglycemia from impaired gluconeogenesis with increased glucose consumption. (Harrison 22e pp.1760-1765)

chunks.text: Promptly and appropriately treated uncomplicated falciparum malaria has a mortality of <0.1%, but risk rises steeply once vital-organ dysfunction occurs or parasitemia exceeds 2%. Cerebral malaria carries roughly 20% mortality in adults and 15% in children even with treatment; about 10% of surviving children (especially with hypoglycemia, severe anemia, repeated seizures, or deep coma) have residual neurologic deficits, most of which improve or resolve within 6 months, though persistent language and cognitive deficits, increased epilepsy risk, and reduced life expectancy occur in some. Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema in adults has >80% mortality. Plasma bicarbonate and lactate are the best biochemical prognosticators. Among complications, poor prognosis is indicated by >20% mature pigment-containing parasites or >5% of neutrophils containing pigment, and by hyperparasitemia. In severe acute renal failure that survives, urine flow returns in a median of 4 days and creatinine normalizes in a mean of 17 days; early dialysis improves survival. (Harrison 22e pp.1763-1765, 1767)

chunks.text: Severe falciparum malaria (WHO-based criteria, Harrison 22e Table 231-2, p.1764) is defined by one or more of: unarousable coma/cerebral malaria (no localizing response, coma >30 min after a generalized convulsion, Glasgow Coma Score <11 or Blantyre <3 in young children); acidemia/acidosis (arterial pH <7.25, base deficit >8 meq/L, or plasma bicarbonate <15 mmol/L; venous lactate >=5 mmol/L; deep labored 'respiratory distress' breathing); severe normochromic normocytic anemia (hematocrit <15% or Hb <50 g/L with parasite density >10,000/uL); renal failure (creatinine >265 umol/L / >3 mg/dL); noncardiogenic pulmonary edema/ARDS (or O2 sat <92% on room air with respiratory rate >30/min); hypoglycemia (glucose <2.2 mmol/L / <40 mg/dL); hypotension/shock (systolic BP <70 mmHg in children 1-5 y or <80 mmHg in adults with impaired perfusion); significant bleeding/DIC; convulsions (>2 generalized seizures in 24 h); hemoglobinuria (macroscopic black/brown/red urine, not due to oxidant drugs or G6PD deficiency); extreme weakness/prostration; hyperparasitemia (>5% in nonimmune, >10% in any patient); and jaundice (bilirubin >50 umol/L / >3 mg/dL) with parasitemia >100,000/uL or other vital-organ dysfunction. Note: criteria thresholds for renal failure are for adults; lower values define severe disease in children. (Harrison 22e p.1764)

chunks.text: Peripheral blood smear (thick and thin film) — Gold standard for diagnosis, species identification, and parasitemia quantification — directly determines treatment choice and monitoring.
Rapid diagnostic test (malaria antigen) — Fast bedside screening tool, useful when smear is not immediately available, though species specificity is more limited than smear.
CBC — Thrombocytopenia is a common supportive finding; hemoglobin helps assess severity (severe anemia is a marker of complicated malaria).
Renal function tests, blood glucose, LFTs — Screens for organ dysfunction that would classify this as severe/complicated malaria requiring IV therapy and higher level of care.
Lactate / blood gas (if unwell) — Acidosis is a severity marker in falciparum malaria with prognostic significance.

chunks.text: Bacterial meningitis is an acute purulent infection of the subarachnoid space accompanied by a CNS inflammatory reaction that can cause decreased consciousness, seizures, raised intracranial pressure and stroke; meninges, subarachnoid space and brain parenchyma are often jointly involved (meningoencephalitis). The leading organisms (S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis) first colonize the nasopharynx, cross or breach the epithelium into the bloodstream, evade neutrophil phagocytosis and complement killing via their polysaccharide capsule, and reach the CSF through the choroid plexus or cerebral capillary endothelium. They multiply readily in CSF because normal CSF has few leukocytes and little complement/immunoglobulin, so opsonization and phagocytosis are poor. Much of the neurologic injury comes from the host inflammatory response rather than direct bacterial damage, so injury can progress even after antibiotics sterilize the CSF. Lysis of bacteria releases cell-wall components (gram-negative LPS; pneumococcal teichoic acid and peptidoglycan) that drive production of TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, chemokines and other mediators by microglia, astrocytes, monocytes, endothelium and CSF leukocytes. These cytokines increase blood-brain barrier permeability (vasogenic edema and protein leakage), the proteinaceous/leukocytic exudate obstructs CSF flow and resorption (obstructive and communicating hydrocephalus, interstitial edema), and neutrophil degranulation plus reactive oxygen/nitrogen species and excitatory amino acids produce cytotoxic edema and cell death (notably in the hippocampal dentate gyrus). Cerebral blood flow rises early then falls with loss of autoregulation; vasculitis and thrombosis of arteries, cortical veins and dural sinuses cause ischemia/infarction. The combined interstitial, vasogenic and cytotoxic edema raises ICP and can lead to coma and herniation (p.1118-1120).

chunks.text: Case-fatality varies by organism: roughly 3-7% for H. influenzae, N. meningitidis or group B streptococcal meningitis, about 15% for Listeria, and around 20% for pneumococcal meningitis. Risk of death rises with decreased consciousness on admission, seizures within 24 h, signs of raised ICP, age (infancy or >50 years), comorbidities such as shock or need for mechanical ventilation, and delay in starting treatment. A markedly low CSF glucose (<40 mg/dL) and very high CSF protein (>300 mg/dL) predict worse outcomes in some series. About 25% of survivors have moderate-to-severe sequelae, commonly decreased intellectual function, memory impairment, seizures, sensorineural hearing loss with dizziness, and gait disturbance (p.1123).

chunks.text: Harrison 22e does not provide a formal graded severity score for acute bacterial meningitis; it frames the disease as a medical emergency (goal: antibiotics within 60 min of arrival) and lists adverse prognostic markers (decreased consciousness on admission, seizures within 24 h, signs of raised ICP, age extremes, comorbidities such as shock/ventilation, treatment delay, very low CSF glucose, very high CSF protein). For distinguishing bacterial from aseptic meningitis in children, the prospectively validated Bacterial Meningitis Score is cited: very low probability (NPV ~99.7%) when all of negative CSF Gram stain, CSF neutrophils <1000/uL, CSF protein <80 mg/dL, peripheral ANC <10,000/uL, and no seizures are met (p.1123-1124).

chunks.text: Lumbar puncture with CSF analysis (cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain, culture) — Confirms the diagnosis, identifies the organism, and guides definitive duration and choice of therapy — but should follow, not precede, empiric antibiotics if there is any delay.
Blood cultures (before antibiotics if no delay incurred) — Frequently positive in bacterial meningitis and may identify the organism if LP is delayed or contraindicated.

CT head (before LP only if specific indications: papilledema, focal neurological deficit, severely altered consciousness, seizures) — Screens for mass effect/herniation risk before LP in specific high-risk presentations — not required routinely and should not delay antibiotics.

veryLikely: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis; likely: Listeria monocytogenes (neonates, elderly, immunocompromised, pregnant); possible: Haemophilus influenzae (unvaccinated populations), Gram-negative bacilli (post-neurosurgery, immunocompromised)
Red flags: Immediate empiric antibiotics required

[guideline] empiric → Ceftriaxone / Vancomycin / Dexamethasone (adjunctive) Reliable CSF penetration and coverage of S. pneumoniae and N. meningitidis, the two dominant pathogens in community-acquired bacterial meningitis.
[guideline] alternative → Ampicillin (added if Listeria risk: age >50, pregnant, immunocompromised)
[guideline] alternative → Meropenem (severe penicillin allergy or healthcare-associated)

chunks.text: Sporozoites inoculated by anopheline mosquitoes reach the liver and undergo pre-erythrocytic schizogony; a single sporozoite yields thousands of merozoites that invade RBCs and multiply (every 48 h for P. falciparum and P. vivax). In P. vivax (and P. ovale) infection, a fraction of intrahepatic forms do not divide but persist as dormant hypnozoites for weeks to a year or more, later reactivating to cause relapses — a feature absent in P. falciparum. In a mixed P. falciparum + P. vivax infection, the falciparum component drives the risk of severe disease through cytoadherence (PfEMP1 binding endothelial receptors), rosetting, and agglutination, causing sequestration of mature parasites in vital organs; only ring forms circulate, so peripheral parasitemia underestimates true burden. P. vivax preferentially invades young reticulocytes and produces lower parasitemia (seldom >2%), while P. falciparum invades RBCs of all ages and can reach very high densities. The simultaneous presence of a vivax hypnozoite reservoir means blood-stage cure of both species does not prevent later vivax relapse (p.1760-1763).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chapter 231 (Malaria), printed pp. 1760-1768

chunks.text: Mixed infections (most commonly P. falciparum together with P. vivax) are frequently under-detected by light microscopy and rapid antigen tests; PCR is the most sensitive method and is increasingly used specifically for speciation and genotyping in mixed infections (p.1767).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chapter 231 (Malaria), printed pp. 1760-1768

chunks.text: Because microscopy and RDTs may detect only the dominant species, a smear or RDT reported as single-species (especially P. falciparum) does not exclude a coexisting vivax/ovale component carrying dormant liver-stage hypnozoites.

source.page: Harrison 22e Chapter 231 (Malaria), printed pp. 1760-1768

chunks.text: P. vivax + P. falciparum is recognized as a distinct co-circulating pattern in endemic mapping, with roughly equal prevalence of the two species in Oceania (p.1761-1762).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chapter 231 (Malaria), printed pp. 1760-1768

chunks.text: Standard combination RDTs typically carry one P. falciparum-specific band plus a pan-malaria or P. vivax band; this design distinguishes falciparum from the 'less dangerous' malarias but is not optimized to flag concurrent dual infection (p.1766).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chapter 231 (Malaria), printed pp. 1760-1768

chunks.text: RDTs may miss low-level P. vivax (and P. ovale/P. malariae) parasitemia and PfHRP2-based tests can be falsely negative where parasites carry HRP2/3 gene deletions — both failure modes can mask one component of a mixed infection (p.1766).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chapter 231 (Malaria), printed pp. 1760-1768

chunks.text: The classic regularly-spaced febrile paroxysm at presentation suggests P. vivax or P. ovale (often relapse); its presence in a patient with confirmed falciparum should raise suspicion of a coexisting vivax/ovale component.

source.page: Harrison 22e Chapter 231 (Malaria), printed pp. 1760-1768

chunks.text: Apparent vivax/ovale relapses arising after treatment of a mixed infection reflect persistence of liver-stage hypnozoites, which are not cleared by standard blood-stage schizonticides.

source.page: Harrison 22e Chapter 231 (Malaria), printed pp. 1760-1768

chunks.text: Treating an apparently single-species falciparum infection as if vivax were absent: the coexisting vivax hypnozoite reservoir is not cleared by blood-stage drugs and later causes relapse — manage mixed infection as falciparum AND provide hypnozoite-directed coverage for vivax.

source.page: Harrison 22e Chapter 231 (Malaria), printed pp. 1760-1768

chunks.text: Relying on microscopy or RDT alone to exclude a second species — both under-detect the minor component; PCR is needed to confirm/exclude mixed infection.

source.page: Harrison 22e Chapter 231 (Malaria), printed pp. 1760-1768

chunks.text: Misreading PfHRP2 RDT positivity that persists for weeks after a prior infection as evidence of the current species mix.

source.page: Harrison 22e Chapter 231 (Malaria), printed pp. 1760-1768

chunks.text: Mistaking persistent P. falciparum gametocytemia after treatment for treatment failure or active infection.

source.page: Harrison 22e Chapter 231 (Malaria), printed pp. 1760-1768

chunks.text: Attributing all post-treatment fever to falciparum recrudescence when it may be a true vivax/ovale relapse from the mixed-infection liver reservoir.

source.page: Harrison 22e Chapter 231 (Malaria), printed pp. 1760-1768

chunks.text: Misidentifying P. knowlesi as P. falciparum on microscopy/RDT, distorting the apparent species picture.

source.page: Harrison 22e Chapter 231 (Malaria), printed pp. 1760-1768

chunks.text: Promptly treated uncomplicated falciparum malaria has a mortality of <0.1%, but risk rises steeply once vital-organ dysfunction occurs or parasitemia exceeds ~2%. In a mixed infection the falciparum component dictates the severe-disease prognosis; cerebral malaria carries ~20% mortality in adults and ~15% in children even with treatment, and ~10% of child survivors have residual neurologic deficits (most improving within 6 months). Poor-prognosis features include hyperparasitemia (>100,000/uL), predominance of mature pigment-containing parasites (>20%), pigment in >5% of neutrophils, hypoglycemia, hyperlactatemia, acidemia, and coagulopathy. The vivax component does not usually drive mortality but, if its hypnozoite reservoir is not addressed, predisposes to later relapse and recurrent anemia (p.1763-1767).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chapter 231 (Malaria), printed pp. 1760-1768

chunks.text: Coma, obtundation, delirium, or abnormal behavior (cerebral malaria) — attributable to the falciparum component

source.page: Harrison 22e Chapter 231 (Malaria), printed pp. 1760-1768

source.page: Harrison 22e Chapter 231 (Malaria), printed pp. 1760-1768

chunks.text: Hyperparasitemia (>2% indicates increased risk; >5-10% defines severe disease) — a falciparum-driven marker

source.page: Harrison 22e Chapter 231 (Malaria), printed pp. 1760-1768

chunks.text: Severity is governed by the P. falciparum component per Harrison Table 231-2 (Manifestations of Severe Falciparum Malaria): major criteria include unarousable coma/cerebral malaria, acidosis (arterial pH <7.25 / lactate >=5 mmol/L), severe normocytic anemia (Hct <15%), renal failure (creatinine >265 umol/L), noncardiogenic pulmonary edema/ARDS, hypoglycemia (<2.2 mmol/L), hypotension/shock, bleeding/DIC, and repeated convulsions; other criteria include hemoglobinuria, prostration, and hyperparasitemia (>5% nonimmune, >10% any patient). Uncomplicated disease = patient can sit/stand unaided and swallow, with no vital-organ dysfunction and parasitemia <2% (p.1763-1764).

chunks.text: Peripheral blood smear (thick and thin film) confirming both species — Definitive method to confirm mixed infection and quantify parasitemia of each species, directly determining treatment approach and monitoring intensity.
Rapid diagnostic test (combination P.f/P.v if available) — Can support or suggest mixed infection rapidly, though smear remains the definitive confirmatory test.
G6PD testing — Mandatory before primaquine administration to avoid precipitating hemolysis in deficient patients.
CBC, renal function, blood glucose, LFTs — Screens for organ dysfunction that would classify this as severe/complicated malaria requiring IV therapy and escalated care.
Mixed Malaria (P. falciparum + P. vivax) (infective) — Tropical Fever
veryLikely: Plasmodium falciparum, Plasmodium vivax
Red flags: Urgent antimalarial therapy required (NOT an antibiotic)
Clostridial myonecrosis / gas gangrene (distinguished from clostridial NF by muscle biopsy)
Streptococcal necrotizing myositis (GAS infection extending into muscle)
Pyomyositis (usually S. aureus; localized, shock uncommon unless toxin-producing)
Synergistic nonclostridial anaerobic myonecrosis (necrotizing cutaneous myositis / synergistic necrotizing cellulitis) — a mixed aerobic-anaerobic variant
Cellulitis / erysipelas (superficial; skin more abnormal but pain mild-moderate)
Halophilic Vibrio vulnificus infection (can be as fulminant as NF; Gulf/Atlantic water exposure or raw seafood in cirrhosis)
Aeromonas soft-tissue infection (freshwater laceration exposure)
Aggressive cellulitis from Vibrio vulnificus or Aeromonas hydrophila
Ecthyma gangrenosum (Pseudomonas, neutropenic hosts)
Clostridial myonecrosis

Soft-tissue plain radiography, CT, and MRI to assess depth of infection and detect tissue gas or a localized abscess — most useful when lesions progress rapidly or SIRS is present; note imaging may show only soft-tissue swelling and is NOT specific for fulminant GAS NF/myonecrosis, where gas is typically absent
Gram stain and aerobic/anaerobic culture of surgically excised tissue to identify GAS vs mixed flora vs MRSA vs Clostridium
Frozen-section histology of aspirate or punch biopsy (valuable in NF), though aspiration/biopsy is negative in ~80% of cases
Serum CPK (markedly elevated when myonecrosis coexists)
Lactate, d-dimer, coagulation, liver and renal function as markers of systemic toxicity/organ failure
Thrombophlebitis (a common early misdiagnosis)
Muscle strain or contusion (the minor trauma at the deep nidus)

NF is infection of the superficial and/or deep fascia investing the muscles of an extremity or trunk, with extensive necrosis of subcutaneous tissue and fascia. Infection spreads rapidly along fascial planes and via venous channels and lymphatics, typically sparing the muscle itself in pure fasciitis. Two main microbiologic patterns: a mixed aerobic-anaerobic (type I) process beginning with a breach of a mucosal barrier (GI/GU tract), and a monomicrobial group A streptococcal (type II) process. In GAS disease, organisms reach deep fascia either by transient bacteremic seeding at a site of minor non-penetrating trauma (no portal) or by spread from cutaneous infection/penetrating trauma. Thrombosis of dermal vessels produces progressive skin necrosis; infarction of cutaneous nerves causes the characteristic late anesthesia. NF caused by Clostridium perfringens or extending into muscle (clostridial/streptococcal myonecrosis) carries very high systemic toxicity with hemolysis. PVL-producing MRSA strains have been reported as a cause.

Pain out of proportion to physical findings is the classic early clue: physical signs may be minimal (only soft-tissue edema and mild erythema) while pain and fever are severe; this disparity helps distinguish NF from superficial cellulitis, where skin appearance is more abnormal but pain is only mild-to-moderate.

Early disease is frequently misdiagnosed (e.g., as thrombophlebitis) and patients may be sent home with analgesics, especially in the strep type that begins deep at a site of non-penetrating minor trauma (bruise, muscle strain) with no visible portal of entry.

Classic late signs evolve sequentially: swelling and brawny edema/tenderness, then dark-red (violaceous) induration, then bullae filled with blue/purple fluid, then friable bluish-maroon-to-black skin; thrombosis of dermal-papillae vessels is extensive by this stage.
Paradoxical decrease in pain or progression to anesthesia over the involved area is an ominous sign reflecting thrombosis of small vessels and infarction of cutaneous nerves.
GAS NF can be preceded by varicella, childbirth, or muscle strain, and most patients deny an antecedent streptococcal infection.
The inoculation site may be inapparent and remote from clinical involvement (e.g., minor hand trauma manifesting as infection over the shoulder or chest).
Myositis/myonecrosis coexists with NF in roughly 20-50% of cases and serum creatine phosphokinase (CPK) may be markedly elevated, signaling deeper muscle involvement.
Early physical findings are minimal relative to pain/fever, leading to underestimation of severity and misdiagnosis as thrombophlebitis or simple cellulitis.
Absence of gas does NOT exclude NF: gas is usually absent when the cause is GAS or MRSA and is seen mainly with mixed/clostridial infection.
Normal or nonspecific imaging does NOT rule out NF — CT/MRI may show only soft-tissue swelling and are not specific for fulminant GAS NF/myonecrosis.
A negative aspirate or frozen-section biopsy does NOT exclude NF (negative in ~80% of cases).
Decreasing pain should not be reassuring — it can signal nerve infarction and disease progression rather than improvement.
Do not wait for imaging or cultures when NF is suspected with systemic toxicity; surgical exploration is both diagnostic and therapeutic.

Mortality for NF is roughly 11-34% overall and rises substantially when associated with toxic shock syndrome. GAS/clostridial fascial-muscle infection historically carried 20-50% mortality with penicillin alone. Survivors of GAS NF often require repeated surgeries including amputation. Clostridial NF/myonecrosis is far more lethal: spontaneous (nontraumatic) myonecrosis mortality exceeds 65% (often C. septicum with underlying malignancy); trunk infection ~63% vs limb ~12% mortality. Any delay in surgery increases the risk of death; early aggressive surgery markedly improves outcomes.
Pain out of proportion to examination findings
Rapidly progressing lesion with signs of systemic inflammatory response / toxicity
Violaceous (blue/purple) bullae, skin sloughing, dusky/mottled erythema
Progression of tenderness to anesthesia over the lesion (cutaneous nerve infarction)
Crepitus or gas in deep tissue (suggests mixed/clostridial infection)
Renal impairment that may precede shock, plus hypotension/multiorgan failure
Urgent surgical exploration supersedes other diagnostic or therapeutic maneuvers — debridement is life-saving and must not be delayed

Microbiologic/clinical typing: Type I = mixed aerobic-anaerobic, begins at a mucosal-barrier breach (GI/GU), common in diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, malignancy, surgery, or abdominal penetrating injury; Fournier gangrene is the perineal/scrotal form. Type II = monomicrobial group A streptococcal (GAS implicated in ~60% of NF cases), can occur in otherwise healthy hosts, two presentations (with vs without a defined portal of entry). PVL-producing MRSA is a recognized monomicrobial cause. NF qualifies as soft-tissue necrosis under the CDC streptococcal toxic shock syndrome case definition (hypotension plus >=2 of: renal impairment, coagulopathy, hepatic impairment, ARDS, generalized erythematous desquamating rash, soft-tissue necrosis/NF/myositis/gangrene). (LRINEC score not described in this source.)

Urgent surgical exploration (diagnostic AND therapeutic) — The definitive diagnostic test — direct visualization of necrotic fascia confirms the diagnosis and simultaneously allows debridement; imaging should not delay surgery when clinical suspicion is high.
Blood cultures and intraoperative tissue/fluid cultures — Identifies the causative organism(s) to guide de-escalation.
CT or MRI (only if diagnosis uncertain and patient stable enough to tolerate delay) — May show fascial thickening/gas, but should never delay surgery in a patient with high clinical suspicion.
CPK — Markedly elevated levels suggest muscle involvement (myonecrosis), affecting the extent of surgical debridement needed.

LRINEC score (Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis) — Can support clinical suspicion using CRP, WBC, hemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, and glucose, though it should not override strong clinical suspicion if score is low.
Necrotizing Fasciitis (infective) — Skin & Soft Tissue

veryLikely: Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus) — monomicrobial type II, Polymicrobial flora including anaerobes and Enterobacteriaceae — type I (more common, often in diabetics/immunocompromised); likely: Staphylococcus aureus (including community-associated MRSA), Clostridium species (if gas gangrene/myonecrosis); possible: Vibrio vulnificus (if marine/brackish water exposure), Aeromonas species (if freshwater exposure)
Red flags: Immediate empiric antibiotics required

[guideline] empiric → Piperacillin-tazobactam + Clindamycin + Vancomycin This combination covers polymicrobial type I infection (pip-tazo), provides antitoxin effect against streptococcal/staphylococcal toxin production (clindamycin, via protein synthesis inhibition), and covers MRSA (vancomycin) — maximal reasonable empiric coverage is justified given the extreme mortality risk.
[guideline] alternative → Meropenem + Clindamycin + Vancomycin (broader gram-negative coverage if indicated)
[guideline] alternative → IVIG (adjunctive, for confirmed streptococcal toxic shock features)
Acute infectious mononucleosis (EBV) — marked cervical adenopathy, exudative pharyngitis, palatine petechiae, gelatinous uvula, splenomegaly (Harrison 22e p.301-302)
Non-group-A streptococcal pharyngitis (group C and group G streptococci) (Harrison 22e p.302)
Gonococcal pharyngitis (Neisseria gonorrhoeae) (Harrison 22e p.302)
Mycoplasma pneumoniae pharyngitis (persistent sore throat with bronchopulmonary symptoms) (Harrison 22e p.300)
Chlamydia pneumoniae pharyngitis (Harrison 22e p.302)
Haemophilus influenzae pharyngitis (cough and otitis media) (Harrison 22e p.300)
Arcanobacterium haemolyticum (scarlatiniform rash) (Harrison 22e p.300)
Acute HIV infection (Harrison 22e p.302)
Acute epiglottitis/supraglottitis — sore throat with dysphagia, odynophagia, hoarseness, stridor or tachypnea, drooling; airway emergency (Harrison 22e p.302)
Peritonsillar abscess — fever, dysphagia, profound throat pain with drooling, trismus, 'hot potato voice', unilateral palate bulge and uvular deviation (Harrison 22e p.302)
Retropharyngeal abscess — post-URI in children with sore throat, dysphagia, deep neck pain, neck stiffness, trismus, drooling; severe cases with dyspnea/stridor (Harrison 22e p.302)
Submandibular abscess / Ludwig angina — swelling of the floor of the mouth displacing the tongue posteriorly, usually after dental infection or extraction (Harrison 22e p.302)
Lemierre syndrome — septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein with metastatic infection (Harrison 22e p.302)
Candida pharyngitis — cottage-cheese exudate that scrapes off leaving a bleeding surface (Harrison 22e p.300)
Rapid GAS antigen test: sensitivity ~80%, specificity ~95%; proper technique (swabbing tonsils/pharynx and any exudate or ulceration) is essential to sensitivity (Harrison 22e p.301)
Throat culture: single-swab sensitivity ~85-90%; can be falsely positive in carriers; not recommended for routine adult evaluation given 24-48 h delay (Harrison 22e p.301)
Heterophil antibody test for EBV mononucleosis (low early sensitivity, rises by week 3) (Harrison 22e p.302)
CBC for atypical lymphocytosis in mononucleosis (absolute lymphocytes >4000/uL or relative >50% with >10% atypical morphology) (Harrison 22e p.302)
CT imaging for suspected head and neck abscess (except obvious peritonsillar abscess) (Harrison 22e p.302)
Lateral neck radiograph in epiglottitis may show the 'thumb sign' (not required for diagnosis) (Harrison 22e p.302)
Gastroesophageal reflux / laryngopharyngeal reflux (Harrison 22e p.300)
Postnasal drainage (Harrison 22e p.300)
Head and neck tumors (Harrison 22e p.300)
Thyroiditis (Harrison 22e p.300)
Leukoplakia mimicking exudate (cannot be scraped off) (Harrison 22e p.300)

Acute pharyngitis (symptoms generally present for days) is most often caused by respiratory viruses; group A beta-hemolytic streptococci (GAS, Streptococcus pyogenes) are a frequent bacterial cause, with other contributors including Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Epstein-Barr virus, HIV, non-group-A streptococci (groups C and G), Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, and Haemophilus influenzae. Complications of GAS pharyngitis arise from both suppurative spread (e.g., peritonsillar abscess, sinusitis, other invasive GAS infection) and nonsuppurative immune-mediated sequelae (acute rheumatic fever, poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, scarlet fever) (Harrison 22e p.300-301).

Sore throat is not synonymous with pharyngitis: it may also arise from submandibular/retropharyngeal/peritonsillar space infections, thyroiditis, gastroesophageal reflux, tumors, or postnasal drainage (Harrison 22e p.300).

In children the Centor criteria are less specific, so GAS pharyngitis should be confirmed by testing; children with pharyngitis but no viral signs (conjunctivitis, runny nose, cough, hoarseness, nonexudative oral lesions) warrant testing (Harrison 22e p.301).
In developed countries the prevalence of rheumatic fever is extremely low, and antibiotic treatment does not prevent poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (Harrison 22e p.300).

Full-blown infectious mononucleosis (EBV) appears in only about one-fourth of cases and is a triad of clinical, hematologic, and serologic findings; new EBV causes 1-6% of pharyngitis in young adults and is rare over age 40 (Harrison 22e p.301).
Heterophil antibody is detectable in only ~40% of mononucleosis patients in the first week but in 80-90% by the third week, so an early negative test does not exclude EBV (Harrison 22e p.302).

Gonococcal pharyngitis is more often asymptomatic than symptomatic; suspect it with persistent sore throat unresponsive to presumptive strep treatment and relevant sexual exposure (Harrison 22e p.302).
Diphtheria produces only mild pharyngitis beneath its characteristic grayish pseudomembrane (Harrison 22e p.302).
Acute HIV infection causes sore throat in roughly half of cases; consider it when sore throat accompanies headache, fever, myalgias, lymphadenopathy, anorexia, and rash (Harrison 22e p.302).
Pharyngeal erythema is most commonly seen with viral infection (common cold, influenza), not bacterial disease (Harrison 22e p.300).

Pharyngeal exudate can be mimicked by Candida (cottage-cheese appearance, scrapes off leaving a bleeding surface) or leukoplakia (cannot be scraped off) — do not equate exudate with bacterial pharyngitis (Harrison 22e p.300).
GAS is the only common cause of sore throat that warrants antibiotics; most non-GAS pharyngitis is viral and self-limited (Harrison 22e p.300).
About 10% of adults with sore throat have GAS; in children the prevalence may reach ~35%, peaking at ages 5-15 years, and is higher in winter and early spring (Harrison 22e p.300).

Risk of GAS pharyngitis is elevated in health care and child care workers, teachers, parents of young children, and contacts of known strep cases; clinicians should watch for local outbreaks in military and institutional settings (Harrison 22e p.300).
GAS carriage is common (up to ~20% of schoolchildren, ~5% of adolescents/young adults); rapid antigen tests and culture cannot distinguish true infection from carriage (Harrison 22e p.301).

In adults meeting zero or one Centor criterion, a positive GAS test is very likely a false positive and/or represents carriage; indiscriminate testing of adults with sore throat is discouraged (Harrison 22e p.301).

Lower the threshold to test/treat GAS in patients with a history of acute rheumatic fever, documented strep exposure in the past week, those in a community strep epidemic, and diabetic or immunocompromised patients (Harrison 22e p.301).
Prescribing antibiotics to the majority of adults with sore throat despite only ~10% having GAS — most cases are viral (Harrison 22e p.300).
Testing adults who meet zero or one Centor criterion: 40-60% of adults with pharyngitis fall here, and a positive test is highly likely to be false-positive or carriage (Harrison 22e p.301).
Relying on throat culture or rapid test to distinguish active infection from GAS carriage — neither can (Harrison 22e p.301).
Applying adult Centor criteria to children, in whom they are less specific (Harrison 22e p.301).
Mistaking Candida or leukoplakia for bacterial pharyngeal exudate (Harrison 22e p.300).
Attempting to examine or swab the posterior pharynx in suspected epiglottitis — this can provoke laryngospasm and should only be done in a controlled setting (Harrison 22e p.302).
Assuming antibiotic treatment of GAS prevents poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis — it does not (Harrison 22e p.300).
A negative early heterophil antibody test does not rule out EBV mononucleosis (Harrison 22e p.302).

Both streptococcal and nonstreptococcal pharyngitis should resolve within 3-5 days. Nonsuppurative complications are rare, and even streptococcal pharyngitis is self-limited in the vast majority of cases; outside the U.S., because complications are rare, some guidelines do not recommend routine GAS testing or antibiotic treatment of sore throat (Harrison 22e p.301).
Shaking chills/rigors, neck swelling beyond lymphadenopathy, trouble swallowing, drooling, or symptoms persisting >5 days without improvement should prompt urgent re-evaluation (Harrison 22e p.301)
Stridor, dyspnea, hoarseness, or tripod/forward-leaning posture with drooling — suggests epiglottitis and impending airway obstruction (Harrison 22e p.302)
Non-GAS pharyngitis that is not resolving in a teenager/young adult with rigors, neck pain or swelling, or extrapharyngeal symptoms — suspect Lemierre syndrome (Harrison 22e p.302)
Trismus, 'hot potato voice', and unilateral palate bulge with uvular deviation — peritonsillar abscess (Harrison 22e p.302)
Grayish pharyngeal pseudomembrane in a traveler from an endemic area — suspect diphtheria (Harrison 22e p.300, 302)

Centor criteria (4 findings, 1 point each): history of fever, absence of cough, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and tonsillar exudate or swelling. For an adult pretest probability of ~10%, post-evaluation probability of GAS is ~2% at 0 points, ~3% at 1, ~8% at 2, ~19% at 3, and ~41% at 4 points (area under the curve 0.79). Conceptually: 0-1 criteria -> neither test nor treat; 2-3 -> rapid antigen test to guide management; 4 -> rapid test or empirical treatment. (Harrison 22e p.300-301).
Rapid antigen detection test (RADT) or throat culture — Confirms or excludes Group A Streptococcus before committing to antibiotics, directly preventing unnecessary use in viral pharyngitis.
Acute Pharyngitis (infective) — Respiratory

veryLikely: Respiratory viruses (most common overall); likely: Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) — when Centor score is high; possible: Fusobacterium necrophorum (consider in older adolescents/young adults with severe symptoms)

[guideline] empiric → Penicillin V (only if GAS confirmed or very high pretest probability) Penicillin remains first-line for confirmed Group A Streptococcal pharyngitis — narrow spectrum, no resistance reported, and prevents rheumatic fever when given for a full 10-day course.
[guideline] alternative → Amoxicillin
[guideline] alternative → Azithromycin (penicillin allergy)

Chronic bacterial prostatitis (CBP) — presents insidiously as recurrent episodes of cystitis, sometimes with pelvic and perineal pain, usually without systemic signs of infection; should be suspected with recurrent UTI not in the context of catheterization (Harrison 22e p.1089, p.1136).
Pyelonephritis — another febrile genitourinary infection that must be excluded as the anatomic source before attributing systemic symptoms to ABP (Harrison 22e p.1136).
Acute cystitis in men — uncommon and warrants caution; urine culture should be obtained in all male UTI to help identify a prostatic focus (Harrison 22e p.1089).
Pyelonephritis — overlapping febrile UTI presentation; distinguished by flank/costovertebral angle pain and an upper-tract source (Harrison 22e p.1089).

Urethritis — urethral pain, pruritus, or discharge should prompt evaluation for sexually transmitted infections (Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, Mycoplasma genitalium) rather than assuming prostatitis (Harrison 22e p.1087).

Urine culture in all male UTI — documenting bacteriuria differentiates bacterial prostatitis from chronic pelvic pain syndrome; dipstick and/or microscopy alone are not sufficient (Harrison 22e p.1089).

Cross-sectional imaging (CT or ultrasound) for men with febrile UTI, including the first episode, if not previously done, to evaluate for urinary tract abnormalities or obstruction (Harrison 22e p.1089).
Evaluation for urinary retention / prostatic focus in men with recurrent cystitis (Harrison 22e p.1089).
Urologic consultation referral if the diagnosis of UTI is unclear or UTI is recurrent (Harrison 22e p.1089).

Chronic pelvic pain syndrome (formerly chronic prostatitis) — a noninfectious disorder that is the far more common cause of prostatic-type symptoms, with NO bacteriuria and NO response to antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.1089).
Benign prostatic hypertrophy with obstructive uropathy / urinary retention — can produce lower urinary tract symptoms and predispose to UTI (Harrison 22e p.1089, p.1131).

Prostatitis can complicate ascending cystitis or arise hematogenously, for example as a metastatic focus of Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia. Infectious prostatitis is almost always bacterial and is far less common than the noninfectious chronic pelvic pain syndrome. In general, most genitourinary infections in men ascend from the urethra to the bladder, with the prostate becoming involved as part of febrile UTI; less than 2% of UTIs are hematogenous, usually from virulent organisms such as S. aureus and Salmonella. Obstruction from prostatic hypertrophy after age 50 promotes urinary stasis and is a major reason UTI incidence in older men approaches that in women (Harrison 22e p.1087, p.1089, p.1131).

Acute bacterial prostatitis (ABP) typically presents as a severe illness with dysuria, urinary frequency, and pain in the prostatic, pelvic, or perineal region, and may be accompanied by fever, rigors, and/or bladder outlet obstruction (Harrison 22e p.1089).

The prostate is involved in the majority of febrile UTI cases in men; ABP should be specifically suspected when a man presents with UTI plus systemic symptoms but no other clear anatomic source such as pyelonephritis (Harrison 22e p.1089, p.1136).

Bacteriuria documented on urine culture is what distinguishes the less common bacterial prostatitis syndromes (acute and chronic) from the far more common chronic pelvic pain syndrome, which is NOT associated with bacteriuria and is NOT improved by antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.1089).

Men with febrile UTI may show an elevated serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) and an enlarged prostate and seminal vesicles on ultrasound, supporting prostatic involvement; PSA is therefore not interpretable as a cancer marker during acute infection (Harrison 22e p.1089).

Prostatitis is largely unrepresented in UTI clinical trial data, so complicated-UTI practice guidelines cannot be assumed to apply to prostatitis; older literature suggests prolonged therapy with prostate-penetrating agents may be needed (Harrison 22e p.1087).

Do not attribute prostatic-type symptoms to bacterial prostatitis without bacteriuria; absence of bacteriuria points to chronic pelvic pain syndrome, which will not respond to antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.1089).
Do not interpret an elevated PSA during febrile male UTI as a cancer marker — acute prostatic infection itself raises PSA and prostate/seminal vesicle size on imaging (Harrison 22e p.1089).

Do not assume complicated-UTI guideline regimens and durations apply to prostatitis, since prostatitis is largely absent from UTI trial data and may require prolonged prostate-penetrating therapy (Harrison 22e p.1087).
Do not overlook a prostatic focus or urinary retention in men presenting with recurrent cystitis (Harrison 22e p.1089).

ABP is typically a severe acute illness but is amenable to therapy with prostate-penetrating antimicrobials. A prostatic abscess is a recognized complication requiring urologic intervention. Chronic bacterial prostatitis recurrences are not uncommon. Men with febrile UTI and none of the warning features (retention, early recurrence, hematuria, voiding difficulty) generally have normal upper and lower urinary tracts on urologic workup, implying a favorable structural prognosis (Harrison 22e p.1089, p.1136).
Bladder outlet obstruction or urinary retention accompanying ABP (Harrison 22e p.1089).
Fever and rigors indicating a severe, systemic illness (Harrison 22e p.1089).
Identification of a prostatic abscess — should prompt urologic specialist consultation (Harrison 22e p.1136).
Symptoms predictive of surgically correctable disease in men with febrile UTI: urinary retention, early UTI recurrence, hematuria at follow-up, and voiding difficulties (Harrison 22e p.1089).

Prostatitis is categorized as acute bacterial prostatitis (ABP) versus chronic bacterial prostatitis (CBP). ABP is a typically severe illness with systemic features (fever, rigors, possible bladder outlet obstruction); CBP presents insidiously as recurrent cystitis with pelvic/perineal pain and typically without systemic signs, often managed in the ambulatory setting. Both are distinct from noninfectious chronic pelvic pain syndrome (Harrison 22e p.1089, p.1136).
Urinalysis and urine culture — Identifies the causative organism; this is preferred over prostatic secretion sampling in the acute setting given bacteremia risk with prostatic massage.
Blood cultures (if febrile/systemically unwell) — Bacteremia is not uncommon in acute prostatitis and positive cultures help confirm the organism.

Post-void residual / bladder scan (if retention suspected) — Urinary retention is a recognized complication requiring catheterization (suprapubic preferred over urethral if prostatitis is causing obstruction).
STI testing (NAAT for gonorrhea/chlamydia) if risk factors present — Identifies sexually transmitted causes requiring different management and partner notification.

chunks.text: M. tuberculosis is an aerobic acid-fast bacillus whose mycolic-acid-rich cell wall confers acid fastness and low permeability (reducing antibiotic efficacy). Transmission is by airborne droplet nuclei (<5-10 um) from a person with infectious pulmonary or laryngeal TB; cavitary cases are most infectious (10^5-10^7 AFB/mL of sputum). Inhaled bacilli reaching the alveoli are phagocytosed by alveolar macrophages; the bacillus arrests phagosome maturation and phagosome-lysosome fusion, replicates, and (via the ESX-1/RD1 secretion system) ruptures the macrophage to infect newly recruited phagocytes. Around 2-4 weeks, cell-mediated (TH1/IFN-gamma-driven, CD4+ T-cell-dependent) macrophage activation and a delayed-type hypersensitivity tissue-damaging response develop; their balance determines disease form. Granulomas (tubercles) of activated macrophages, epithelioid and giant cells form, with central caseous (cheese-like) necrosis in which low oxygen and pH inhibit but do not kill bacilli. When the macrophage-activating response is weak, delayed hypersensitivity causes progressive caseous liquefaction, bronchial and vascular erosion, and cavity formation; bacilli multiply within cavities and are discharged into airways, driving transmission and bronchogenic spread of satellite lesions. Lymphohematogenous dissemination can seed distant organs (miliary disease, meningitis). The continuum from infection to disease is governed largely by host immune competence; only ~10% of immunocompetent infected persons progress to active disease over a lifetime, about half within ~18 months. (pp.1380-1385)

chunks.text: Untreated, TB is often fatal: about one-third of patients die within 1 year of diagnosis, and historically ~70% (weighted mean) of smear-positive cases died within 10 years; paucibacillary smear-negative disease had a lower ~20% case-fatality at 5 years, and ~60% of 5-year survivors underwent spontaneous remission. With timely, proper drug-susceptible treatment the vast majority are cured. Improper therapy lowers mortality but generates chronic infectious, often drug-resistant cases. A substantial proportion of cured survivors suffer post-TB lung disease - chronic airflow impairment, dyspnea, residual cough, bronchiectasis, pulmonary hypertension, and predisposition to aspergilloma/chronic pulmonary aspergillosis in residual cavities. chunks.text: Drug-induced fever - virtually any drug, even after long-term use; common culprits include allopurinol, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, phenytoin, sulfasalazine, furosemide, and antimicrobials (sulfonamides, minocycline, vancomycin, beta-lactams, isoniazid); fever persisting >72h after stopping the drug makes it an unlikely cause (pp.150, 153)

chunks.text: FUO is a syndrome, not a single disease - a final prolonged febrile illness in which intensive standard evaluation has failed to localize a cause. Etiologies cluster into four groups: infections, noninfectious inflammatory diseases (NIIDs: autoimmune, autoinflammatory, granulomatous, and vasculitides), malignancy, and miscellaneous, with a substantial undiagnosed fraction. The spectrum has shifted over time: intraabdominal abscesses, tumors, and infective endocarditis have declined as CT, ultrasound, blood culture, and echocardiography improved, while entities such as acute HIV and autoinflammatory syndromes are now recognized. NIIDs may precede their typical clinical or laboratory features by months, requiring prolonged observation. The 'FUO paradox' describes how, despite better imaging (CT/MRI/PET-CT), the undiagnosed proportion is now higher (>50% in some Western cohorts) because most febrile illnesses are diagnosed before 3 weeks elapse, leaving only the most difficult cases to meet FUO criteria (pp.149-150).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.22 (Mulders-Manders & Rovers), pp.149-154 (file pages 192-197)

chunks.text: Current (post-Petersdorf) FUO definition requires all of: fever >=38.3C (101F) on at least two occasions, illness lasting at least 3 weeks, no known immunocompromised state, and a diagnosis still uncertain after thorough history, examination, and a defined set of obligatory investigations (p.149).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.22 (Mulders-Manders & Rovers), pp.149-154 (file pages 192-197)

chunks.text: Geography shapes the differential: infections (especially TB) dominate non-Western cohorts, while noninfectious inflammatory diseases (NIIDs) are the most common cause in Western cohorts, accounting for up to one-third of cases (p.150).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.22 (Mulders-Manders & Rovers), pp.149-154 (file pages 192-197)

chunks.text: Investigation of cryoglobulins is a useful low-cost screening test in FUO given the frequent absence of specific symptoms (p.153).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.22 (Mulders-Manders & Rovers), pp.149-154 (file pages 192-197)

chunks.text: Inflammation of unknown origin (IUO) shares the FUO definition but lacks the temperature criterion (elevated CRP/ESR with normal temperature); its causes and workup are identical to FUO (p.149).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.22 (Mulders-Manders & Rovers), pp.149-154 (file pages 192-197)

chunks.text: FUO usually reflects an ATYPICAL presentation of a COMMON disease rather than a rare disease; pattern recognition explains the higher diagnostic yield at expert centers (pp.150, 153).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.22 (Mulders-Manders & Rovers), pp.149-154 (file pages 192-197)

chunks.text: The cornerstone of the workup is the search for potentially diagnostic clues (PDCs) - all localizing signs, symptoms, and abnormalities pointing toward a diagnosis - via repeated history, examination, and obligatory tests; further testing should be PDC-driven (pp.152-153).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.22 (Mulders-Manders & Rovers), pp.149-154 (file pages 192-197)

chunks.text: Examination should pay special attention to the eyes, lymph nodes, temporal arteries, liver, spleen, prior surgical sites, the entire skin surface, and mucous membranes (p.152).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.22 (Mulders-Manders & Rovers), pp.149-154 (file pages 192-197)

chunks.text: History should capture fever pattern (continuous vs recurrent) and duration, prior medical history, current/recent drugs, family and sexual history, country of origin, recent and remote travel, environmental/hobby exposures, and animal contacts (p.152).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.22 (Mulders-Manders & Rovers), pp.149-154 (file pages 192-197)

chunks.text: Giant cell arteritis is notably prevalent among FUO patients, with rates up to 17% in the elderly; temporal artery biopsy is still recommended for patients >=55 years (p.153).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.22 (Mulders-Manders & Rovers), pp.149-154 (file pages 192-197)

chunks.text: FUO with headache should prompt CSF microbiologic examination for herpes simplex virus (especially type 2), Cryptococcus neoformans/gattii, and M. tuberculosis (p.153).

chunks.text: In patients with recurrent/episodic FUO, ask the patient to return DURING a febrile episode; further tests should be done during an inflammatory episode since abnormalities may be absent between episodes (pp.152-153).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.22 (Mulders-Manders & Rovers), pp.149-154 (file pages 192-197)

chunks.text: Starting empirical therapeutic trials before a diagnosis - should be AVOIDED except when the patient is rapidly deteriorating, because most undiagnosed patients resolve spontaneously (p.154).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.22 (Mulders-Manders & Rovers), pp.149-154 (file pages 192-197)

chunks.text: Continuing antibiotics/glucocorticoids during workup - they mask disease: cultures become unreliable and glucocorticoids shrink lymph nodes regardless of cause; stop them before further testing (p.152).

chunks.text: Early empirical glucocorticoids - can mask fever while infection or lymphoma spreads and reduce the chance of diagnosing a treatable malignancy; avoid until infection and lymphoma are sufficiently excluded (p.155).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.22 (Mulders-Manders & Rovers), pp.149-154 (file pages 192-197)

chunks.text: Ordering more screening tests without PDCs - low yield; immunologic and microbiologic serologies without PDCs more often give false-positives; better to wait for new PDCs unless the patient deteriorates (pp.153-154).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.22 (Mulders-Manders & Rovers), pp.149-154 (file pages 192-197)

chunks.text: Over-culturing - performing >3 blood cultures or >1 urine culture is useless absent PDCs (p.153).

chunks.text: Failing to recognize PDCs already present in available information is a frequent cause of diagnostic delay (p.154).

chunks.text: Interpreting a negative TST/IGRA as excluding TB - it does not; results may be indeterminate in miliary TB, malnutrition, immunosuppression, or with anti-IFN-gamma autoantibodies (p.153).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.22 (Mulders-Manders & Rovers), pp.149-154 (file pages 192-197)

chunks.text: Misreading PET/CT - physiologic FDG uptake in brain, heart, bowel, kidneys, and bladder can obscure pathology (e.g., cardiac uptake masking endocarditis - mitigate with a pre-scan low-carbohydrate diet) (p.153).
