chunks.text: Prognosis depends chiefly on the underlying diagnosis. When FUO remains unexplained after extensive evaluation, outlook is favorable: large cohorts report high rates of spontaneous fever resolution and mortality of 8% or less over several years of follow-up. The greatest mortality risk is during the early diagnostic phase. A normal 18F-FDG-PET/CT is associated with higher rates of spontaneous resolution and may help predict who will resolve. A symptom duration >12 months and a normal PET/CT both lower the chance of ever reaching a final diagnosis (pp.150, 154).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.22 (Mulders-Manders & Rovers), pp.149-154 (file pages 192-197)

chunks.text: Clinical deterioration without new PDCs - the trigger to escalate workup (rather than wait) and the situation where empirical therapy may be justified (pp.152-153)

chunks.text: FUO categories (by host/setting), each requiring a distinct approach: (1) classic FUO - the immunocompetent adult per the formal definition; (2) nosocomial FUO; (3) neutropenic FUO; and (4) HIV-associated FUO. The contemporary Harrison definition explicitly EXCLUDES immunocompromised states, which need a different, more aggressive approach. Etiologies are grouped into four diagnostic categories - infections, noninfectious inflammatory diseases (NIIDs), malignancy, and miscellaneous - with a large 'no diagnosis' fraction (pp.149-150).

chunks.text: Repeat detailed history and serial examinations — New localizing signs often emerge over time and are the single most valuable step in PUO workup.
CBC, ESR, CRP, LFTs, RFTs, urinalysis — First-tier screening tests that can reveal a localizing clue (e.g., abnormal LFTs pointing to liver abscess or biliary source).
Blood cultures (multiple sets, including for fastidious organisms if endocarditis suspected) — Identifies bacteremic causes including culture-negative endocarditis pathogens with extended incubation.
Chest X-ray and abdominal ultrasound — First-line imaging to screen for occult infection (TB, abscess) or malignancy.
CT chest/abdomen/pelvis (second-tier) — More sensitive for occult abscess, lymphadenopathy, or malignancy if first-tier workup is unrevealing.
Echocardiography (if any murmur, risk factors, or persistent bacteremia) — Screens for infective endocarditis as a cause of prolonged fever.
Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (infective) — Systemic
veryLikely: Diagnosis-dependent — broad differential includes infective (TB, enteric fever, infective endocarditis, abscess), neoplastic (lymphoma), and autoimmune/rheumatologic causes

Complicated UTI (fever in a patient with structural/functional urinary abnormality, immunocompromise, or instrumentation) (Harrison 22e p.1133-1134)
Sexually transmitted infection mimicking UTI, particularly Chlamydia trachomatis cervicitis/urethritis (Harrison 22e p.1133-1134)
Renal/ureteral calculus with obstruction (renal colic) presenting with flank pain and pyuria (Harrison 22e p.2493)
Acute prostatitis (Harrison 22e p.1137)
Cervicitis or urethritis due to Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Harrison 22e p.1133-1134)
Vaginitis (Candida albicans, Trichomonas vaginalis) or herpetic urethritis causing dysuria (Harrison 22e p.1133-1134)

Upper-tract imaging (CT or renal ultrasound) to evaluate for obstruction, abscess, or anatomic abnormality, especially in men, in patients not responding within 72 hours, or when complicated infection is suspected (Harrison 22e p.1132, 1137)

Urine dipstick (nitrite, leukocyte esterase) and microscopic urinalysis as point-of-care tests; note nitrites detect only Enterobacterales and may be falsely negative with non-Enterobacterales organisms (Harrison 22e p.1134-1135)
Imaging for gas in renal/perinephric tissues when emphysematous pyelonephritis is suspected in a diabetic patient (Harrison 22e p.1090)
Renal/ureteral stone with proximal obstruction, which may present exactly as acute pyelonephritis (Harrison 22e p.2493)
Interstitial cystitis or noninfectious vulvovaginal irritation causing dysuria (Harrison 22e p.1133-1134)
Sloughed renal papilla or blood clot causing ureteral obstruction without infection (Harrison 22e p.2493)
Musculoskeletal flank/back pain, herpes zoster, abdominal aortic aneurysm, duodenal ulcer (differential for flank pain) (Harrison 22e p.2493)

Pyelonephritis usually develops as an ascending infection: uropathogens move from the urethra to the bladder and then continue up the ureter to the renal parenchyma, which is the route for most renal parenchymal infection. Its microbiology therefore mirrors that of acute cystitis. A minority arises hematogenously (<2% of UTIs overall), typically with relatively virulent organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus and Salmonella; isolation of either from urine should prompt consideration of concomitant bacteremia, and hematogenous seeding can produce focal renal abscesses. Anatomic factors causing urinary obstruction or retention (congenital anomalies, cystocele, pelvic-organ prolapse, neurogenic bladder, benign prostatic hypertrophy) impede the protective flushing action of micturition and predispose to renal involvement. A foreign body such as a stone or catheter provides an inert surface for colonization (Harrison 22e p.1088, 1130-1131).

Fever is the principal feature distinguishing pyelonephritis from simple cystitis; presence of fever, back/flank pain, rigors, nausea or vomiting signals infection that has extended beyond the bladder (Harrison 22e p.1086-1090, 1133).

Severity spans a wide spectrum: mild disease may present only with low-grade fever with or without costovertebral angle pain, whereas severe disease manifests with high fever, rigors, nausea, vomiting, and flank pain; onset is generally acute and may or may not be preceded by cystitis symptoms (Harrison 22e p.1090).
Pyelonephritis represents tissue-invasive disease and patients are often systemically ill, so the threat of progression to bacteremia and urosepsis is real (Harrison 22e p.1090, 1137, 1329).

In a woman presenting with at least one localizing urinary symptom (dysuria, frequency, hematuria, or back pain) and no complicating factors, the combined probability of acute cystitis or pyelonephritis is about 50% (Harrison 22e p.1133).

Men with febrile UTI should undergo upper-tract imaging (CT or ultrasound) if not done previously, to evaluate for urinary tract abnormality or obstruction, and elevated PSA with enlarged prostate/seminal vesicles suggests prostatic involvement (Harrison 22e p.1132).

Pregnant patients are at unusually high risk of developing pyelonephritis, which can adversely affect pregnancy outcome (preterm delivery, low birth weight); this underlies routine prenatal screening for asymptomatic bacteriuria (Harrison 22e p.1086, 1329).

Treating presumed UTI when the true cause is an STI (e.g., C. trachomatis); vaginal discharge should prompt STI consideration since symptoms alone do not reliably distinguish them (Harrison 22e p.1133-1134).

Stopping the workup at an abnormal urinalysis in a catheterized or febrile patient: pyuria and bacteriuria are expected with catheterization and do not by themselves establish UTI as the cause of fever (Harrison 22e p.1133-1135).
Mistaking an obstructing stone with proximal infection for uncomplicated pyelonephritis and missing the need for emergent drainage (Harrison 22e p.2493).
Misattributing xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis to renal malignancy because its mass effect can mimic tumor (Harrison 22e p.1090).
Delayed/withheld antimicrobial therapy in true UTI carries a small increased risk of progression to pyelonephritis (Harrison 22e p.1136).

Most pyelonephritis treated effectively resolves, though fever may take 5-7 days to clear completely even with appropriate therapy. Renal parenchymal damage and loss of renal function are uncommon and occur primarily in association with urinary obstruction (preexisting, or, rarely, de novo in diabetic patients with papillary necrosis). Chronic bacterial pyelonephritis is rarely a cause of chronic renal failure because it seldom affects both kidneys. Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis arises from chronic obstruction (often staghorn calculus) plus chronic infection causing suppurative destruction of renal tissue and frequently requires nephrectomy (Harrison 22e p.1090, 1137, 1329, 2493).

Acute papillary necrosis with sloughed papillae obstructing the ureter, producing obstructive uropathy that requires intervention to relieve obstruction and preserve renal function (Harrison 22e p.1090, 1137)
UTI in the setting of ureteral obstruction is a medical emergency requiring immediate restoration of drainage by ureteral stent or percutaneous nephrostomy (Harrison 22e p.2493)

Emphysematous pyelonephritis: gas production in renal and perinephric tissues, occurring almost exclusively in patients with poorly controlled diabetes; a particularly severe form (Harrison 22e p.1090)
Continued fever and/or bacteremia despite antibacterial therapy should raise suspicion for intraparenchymal, perinephric, or renal cortical abscess (Harrison 22e p.1090, 1137)
Failure of clinical response within 72 hours warrants evaluation for an uncontrolled source of infection (Harrison 22e p.1137)
Persistently elevated/increasing fever, flank pain, and rising neutrophil counts should prompt evaluation for intrarenal/perinephric abscess and/or obstruction (Harrison 22e p.1329)
Bilateral papillary necrosis may present first as a rapid rise in serum creatinine (Harrison 22e p.1090)

Harrison describes a clinical spectrum rather than a formal score: mild pyelonephritis (low-grade fever, with or without lower back or costovertebral angle pain) versus severe pyelonephritis (high fever, rigors, nausea, vomiting, flank pain). Distinct severe/complicated entities include emphysematous pyelonephritis (gas-forming, almost exclusively in poorly controlled diabetes), xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis (chronic obstruction plus infection causing suppurative renal destruction), and pyelonephritis complicated by papillary necrosis with obstruction or by intrarenal/perinephric abscess. Acute pyelonephritis is one of the systemic UTI presentations that may be grouped as urosepsis or febrile UTI, with or without bacteremia (Harrison 22e p.1090, 1329).
Urine culture and sensitivity — Confirms organism and susceptibility, essential for targeted therapy and de-escalation.
Blood cultures — Pyelonephritis carries meaningful bacteremia risk; positive cultures confirm systemic involvement and guide duration.
Renal ultrasound or CT (if no improvement in 48-72 hours) — Evaluates for obstruction or abscess if the patient fails to improve on appropriate therapy.

chunks.text: Rickettsiae and Orientia are obligately intracellular gram-negative coccobacilli that primarily infect vascular endothelial cells. After tick saliva inoculates organisms into the dermis (in RMSF after roughly 6 h of feeding), they spread lymphohematogenously and infect contiguous foci of endothelium throughout the body, producing a widespread infectious vasculitis with increased vascular permeability. The resulting edema, hypovolemia, and tissue ischemia (rather than occlusive thrombosis) drive the organ injury: prerenal azotemia, noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, and CNS dysfunction. Platelet consumption causes thrombocytopenia in about a third to half of RMSF cases, but frank DIC with hypofibrinogenemia is rare; the coagulation changes appear to be homeostatic responses to endothelial injury forming nonocclusive hemostatic plugs (p.1454, p.1456).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.137-141 (Ch.21 Fever and Rash); p.1454-1459 (Ch.192 Rickettsial Diseases); p.1488 (Ch.189 Leptospirosis differential)

chunks.text: All acute rickettsial illnesses look alike for roughly the first 5 days: fever, headache, and myalgias, often with nausea, vomiting, or cough; the distinguishing features (rash, eschar, pneumonitis, meningoencephalitis) emerge only as the illness progresses (p.1454).

chunks.text: An inoculation eschar (tache noire) is a necrotic, often painless black-crusted lesion with a surrounding erythematous halo at the bite site; it can appear during the incubation period and is common in Mediterranean spotted fever (~50%), African tick-bite fever (~90%), and rickettsialpox (~90%), but is essentially absent in classic RMSF (<1%) and in epidemic/murine typhus (p.1455).

chunks.text: African tick-bite fever (R. africae) is the rickettsiosis most often imported into Europe and North America via travelers returning from sub-Saharan Africa; because Amblyomma ticks feed in groups, multiple eschars and regional lymphadenopathy are characteristic, and rash may be vesicular, sparse, or absent (p.1457-1458).

chunks.text: In RMSF the rash is centrifugal and evolving: erythematous macules begin on wrists and ankles, spread to extremities and trunk, and only later involve palms and soles; macules progress to non-blanching petechiae as vascular damage advances (p.1456).

chunks.text: Outcome is strongly time-dependent: untreated RMSF carries mortality of roughly 20-25% (historic) with confirmed-case fatality around 9-10% where R. rickettsii is the sole agent, versus ~3-5% when treated early; delayed recognition and treatment markedly increase death. For unclear reasons RMSF case-fatality approaches 50% in Mexico and Brazil. Severe Mediterranean spotted fever has mortality near 50% without treatment but improves dramatically with even a single day of appropriate therapy. Untreated epidemic typhus historically killed up to 60% and still exceeds 10-15% in outbreaks. Many survivors of severe RMSF recover fully, but permanent neurologic deficits and gangrene requiring amputation can follow severe illness (p.1456-1457; p.1488 / Ch.21).

chunks.text: Harrison does not give a formal grading scale, but stratifies along a spectrum: (1) self-limited febrile illness that resolves without evolution; (2) classic disease with rash and/or eschar; and (3) severe/complicated disease with organ involvement - pneumonitis/ARDS, meningoencephalitis, acute kidney injury, hemorrhage/skin necrosis/gangrene, sepsis/septic shock, and (rarely) fulminant RMSF fatal within 5 days. Higher-risk groups include children <10 years, adults >70 years, the immunosuppressed, and (for fulminant RMSF) males with G6PD deficiency (p.1454-1457).

SBP is spontaneous infection of ascitic fluid in the absence of an intraabdominal surgical source. The presumed mechanism is bacterial translocation: gut flora cross an edematous, leaky intestinal wall into mesenteric lymph nodes, producing bacteremia that seeds the ascites, which is a good growth medium. Susceptibility in cirrhosis reflects impaired hepatic filtration from a diseased liver and altered portal circulation, low ascitic complement levels (lower than in non-cirrhotic ascites), and diminished opsonic and phagocytic function of PMNs in advanced liver disease. Cirrhosis is also associated with gut dysbiosis (increased Enterobacteriaceae), small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth, reduced Paneth-cell defensins, decreased intestinal motility, reduced pancreatobiliary secretions, and portal-hypertensive enteropathy, all of which promote pathologic translocation. SBP occurs in up to ~30% of hospitalized cirrhotics with ascites but is an uncommon event overall, affecting 10% or fewer of cirrhotic patients. (Harrison 22e p.1070, 2715)
An ascitic-fluid PMN (neutrophil) count of at least 250/microL is diagnostic of SBP, irrespective of whether cultures grow an organism (Harrison 22e p.329, 372, 1070).
SBP virtually always arises on a background of preexisting ascites, which predates the infection (Harrison 22e p.1070).

A repeat paracentesis after 48 hours of therapy should confirm at least a 25% fall in the ascitic PMN count from baseline; failure to fall, or persistent ascitic leukocytosis after treatment, should prompt a search for an alternative or secondary diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.329, 1071).

Fever is the single most common manifestation, present in roughly 80% of cases; abdominal pain, acute onset, and peritoneal signs aid diagnosis but their absence does not rule SBP out (Harrison 22e p.1070).
Abdominal tenderness is found in only about 40% of patients and rebound tenderness is uncommon, so a benign abdomen does not exclude the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.329).

SBP can present with no abdominal symptoms at all, instead manifesting as new or worsening hepatic encephalopathy, altered mental status, jaundice, or acute kidney injury without another explanation (Harrison 22e p.329, 1070, 2715).

In any cirrhotic patient hospitalized with ascites who deteriorates or shows signs of infection, a diagnostic paracentesis is mandatory; tapping within 12 hours of admission lowers mortality through early SBP detection (Harrison 22e p.329, 2715).

Ascitic fluid should be injected directly into blood-culture bottles at the bedside to improve yield, and blood cultures drawn simultaneously, since the organism burden in the fluid is low and bacteremia frequently coexists (Harrison 22e p.329, 1070).
Culture samples should be obtained before antibiotics are started to maximize recovery of the organism (Harrison 22e p.1070).
SBP is almost always monomicrobial; a single isolate is the rule (Harrison 22e p.329, 1070).
Gram stain of ascitic fluid is frequently negative in SBP and a negative result should not deter treatment (Harrison 22e p.1070).
Diagnosis rests on the ascitic PMN count >=250/microL, not on a positive culture; ascitic cultures are often negative because the organism burden is low (Harrison 22e p.329, 1070).

Recovery of more than one organism (a mixed flora, especially with anaerobes) alongside an elevated PMN count points to SECONDARY peritonitis from a ruptured viscus or abscess, not SBP, and demands a search for a surgical source (Harrison 22e p.329, 1071).
Multiple organisms WITHOUT an elevated PMN count suggest bowel perforation by the paracentesis needle rather than true infection (Harrison 22e p.329).

Failing to perform a diagnostic paracentesis in a decompensated cirrhotic who deteriorates (encephalopathy, AKI, sepsis) misses SBP, since the abdomen may be benign and tenderness is present in only ~40% (Harrison 22e p.329, 2715).
A low ascitic total protein (<1.0-1.5 g/dL) reflects low opsonic activity and identifies patients at higher risk for SBP; this group warrants heightened suspicion (Harrison 22e p.330, 1071).

The 250/microL PMN threshold is specific to SBP and should not be applied to secondary peritonitis or to peritoneal-dialysis peritonitis, where lower leukocyte cutoffs are used (Harrison 22e p.1070, p.2486 context).
Gastric acid suppression (e.g., proton-pump inhibitors) has been associated with increased SBP risk in observational data (Harrison 22e p.1071).

SBP is a common and potentially lethal complication of cirrhotic ascites and carries significant morbidity and mortality, largely because it tends to occur in patients with the most advanced liver disease. In-hospital mortality is roughly 17-25%; one tertiary-center series reported ~23% mortality at 30 days and ~37% at 90 days. Recurrence is high, with up to ~70% of patients having another episode within a year. Patients with PBP usually respond to appropriate antibiotics within about 72 hours. The underlying prognosis of cirrhosis with ascites is itself poor, with under 50% surviving 2 years after ascites onset in some series, so SBP should prompt consideration of liver transplantation. (Harrison 22e p.1071, 2715-2716, 373)
New or worsening hepatic encephalopathy or altered mental status in a cirrhotic with ascites (Harrison 22e p.329, 1070, 2715)
Unexplained acute kidney injury, jaundice, or nonlocalizing malaise/fatigue in a susceptible patient (Harrison 22e p.1070)
Multiple organisms recovered from ascitic fluid, especially with anaerobes, suggesting secondary peritonitis requiring source control (Harrison 22e p.329, 1071)
Free air under the diaphragm on imaging, signaling perforation (Harrison 22e p.1070)
Concurrent GI/variceal bleeding, which markedly increases SBP frequency (Harrison 22e p.330, 2716)
Failure of the ascitic PMN count to fall, or persistence of WBCs after therapy, indicating treatment failure or an alternative diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.329, 1071)

Harrison does not provide a formal severity grading system specific to SBP. Risk stratification is framed around predictors of poor outcome and renal injury: higher SBP risk in patients with low ascitic-fluid total protein (<1.0-1.5 g/dL), impaired renal function (creatinine >=1.2 mg/dL, BUN >=25 mg/dL, or serum sodium <=130 mEq/L), and advanced liver failure (Child-Turcotte-Pugh score >=9, bilirubin >=3 mg/dL); these are used to identify candidates for prophylaxis. The greatest benefit of adjunctive albumin is seen in those presenting with serum creatinine >=1 mg/dL, BUN >=30 mg/dL, or total bilirubin >=5 mg/dL. (Harrison 22e p.1071)

Diagnostic paracentesis with ascitic fluid cell count and culture — Defines the diagnosis (neutrophil count ≥250/mm³) and identifies the organism for targeted therapy — essential before committing to a full antibiotic course where feasible.
Blood cultures — Frequently positive and may identify the organism even when ascitic fluid culture is negative (culture-negative neutrocytic ascites).
Renal function tests — Guides decision on adjunctive albumin and assesses for hepatorenal syndrome, a major complication of SBP.
Liver function tests and coagulation profile — Establishes baseline severity of underlying liver disease, relevant to prognosis and overall management.
Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (infective) — Hepatobiliary / GI

[guideline] alternative → Ceftriaxone

Other rickettsioses presenting with eschar, rash, fever and headache (e.g., Mediterranean spotted fever, African tick-bite fever, rickettsialpox, murine and epidemic typhus) (Harrison 22e p.1455-1456).
Atypical/community-acquired pneumonia, given the cough and dyspnea of pulmonary involvement (Harrison 22e p.1126).
Other undifferentiated tropical febrile illnesses with thrombocytopenia and transaminitis.
Serology is the mainstay of laboratory diagnosis: indirect fluorescent antibody, indirect immunoperoxidase, enzyme immunoassays, and rapid lateral-flow chromatographic tests (Harrison 22e p.1460).
PCR amplification of Orientia genes is effective when performed on eschar material, but is less sensitive on blood (Harrison 22e p.1460).
Platelet count: thrombocytopenia is a characteristic laboratory finding in scrub typhus (as in other rickettsioses) (Harrison 22e p.1455).
WBC count is typically normal or low (Harrison 22e p.1455).
Serum sodium: hyponatremia is a recognized associated finding across the rickettsioses (Harrison 22e p.1455).
Hepatic aminotransferases: mild to moderate elevation is commonly seen (Harrison 22e p.1455).

Scrub typhus is caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi, an obligate intracellular organism placed in a separate genus within the family Rickettsiaceae. It differs substantially from Rickettsia species both genetically and in cell-wall composition, notably lacking lipopolysaccharide. Disease results from infection of vascular endothelial cells with increased vascular permeability (a mechanism shared across the rickettsioses). The organism is maintained in nature by transovarial transmission within trombiculid mites; infected larval mites (chiggers, the only mite stage that feeds on a vertebrate host) inoculate the organism into the skin during feeding. Severe disease reflects widespread vascular injury, producing the encephalitis and interstitial pneumonia that characterize advanced cases. Closely related Orientia species (O. chuto, Candidatus O. chiloensis) cause scrub typhus-like illness in newly recognized foci (Harrison 22e p.1455-1456, p.1460, p.3773).

The classic triad of an inoculation eschar at the chigger feeding site, regional lymphadenopathy, and a maculopapular rash is the textbook description, but these signs are seldom seen in indigenous (local endemic) patients (Harrison 22e p.1460).
Among returning travelers, fewer than 50% develop an eschar and fewer than 40% develop a rash; when a rash does appear it typically emerges on day 4-6 of illness (Harrison 22e p.1460).

Eschar formation occurs at the site of mite/chigger feeding and may develop during the incubation period; an eschar is a useful diagnostic clue that should prompt consideration of scrub typhus (Harrison 22e p.1455).

Onset after a 6-21 day incubation is characterized by fever, headache, myalgia, cough, and gastrointestinal symptoms; some patients recover spontaneously after a few days while others progress to severe disease (Harrison 22e p.1460).
Chigger bites may be asymptomatic, so the absence of a recalled bite does not exclude the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.3773).

Immunity to scrub typhus is short-lived: protection against the homologous strain wanes over 1-3 years, and the organism's marked antigenic diversity means cross-protective immunity can be lost in as little as 1 month, so reinfection is possible (Harrison 22e p.1460).

Relying on the classic triad: eschar, rash, and lymphadenopathy are frequently absent (eschar <50% and rash <40% of travelers; signs seldom seen in indigenous patients), so a negative skin exam does not exclude scrub typhus (Harrison 22e p.1460).
Expecting a recalled bite: chigger bites may be asymptomatic and the mites are tiny and rarely noticed (Harrison 22e p.3773).

Assuming geographic exclusion: although classically eastern/southern Asia, northern Australia, and Pacific/Indian Ocean islands, emerging and reemerging foci (e.g., Chile, parts of South/Central America, Africa, Arabian peninsula via related Orientia species) challenge the traditional epidemiology (Harrison 22e p.1460, p.3773).
Note that PCR on blood is less sensitive than PCR on eschar material (Harrison 22e p.1460).
Some Thai isolates are poorly responsive to doxycycline or chloramphenicol (Harrison 22e p.1460).

Illness ranges from mild and self-limiting to fatal. The case-fatality rate for untreated classic cases is about 6% and would likely be lower if all mild cases were captured; overall reported mortality varies widely by location (cited as 1% to 70%). Risk of death rises with increasing age and with the presence of myocarditis, delirium, pneumonitis, or signs of hemorrhage. Recognized in time, the disease responds well to appropriate antibiotic therapy (Harrison 22e p.1035, p.1460).
Altered mental status / encephalitis (meningoencephalitis is a feature of severe disease) (Harrison 22e p.1035, p.1455).
Interstitial pneumonia / pneumonitis with dyspnea or progression toward respiratory failure (Harrison 22e p.1035, p.1460).
Myocarditis (Harrison 22e p.1035).
Signs of disseminated intravascular coagulation or hemorrhage (Harrison 22e p.1035).
Renal failure (Harrison 22e p.1035).
Progressive hypotension and multiorgan failure (a severe-disease pattern shared by the rickettsioses) (Harrison 22e p.1455).

Harrison does not give a formal severity score; it contrasts mild/self-limiting illness with severe disease. Severe scrub typhus is marked by encephalitis/meningoencephalitis and interstitial pneumonia due to vascular injury, and may progress to myocarditis, DIC, renal failure, hypotension, and multiorgan failure (Harrison 22e p.1035, p.1455, p.1460).

Careful skin examination for eschar — Eschar (a painless, often overlooked necrotic lesion at the chigger bite site) is highly specific for scrub typhus when found — actively look in skin folds, axillae, groin.
Scrub typhus IgM ELISA / Weil-Felix (less specific) — Confirms diagnosis serologically, though treatment should not wait for results when clinical suspicion is high.
CBC, LFTs, renal function — Assesses organ involvement; transaminitis and thrombocytopenia are common supportive findings.
Chest X-ray (if respiratory symptoms) — Screens for ARDS, a recognized complication of severe/delayed scrub typhus.

chunks.text: Sepsis arises when an infection provokes a dysregulated, self-amplifying host response rather than a contained local one. Pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs, e.g., LPS, bacterial cell-wall components, microbial nucleic acids) and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs, e.g., histones, HMGB1, S100 proteins, mitochondrial/double-stranded DNA, ATP released from injured cells) are sensed by pattern-recognition receptors (TLRs, CLRs, RAGE, RIG-I, NOD-like receptors) on innate immune and parenchymal cells. This triggers exuberant release of cytokines and chemokines and upregulation of vascular adhesion molecules. Myeloid cells (neutrophils, monocytes, M1 macrophages, dendritic cells) drive injury through phagocytosis, degranulation, reactive oxygen/nitrogen species, and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), while emergency granulopoiesis releases immature neutrophils (a poor-prognosis marker). Lymphoid responses are dysregulated, with lymphocyte apoptosis, exhaustion, and myeloid-derived suppressor cells producing a state of immunosuppression that predisposes survivors to secondary infection. The endothelium is activated and injured: glycocalyx breakdown, loss of VE-cadherin/tight junctions, and apoptosis cause capillary leak, interstitial edema, and a widened oxygen-diffusion distance. A prothrombotic shift (increased tissue factor, vWF, PAI-1; depleted antithrombin, tissue factor pathway inhibitor, and protein C; complement activation with C3a/C5a and the C5b-9 membrane attack complex) generates microvascular thrombi and, once clotting factors and platelets are consumed, bleeding. Excess nitric oxide drives systemic vasodilation. The net result is impaired oxygen delivery, uptake, and utilization; even when oxygen delivery is adequate, mitochondrial and metabolic dysfunction impairs ATP generation and ion homeostasis, producing multiorgan cellular injury and dysfunction (p.2317-2319).

source.page: 2310-2324 (Harrison 22e; principal sepsis chapter 315, p.2316-2324; shock chapter 314, p.2310-2316; ICU scoring chapter 311, p.2291-2292)

chunks.text: Sepsis-3 (2016) reframes sepsis as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection, not merely a systemic inflammatory state; the older SIRS-based criteria and the term 'severe sepsis' were discarded for poor specificity (p.2316).

source.page: 2310-2324 (Harrison 22e; principal sepsis chapter 315, p.2316-2324; shock chapter 314, p.2310-2316; ICU scoring chapter 311, p.2291-2292)

chunks.text: Lactate is central to risk-stratifying sepsis: elevation reflects tissue hypoperfusion/anaerobic metabolism, correlates with worse outcome, and serial measurements help track response to resuscitation (p.2313).

source.page: 2310-2324 (Harrison 22e; principal sepsis chapter 315, p.2316-2324; shock chapter 314, p.2310-2316; ICU scoring chapter 311, p.2291-2292)

chunks.text: Most sepsis is community-onset (~88%); the urinary tract is the single most common primary site, followed by respiratory, intra-abdominal, and skin/soft-tissue sources (p.2316).

chunks.text: Hospital-onset sepsis tends to involve sicker, more comorbid patients with more intra-abdominal infection and bacteremia from Enterococcus, Candida, and Pseudomonas, and carries higher ICU admission and mortality (p.2317).

chunks.text: Operationally, sepsis is identified by an acute rise of >=2 points in the SOFA score over baseline in a patient with suspected or confirmed infection (p.2320).

chunks.text: Septic shock is the subset of sepsis with persistent hypotension needing vasopressors to keep MAP >65 mmHg PLUS lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation, reflecting circulatory, cellular, and metabolic derangement that markedly raises mortality (p.2310, 2320).

chunks.text: Overall in-hospital mortality is roughly 15% among hospitalized adults with sepsis, rising to up to ~40% with septic shock; globally an estimated ~11 million sepsis-related deaths occur yearly (about one in five deaths worldwide). Mortality climbs with age and is higher in men. Elevated SOFA scores and machine-learning-defined phenotypes track population-level outcome (e.g., alpha/beta/gamma/delta phenotypes with ~2%/5%/15%/32% mortality) but cannot reliably predict an individual patient's outcome. Survivorship carries a heavy long-term burden: physical (prolonged fatigue, muscle loss, weakness, reduced functional capacity), cognitive (cognitive decline, dementia), and psychological (depression, reduced quality of life) sequelae, plus increased risk of cardiovascular events, recurrent infection, and readmission. About half of survivors are rehospitalized within a year and roughly one in six die within the first year, with most post-sepsis deaths in the first 6 months and elevated death risk persisting up to ~2 years (p.2316-2317, 2324). No FDA-approved host-targeted/immunomodulatory therapy exists for sepsis (p.2324).

chunks.text: Sepsis-3 (Singer et al., JAMA 2016) is the current framework: (1) Infection (suspected or confirmed) without organ dysfunction is not sepsis. (2) Sepsis = suspected/confirmed infection with an acute increase of >=2 points in the SOFA score from baseline (life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response). The SOFA score grades six systems 0-4: respiratory (PaO2/FiO2), coagulation (platelets), liver (bilirubin), cardiovascular (MAP / vasopressor requirement), CNS (Glasgow Coma Scale), and renal (creatinine / urine output). (3) Septic shock = sepsis with vasopressor requirement to maintain MAP >65 mmHg AND serum lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation. qSOFA (>=2 of RR >=22/min, altered mentation, SBP <=100 mmHg) is a rapid bedside risk-stratification prompt for poor outcome in suspected infection, not a diagnostic criterion. The prior 1991/1992 SIRS-based definitions and the term 'severe sepsis' are obsolete under Sepsis-3 (p.2292, 2316, 2320).

source.page: 2310-2324 (Harrison 22e; principal sepsis chapter 315, p.2316-2324; shock chapter 314, p.2310-2316; ICU scoring chapter 311, p.2291-2292)

chunks.text: Blood cultures (x2, before antibiotics if feasible) — Identifies the causative organism and susceptibility for de-escalation.
Lactate — Core Sepsis-3/Surviving Sepsis Campaign marker of tissue hypoperfusion; guides resuscitation and risk-stratification toward septic shock.
Source-specific cultures (urine, sputum, wound, CSF as guided by clinical exam) — Identifies and confirms the infectious source to allow targeted therapy.
CBC, renal function, liver function, coagulation profile — Assesses organ dysfunction (SOFA components) and supports staging severity.
Imaging directed by suspected source (CXR, abdominal ultrasound/CT) — Localizes the source and identifies any need for source control (drainage, debridement).
Sepsis (infective) — Systemic

veryLikely: Organism depends entirely on the suspected source (e.g., E. coli for urosepsis, S. pneumoniae for pulmonary sepsis); likely: Polymicrobial flora if source is intra-abdominal; possible: Resistant organisms if healthcare-associated or recent antibiotic exposure
Red flags: Immediate empiric antibiotics required

[guideline] empiric → Piperacillin-tazobactam (broad empiric, source unclear) / Add Vancomycin if MRSA risk, line-associated, or skin/soft tissue source Broad empiric gram-positive, gram-negative, and anaerobic coverage is reasonable when the source is not yet localized, pending rapid source identification to allow narrowing.
[guideline] alternative → Source-directed narrow-spectrum therapy (preferred once source identified)
Other causes of distributive shock: pancreatitis, severe burns, liver failure, anaphylaxis, neurogenic shock from brain/spinal cord injury, and adrenal insufficiency/adrenal crisis (p.2353-2354)

chunks.text: Septic shock is the most common form of distributive shock, in which the primary hemodynamic derangement is a fall in systemic vascular resistance (vasoplegia) rather than a primary loss of preload or pump function. The vasodilatory profile is distinctive: SVR is reduced, cardiac output is typically increased as a compensatory response, and both central venous pressure (CVP) and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) tend to be low (p.2353-2354). Arterial and venous vasodilation is mediated in part by excess nitric oxide; vasopressin deficiency may also contribute to refractory hypotension. The dysregulated host response begins when pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs, e.g. LPS, microbial nucleic acids) and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs, e.g. histones, HMGB1, mitochondrial DNA, ATP) are sensed by pattern-recognition receptors (TLRs, CLRs, RAGE, RIG-I, NOD receptors) on neutrophils, monocytes/macrophages, and parenchymal cells, triggering proinflammatory cytokine/chemokine release and upregulation of endothelial adhesion molecules. Activated neutrophils release reactive oxygen species and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs); endothelial activation/injury, glycocalyx degradation, and loss of VE-cadherin tight junctions cause capillary leak, interstitial edema, and increased oxygen-diffusion distance. A prothrombotic state arises from tissue-factor-driven coagulation, platelet/vWF microthrombi, complement activation (C3a, C5a, C5b-9 membrane attack complex), reduced anticoagulants (antithrombin, tissue factor pathway inhibitor, activated protein C), and impaired fibrinolysis (elevated PAI-1); consumption of clotting factors and platelets can then produce hemorrhage. The net effect is hypotension (from vasodilation, myocardial depression, and hypovolemia), microcirculatory dysfunction, and mitochondrial/metabolic failure, so that oxygen delivery, uptake, and utilization are all impaired and cellular injury occurs even when bulk oxygen delivery appears adequate (p.2317-2320). Sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy can add a cardiogenic component, producing mixed shock (p.2355).

chunks.text: Septic shock carries up to ~40% mortality, far higher than the ~15% overall mortality among US hospitalized adults with sepsis (p.2316). In emergency-department shock cohorts, septic and cardiogenic shock have the highest 90-day mortality (reported ~56% and ~52% respectively), and septic shock predominates among ICU shock (~62% of ICU shock patients in one multicenter series), whereas hypovolemic shock has lower mortality (p.2355). Mortality rises with age and is higher in men; comorbidities such as diabetes, obesity, neurologic/respiratory/cardiac disease, renal or hepatic insufficiency, cancer, and immunosuppression worsen outcomes (p.2317). SOFA scores predict mortality at the population level but not for individual patients; proposed clinical 'phenotypes' (alpha/beta/gamma/delta) carried roughly 2%, 5%, 15%, and 32% mortality (p.2317). Survivors face substantial long-term sequelae: physical (fatigue, muscle loss, weakness), cognitive and psychological (cognitive decline, dementia, depression), and increased risk of cardiovascular events, recurrent infection, and readmission. Roughly half of survivors are rehospitalized within 1 year and about one in six die within the first year, with most post-sepsis deaths in the first 6 months and elevated risk persisting up to 2 years (p.2321).

chunks.text: Sepsis-3 spectrum: (1) Sepsis = life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response to infection, operationalized as an acute increase of >=2 points in the SOFA score in a patient with suspected/confirmed infection. (2) Septic shock = a subset of sepsis with profound circulatory, cellular, and metabolic abnormalities and higher mortality, operationally defined as a septic patient who, despite adequate fluid resuscitation, requires vasopressors to maintain MAP >65 mmHg AND has serum lactate >2 mmol/L. qSOFA (RR>=22, GCS<15, SBP<=100; score >=2) is a rapid risk-stratification screen, not a diagnosis. The historical Sepsis-1/2 terms 'severe sepsis' and SIRS-based septic shock (SBP<90 or drop >=40 mmHg) have been superseded (p.2316, p.2320).

Pneumonia results from proliferation of microbial pathogens in the alveoli combined with the host inflammatory response. Organisms reach the lower respiratory tract by inhalation, microaspiration of oropharyngeal flora, or direct mucosal spread; mechanical defenses (nasal hairs/turbinates, the branching airway, mucociliary clearance, gag and cough reflexes) are insufficient to fully exclude bacteria, and the lung is now understood to harbor a microbiota rather than being sterile. An inflammatory/epithelial-endothelial injury event releases cytokines, chemokines, and catecholamines that can selectively promote growth of organisms such as S. pneumoniae and P. aeruginosa, generating a positive-feedback loop; in CAP the trigger is often a viral infection compounded by microaspiration. Inflammatory mediators (IL-6, TNF) cause fever, while IL-8 and G-CSF recruit neutrophils; mediators from macrophages and neutrophils produce alveolar-capillary leak with impaired oxygenation, hypoxemia, and radiographic infiltrates. Some pathogens interfere with hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, worsening hypoxemia. Reduced compliance from capillary leak, increased respiratory drive and secretions, and intrapulmonary shunting drive worsening dyspnea, and when severe, reductions in lung volume/compliance and shunting can precipitate respiratory failure. Pathologically, classic (lobar pneumococcal) pneumonia evolves through edema, red hepatization, gray hepatization, and resolution phases.
Neither the Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) nor CURB-65 accurately determines the need for ICU admission; they predict mortality/site of care but not ICU need (p.1026).
Gross hemoptysis suggests necrotizing pneumonia, e.g., due to CA-MRSA (p.1024).
In the elderly, severe CAP may present atypically as new-onset or worsening confusion or decompensation of a chronic illness with few classic respiratory findings (p.1025).
Recent data show a mortality benefit for corticosteroids in severe CAP, particularly when there is a high level of systemic inflammation (CRP >15 mg/dL) (p.1029).

Patients with septic shock requiring vasopressors or acute respiratory failure requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation meet a major criterion and should be admitted directly to an ICU (p.1026).
Presence of three or more of the nine minor severe-CAP criteria warrants admission to an ICU or high-level monitoring unit (p.1026).

Late or delayed ICU admission is associated with increased mortality; less-ill patients placed on a general ward who then deteriorate fare worse than equally ill patients monitored in the ICU from the outset (p.1026).
In ICU-admitted CAP specifically, treatment directed at an identified pathogen may be superior to empirical therapy, so etiologic workup carries more weight in severe disease (p.1025).
The microbial spectrum of severe (ICU) CAP differs from milder CAP: Legionella tends to cause more serious disease, and S. aureus and gram-negative bacilli become more prominent (p.1024).

Prior respiratory-tract isolation of MRSA or P. aeruginosa within the past year is a stronger (more robust) risk factor for these pathogens than recent hospitalization plus parenteral antibiotic exposure (p.1028).
Procalcitonin (PCT) is insufficiently accurate to diagnose bacterial CAP and must NOT be used as a basis for withholding initial antibiotics; CRP is even less sensitive than PCT (p.1026).

If only a viral pathogen (e.g., influenza or SARS-CoV-2) is found and no bacterial pathogen is evident, antibacterial therapy can be stopped — BUT in severe illness, bacterial-viral co-infection must still be considered (p.1028).
Using PSI or CURB-65 to decide ICU admission - neither is accurate for that purpose (p.1026).
Withholding initial antibiotics based on a low procalcitonin - PCT is too inaccurate to exclude bacterial CAP (p.1026).
Assuming hospitalization alone is a significant risk factor for MRSA or P. aeruginosa - it is no longer considered so; severity plus specific risk factors drive coverage decisions (p.1028).
Requiring all three drug-resistance risk factors (recent hospitalization, recent oral/IV antibiotics, local validation) before considering resistant pathogens - any can apply (p.1028).
Stopping antibacterials when a virus is identified in a severely ill patient without considering bacterial-viral co-infection (p.1028).

Attributing failure to improve to the wrong cause: consider resistant or unexpected pathogen (CA-MRSA, M. tuberculosis, fungus), a sequestered focus (lung abscess, empyema), wrong drug/dose, or nosocomial superinfection (p.1029).
Routinely covering anaerobes in aspiration-related severe CAP - unnecessary unless poor dentition, lung abscess, or necrotizing pneumonia (p.1027).

Prognosis depends on age, comorbidities, and site of treatment. For hospitalized CAP, overall mortality ranges from 12% to 40%, the higher end reflecting ICU-level disease and care-process factors such as timely administration of appropriate antibiotics (vs <5% for outpatients). CURB-65 scores >=3 carry an overall ~22% mortality and may indicate ICU admission; PSI class 5 has a ~29.2% mortality. CAP is a leading infectious cause of death in patients >65 years; about 18% of hospitalized CAP patients are readmitted within a month, and recent data show 1-year mortality after CAP (especially in older patients) exceeds 30-day mortality. Severe-CAP complications (respiratory failure, shock, multiorgan failure) and pneumonia-associated cardiovascular events worsen outcomes.

IDSA/ATS severe-CAP criteria (Harrison 22e Table 131-3, p.1026). MAJOR criteria (either qualifies for ICU): (1) respiratory failure requiring invasive mechanical ventilation; (2) septic shock requiring vasopressors. MINOR criteria (>=3 warrant ICU/high-level monitoring): respiratory rate >=30 breaths/min; PaO2/FiO2 ratio <=250; multilobar infiltrates; confusion/disorientation; uremia (BUN >=20 mg/dL); leukopenia (WBC <4000/uL); thrombocytopenia (platelets <100,000/uL); hypothermia (core temperature <36 C); and hypotension requiring aggressive fluid resuscitation. Prognostic tools PSI (5 mortality classes, class 5 ~29.2%) and CURB-65 (confusion, urea >7 mmol/L, RR >=30, SBP <=90 or DBP <=60 mmHg, age >=65; score >=3 ~22% mortality) assess severity/site of care but are NOT accurate for determining ICU need.
Blood cultures (x2) — Bacteremia rate is higher in severe CAP; identifies organism and susceptibility for de-escalation.
Sputum culture and Gram stain — Helps target and de-escalate empiric therapy.
Urinary antigen (pneumococcal and Legionella) — Rapid, useful for severe presentations to guide targeted therapy.
ABG — Quantifies hypoxia/hypercapnia and guides ventilatory support decisions.
Chest X-ray / CT chest — Defines extent (multilobar disease, effusion, cavitation) which affects prognosis and management.
Lactate — Screens for tissue hypoperfusion and helps gauge severity/sepsis overlap.
Severe Community Acquired Pneumonia (infective) — Respiratory

chunks.text: Sinusitis is inflammation of the paranasal sinuses; when the nasal passages are also involved the term rhinosinusitis is used. Most acute disease begins as a viral process. Bacterial sinusitis, when it occurs, is usually a secondary superinfection of the obstructed/inflamed sinus and is most often caused by S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, or M. catarrhalis. Nonspecific URI is an acute infection of the respiratory tract above the vocal cords, most commonly caused by respiratory viruses acquired through direct contact with infected people, contaminated surfaces, and large and small respiratory droplets. Susceptibility depends on prior exposure and immunity, general health, genetics, microbiome factors, and psychosocial factors including stress. Because immunity is serotype-specific (rhinovirus, adenovirus) or weak/short-lived (coronaviruses, parainfluenza, RSV, metapneumovirus), reinfection is frequent (Harrison 22e pp.295-296).

The nonspecific URI ('common cold') is defined as a respiratory tract infection in which no single symptom predominates, distinguishing it clinically from more localized syndromes such as pharyngitis, sinusitis, or otitis media (Harrison 22e p.296).

The overwhelming majority of acute respiratory infections are caused by common respiratory viruses and are self-limited; antibiotics neither speed resolution nor prevent complications, which is why at least half of ambulatory antibiotic prescriptions for these infections are inappropriate (Harrison 22e p.295).

Nasal mucus in a viral URI can range anywhere from watery to frankly purulent, so purulent or discolored nasal discharge by itself does not indicate bacterial infection or warrant antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.296).

Symptoms typically begin gradually after a 2-8 day incubation, peak early, and usually last 5-10 days but may persist up to 14 days; patients remain infectious as long as symptoms are present (Harrison 22e pp.296-297).

Adults average 2-4 URIs per year and children 6-10 per year; reinfection is common because immunity to the many rhinovirus and adenovirus serotypes is serotype-specific and immunity to coronaviruses, parainfluenza, RSV, and metapneumovirus is weak or short-lived (Harrison 22e pp.295-296).
Myalgias may occur but are usually less prominent than in influenza, a useful bedside discriminator from influenza (Harrison 22e p.296).

Making a specific viral diagnosis is not practical, cost-effective, or necessary; multiplex RT-PCR panels may be overly sensitive and yield false positives from recent prior infection (Harrison 22e p.296).
URI can be reduced by hand hygiene, physical distancing, masking, isolation of ill persons, and environmental cleaning (Harrison 22e p.295).

Prescribing antibiotics for a viral URI: they do not shorten illness or prevent complications and risk adverse drug effects, microbiome disruption, C. difficile infection, increased cost, and antibiotic resistance (Harrison 22e p.295).
Interpreting purulent nasal discharge as evidence of bacterial infection; viral URI mucus normally ranges from watery to purulent (Harrison 22e p.296).

Drivers of inappropriate prescribing include time pressure, fear of missing a rare bacterial diagnosis, concern about a rare complication, low salience of antibiotic harms, and the mistaken belief that patients demand antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.295).

Delayed antibiotic prescriptions are conceptually flawed for self-limited respiratory infections, shift decision-making to patients, and send a mixed message; they should be avoided (Harrison 22e p.296).
Procalcitonin testing has been ineffective and CRP testing not durable for reducing inappropriate ambulatory antibiotic use (Harrison 22e p.296).

Many popular cold remedies are ineffective, of questionable benefit, or harmful, including echinacea, zinc, inhaled steam, vitamin C, vitamin D, garlic, antihistamines, intranasal corticosteroids, saline nasal irrigation, and antiviral drugs (Harrison 22e p.296).
Cough and cold medicines should not be used in children under 6 years because of the risk of adverse effects (Harrison 22e p.296).

Nonspecific URI is self-limited. Symptoms peak early and generally resolve within 5-10 days, though some last up to 14 days. Although the cold can occasionally be complicated by otitis media or bacterial sinusitis, for any individual patient an antibiotic is more likely to cause an adverse reaction than to prevent a complication (Harrison 22e pp.296-297).

chunks.text: The endotracheal tube is the single most important risk factor for VAP. While it blocks large-volume aspiration, it worsens microaspiration of secretions that pool above the cuff, and the tube plus suctioning damages tracheal mucosa and promotes tracheal colonization. Pathogenic bacteria form a glycocalyx biofilm on the tube surface that shields them from antibiotics and host defenses; suctioning can dislodge organisms that reinoculate the trachea, and biofilm fragments can embolize to distal airways carrying bacteria. Ventilator circuit tubing can harbor organisms that wash back if manipulated, so circuits are changed only when soiled or with a new patient. In critically ill patients, normal oropharyngeal flora is replaced by pathogens, driven mainly by antibiotic selection pressure, cross-infection, severe systemic illness, and malnutrition. Severely ill patients with sepsis or trauma appear to enter a state of immunoparalysis several days after ICU admission, coinciding with peak VAP risk; the mechanism is unclear but hyperglycemia and frequent transfusions adversely affect immunity (p.1029-1030).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chap. 131 (Pneumonia) p.1029-1033 and Chap. 147 (Health Care-Associated Infections) p.1147-1148

chunks.text: Crude mortality rates for VAP are reported as high as 50-70%, but the clinically meaningful figure is attributable mortality, since many patients have underlying diseases that would be fatal regardless. Attributable mortality exceeded 25% in one matched-cohort study, while more recent estimates are lower (5-10%); VAP complicating COVID-19 has higher attributable mortality. Mortality varies with patient type and ICU; VAP in trauma patients is generally not associated with attributable mortality (these patients were often previously healthy). The causative pathogen matters: MDR pathogens carry significantly greater attributable mortality than non-MDR pathogens, and infection with organisms such as S. maltophilia mainly marks a severely immunocompromised host at high risk. Beyond death, the major complication is prolonged mechanical ventilation with longer ICU and hospital stays; long-term sequelae of necrotizing infection include bronchiectasis and parenchymal scarring with recurrent pneumonia, prolonged oxygen need, a catabolic state, and (in the elderly) loss of independent function (p.1032-1033).

chunks.text: None of the hepatitis viruses is ordinarily directly cytopathic to hepatocytes; the clinical manifestations and outcome of acute liver injury are largely determined by the host immune (chiefly cell-mediated/cytolytic T-cell) response to infected hepatocytes. In hepatitis B the existence of inactive carriers with normal histology and the more severe disease seen with defective cellular immunity support an immune-mediated mechanism; in immunocompetent adults the degree of liver injury correlates with the level of HBV replication (HBV DNA). HBV enters hepatocytes via the sodium taurocholate cotransporting polypeptide (NTCP) receptor and replicates through reverse transcription of a pregenomic RNA, forming covalently closed circular DNA in the nucleus. HDV likewise enters via NTCP but depends on HBV helper function for complete virions and liver injury (p.2643-2645, p.2651).

chunks.text: Five hepatotropic viruses cause almost all acute viral hepatitis: HAV, HBV, HCV, HDV (delta), and HEV. All are RNA viruses except HBV, which is a DNA virus that replicates via reverse transcription like a retrovirus (p.2643).

chunks.text: Hepatitis A and acute hepatitis B in previously healthy persons usually resolve completely (HBV self-limited in ~95-99% of healthy adults; HAV essentially always), with an overall case-fatality of ~0.1% (1% among hospitalized acute hepatitis B). Hepatitis A and E cause no chronic liver disease in immunocompetent hosts. Acute hepatitis C becomes chronic in ~85-90%; among chronic HCV, cirrhosis develops in up to ~20% over 10-20 years, with an annual decompensation risk ~4% and annual HCC risk ~1-4% (about 3.36%) once cirrhotic - rates declining with effective direct-acting antiviral therapy. Chronic hepatitis B carries an enhanced HCC risk, especially with infection in infancy/childhood and high HBV DNA/HBeAg; risk of cirrhosis and HCC rises with the level of HBV replication. Waterborne hepatitis E (genotypes 1 and 2) in India/Asia has a case-fatality of 1-2%, rising to 10-20% in pregnant women. Acute HBV-HDV co-infection mortality is usually similar to HBV alone (~5% in some injection-drug-user outbreaks), but HDV superinfection of chronic HBV markedly worsens outcome (annual cirrhosis rate ~4% in chronic hepatitis D; annual HCC ~3% once cirrhotic) (p.2658-2660).

Features indicating severe hepatocellular disease warranting prompt hospital admission include prolonged prothrombin time, low serum albumin, hypoglycemia, and very high serum bilirubin; presenting ascites, edema, or encephalopathy indicate a poorer prognosis. Progression to fulminant hepatitis (massive hepatic necrosis) is marked by encephalopathy with rapidly shrinking liver size, rapidly rising bilirubin, and markedly prolonged PT even as aminotransferases fall (p.2658-2659).

Coagulation profile (PT/INR) — A rising INR is the key early warning sign of evolving acute liver failure and should be tracked closely.
Mental status assessment (serial) — Screens for hepatic encephalopathy, the clinical hallmark of progression to acute liver failure requiring urgent escalation of care.

Viral meningitis is inflammation of the meninges, most often caused by enteroviruses, with a self-limited course in immunocompetent hosts. Inflammation is largely confined to the meninges, producing meningeal irritation without the parenchymal brain involvement that characterizes encephalitis; preservation of higher cerebral function distinguishes meningitis from encephalitis. CSF oligoclonal IgG bands directed against viral proteins can occur, though they are nonspecific (Harrison 22e p.1166-1167).

Profound alterations in consciousness (stupor, coma, marked confusion), seizures, focal neurologic signs, or neuroimaging evidence of parenchymal involvement do NOT occur in viral meningitis; their presence points instead to encephalitis or another CNS process (p.1166).

Consider LCMV when aseptic meningitis occurs in late fall/winter with exposure to house mice or pet/laboratory rodents or their excreta, particularly when accompanied by leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, or abnormal liver function tests (p.1169).

Headache is almost invariably present, often frontal or retroorbital, with photophobia and pain on eye movement; nuchal rigidity is usually present but may be mild, appearing only near the limit of neck anteflexion (p.1166).

A specific viral cause is identified in 60-90% of cases using combined CSF PCR, culture, and serology; roughly two-thirds of culture-negative 'aseptic' meningitis cases have a viral etiology found by CSF PCR (p.1166).
Enteroviruses account for >85% of cases with an identified etiology and predominate in summer and fall, especially in children <15 years (p.1167-1168).

HSV-2 causes most adult uncomplicated HSV meningitis (HSV-1 causes ~90% of HSV encephalitis); ~20% of HSV meningitis patients develop recurrent attacks, and most recurrent/'aseptic' meningitis, including cases formerly called Mollaret's meningitis, is due to HSV (p.1168).
Many HSV meningitis patients give no history and show no active genital herpes lesions at presentation, so absence of genital lesions does not exclude the diagnosis (p.1168).
VZV is increasingly recognized as a cause of meningitis even WITHOUT rash, so absence of chickenpox or shingles does not exclude it (p.1168).

Cranial nerve palsies (most often V, VII, or VIII) are more common in HIV meningitis than in other viral meningitides; HIV seroconversion may be delayed, so seronegative suspected cases warrant repeat testing (p.1168).

Mumps meningitis is suggested by parotitis, orchitis, oophoritis, pancreatitis, or raised serum amylase/lipase, but their absence does not exclude it; a documented prior mumps infection (lifelong immunity) does exclude it (p.1168-1169).
Failing to recognize partially or incompletely treated bacterial meningitis, which can produce a lymphocytic-predominant CSF that mimics viral meningitis (p.1167)
Up to 15% of enteroviral meningitis patients (most often young infants) have a NORMAL CSF leukocyte count, so a normal cell count does not exclude the diagnosis (p.1168)

PMNs may predominate during the first 48 h of viral meningitis (e.g., echovirus 9, WNV, EEE, mumps); WNV PMN pleocytosis occurs in ~45% and can persist a week or more before shifting to lymphocytes — do not assume early neutrophilia means bacterial infection (p.1167-1168)
Treating a normal CSF glucose as ruling out viral meningitis is wrong, but conversely low CSF glucose can occur in 10-30% of mumps or LCMV and rarely with enteroviruses, HSV-2, or VZV (p.1167)
CSF viral culture has generally poor sensitivity for viral meningitis (unlike its utility in bacterial infection), so reliance on culture alone underdiagnoses (p.1167)
Enterovirus detected in stool is NOT diagnostic of acute CNS infection — it may reflect residual shedding from a prior infection or asymptomatic carriage during epidemics (p.1167)
Enteroviral RT-PCR has low sensitivity for EV71; specific testing may be required (p.1168)
EBV CSF PCR false-positives may reflect viral reactivation or latent viral DNA in recruited lymphocytes rather than true EBV meningitis (p.1168)
Routine serology is unhelpful for high-seroprevalence viruses (HSV, VZV, CMV, EBV) (p.1167)

In adults the prognosis for full recovery from viral meningitis is excellent; treatment of almost all cases is primarily symptomatic. Rare adult patients have persisting headache, mild mental impairment, incoordination, or generalized asthenia for weeks to months. Outcome is less certain in infants and neonates (<1 year), in whom intellectual impairment, learning disabilities, hearing loss, and other lasting sequelae have been reported. Enteroviral meningitis outside the neonatal period is usually benign with recovery without sequelae, but chronic/severe infection can occur in neonates and in people with hypo- or agammaglobulinemia (Harrison 22e p.1168-1169).
Depressed or markedly altered consciousness (stupor, coma, marked confusion) — suggests encephalitis or alternative diagnosis, not simple viral meningitis (p.1166)
Seizures (p.1166)
Focal neurologic signs/symptoms or neuroimaging abnormalities indicating parenchymal brain involvement (p.1166)
CSF PMN pleocytosis without an established diagnosis — should prompt consideration of bacterial or parameningeal infection (p.1166-1167)

Lymphocytic pleocytosis WITH low CSF glucose (hypoglycorrhachia) — should raise suspicion of fungal, tuberculous, or Listeria meningoencephalitis, or noninfectious causes such as sarcoid or neoplastic meningitis (p.1167)
Atypical CSF profile or immunocompromising condition/treatment — warrants hospitalization and neuroimaging (p.1167)

Harrison does not give a formal severity grading for viral meningitis; it instead frames disposition by risk. Immunocompetent patients with a classic CSF profile (lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose, negative Gram stain), no focal signs, and no significant alteration in consciousness may not require hospitalization if home monitoring and follow-up are assured. Hospitalization is indicated for immunocompromised patients, those with significant alteration in consciousness, seizures, or focal signs suggesting encephalitis/parenchymal involvement, and those with an atypical CSF profile (Harrison 22e p.1169).

Lumbar puncture with CSF cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain, culture — The decisive test distinguishing viral from bacterial meningitis and guiding the decision to continue or stop empiric antibacterial therapy.
CSF viral PCR (enterovirus, HSV) — Identifies the specific viral cause; HSV PCR specifically changes management since HSV meningitis/encephalitis is treated with acyclovir.
Blood cultures — Performed alongside LP workup to support the broader diagnostic picture, particularly if bacterial meningitis cannot yet be excluded.

veryLikely: Enteroviruses (most common cause overall); likely: Herpes simplex virus type 2, Varicella zoster virus; possible: HIV (acute seroconversion), Mumps (in unvaccinated populations)
Acute mesenteric ischemia (SMA embolism/thrombosis) — also causes severe diffuse abdominal pain, classically pain out of proportion to exam findings (p.154).
Thoracic / thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm, which is often contiguous with infradiaphragmatic disease (p.2208).
Mycotic (infective) aortic aneurysm from staphylococcal, streptococcal, Salmonella, or fungal seeding — typically saccular and often with positive blood cultures (p.2209).
Syphilitic aortitis — uncommon cause, predominantly involves the ascending aorta/arch rather than the abdominal aorta (p.2209).
Tuberculous aneurysm — typically affects the thoracic aorta via contiguous spread from hilar nodes or abscess (p.2209).
Abdominal ultrasound — delineates transverse and longitudinal dimensions, can detect mural thrombus, and is the tool for serial size surveillance and screening (p.2211).
Plain abdominal radiograph — may show a calcified aneurysm outline, but ~25% are non-calcified and not visualized (p.2211).
Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI — accurate for location and size and for planning open or endovascular repair (p.2211).
Contrast aortography may underestimate true diameter when mural thrombus reduces luminal size, and carries risks of bleeding, allergy, and atheroembolism (p.2211).
Renal/ureteric colic — rupturing AAA pain radiating to flank or genitalia can mimic urolithiasis (p.154).
Rectus sheath hematoma — abdominal wall mass and pain, especially on anticoagulants (p.154).

Aneurysm is a pathologic dilation of the aortic wall; a true aneurysm involves all three wall layers, versus a pseudoaneurysm in which intima and media are disrupted and the dilated segment is contained only by adventitia (and sometimes perivascular clot). Most abdominal aortic aneurysms are degenerative and atherosclerotic. Wall failure results from degradation or abnormal production of the structural matrix proteins elastin and collagen, driven by inflammation, oxidative stress, proteolysis, and biomechanical wall stress. B- and T-lymphocytes, macrophages, inflammatory cytokines, and matrix metalloproteinases degrade elastin and collagen, reducing tensile strength and the aorta's ability to tolerate pulsatile stretch; histology shows elastin/collagen destruction, loss of vascular smooth muscle, neovascularization, and inflammation (p.2208).
Most abdominal aortic aneurysms are asymptomatic and are found as an incidental imaging finding or as a palpable, pulsatile, expansile, nontender mass on routine abdominal exam (p.2211).
New aneurysmal pain is usually a harbinger of rupture and constitutes a medical emergency; however, acute rupture more often occurs without any prior warning (p.2211).
Acute pain plus hypotension is the presentation of frank rupture and mandates emergency open or endovascular repair (p.2211).
At least 90% of abdominal aortic aneurysms >4.0 cm are atherosclerotic, and most lie below the level of the renal arteries (infrarenal) (p.2211).
Cigarette smoking is the most potent modifiable risk factor; incidence rises with age and the condition is more common in men (p.2211).
Mural thrombus within the aneurysm sac can be a source of peripheral (distal) embolization (p.2211).
A rupturing AAA can be misattributed to renal/ureteric colic when pain radiates to the flank or genitalia (p.154).
Plain x-ray cannot exclude an aneurysm because roughly a quarter are non-calcified (p.2211).
Aortography may underestimate aneurysm diameter when mural thrombus narrows the lumen (p.2211).
Premonitory pain may persist for several days before rupture and collapse, so an evolving symptomatic aneurysm should not be dismissed (p.154).

Prognosis depends on aneurysm size and on the severity of coexisting coronary and cerebrovascular disease. Rupture risk rises sharply with diameter: the 5-year rupture risk is roughly 1-2% for aneurysms <5 cm versus 20-40% for aneurysms >5 cm. At smaller diameters the rupture risk is higher in women than in men (p.2211-2212).
New or worsening aneurysmal pain (abdomen, lower back, chest, or scrotum) signals impending rupture (p.2211).
Abdominal pain radiating to sacrum, flank, or genitalia should always raise suspicion of a rupturing AAA (p.154).
Acute pain with hypotension indicates rupture — emergency repair required (p.2211).

Rupture-risk stratification is driven by maximal aortic diameter. Per Harrison: a true abdominal aortic aneurysm is dilation 50% greater than the adjacent normal segment; aneurysms >=4.0 cm affect 1-2% of men >50. 5-year rupture risk is ~1-2% for <5 cm and ~20-40% for >5 cm. Repair thresholds: any size if rapidly expanding or symptomatic; for asymptomatic aneurysms repair is indicated at >=5.5 cm in men and >=5.0 cm in women, with smaller aneurysms followed by ultrasound surveillance (p.2210-2212).

chunks.text: Myocardial ischemia (angina pectoris) arises from an imbalance between myocardial oxygen demand (raised by heart rate, ventricular wall stress, and contractility) and oxygen supply (set by coronary blood flow and arterial oxygen content). ACS is typically precipitated by acute coronary atherothrombosis. When ischemia is sufficiently severe and prolonged (as little as ~20 min), irreversible cellular injury and MI occur. Symptoms can also be driven predominantly by increased demand (e.g., intense psychological stress) or reduced delivery (anemia, hypoxia, hypotension), underlying the type 2 MI concept (Harrison 22e p.145).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.145-152 (Chap. 15, Chest Discomfort)

chunks.text: ACS encompasses unstable angina, NSTEMI, and STEMI, and the term is generally reserved for ischemia precipitated by acute coronary atherothrombosis (Harrison 22e p.145).

chunks.text: Unstable ischemic heart disease is sub-classified by whether acute myocardial injury is detectable and whether ST-segment elevation is present: unstable angina = no detectable acute injury; NSTEMI/STEMI = acute injury without/with ST elevation (Harrison 22e p.145).

chunks.text: Type 1 MI (acute coronary thrombosis) is distinguished from type 2 MI, which results from another imbalance of myocardial oxygen supply and demand; type 2 may be driven by anemia, hypoxia, hypotension, or intense psychological stress (Harrison 22e p.145, p.150).

chunks.text: Among unselected ED chest-pain populations, only ~10-20% (as low as 5%) are ultimately diagnosed with ACS, while gastrointestinal causes predominate; historically 2-6% of patients discharged with presumed non-ischemic pain were later found to have had a missed MI. In patients stratified as low risk (excluding ST elevation or definite noncardiac pain), the estimated 30-day major cardiovascular event rate was ~2.5%. Validated clinical decision pathways combining ECG and serial high-sensitivity troponin can achieve ACS miss rates <0.5%, and a single very low hs-troponin >2-3 h after symptom onset carries a negative predictive value >99% for MI (Harrison 22e p.145, p.150-151).

chunks.text: ACS is categorized along two clinical decision-making lines. (1) Diagnostic/disposition risk in undifferentiated chest pain uses clinical decision pathways such as the HEART score (history, ECG, age, risk factors; low risk 0-3) and EDACS, combined with serial high-sensitivity troponin, to classify patients as low/intermediate/high risk. (2) Prognostic risk in established ACS uses the TIMI and GRACE risk scores (Chap. 286) to estimate event risk - these are explicitly not intended for diagnostic use. Common high-risk elements across tools: typical ACS symptoms, older age, known/atherosclerotic risk factors, ischemic ECG changes, and elevated troponin (Harrison 22e p.151).

chunks.text: Acute leukaemia is a clonal proliferation of immature, poorly differentiated haematopoietic precursors (blasts) that infiltrate marrow, blood and other tissues; AML arises from myeloid progenitors and ALL from lymphoid (B- or T-lineage) progenitors. Genome sequencing indicates most AML arises from a small number of mutations that accumulate with age - up to 5-6% of normal people over 70 carry premalignant clones (clonal haematopoiesis of indeterminate potential, CHIP, commonly DNMT3A/TET2/ASXL1), which carries a ~10-fold increased risk of haematologic malignancy though additional 'hits' are required to progress to overt leukaemia. Genetic lesions drive both phenotype and behaviour: for example t(15;17)/PML-RARA defines APL and predisposes to DIC, while NPM1 and FLT3 mutations associate with high leukocyte counts. Marrow replacement by blasts produces anaemia, neutropenia and thrombocytopenia, accounting for the dominant clinical features (Harrison 22e p.825-828, p.844).

chunks.text: Outcome is dominated by age and genetics. In AML, cytogenetic/molecular findings at diagnosis are the strongest predictors: t(15;17)/APL has a very good prognosis (~85% cured), core-binding-factor AML (t(8;21), inv(16)) is favourable (~55% cured), normal-karyotype AML is intermediate (~40% cured), and TP53 mutation, complex karyotype, t(6;9), inv(3) or monosomy 7 are adverse with little chance of cure without transplant. NPM1 mutation without FLT3-ITD is favourable, whereas FLT3-ITD is adverse. Advancing age, poor performance status, antecedent haematologic disorder/preceding cytopenias, therapy-related disease and high presenting WBC all worsen outcome; only ~32% of AML patients survive 5 years overall. In ALL, outcome is strongly age-dependent - cure rates ~90% in children falling to <10% in elderly/frail adults; achievement of molecular complete remission (MRD negativity) is the most important on-treatment prognostic factor (Harrison 22e p.825-828, p.846-847).

Acute adrenal insufficiency reflects an absolute or relative deficiency of cortisol, in primary disease compounded by loss of aldosterone (mineralocorticoid). Glucocorticoid deficiency impairs vascular tone, gluconeogenesis and loss of feedback inhibition of AVP release (contributing to hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia), while mineralocorticoid deficiency causes renal salt wasting with volume depletion, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and rising creatinine. The result is hypotension that may decompensate into hypovolaemic shock. Crisis is usually unmasked by a stressor that exceeds the inadequate cortisol reserve — intercurrent illness, surgery or other stress, or increased glucocorticoid inactivation as in hyperthyroidism (p.3111).
Adrenal crisis typically emerges after a prolonged prodrome of nonspecific complaints rather than appearing out of the blue (p.3111).
Crisis is more frequent in PRIMARY adrenal insufficiency because both glucocorticoid AND mineralocorticoid secretion are lost (p.3111).
Postural hypotension can progress to frank hypovolaemic shock (p.3111).
Prospective data: about 8.3 adrenal crises per 100 patient-years and roughly 0.5 crisis-related deaths per 100 patient-years (p.3111).
Adrenal crisis is classified as a form of endocrine/distributive shock (p.2353).
In suspected crisis, it is reasonable to draw a baseline cortisol (and ACTH), start replacement, and defer formal stimulation testing — diagnostic testing must never delay treatment (p.3111).

Starting thyroid hormone replacement in an undiagnosed patient can precipitate adrenal crisis, because thyroid hormone shortens cortisol half-life; screen for adrenal insufficiency before treating hypothyroidism in possible polyendocrine syndrome (p.3133).
Do NOT let diagnostic testing delay treatment in suspected crisis (p.3111).

Random/baseline serum cortisol has limited diagnostic value because levels may be coincidentally low from normal diurnal rhythm, and many secondary cases have near-normal baseline cortisol that only fails on stimulation testing (p.3111).
Do NOT start thyroid hormone before excluding/treating adrenal insufficiency — it can precipitate crisis (p.3133).
Hyperthyroidism increases glucocorticoid inactivation and can trigger crisis (p.3111).
Adrenal insufficiency can be masked by concurrent primary hypothyroidism, which prolongs cortisol half-life (p.3133).
Acute adrenal insufficiency is potentially lethal (p.636). Even with established care, crises and crisis-related deaths continue to occur (~8.3 crises and ~0.5 deaths per 100 patient-years) (p.3111).

chunks.text: In prerenal states, a fall in true or effective arterial volume lowers mean arterial pressure and triggers sympathetic activation, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, and vasopressin release; GFR is sustained by prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriolar dilatation and angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction. Once mean arterial pressure falls below about 80 mmHg, GFR declines steeply. This autoregulation explains why NSAIDs (which block prostaglandin-mediated afferent dilatation) and ACE inhibitors/ARBs (which reduce efferent constriction) can precipitate hemodynamically mediated AKI when volume or perfusion pressure is already reduced, and why patients with bilateral renal artery stenosis (or stenosis of a solitary kidney) are especially susceptible to a precipitous GFR fall on ACEi/ARBs. Sustained hypoperfusion progresses to ischaemic ATN. Nephrotoxic ATN results from a combination of intrarenal vasoconstriction, direct tubular toxicity, and intratubular obstruction (p.340).

chunks.text: Anaphylaxis is driven by mediators released chiefly from mast cells, basophils, and eosinophils. The most common mechanism is allergen cross-linking of IgE bound to FcepsilonRI on mast cells and basophils, triggering degranulation. Preformed granule contents include histamine, proteases (tryptase, chymase), proteoglycans (heparin, chondroitin sulfate), and TNF-alpha; newly generated arachidonic-acid products include cysteinyl leukotrienes, prostaglandin D2, and platelet-activating factor (PAF). Histamine produces flushing, urticaria, pruritus and, at high levels, hypotension and tachycardia; cysteinyl leukotrienes and PGD2 cause bronchoconstriction and increased microvascular permeability, with PGD2 also recruiting eosinophils and basophils. Serum PAF correlates with severity and is inversely related to PAF acetylhydrolase. Tryptase and chymase activate complement (generating the anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a) and the kallikrein-kinin system, with mediator effects likely additive or synergistic. Reactions can also be non-IgE-mediated: direct mast-cell activation (e.g., via MRGPRX2 by neuromuscular blockers, quinolones, icatibant; or opiates, vancomycin, radiocontrast, NSAIDs), complement activation (e.g., Cremophor-solubilized paclitaxel), or contact-system/bradykinin generation (e.g., oversulfated chondroitin sulfate heparin contaminant). (p. 2812-2813)

chunks.text: Anemia results from a defect in any of the three requirements for normal red-cell production: renal erythropoietin (EPO) output, a functioning erythroid marrow, and adequate substrate (especially iron). EPO rises logarithmically once haemoglobin falls below ~100-120 g/L, but in chronic kidney disease and chronic inflammation EPO is inappropriately low for the degree of anemia. With adequate EPO and substrate, marrow red-cell output can rise four- to fivefold over 1-2 weeks. Mechanistically anemia is either hyperproductive/regenerative (blood loss or haemolysis, with reticulocytosis) or hypoproliferative (nutritional deficiency, marrow replacement, absent precursors, stem-cell defects, or EPO deficiency). Inflammatory cytokines such as TNF lower EPO and raise hepcidin, which blocks iron absorption and release from stores, producing the anemia of inflammation (p.443-450).
