chunks.text: Two complementary classifications. (1) By red-cell size (Wintrobe): microcytic (iron deficiency, thalassaemia, sideroblastic, anemia of inflammation), normocytic (renal disease, marrow invasion, myeloma, aplastic anemia, pure red cell aplasia, endocrinopathies), and macrocytic - subdivided into oval macrocytes (B12/folate deficiency, myelodysplasia, drugs) and round macrocytes (alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, hypoxia, reticulocytosis, smoking, dysproteinemia). (2) By mechanism: hyperproductive (blood loss, haemolysis - reticulocytes high) versus underproductive/hypoproliferative (nutritional deficiency, absent precursors, lack of EPO, marrow replacement, stem-cell defects - reticulocytes low/inappropriate). The absolute reticulocyte count plus MCV drive the diagnostic algorithm (p.448-451). For acute blood loss: vascular instability appears with sudden loss of ~25% of total blood volume, and >30% loss exceeds compensatory mechanisms (p.851).

chunks.text: ACE inhibitors block angiotensin-converting enzyme, which normally also degrades the vasodilator peptide bradykinin; inhibition leads to delayed bradykinin breakdown and accumulation, increasing vascular permeability in the deep dermis and subcutaneous/submucosal tissues and producing angioedema (pp. 2807, 2024). This is mechanistically the same bradykinin pathway implicated in hereditary angioedema, where deficient or dysfunctional C1 inhibitor (C1INH) fails to restrain activated factor XII (Hageman factor) and kallikrein, generating excess bradykinin (p. 2808). Because the mechanism is bradykinin- rather than histamine-/IgE-mediated, there is no associated urticaria or pruritus, and the process is fundamentally distinct from allergic mast-cell-driven angioedema (p. 2808). The same bradykinin-accumulation mechanism explains the increased angioedema risk seen with combined ACE/neprilysin inhibition, since neprilysin also degrades bradykinin (Ch. 265, p. 1995).

[guideline] management
Acute myocardial infarction / acute coronary syndrome (chest pain, and dissection can occlude a coronary ostium) (Harrison 22e p.2169)
Pulmonary embolism (Harrison 22e p.108)
Pericarditis (Harrison 22e p.106)
Esophageal pain / spasm, which can mimic angina (Harrison 22e p.106)
CT (with contrast) — most commonly used given proximity of scanners to emergency rooms and rapidity; sensitivity and specificity >90% for the intimal flap and extent (Harrison 22e p.2169)
MRI — highly accurate for intimal flap, extent, intramural hemorrhage and penetrating ulcers; sensitivity and specificity >90% (Harrison 22e p.2169)

Transesophageal echocardiography — ~98% sensitivity and ~90% specificity for ascending and descending dissection (but not the arch); also assesses aortic regurgitation and pericardial effusion (Harrison 22e p.2169)
Transthoracic echocardiography — rapid bedside test, overall sensitivity 60-85% (>80% for proximal ascending dissection), less useful for arch and descending aorta (Harrison 22e p.2169)
Chest x-ray — may show widened superior mediastinum and/or pleural effusion (Harrison 22e p.2169)
ECG — to look for ischemia and help differentiate from MI (Harrison 22e p.2169)
Penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer of the aorta (Harrison 22e p.2168)
Acute intramural hematoma of the aorta (Harrison 22e p.2168)
Aortic rupture (Harrison 22e p.2168)

Dissection begins with a tear of the intima, most often along the high-shear right lateral wall of the ascending aorta or in the descending thoracic aorta just below the ligamentum arteriosum. Pulsatile flow dissects along the elastic lamellar plates of the media to create a false lumen; the initiating event may be a primary intimal tear with secondary dissection into the media, or a medial hemorrhage that secondarily disrupts the intima. The dissection usually propagates distally (sometimes proximally), may be limited distally by atherosclerotic plaque, and can re-enter the true lumen through a secondary distal intimal disruption. Underlying medial degeneration and conditions that raise aortic wall stress predispose to dissection. Two related radiologic/pathologic variants are intramural hematoma (rupture of vasa vasorum bleeding into the wall, without an intimal flap) and penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer (plaque erosion into the media); both can progress to dissection and rupture (Harrison 22e p.2168-2169).
Pain characteristically migrates as the dissection propagates, often shifting to the interscapular region of the back (Harrison 22e p.2169).
Systemic hypertension coexists in about 70% of patients with aortic dissection (Harrison 22e p.2168).
Peak incidence is in the sixth and seventh decades, with men affected about twice as often as women (Harrison 22e p.2169).

A normal ECG showing no ischemia helps distinguish dissection from myocardial infarction in a patient with chest pain, though dissection can rarely involve a coronary ostium and cause an actual MI (Harrison 22e p.2169).

On chest x-ray, ascending dissection often produces a widened superior mediastinum; a pleural effusion (usually left-sided) may appear and is typically serosanguineous rather than a sign of rupture unless accompanied by hypotension and a falling hematocrit (Harrison 22e p.2169).
Although 'tearing' or 'ripping' pain is classic, acute aortic emergencies also commonly present with knifelike pain (Harrison 22e p.106).
Stanford type A or B classification is more practical for management than DeBakey, because DeBakey types I and II are managed similarly (Harrison 22e p.2168).

Aortic dissection is a classic disease that is misdiagnosed as acute myocardial infarction — a dangerous error because anticoagulant/thrombolytic therapy for presumed MI can be catastrophic (Harrison 22e p.102, p.2169).
A left pleural effusion in dissection is usually serosanguineous and does not by itself indicate rupture unless there is accompanying hypotension and a falling hematocrit (Harrison 22e p.2169).
Transthoracic echocardiography is insensitive for arch and descending dissections, so a negative TTE does not exclude dissection (Harrison 22e p.2169).

In-hospital mortality after surgical treatment of dissection is reported at about 15-25%; for medically treated uncomplicated type B dissection it is about 12%. Major perioperative causes of death and morbidity include myocardial infarction, paraplegia, renal failure, tamponade, hemorrhage, and sepsis. With careful follow-up the long-term outlook after discharge is generally good, with roughly 60% 10-year survival; patients with Marfan syndrome are at high risk for post-dissection complications (Harrison 22e p.2170).
Sudden, very severe tearing chest or interscapular back pain with diaphoresis, especially when it migrates (Harrison 22e p.2169)

New aortic regurgitation murmur (bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure, diastolic murmur along the right sternal border) in a patient with chest pain — common (>50%) in proximal dissection (Harrison 22e p.2169)
Pulse deficit or loss of pulses (Harrison 22e p.2169)
Hypotension with hemopericardium / cardiac tamponade signs (suggests retrograde type A dissection) (Harrison 22e p.2169)
Acute neurologic deficit — hemiplegia/hemianesthesia (carotid involvement) or paraplegia (spinal cord ischemia) (Harrison 22e p.2169)
Acute pulmonary edema (Harrison 22e p.2169, p.107)
Falling hematocrit with hypotension and pleural effusion (suggests rupture) (Harrison 22e p.2169)

Stanford classification: type A involves the ascending aorta (proximal dissection) regardless of tear site or distal extension; type B is limited to the arch and/or descending aorta (distal dissection). DeBakey classification: type I — intimal tear in ascending aorta with propagation to arch, descending and possibly abdominal aorta; type II — limited to the ascending aorta; type III — tear in the descending aorta with distal propagation. Stanford A/B is more practical for management since DeBakey I and II are managed similarly (Harrison 22e p.2168).

[guideline] management

Aortic sclerosis (focal leaflet thickening/calcification without obstruction; Doppler jet velocity 2.5 m/s or less) can produce a grade 2-3 midsystolic murmur acoustically identical to AS (Harrison 22e p.1908).
Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (subvalvular dynamic outflow obstruction) (Harrison 22e p.328, 1934).
Subaortic membrane (fixed subvalvular obstruction that can mimic valvular AS) (Harrison 22e p.1934).
Supravalvular aortic stenosis (exceedingly rare) (Harrison 22e p.1934).
Pulmonic stenosis (midsystolic murmur, second left interspace) (Harrison 22e p.329).
Atrial septal defect with increased pulmonic flow producing a midsystolic murmur with fixed splitting of S2 (Harrison 22e p.329).
Mitral regurgitation, given the apical Gallavardin transmission of the AS murmur (Harrison 22e p.328).

Transthoracic echocardiography to assess valve anatomy (tricuspid/bicuspid, leaflet calcification, excursion), stenosis severity, LV size/wall thickness/function, and aortic root and proximal ascending aorta (Harrison 22e p.329, 1933).
Doppler estimation of transvalvular peak velocity and pressure gradient (Harrison 22e p.1933).
Continuity-equation estimation of aortic valve area, the most accurate echo technique, especially when gradients are underestimated by LV dysfunction (Harrison 22e p.1933-1934).
Dobutamine stress echocardiography to evaluate low-flow/low-gradient AS and determine whether the valve can open further (Harrison 22e p.1934).
Cardiac MRI for quantitative assessment of severity (Harrison 22e p.1933).
Carotid pulse examination for parvus et tardus contour (Harrison 22e p.329, 1905).
Hyperdynamic flow murmurs without structural disease (fever, thyrotoxicosis, pregnancy, anemia, normal childhood/adolescence) can produce midsystolic murmurs (Harrison 22e p.1908).

Aortic stenosis is most often caused by gradual progression of valvular calcification of either normal trileaflet or congenitally bicuspid valves, producing fixed left ventricular outflow obstruction. The pressure overload drives left ventricular hypertrophy, which manifests on the ECG as LVH that increases with severity. The combination of increased myocardial oxygen demand and impaired endocardial perfusion can cause ischemia/angina even with normal coronaries. Syncope in AS reflects a structural disorder compromising cardiac output, and inappropriate reflex vasodilation may be provoked by increased ventricular contractility against the fixed obstruction (Harrison 22e p.203-204, 285, 329, 1933).

The murmur of AS is a crescendo-decrescendo (midsystolic/ejection) murmur, usually loudest in the second right intercostal space and radiating into the carotids; it is the most common midsystolic murmur in adults (Harrison 22e p.328).

Apical transmission of the AS murmur, where it becomes higher-pitched, is common (Gallavardin effect) and may be mistaken for mitral regurgitation; the AS murmur intensifies in the beat following a premature beat and varies directly with cardiac output, whereas the MR murmur stays constant beat-to-beat (Harrison 22e p.328).

Auscultatory features pointing to severe AS include a soft or absent A2, paradoxical splitting of S2, a late-peaking systolic murmur, an apical S4, and (at normal output) a systolic thrill and a grade 4 or louder murmur (Harrison 22e p.328).

An early ejection sound (click) in children/young adults signifies a flexible, noncalcified bicuspid valve and localizes obstruction to the valvular level rather than sub- or supravalvular (Harrison 22e p.328).
Bicuspid aortic valve is one of the most common congenital anomalies and predisposes to both aortic stenosis and aortic regurgitation (Harrison 22e p.1933).

AS can precipitate myocardial ischemia and anginal chest pain even without obstructive coronary atherosclerosis, by creating extreme myocardial oxygen demand with impaired endocardial blood flow (type 2 ischemia mechanism) (Harrison 22e p.285).

Heyde's syndrome is the association of aortic stenosis with bleeding gastrointestinal vascular ectasias (acquired von Willebrand disease); such patients appear to benefit from aortic valve replacement (Harrison 22e p.361).

Avoid aggressive preload/afterload reduction: aggressive treatment of cardiac failure with diuretics and/or vasodilators can precipitate orthostatic hypotension in patients with structural disease such as AS (Harrison 22e p.203).
Transvalvular pressure gradients underestimate severity in severe LV dysfunction; rely on valve area by continuity equation (Harrison 22e p.1933-1934).
In low-flow/low-gradient AS the valve may behave stenotic simply because of the low gradient; provocative dobutamine testing is needed to distinguish true severe stenosis (Harrison 22e p.1934).
The carotid parvus-et-tardus sign is less discriminatory in older patients with stiffened arteries (Harrison 22e p.329).
Aortic sclerosis can produce a murmur indistinguishable on auscultation from significant AS (Harrison 22e p.1908).

Patients with good left ventricular function can tolerate severe AS for a considerable period, so valve area or gradient alone should not dictate timing of surgery, which remains a clinical decision (Harrison 22e p.1934).
A weak and delayed carotid pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus) indicates severe AS (Harrison 22e p.329, 1905).
Soft or absent A2, paradoxical splitting of S2, late-peaking murmur, and an apical S4 indicate severe AS (Harrison 22e p.328).
A softening AS murmur in the setting of heart failure/low cardiac output is misleading and does not indicate mild disease (Harrison 22e p.328).
Syncope (including reflex/exertional) from AS reflects structural compromise of cardiac output (Harrison 22e p.203-204).

Echo: peak instantaneous velocities of 3.0 m/s or higher (often >4.0 m/s) correspond to gradients of ~36 and ~64 mmHg and indicate at least moderate AS; aortic valve area <1.0 cm2 is generally severe and <0.6 cm2 critical (Harrison 22e p.1933-1934). Catheterization: a valve area <1.0 cm2 with a mean gradient >40 mmHg indicates severe AS (Harrison 22e p.1950). Aortic sclerosis (non-obstructive) is defined by a Doppler jet velocity of 2.5 m/s or less (Harrison 22e p.1908).

chunks.text: Asthma is characterized by episodic, usually reversible airway obstruction with airway hyperresponsiveness, generally accompanied by airway inflammation (most often eosinophilic, sometimes neutrophilic, occasionally with no obvious inflammation). Exacerbations are episodes of acute bronchospasm driven by luminal narrowing from airway smooth-muscle constriction, airway edema and mucus secretion, superimposed on chronic airway inflammation. Triggers activate mast cells/basophils and inflammatory cells (releasing bronchoconstrictors and mediators) and stimulate sensory nerves acting on smooth muscle. Allergen exposure can cause an immediate (early) bronchospasm and a late response 2-24 h later with airway narrowing and inflammation. Structural airway-wall thickening (smooth-muscle hypertrophy/hyperplasia, subepithelial collagen deposition, edema, mucosal inflammation) increases the tendency to narrow disproportionately. In severe airflow obstruction there may be air trapping with dynamically elevated FRC and increased residual volume; mild hypoxemia from ventilation-perfusion mismatch (oxygen-responsive) is common (p.2216-2217, p.2221, p.2222-2223).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chapter 298 (Asthma, Israel), p.2215-2228

chunks.text: An exacerbation is an episode of acute bronchospasm that may be severe enough to require emergency care or hospitalization and can be fatal (p.2216).

chunks.text: Asthma causes significant morbidity and mortality; roughly 3000-4000 people die from asthma each year in the United States. Death can occur even in mild asthma (at lower rates than severe asthma). Mortality in patients over 65 is about five times that of younger cohorts. High-risk features for asthma death (Table 298-6) include prior ICU admission or intubation for asthma, illicit drug use, depression, a new diagnosis within the past year, two or more emergency visits in the past 6 months, severe psychosocial problems, lower socioeconomic status, and being on daily prednisone before admission. Severe exacerbations may accelerate long-term lung-function decline (p.2221, p.2227).

chunks.text: Harrison stratifies acute deteriorations practically rather than by a fixed table. Mild-to-moderate deteriorations can initially be managed with frequent beta2-agonists; failure to control with hourly beta2-agonists for several hours warrants urgent care. In urgent/ED care, PEFR or FEV1 guides severity: PEFR >60% predicted usually responds to beta2-agonists alone, whereas failure to reach PEFR >60% or persistent severe tachypnea over 4-6 h indicates a severe attack needing admission. Life-threatening / near-fatal features include silent chest, respiratory exhaustion, and a normal or rising PaCO2 signaling impending respiratory failure; status asthmaticus denotes a severe refractory attack with high airway resistance making ventilation difficult (p.2227).

[guideline] management
Multifocal atrial tachycardia (>=3 distinct P-wave morphologies with clear isoelectric intervals and a slower atrial rate than AF; typically in chronic pulmonary disease and acute illness) (p.1989).

Other supraventricular tachycardias including atrial flutter, focal atrial tachycardia, AV nodal reentry, and AV reciprocating tachycardia, distinguished by 12-lead ECG appearance and response to AV nodal blockade (p.1976-1977).
Preexcited (accessory-pathway) AF, presenting as an irregular wide-complex tachycardia with bizarre, beat-to-beat-variable QRS morphology (p.1985-1986).
Transesophageal echocardiography to exclude left atrial appendage thrombus before cardioversion when AF duration is >48 h or unknown (p.1992).
Cardiac CT angiography with delayed-acquisition imaging as an alternative to TEE for left atrial appendage thrombus detection, with high sensitivity and specificity (p.1992).
Ambulatory ECG monitoring, implantable loop recorders, or wearable/home ECG devices to capture intermittent or subclinical episodes (p.1991, 1993).

AF is characterized by disorganized, rapid, irregular atrial electrical activation with loss of organized atrial mechanical contraction; the AV node filters these impulses to produce an irregular ventricular rate. The pathophysiology is multifactorial and incompletely understood, with a proposed 'final common pathway' in which risk factors (age, cardiovascular disease, hypertension, diabetes, obesity, alcohol, sleep-disordered breathing) drive electrophysiologic changes in atrial tissue. Altered membrane channel regulation produces abnormal excitability; pulmonary vein musculature (and other foci such as the posterior left atrial wall, superior vena cava, coronary sinus, vein of Marshall) shows enhanced automaticity generating ectopic beats that initiate AF. Progressive cellular and tissue remodeling shortens atrial refractory periods and creates functional reentry, with eventual fibrosis and left atrial enlargement, explaining the typical progression from paroxysmal to persistent to long-standing persistent disease. Loss of atrial systole reduces cardiac output, and variable ventricular filling produces variable stroke volume (p.1990-1992).
AF is the most common sustained arrhythmia; prevalence rises steeply with age (~20% of those over 80), and the lifetime risk for a 40-year-old man is roughly one in four (p.1990).
On the ECG, AF shows absence of organized atrial activity (no P waves) with an irregularly irregular ventricular response; the chaotic atrial activity is often best seen in lead V1 (p.1990, 1991).

The conducted ventricular rate is variable and usually rapid (commonly 110-160/min), but may exceed 200/min, or be inappropriately slow when there is high vagal tone or AV nodal conduction disease (p.1990).
Many patients are unaware of the irregular heartbeat, so AF is frequently asymptomatic; absence of AF on intermittent monitoring does not establish low risk (p.1990, 1993).

AF is categorized by temporal pattern: paroxysmal (self-terminating, usually within 7 days), persistent (continuous >7 days but <1 year), and long-standing persistent (>1 year); these patterns correlate with progressive left atrial enlargement and scar burden (p.1990, 1991).

Stroke and bleeding risks are estimated as concepts using the CHA2DS2-VASc score (stroke risk: congestive heart failure, hypertension, age, diabetes, prior stroke/TIA, vascular disease, sex) and HAS-BLED score (bleeding risk), respectively (p.1993).

AF burden does not predict stroke risk; the approach to paroxysmal AF is the same as for persistent AF, and even apparently infrequent episodes carry risk because asymptomatic episodes are common (p.1993).
Subclinical AF detectable only on long-term continuous monitoring is associated with roughly 2.5-fold increased stroke risk (p.1993).
AF detected after cryptogenic stroke using insertable cardiac monitors in up to ~8.9% of patients within 6 months, supporting prolonged rhythm monitoring in this setting (p.1990).
Relying on AF burden or symptom frequency to gauge stroke risk is mistaken; anticoagulation decisions should rest on the risk-factor profile, not how often AF is documented (p.1993).
A normal intermittent monitor does not exclude clinically important AF, since asymptomatic episodes are common (p.1993).

Cardioverting AF of >48 h (or unknown) duration without anticoagulation or thrombus exclusion risks thromboembolism, which can occur even days later because of post-conversion atrial stunning (delayed recovery of mechanical function) (p.1992).
Nonvalvular AF (AF without mitral stenosis) differs in management from valvular AF; rheumatic mitral stenosis and mechanical valves carry especially high thromboembolic risk (p.1993).

AF is not benign: it carries a 1.5- to 1.9-fold increased mortality after adjusting for underlying cardiac disease, and causes approximately 25% of all strokes. It increases the risk of dementia, MRI-detected silent embolic infarcts, congestive heart failure, and cardiomyopathy. Tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy is generally reversible once ventricular rate is controlled. AF tends to be progressive, with no definitive durable cure, and patients maintaining sinus rhythm generally have better survival than those who remain in AF (p.1990, 1992, 1994).
Acute AF with significant haemodynamic compromise, pulmonary oedema, or evidence of coronary ischaemia indicates need for emergent cardioversion (p.1992).

Preexcited AF over an accessory pathway with very rapid repetitive conduction (minimum R-R <250 ms occurs in ~25% of preexciting pathways) is potentially life-threatening, predisposing to ventricular fibrillation and sudden death (p.1985-1986).
Syncope or presyncope from bradycardia/pauses, including offset pauses on spontaneous conversion to sinus rhythm, suggesting coexisting sinus node dysfunction (tachy-brady syndrome) (p.1992).
Sustained uncontrolled rapid ventricular rates risk precipitating heart failure and tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy (p.1990, 1992).

By temporal pattern (Table 258-1): paroxysmal AF (self-terminates or is cardioverted within 7 days; normal-to-mildly enlarged left atrium, low scar burden), persistent AF (continuous >7 days but <1 year; mild-to-severe LA enlargement, moderate scar), and long-standing persistent AF (>1 year; severely enlarged LA, high scar burden). A newer staged framework (at risk of AF, pre-AF, AF, permanent AF) reframes AF as a disease continuum. Mitral stenosis defines valvular versus nonvalvular AF for risk purposes (p.1991, 1993, 1996).

chunks.text: Biliary colic results from transient obstruction of the cystic duct (or common bile duct) by a gallstone migrating out of the gallbladder. The obstruction raises intraluminal pressure and distends the viscus; because repetitive biliary contractions cannot overcome or relieve the blockage, a steady visceral pain is generated. When the stone disimpacts or falls back, pressure normalizes and the pain resolves spontaneously, so an uncomplicated episode is self-limited and is NOT accompanied by inflammation, fever, or sustained cholestasis. Underlying stones are usually cholesterol stones (>90% in Western populations), which form when bile becomes supersaturated with cholesterol, cholesterol monohydrate crystals nucleate, and gallbladder hypomotility allows stasis and stone growth; gallbladder emptying is frequently impaired in stone formers. Distinct mechanisms (mechanical, chemical from lysolecithin, and bacterial) convert simple obstruction into acute cholecystitis when the cystic duct stays blocked (p.2727-2732).

chunks.text: Uncomplicated biliary colic is self-limited; the individual attack resolves once the transient obstruction clears. The natural history of the underlying gallstones is generally favorable: 60-80% of asymptomatic stone carriers stay symptom-free for up to 25 years, the chance of developing symptoms is only ~2-4% per year in the first 5 years after diagnosis (falling to 1-2% thereafter), and the yearly incidence of complications is only ~0.1-0.3%. The cumulative risk of death from gallstone disease under expectant management is small. However, once biliary pain has occurred, the likelihood of recurrent attacks and of complications requiring intervention rises substantially; younger patients at diagnosis are more likely to become symptomatic than those over 60 (p.2731).

chunks.text: Mechanical obstruction of a hollow viscus classically elicits intermittent (colicky) pain that is less well localized than the parietal pain of peritoneal irritation; distension of the viscus may also produce steady pain with only occasional paroxysms. With superimposed strangulating obstruction, traction on the root of the mesentery can refer pain to the lower lumbar region. As the obstructed proximal bowel progressively dilates it loses muscular tone, so colicky pain may wane and peristaltic sounds may weaken. Obstruction must be distinguished from adynamic ileus (loss of peristalsis) and from colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie's syndrome), in which the bowel is dilated without a mechanical lesion (Harrison 22e pp.110-113, p.327).

[guideline] management

Metastatic brain tumour - three times more common than all primary brain tumours combined in adults; commonest sources lung and breast, with melanoma having the greatest propensity to metastasize to brain (p.716, p.723)
Diffuse glioma - the most common malignant PRIMARY brain tumour; subdivided into IDH-mutant astrocytoma, IDH-mutant 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendroglioma, and IDH wild-type glioblastoma (p.717-718)
Meningioma - now the most common primary brain tumour overall (~35%); extra-axial dural-based lesion, WHO grades I-III (p.720-721)
Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) - ~9% of primary brain tumours, presents with progressive unilateral hearing loss/tinnitus/dizziness (p.721)
Primary CNS lymphoma - densely enhancing, often periventricular/basal ganglia/corpus callosum; associated with immunosuppression and EBV in HIV (p.720)
Pituitary adenoma - amenorrhoea/galactorrhoea with headache suggests a prolactinoma (p.157, p.721)
Pineal-region tumour presenting with Parinaud's syndrome and hydrocephalus (p.720)
Colloid cyst of the third ventricle - intermittent hydrocephalus, rarely sudden death (p.722)
Brain abscess - shares a ring-enhancing radiographic appearance with metastasis and high-grade glioma (p.723)
Cerebral toxoplasmosis - in immunocompromised patients, multiple ring-enhancing lesions can be hard to distinguish from PCNSL or metastases (p.721)
MRI with gadolinium is the preferred test; CT only if MRI cannot be done (p.716)
Neuroimaging is often the only test needed to diagnose a brain tumour; laboratory tests are rarely useful (p.716)
FLAIR sequences to detect non-enhancing low-grade gliomas (p.716, p.718)
Functional MRI for presurgical mapping of eloquent cortex (p.716)
PET, MR perfusion and MR spectroscopy to assess metabolic activity and help separate tumour progression from radiation/treatment necrosis (p.716)
CSF cytology / flow cytometry when leptomeningeal involvement is suspected (gold standard but positive in only ~50% on first LP, still misses ~10% after three samples) (p.720, p.724)

Stereotactic biopsy for histologic diagnosis when imaging is insufficient; in suspected PCNSL withhold glucocorticoids until biopsy because they are cytolytic and can render tissue non-diagnostic (p.720)
HIV testing and body PET/CT, spine MRI, CSF and slit-lamp eye exam to stage suspected PCNSL (p.720-721)
Serum tumour markers (e.g. beta-hCG) occasionally elevated in metastatic disease (p.716)
Demyelinating lesion - can mimic the nonspecific appearance of a brain metastasis (p.723)
Neurosarcoidosis - listed among lesions resembling metastatic disease on imaging (p.723)
Radiation necrosis in a previously irradiated patient - mimics tumour and may need PET/MR perfusion to distinguish recurrence from treatment effect (p.716, p.723)

General/raised-ICP symptoms arise as the enlarging tumour plus surrounding vasogenic edema raises intracranial pressure or obstructs CSF circulation, producing hydrocephalus; focal deficits reflect local invasion or compression (p.716). Primary tumours develop through stepwise acquisition of genetic changes - loss of tumour-suppressor genes (p53, CDKN2A/B, PTEN) and amplification/overexpression of oncogenes such as EGFR and PDGFR - and glioblastomas in particular show marked molecular heterogeneity (p.717). The 2021 WHO CNS classification integrates molecular markers (e.g. IDH mutation, 1p/19q co-deletion) with histology into the diagnosis (p.717-718). Brain metastases spread hematogenously, lodging in terminal arterioles at the grey-white junction in watershed territory, so distribution follows blood flow (~85% supratentorial, ~15% posterior fossa) (p.723).

Presenting features split into general (raised-ICP) symptoms - headache +/- nausea/vomiting, cognitive change, personality change, gait disorder - and focal/lateralizing signs such as hemiparesis, aphasia or visual field loss; many patients have both (p.716).

The classic morning-predominant headache that eases through the day occurs in only a minority of patients; brain-tumour headache is more often a nondescript dull ache, and migraine produces this pattern far more often than tumour (p.716, p.157).
Vomiting preceding headache by weeks is highly characteristic of posterior fossa tumours, and headache disturbs sleep in about 10% (p.157).
Seizures from a brain tumour always have a focal onset whether or not this is clinically apparent (p.716).
New de novo headache in a patient with known malignancy should raise suspicion of cerebral metastases or carcinomatous (leptomeningeal) meningitis (p.157).

On MRI, malignant tumours (primary or metastatic) typically enhance with gadolinium, have central necrosis and surrounding white-matter edema, whereas low-grade gliomas usually do NOT enhance and are best seen as increased signal on FLAIR (p.716).
Meningiomas and vestibular schwannomas are extra-axial, densely enhancing lesions; a meningioma characteristically shows a dural tail and compresses but does not invade brain (p.716, p.721).

Leptomeningeal disease produces multilevel neuraxis signs (radiculopathies, cranial neuropathies, seizures, confusion, raised-ICP encephalopathy); isolated focal deficits like hemiparesis are rarely from it unless brain is directly infiltrated (p.724).
Parinaud's syndrome (impaired upgaze and accommodation) points to a pineal-region mass (p.720).

A ring-enhancing lesion is non-specific - the differential includes brain abscess, toxoplasmosis, PCNSL, demyelination, sarcoidosis, radiation necrosis and primary brain tumour, so do not assume tumour without context (p.721, p.723).

Withholding the diagnosis of glioma can be hard for diffusely infiltrative non-enhancing tumours (formerly gliomatosis cerebri), which often present only with cognitive decline and confluent FLAIR signal without mass effect (p.718).
Do not give glucocorticoids before biopsy in suspected PCNSL - their cytolytic effect can yield non-diagnostic tissue (p.720).
Prophylactic antiepileptic drugs have no role in tumour patients who have not had a seizure (only perioperative use is sometimes appropriate) (p.716).
A normal or migrainous headache pattern is far more often migraine than tumour - tumour headache is frequently nondescript (p.157).
Imaging-negative leptomeningeal disease is common; a single negative CSF cytology does not exclude it (positive in only ~50% on first LP) (p.724).

Outcome is tumour-specific. Low-grade (grade 2) IDH-mutant astrocytoma usually transforms to higher grade with median survival around 10 years; high-grade IDH-mutant astrocytoma roughly 3-9 years (p.718). Oligodendrogliomas (IDH-mutant, 1p/19q co-deleted) are more therapy-responsive with median survival in excess of 10 years (p.718). Glioblastoma (IDH wild-type) is the most common malignant primary tumour and invariably recurs; with standard combined therapy median survival is ~15-18 months and 5-year survival ~10%; adverse factors include older age, unmethylated MGMT promoter, poor performance status and unresectable tumour (p.718-719). Diffuse midline glioma H3K27-altered carries a poor prognosis (~1 year) regardless of grade (p.719). Pilocytic astrocytoma (grade 1) and completely resected meningiomas/ependymomas can be cured (p.719-721). Brain metastases treated with WBRT have median survival of only ~4-6 months, though SRS achieves local control in 80-90% and occasional cure (p.724).
Progressive, subacute focal/lateralizing deficit (hemiparesis, aphasia, visual field loss) (p.716)
New-onset focal-onset seizures (p.716)
Morning-predominant headache or headache with raised-ICP features (nausea/vomiting, worse with exertion or position change) (p.716, p.157)
Vomiting preceding headache by weeks - suggests a posterior fossa mass (p.157)
New de novo headache in a patient with known systemic cancer (p.157)
Personality change/apathy that may be mistaken for depression (p.716)

WHO CNS grading (2021 integrated histologic + molecular classification): diffuse gliomas graded 2-4 by histologic malignancy and molecular markers, with CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion conferring grade 4 to otherwise lower-grade IDH-mutant astrocytomas; pilocytic astrocytoma is grade 1. Meningiomas are graded I (benign), II (atypical) and III (malignant) by increasing aggressiveness (p.717-718, p.720-721).

chunks.text: A profound fall in myocardial contractility initiates a self-perpetuating spiral: reduced cardiac output and stroke volume lower blood pressure and coronary perfusion, worsening ischaemia and further depressing contractility, which left untreated leads to death. Ineffective stroke volume is the inciting event, but inadequate circulatory compensation also contributes. Early peripheral vasoconstriction may transiently improve coronary and peripheral perfusion but raises afterload and can worsen ischaemia. Over time, systemic inflammation from acute cardiac injury induces pathologic vasodilatation; inflammatory cytokines and inducible/endothelial nitric oxide synthase increase NO and its by-product peroxynitrite, which are negatively inotropic and cardiotoxic. Lactic acidosis and hypoxaemia compound the cycle because severe acidosis blunts the efficacy of endogenous and exogenous catecholamines. Bleeding and transfusion during ICU care can further trigger inflammation. Left-ventricular failure accounts for roughly 80% of cardiogenic shock complicating acute MI, with acute severe mitral regurgitation, ventricular septal rupture, predominant RV failure, and free-wall rupture/tamponade making up the remainder (p.2325).

chunks.text: In-hospital mortality ranges from roughly 40-60% depending on shock severity and underlying cause; cardiogenic and septic shock carry the highest mortality among shock types (90-day mortality around 52% for cardiogenic shock in one ED cohort). Untreated shock progresses through compensated (preshock), decompensated, and finally irreversible stages with permanent organ dysfunction and multi-organ failure. Reperfusion and modern care have reduced the incidence of shock complicating acute MI to about 5-10% (p.2311, p.2325).

chunks.text: CKD results from two overlapping processes: (1) initiating mechanisms specific to the underlying cause (developmental/genetic, immune-complex, inflammatory, metabolic, microvascular, or toxic injury to vascular, glomerular, or tubulointerstitial compartments), and (2) a nonspecific final common pathway in which loss of nephron mass triggers compensatory hyperfiltration and hypertrophy of remaining nephrons. Intrarenal renin-angiotensin activation with blunted tubuloglomerular feedback raises intraglomerular pressure; this adaptation becomes maladaptive, distorting glomerular architecture, impairing podocyte function and the filtration barrier, and producing progressive sclerosis and nephron dropout. The uremic syndrome arises from three spheres of dysfunction: accumulation of retained solutes (urea and creatinine are only readily-measured but incomplete surrogates for many retained toxins), loss of non-excretory kidney functions (fluid/electrolyte homeostasis, hormone production/regulation - EPO, calcitriol, with altered PTH, FGF-23, insulin), and progressive systemic inflammation (elevated CRP, falling albumin/fetuin) feeding a malnutrition-inflammation-atherosclerosis/calcification syndrome (p.2385-2389).

Harrison Table 319-3 stages (abnormality >3 months): Stage 1 (>60 with abnormal urinalysis/imaging), Stage 2 (>60, mild progression risk), Stage 3a (45-60), Stage 3b (30-45), Stage 4 (15-30, prepare for RRT), Stage 5 (<15, highest RRT need). chunks.text: A range of stimuli converge on a final common pathway of airway inflammation and worsening respiratory symptoms. The underlying COPD substrate is fixed airflow obstruction (chronically reduced, non-normalizing FEV1/FVC) compounded by hyperinflation and air trapping; a flattened diaphragm becomes mechanically disadvantaged, raising the work of breathing during any acute decompensation. Gas exchange is impaired chiefly by ventilation-perfusion mismatching (shunt is minimal), which explains why modest supplemental oxygen usually corrects COPD hypoxemia. Hypoxemia tends not to appear until FEV1 falls below ~50% predicted, and CO2 retention is not expected until FEV1 is below ~25% predicted. Acutely, worsening obstruction and dynamic hyperinflation can precipitate alveolar hypoventilation with rising arterial CO2 and respiratory acidosis (p.2251-2252, p.2255, p.2258).

source.page: 2249-2259 (Chapter 303, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease); 1756 (Aspergillus/COPD exacerbation note)

chunks.text: An exacerbation is an episodic acute worsening of respiratory symptoms (increased dyspnea, cough, and/or change in sputum amount or character), typically evolving over less than 14 days; it may or may not be accompanied by fever, myalgias, or sore throat (p.2258).

source.page: 2249-2259 (Chapter 303, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease); 1756 (Aspergillus/COPD exacerbation note)

chunks.text: Cor pulmonale (overt right heart failure) is now relatively uncommon since supplemental oxygen became standard, but pulmonary hypertension should be considered in patients with persistent activity limitation or lower-extremity edema; it typically arises with FEV1 <25% predicted and chronic hypoxemia (Pao2 <55 mmHg), though some develop it from vascular destruction independent of obstruction severity (p.2252, p.2254).

source.page: 2249-2259 (Chapter 303, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease); 1756 (Aspergillus/COPD exacerbation note)

chunks.text: COPD exacerbation is fundamentally a clinical diagnosis; spirometry/pulmonary function testing has not been shown to help diagnose or manage an exacerbation, in contrast to its role in asthma (p.2259).

source.page: 2249-2259 (Chapter 303, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease); 1756 (Aspergillus/COPD exacerbation note)

chunks.text: The single strongest predictor of future exacerbations is a prior exacerbation, and the greatest single risk factor for hospitalization is a previous hospitalization for exacerbation (p.2258).

source.page: 2249-2259 (Chapter 303, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease); 1756 (Aspergillus/COPD exacerbation note)

chunks.text: Exacerbation frequency rises as airflow obstruction worsens; patients with severe obstruction (FEV1 <50% predicted) average about 1-3 episodes per year, though some severely obstructed patients exacerbate infrequently (p.2258).

source.page: 2249-2259 (Chapter 303, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease); 1756 (Aspergillus/COPD exacerbation note)

chunks.text: Assess both the severity of the current exacerbation and the severity of the underlying COPD, because the more severe either component, the greater the likelihood of needing hospital admission (p.2258).

source.page: 2249-2259 (Chapter 303, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease); 1756 (Aspergillus/COPD exacerbation note)

chunks.text: Examination should focus on degree of distress, tachycardia, tachypnea, accessory muscle use, cyanosis, ability to speak in full sentences, mental status, and paradoxical abdominal wall motion (p.2258).

source.page: 2249-2259 (Chapter 303, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease); 1756 (Aspergillus/COPD exacerbation note)

chunks.text: Blood eosinophil count (from CBC differential) is used to stratify exacerbation risk and to guide whether inhaled corticosteroids are added; counts below 100 cells/microliter derive no benefit while benefit rises above 100 and is favored above 300 (p.2255, p.2256).

source.page: 2249-2259 (Chapter 303, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease); 1756 (Aspergillus/COPD exacerbation note)

chunks.text: Non-infective precipitants are well recognized: air pollution (including extreme-heat days), allergens, pulmonary embolism, and medication nonadherence; in a notable minority no precipitant is identified (p.2253, p.2258).

source.page: 2249-2259 (Chapter 303, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease); 1756 (Aspergillus/COPD exacerbation note)

chunks.text: Environmental exposure and Aspergillus sensitization can drive some COPD exacerbations, relevant to the eosinophilic/allergic exacerbation phenotype (p.1756).

source.page: 2249-2259 (Chapter 303, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease); 1756 (Aspergillus/COPD exacerbation note)

chunks.text: Withholding needed supplemental oxygen for fear of CO2 retention: oxygen targeted to SpO2 88-92% is appropriate, and although it may modestly raise arterial Pco2 in some hypercarbic patients by altering ventilation-perfusion relationships, this should not deter correction of hypoxemia (p.2259).

source.page: 2249-2259 (Chapter 303, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease); 1756 (Aspergillus/COPD exacerbation note)

chunks.text: Relying on spirometry to diagnose or manage an acute exacerbation, which is not supported by evidence (unlike in asthma) (p.2259).

source.page: 2249-2259 (Chapter 303, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease); 1756 (Aspergillus/COPD exacerbation note)

chunks.text: Overlooking pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, pneumonia, or heart failure, since each can mimic or accompany an exacerbation (p.2258, p.2259).

source.page: 2249-2259 (Chapter 303, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease); 1756 (Aspergillus/COPD exacerbation note)

chunks.text: Attributing all exacerbations to bacterial infection: PCR-based studies show viral respiratory infections may cause more than 50% of exacerbations, and in a notable minority no specific precipitant is identifiable (p.2258).

source.page: 2249-2259 (Chapter 303, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease); 1756 (Aspergillus/COPD exacerbation note)

chunks.text: Mechanical ventilatory support for a COPD exacerbation carries a hospital mortality of roughly 17-49%. After a hospitalization for COPD, about 20% of patients are rehospitalized within 30 days and 45% within a year, with mortality around 20% in the year following discharge. Exacerbations are also associated with greater longitudinal loss of lung function (notably in those with better baseline function) and account for the majority of COPD-related health-care expenditure (p.2253, p.2259).

source.page: 2249-2259 (Chapter 303, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease); 1756 (Aspergillus/COPD exacerbation note)

chunks.text: Respiratory acidosis with hypercarbia (Paco2 >45 mmHg and pH <=7.35) indicating acute respiratory failure and a need for ventilatory support (p.2255, p.2259)

source.page: 2249-2259 (Chapter 303, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease); 1756 (Aspergillus/COPD exacerbation note)

chunks.text: New or worsening hypoxemia (p.2259)

source.page: 2249-2259 (Chapter 303, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease); 1756 (Aspergillus/COPD exacerbation note)

chunks.text: Mental status change (confusion, sleepiness), inability to speak in complete sentences, or impaired cooperation (p.2258, p.2259)

source.page: 2249-2259 (Chapter 303, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease); 1756 (Aspergillus/COPD exacerbation note)

chunks.text: Paradoxical abdominal wall motion, marked accessory muscle use, and central cyanosis signaling impending respiratory failure (p.2258)

source.page: 2249-2259 (Chapter 303, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease); 1756 (Aspergillus/COPD exacerbation note)

chunks.text: Significant comorbidity such as heart failure, or an unsafe living situation, favoring inpatient management (p.2259)

source.page: 2249-2259 (Chapter 303, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease); 1756 (Aspergillus/COPD exacerbation note)

chunks.text: New digital clubbing is NOT a feature of COPD itself and should prompt a search for another cause such as lung cancer (p.2254)

source.page: 2249-2259 (Chapter 303, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease); 1756 (Aspergillus/COPD exacerbation note)

chunks.text: Underlying COPD severity is graded by post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.7 plus FEV1 % predicted: GOLD 1 (mild) >=80%, GOLD 2 (moderate) 50-79%, GOLD 3 (severe) 30-49%, GOLD 4 (very severe) <30%. The GOLD ABE assessment further classifies patients using symptom burden (mMRC dyspnea scale or CAT score) and annual exacerbation history: groups A and B for those with 0-1 moderate exacerbations not leading to hospitalization (A = mMRC 0-1/CAT <10, B = mMRC >=2/CAT >=10), and group E for those with >=2 moderate exacerbations or >=1 leading to hospitalization. The ATS/ERS alternative grades obstruction by FEV1 z-scores rather than percent predicted. For an acute exacerbation, severity itself is a clinical determination; an expert-consensus scheme stages it using dyspnea, vital signs, CRP, and arterial blood gases (p.2255, p.2256, p.2259).

source.page: 2249-2259 (Chapter 303, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease); 1756 (Aspergillus/COPD exacerbation note)

Intradural extramedullary tumours (meningioma, neurofibroma/schwannoma) - usually slow-growing and benign; long symptom duration favours an intradural origin (p.3606)

chunks.text: Because the cord packs nearly the entire motor output and sensory input of the trunk and limbs into a small cross-section, even a small compressive mass causes disproportionately severe, often reversible-if-treated-early, deficits (p.3559). In neoplastic compression, metastases lodge in the vertebral body or pedicle (the axial skeleton is rich in marrow); the enlarging deposit compresses the underlying dura, or a paravertebral mass (lymphoma, myeloma, paediatric tumours) extends through the intervertebral foramen into the canal. Expanding extradural tumour injures axons and myelin mechanically and compromises blood flow, producing ischaemia and infarction (pp.589, 3563). In spinal epidural abscess, as the collection expands it causes additional cord damage through venous congestion and thrombosis, so that once weakness appears deterioration can be rapid and irreversible (p.3606). The thoracic spine is the commonest site of metastatic compression (~70%), followed by lumbosacral (~20%) and cervical (~10%) (p.631).

source.page: Harrison 22e: Ch. 453 Diseases of the Spinal Cord pp.3602-3607; Ch. 80 Oncologic Emergencies (MSCC) pp.631-633; Ch. 95 Epidural Metastasis pp.767-768; Ch. 19 Neck Pain pp.173-175; Ch. 26 Acute Paraparesis p.213; Ch. 136 Vertebral Osteomyelitis / Spinal Epidural Abscess p.1105

chunks.text: A horizontally demarcated sensory level (identified by moving a pinprick or cold stimulus up the trunk) below which sensory, motor and autonomic function is impaired is the hallmark of a cord lesion; for the spinothalamic tract the true level may sit one to two segments above the clinically detected level (p.3603).

source.page: Harrison 22e: Ch. 453 Diseases of the Spinal Cord pp.3602-3607; Ch. 80 Oncologic Emergencies (MSCC) pp.631-633; Ch. 95 Epidural Metastasis pp.767-768; Ch. 19 Neck Pain pp.173-175; Ch. 26 Acute Paraparesis p.213; Ch. 136 Vertebral Osteomyelitis / Spinal Epidural Abscess p.1105

chunks.text: The upper border of sensory loss often lies one or two vertebrae BELOW the actual site of compression, so the radiographic target may be higher than the clinical level suggests (p.631).

source.page: Harrison 22e: Ch. 453 Diseases of the Spinal Cord pp.3602-3607; Ch. 80 Oncologic Emergencies (MSCC) pp.631-633; Ch. 95 Epidural Metastasis pp.767-768; Ch. 19 Neck Pain pp.173-175; Ch. 26 Acute Paraparesis p.213; Ch. 136 Vertebral Osteomyelitis / Spinal Epidural Abscess p.1105

chunks.text: Pain is usually the first symptom of metastatic compression and can precede neurological signs by days to months; it characteristically worsens when supine/recumbent and at night, helping distinguish it from degenerative disk pain which is often relieved by lying down (pp.631, 768, 3605).

source.page: Harrison 22e: Ch. 453 Diseases of the Spinal Cord pp.3602-3607; Ch. 80 Oncologic Emergencies (MSCC) pp.631-633; Ch. 95 Epidural Metastasis pp.767-768; Ch. 19 Neck Pain pp.173-175; Ch. 26 Acute Paraparesis p.213; Ch. 136 Vertebral Osteomyelitis / Spinal Epidural Abscess p.1105

chunks.text: Lhermitte's sign (an electric tingling shooting down the back and limbs on neck flexion/extension) can be an EARLY clue to cervical cord compression (p.631).

source.page: Harrison 22e: Ch. 453 Diseases of the Spinal Cord pp.3602-3607; Ch. 80 Oncologic Emergencies (MSCC) pp.631-633; Ch. 95 Epidural Metastasis pp.767-768; Ch. 19 Neck Pain pp.173-175; Ch. 26 Acute Paraparesis p.213; Ch. 136 Vertebral Osteomyelitis / Spinal Epidural Abscess p.1105

chunks.text: Loss of bowel/bladder control is usually a LATE feature; motor and sensory loss typically precede sphincter disturbance (p.631).

source.page: Harrison 22e: Ch. 453 Diseases of the Spinal Cord pp.3602-3607; Ch. 80 Oncologic Emergencies (MSCC) pp.631-633; Ch. 95 Epidural Metastasis pp.767-768; Ch. 19 Neck Pain pp.173-175; Ch. 26 Acute Paraparesis p.213; Ch. 136 Vertebral Osteomyelitis / Spinal Epidural Abscess p.1105

chunks.text: Useful trunk sensory landmarks for localising a thoracic level are the nipples (T4) and umbilicus (T10) (p.3604).

source.page: Harrison 22e: Ch. 453 Diseases of the Spinal Cord pp.3602-3607; Ch. 80 Oncologic Emergencies (MSCC) pp.631-633; Ch. 95 Epidural Metastasis pp.767-768; Ch. 19 Neck Pain pp.173-175; Ch. 26 Acute Paraparesis p.213; Ch. 136 Vertebral Osteomyelitis / Spinal Epidural Abscess p.1105

chunks.text: Spinal column infection (osteomyelitis/abscess) characteristically crosses the disk space to involve the adjacent vertebral body, whereas tumour tends to respect the disk space - a distinguishing imaging feature (p.3605).

source.page: Harrison 22e: Ch. 453 Diseases of the Spinal Cord pp.3602-3607; Ch. 80 Oncologic Emergencies (MSCC) pp.631-633; Ch. 95 Epidural Metastasis pp.767-768; Ch. 19 Neck Pain pp.173-175; Ch. 26 Acute Paraparesis p.213; Ch. 136 Vertebral Osteomyelitis / Spinal Epidural Abscess p.1105

chunks.text: Vertebral collapse is not a reliable marker of malignancy - about 20% of collapses, especially in older and postmenopausal patients, are due to osteoporosis rather than tumour (p.632).

source.page: Harrison 22e: Ch. 453 Diseases of the Spinal Cord pp.3602-3607; Ch. 80 Oncologic Emergencies (MSCC) pp.631-633; Ch. 95 Epidural Metastasis pp.767-768; Ch. 19 Neck Pain pp.173-175; Ch. 26 Acute Paraparesis p.213; Ch. 136 Vertebral Osteomyelitis / Spinal Epidural Abscess p.1105

chunks.text: Pedicle erosion (the 'winking owl' sign) is the earliest plain-film sign of vertebral tumour, but plain films are insensitive and a normal film does not exclude malignancy (p.632).

chunks.text: Mistaking a myelopathy for polyneuropathy or Guillain-Barre syndrome: ascending paraesthesias suggest neuropathy, but a sharply demarcated sensory level plus bladder disturbance points to a cord origin (pp.213, 3605).

chunks.text: Acute severe transverse lesions cause initial FLACCID weakness and areflexia ('spinal shock') that can be misread as anterior horn cell disease or acute polyneuropathy before hyperreflexia supervenes over days to weeks (p.3604).

chunks.text: Cauda equina syndrome (low back/radicular pain, saddle/perineal sensory loss, asymmetric leg weakness, sphincter and sexual dysfunction, lost ankle/bulbocavernosus/anal reflexes) reflects nerve-root rather than cord compression and must be distinguished from conus and cord syndromes - mass lesions low in the canal often produce a mixed picture (pp.132, 632, 3604).

chunks.text: Outcome is strongly time- and function-dependent: treatment is most successful in patients who are still ambulatory and have intact sphincter control when therapy begins, and a good response is expected in those ambulatory at presentation - treatment usually prevents new weakness and up to a third regain some motor function (pp.632, 3606). Motor deficits fixed for more than 12 h seldom improve, and beyond 48 h substantial recovery is unlikely (p.3606). For spinal epidural abscess, prompt diagnosis and treatment allow significant recovery in up to two-thirds, but surgery is unlikely to reverse deficits fixed for more than a few days (p.3607). Recovery from paraparesis is better after surgery than radiotherapy alone, though survival may be short with widespread metastatic disease (p.768).

chunks.text: Gout arises from an increased body urate pool due to chronic hyperuricemia, leading to supersaturation and crystallization of monosodium urate (MSU) within joints and connective tissue. Hyperuricemia is predominantly due to impaired renal urate excretion (~90%) and less often urate overproduction (~10%); a minority (~10%) of cases reflect inherited metabolic disorders (PRPP synthetase superactivity, HPRT deficiency). Crystal shedding from inert synovial deposits, triggered by metabolic factors, diuresis, rapid urate changes (including urate-lowering therapy initiation), local trauma, or medical illness, activates resident synovial phagocytes (monocytes/macrophages, mast cells) and the NLRP3 inflammasome, generating IL-1beta and other proinflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-8, TNF-alpha). Phagocytosis of MSU crystals by neutrophils with a respiratory burst amplifies the acute inflammatory response. Persistent MSU deposition produces tophi (granulomatous inflammation around crystals) and chronic erosive gouty arthritis. In CPPD, increased cartilage inorganic pyrophosphate (largely from extracellular ATP breakdown, regulated by the ANKH transporter) combines with calcium to form CPP crystals; their release similarly drives inflammasome-mediated inflammation, analogous to hyperuricemia in gout. Apatite and calcium oxalate crystals can likewise stimulate synovial cell proliferation and release of proteases, collagenases, and prostaglandin E2, contributing to joint destruction (Harrison 22e p.2956-2962).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.384, p.2956-2962

chunks.text: Initial gout flares are usually monoarticular; the first metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra) is involved in 70-90% of cases, followed by tarsal joints, ankles, and knees. Oligo- and polyarticular flares emerge over time (Harrison 22e p.2958).

chunks.text: Untreated gout flares typically resolve spontaneously within 1-2 weeks, but recurrent flares over years can progress to chronic gouty arthritis with persistent low-grade synovitis, subcutaneous tophi, joint deformity, and erosive bony destruction. Controlling the underlying chronic hyperuricemia (urate-lowering therapy to a subsaturation target) can prevent recurrent flares and dissolve tophi, generally requiring lifelong therapy. For chronic CPPD there is no means to remove established CPP crystal deposits from cartilage and synovium (unlike urate lowering in gout), and progressive destructive large-joint disease may require joint replacement. Apatite-associated destructive arthropathy (e.g., Milwaukee shoulder) progresses indolently and may also lead to joint replacement (Harrison 22e p.2958-2962).

Diagnostic paracentesis with serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG): ≥1.1 g/dL indicates portal-hypertensive ascites, <1.1 g/dL indicates non-portal-hypertensive cause (p.371)
Serial serum creatinine and exclusion of volume depletion/intrinsic renal disease when HRS is suspected (p.2759)
Ascitic fluid cell count/differential, total protein, Gram stain and culture inoculated into blood-culture bottles at the bedside (p.371)
In high-SAAG ascites, ascitic protein <2.5 g/dL suggests cirrhosis vs ≥2.5 g/dL suggesting cardiac/early Budd-Chiari sinusoidal sources (p.371)

Transient elastography (liver stiffness) to stage fibrosis and predict variceal hemorrhage, ascites, and liver-related death (p.2676)
Hepatic venous pressure gradient measurement in selected cases to confirm sinusoidal portal hypertension (p.370, p.2757)
Pulse oximetry as a screen for hepatopulmonary syndrome (p.2673)

Decompensation is driven by portal hypertension plus renal sodium and water retention. Portal hypertension (elevation of the hepatic venous pressure gradient >5 mmHg) arises from two simultaneous processes: increased intrahepatic resistance from fibrosis disrupting sinusoidal architecture, stellate-cell-mediated smooth-muscle contraction, regenerative nodules, microthrombi, and reduced intrahepatic endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) causing intrahepatic vasoconstriction; and increased splanchnic blood flow from systemic vasodilation. Systemically, raised nitric oxide, VEGF and TNF cause splanchnic arterial vasodilation, pooling blood and reducing effective circulating volume; the kidneys sense this as hypovolemia and activate ADH, the sympathetic nervous system and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, producing free-water and sodium retention (ascites/edema). Encephalopathy results from gut-derived neurotoxins bypassing the liver via portosystemic shunting and reduced hepatic mass. (p.370, p.2756, p.2759)

Compensated cirrhosis can be asymptomatic for a decade or more; the transition to decompensation is marked by the first major event — ascites/edema, variceal hemorrhage, hepatic encephalopathy, or jaundice. (p.2756, p.2754)
Once clinically significant portal hypertension (HVPG ≥5 mmHg, with substantial decompensation risk at ≥10 mmHg) progresses to overt decompensation, median survival is under 2 years. (p.2756)

Encephalopathy in chronic liver disease is almost always triggered by an identifiable precipitant (GI bleeding, infection, volume depletion/overdiuresis, hyponatremia, constipation, uremia, sedatives/narcotics) rather than spontaneous progression. (p.2673, p.2759)

Ammonia levels correlate poorly with the severity of encephalopathy or liver disease; the diagnosis of hepatic encephalopathy is clinical, and most hepatologists do not rely on ammonia to make the diagnosis or follow progress. (p.2759)
A new or worsening encephalopathy episode mandates a search for occult infection — if ascites is present it should be tapped to exclude SBP. (p.2759)
A hyperdynamic circulation (widened pulse pressure, increased cardiac output, reduced peripheral resistance from splanchnic vasodilation) is a hallmark of advanced cirrhosis. (p.2673)

Acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF) is acutely decompensating cirrhosis with one or more extrahepatic organ failures, behaves like a sepsis syndrome, and carries 28-day mortality of 20-70% rising with the number of failing organs; it is most often precipitated by bacterial/fungal infection or alcoholic hepatitis. (p.2760)
Relying on ammonia levels to diagnose or track hepatic encephalopathy — they correlate poorly with disease severity (p.2759)
Attributing altered mental status to encephalopathy without excluding electrolyte disturbance, sedatives, and renal/respiratory failure (p.2673)
Failing to tap the ascites in a decompensated cirrhotic with new symptoms — abdominal tenderness is present in only ~40% of SBP and rebound is uncommon, so SBP can be clinically silent (p.372)

Multiple organisms on ascitic culture with a raised PMN count indicate secondary (not spontaneous) peritonitis and a surgical source; multiple organisms without raised PMN suggest bowel perforation by the paracentesis needle (p.372)
Withholding paracentesis for fear of coagulopathy — paracentesis is safe even in coagulopathic patients (p.371)
Restricting dietary protein for encephalopathy — its harm to nutrition outweighs benefit and it is strongly discouraged (p.2760)

Decompensation defines a poor-prognosis state: with clinically significant portal hypertension that decompensates, median survival is under 2 years, and fewer than 50% of patients survive 2 years after the onset of ascites. Encephalopathy in chronic liver disease is a poor prognostic sign. HRS (both AKI and CKD types) carries a poor prognosis unless liver transplantation is achieved. ACLF 28-day mortality ranges from 20-70%, rising with the number of organ failures. Severity and transplant priority are graded by Child-Pugh class and the MELD/MELD-Na (MELD 3.0) systems. (p.371, p.2675-2676, p.2756, p.2759-2760)
Variceal hemorrhage carries a 20-30% mortality per bleeding episode and is an immediate life-threatening event (p.2756)
A stepwise progressive rise in creatinine with large-volume ascites suggests hepatorenal syndrome (HRS-AKI), a poor-prognosis functional renal failure (p.2759)
ACLF with four or more organ failures persisting after 3-7 days of ICU support, when transplant is not an option, signals a transition toward palliative care (p.2760)
Avoid NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, and use ACE inhibitors/ARBs cautiously — they precipitate renal failure in cirrhotic ascites (p.371, p.2758)
New-onset or worsening encephalopathy, jaundice, or tense ascites in known cirrhosis should prompt an urgent search for a precipitant (p.2759)

Child-Pugh score (5 factors: bilirubin, albumin, prothrombin time/INR, ascites, encephalopathy; range 5-15) classifies cirrhosis as class A (5-6, compensated), B (7-9), or C (10-15); a score ≥7 (class B) defines decompensation. MELD score uses INR, bilirubin, and creatinine to predict short-term mortality and allocate organs; it was extended with serum sodium and reweighted as MELD-Na / MELD 3.0 for transplant listing. PELD is the pediatric equivalent. Clinically significant portal hypertension is defined by HVPG ≥10 mmHg. (p.2675-2676, p.2756, p.2754)

chunks.text: DIC arises from uncontrolled thrombin generation triggered by multiple mechanisms, with simultaneous disruption of physiologic anticoagulant pathways and abnormal fibrinolysis. In sepsis and trauma, activation of inflammatory pathways increases tissue factor expression, activates neutrophils and monocytes with cytokine release and neutrophil extracellular trap formation, and releases polyphosphates that cross-talk with the coagulation system (thrombo-inflammation); endothelial damage causes loss of native antithrombotic properties. The result is systemic fibrin deposition in small and mid-size vessels causing microvascular occlusion, ischemic organ damage, and red cell fragmentation/hemolysis. Sustained activation consumes platelets and clotting factors, producing systemic bleeding that is aggravated by secondary hyperfibrinolysis in late stages. Purpura fulminans is a severe form of DIC with extensive cutaneous thrombosis, predominantly in young children after viral or bacterial infection, especially with inherited or acquired protein C pathway deficiency (p.976).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.976-978 (Ch. 121, Coagulation Disorders); p.974 (Ch. 120, thrombocytopenia algorithm)

chunks.text: DIC is an acquired syndrome of intravascular activation of coagulation with loss of localization, which can damage the microvasculature and, if severe enough, cause organ dysfunction (ISTH 2001 definition) (p.976).

chunks.text: The central event is uncontrolled thrombin generation, compounded by disruption of physiologic anticoagulant mechanisms and abnormal fibrinolysis, producing systemic fibrin deposition in small and mid-size vessels (p.976).

chunks.text: Fibrin deposition can compromise blood supply to lung, kidney, liver and brain, causing organ failure; pulmonary microvascular thrombosis is a component of ARDS (p.976).

[guideline] management

Alcoholic ketoacidosis — high-anion-gap acidosis (predominantly beta-hydroxybutyrate) without hyperglycaemia, usually with preserved renal function, in chronic alcohol use with vomiting and poor intake (p.413).
Starvation ketoacidosis — ketoacidosis with normal or low glucose (p.413).
Other high-anion-gap acidoses: lactic acidosis, toxic ingestions (e.g. salicylates), and renal failure/uraemia (p.413).
Plasma beta-hydroxybutyrate measured directly (more reliable than urine nitroprusside ketones) (p.413).
Anion gap calculation, including assessment for a mixed non-anion-gap / high-anion-gap acidosis when the change in bicarbonate exceeds the change in anion gap (p.413).
Acute pancreatitis can mimic DKA (and vice versa), with overlapping abdominal pain; DKA may itself be accompanied by amylase elevation, complicating the distinction (p.2788).

DKA results from increased fatty acid metabolism with accumulation of the ketoacids acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate, producing hyperglycaemia, ketonaemia and a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. It typically occurs in insulin-dependent diabetes when insulin is stopped or when an intercurrent illness (e.g. infection, gastroenteritis, pancreatitis, myocardial infarction) acutely raises insulin requirements. In euglycaemic DKA caused by SGLT2 inhibitors, glycosuria drives an osmotic diuresis and volume depletion while plasma glucose stays in the normal range despite the ketoacidosis (p.413).
An acetone-like fruity odour on the breath is a classic bedside clue to ketoacidosis (p.93).
Urine dipstick (nitroprusside reaction) detects acetoacetate but not beta-hydroxybutyrate, so it can underestimate the true degree of ketosis; measure plasma beta-hydroxybutyrate directly (p.413).

As the circulation is restored with fluids, beta-hydroxybutyrate is converted to acetoacetate, so the nitroprusside ketone reading may paradoxically become more positive during treatment rather than reflecting worsening disease (p.413).
Glucose may be normal or only mildly raised in euglycaemic DKA (SGLT2-inhibitor associated) and in starvation ketoacidosis, so a normal glucose does not exclude ketoacidosis (p.413).
Excretion of ketoacids obligates loss of cations (sodium, potassium), worsening volume depletion and promoting chloride retention (p.413).
Relying on urine ketone dipstick, which misses beta-hydroxybutyrate and underestimates ketosis (p.413).
Interpreting a rising nitroprusside ketone result during fluid resuscitation as deterioration, when it reflects the beta-hydroxybutyrate-to-acetoacetate shift (p.413).
Assuming a normal/near-normal glucose excludes DKA, missing euglycaemic DKA on SGLT2 inhibitors (p.413).
Over-resuscitation with isotonic saline causing volume overload and/or hyperchloraemic acidosis (p.413).

Mucormycosis risk: DKA patients are at high risk of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis; acidosis frees iron from carrier proteins and beta-hydroxybutyrate upregulates fungal adherence/penetration receptors — consider in a DKA patient with sinus/orbital/facial signs (p.1761).
Severe acidaemia (pH <7.00) or shock identifies the small subset where bicarbonate may be considered; cerebral oedema risk limits its use (p.413).
Hyperchloraemic (non-anion-gap) acidosis and volume overload can be precipitated by aggressive isotonic saline during treatment (p.413).

[guideline] management
Characterise overall physiologic state and toxidrome from vital signs and neuromuscular exam (p.3704)
Anion gap (raised AGMA in methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylate, or any poisoning causing organ failure, seizures or shock; low anion gap with bromide, calcium, iodine, lithium, magnesium) (p.3705)
Osmolal gap (>10 mmol/L suggests a low-molecular-weight solute such as an alcohol or glycol) (p.3705)
Serum lactate (low relative to anion gap in alcohol/glycol intoxication, high and near the anion gap in hypoperfusion) (p.3705)
Glucose, electrolytes, ketones (hypo-/hyperglycaemia and hypo-/hyperkalaemia patterns can implicate specific agents) (p.3705)
ECG (bradycardia/AV block, QRS and QT prolongation, ventricular tachyarrhythmias suggest specific agent classes) (p.3706)
Abdominal/chest radiograph (radiopaque densities suggest heavy metals, drug packets, iron, enteric-coated or salicylate tablets; CXR for pulmonary edema/aspiration) (p.3706)

Quantitative serum levels (acetaminophen, alcohols incl. ethylene glycol/methanol, anticonvulsants, barbiturates, digoxin, iron, lithium, salicylate, theophylline, carboxyhemoglobin, methemoglobin) guide management (p.3706)
Coagulation (PT/INR) for warfarin/rodenticide risk stratification, though unreliable for direct oral anticoagulant overdose (p.3705)
Psychogenic illness / anxiety reaction (mass hysteria, fear of poisoning) producing symptoms inconsistent with the exposure history (p.3705)
Structural CNS lesion - focal neurologic findings are uncommon in poisoning and should prompt evaluation for a structural cause (p.3703)

Poisoning is a dose-related adverse effect from exposure to a chemical, drug or other xenobiotic. Responses to a given dose vary with genetic polymorphism, enzyme induction or inhibition by co-ingestants, and acquired tolerance. Toxicity may be local or systemic depending on route, the agent's physicochemical properties and mechanism, and its severity/reversibility depends on the functional reserve of the patient or target organ (influenced by age and pre-existing disease) (p.3703).

Diagnosis of an unknown poisoning rests on pattern recognition: first classify the overall physiologic state as stimulated, depressed, discordant, or normal, then look for a recognizable toxidrome (p.3704).

Most patients who are or become asymptomatic by 6 h after ingestion are unlikely to develop later toxicity and may be discharged, but longer observation is required after 'toxic time-bomb' ingestions (p.3707).

Core temperature is the single most reliable predictor of poor outcome in stimulant (e.g. cocaine) poisoning or in drug/alcohol/GHB withdrawal, so it must be measured even in difficult or combative patients (p.3704).

Mydriasis is common to all stimulant states but is most marked with anticholinergics (muscarinic loss of pupil reactivity); cocaine and other sympathomimetics enlarge pupils yet retain some light reactivity (p.3704).

The anticholinergic toxidrome is distinguished from other stimulant states by hot, dry, flushed skin, decreased bowel sounds and urinary retention, whereas sympathomimetic states cause diaphoresis and increased bowel activity (p.3704).
Miosis points to a depressed state from opioids or cholinergic agents; muscarinic/nicotinic features separate cholinergic poisoning from opioid poisoning (p.3704-3705).

In opioid and sedative-hypnotic poisoning, vital-sign derangements are secondary to CNS depression and do not appear until consciousness is markedly reduced (grade 3-4 depression); marked cardiovascular depression with preserved consciousness instead suggests a peripherally acting sympatholytic (p.3705).
Rotatory nystagmus among stimulated patients is essentially specific to phencyclidine and ketamine (p.3704).

A near-normal exam may reflect a nontoxic exposure, psychogenic illness, or a 'toxic time-bomb' (slowly absorbed, slowly distributed, requiring metabolic activation, or disrupting metabolism); once-daily reformulations have made these increasingly common (p.3705).
Rapid response of altered mental status to IV dextrose, naloxone or flumazenil is virtually diagnostic of hypoglycemia, opioid poisoning and benzodiazepine intoxication respectively (p.3706).

Rapid hospital urine drug-of-abuse screens are screening tests only, cannot confirm the exact substance, and are not diagnostic or forensic; false positives (e.g. fluoroquinolones triggering false-positive opiate screens) and false negatives are common (p.3706).

A negative drug screen does not exclude poisoning - the agent may be undetectable by the assay (e.g. synthetic cannabinoids/spice, cathinones/bath salts, kratom) or present below the limit of detection at the time of sampling; repeat testing later may turn positive (p.3706).

Qualitative drug screens are not clinically useful or cost-effective when the patient is asymptomatic or the picture fits the reported history; reserve them for severe or unexplained toxicity (coma, seizures, cardiovascular instability, acidosis, nonsinus rhythms) (p.3706).
Blood levels obtained during absorption/distribution may exceed tissue levels and may not correlate with toxicity (p.3707).
In polydrug overdose a clear toxidrome may be obscured when different drug classes counteract each other's physiologic effects (p.3704).
Physostigmine fully reverses anticholinergic poisoning but can also produce some arousal in CNS depression of any cause, so arousal alone is not specific (p.3706).
Overdose effects begin sooner, peak later and last longer than therapeutic-dose effects, and an agent's published (therapeutic) pharmacokinetics differ from its toxicokinetics in overdose (p.3707).

Overall mortality is low (<1% of all poison exposures) but rises to 1-2% among hospitalised patients with intentional (suicidal) overdose or complications of drugs of abuse, who account for most serious poisonings. About 20-25% of exposures need bedside professional evaluation and ~5% need hospitalisation. Acetaminophen is the pharmaceutical most often implicated in fatal poisoning, while carbon monoxide is the leading overall cause of poisoning death (often fatal before discovery). Most patients asymptomatic at 6 h are unlikely to deteriorate (p.3703, p.3707).
Temperature elevation (grade 4 stimulation) - most reliable predictor of poor outcome in stimulant poisoning and withdrawal (p.3704)
Coma, seizures or cardiovascular collapse (grade 4 physiologic stimulation or depression) (p.3705)
Focal neurologic findings - uncommon in poisoning and suggest a structural CNS lesion (p.3703)
Suspicion of 'body packing'/'body stuffing' in patients ill after foreign travel or arrest (p.3703)
High blood levels of agents with more toxic metabolites (acetaminophen, ethylene glycol, methanol) signalling need for antidote or dialysis (p.3707)

Harrison grades physiologic stimulation and depression in poisoning/withdrawal (Table 470-2): Stimulation - grade 1 anxious/tremulous with normal vital signs; grade 2 agitated, mildly-moderately raised vitals but can follow commands; grade 3 delirious with motor hyperactivity and markedly raised vitals, possible tachyarrhythmias; grade 4 coma, seizures, cardiovascular collapse. Depression - grade 1 lethargic but arousable to voice/touch; grade 2 responds to pain not voice, brainstem reflexes intact; grade 3 unresponsive to pain, depressed brainstem reflexes, reduced tone/respiration/temperature; grade 4 flaccid, absent brainstem reflexes and respirations, depressed cardiovascular signs (p.3705).

chunks.text: DVT arises from Virchow's triad of venous stasis, hypercoagulability and endothelial injury, now understood to be typically coupled with an inflammatory trigger. Activated platelets release proinflammatory microparticles that recruit neutrophils to form neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs); these histone-rich, web-like networks promote platelet aggregation and platelet-dependent thrombin generation. Thrombi form and propagate in an environment of stasis, low oxygen tension and upregulated proinflammatory genes. Lower-extremity thrombi usually begin in the calf veins and can propagate proximally to the popliteal, femoral and iliac veins; detached thrombi embolize through the vena cava and right heart into the pulmonary circulation, and rarely cross a patent foramen ovale or atrial septal defect to cause paradoxical (arterial) embolism. VTE shares inflammation, hypercoagulability and endothelial injury with arterial atherothrombosis, so VTE patients have more than double the risk of future MI or stroke and vice versa. Common genetic prothrombotic states are factor V Leiden (resistance to protein C) and the prothrombin gene mutation (raised prothrombin level); deficiencies of antithrombin, protein C and protein S also predispose but are rare; antiphospholipid syndrome is an acquired thrombophilia causing both venous and arterial thrombosis (Harrison 22e p.2156-2158).

chunks.text: Postthrombotic syndrome (chronic venous insufficiency) is the main long-term morbidity: damaged venous valves cause ankle/calf swelling and leg aching after prolonged standing, and in its most severe form deep skin ulceration near the medial malleolus. Notably, graduated compression stockings prescribed for asymptomatic newly diagnosed acute DVT do NOT prevent postthrombotic syndrome (they are used only for symptomatic swelling relief). Recurrence risk after stopping anticoagulation is stratified (ESC 2019) as low (<3%/yr, e.g., major surgery/trauma), intermediate (3-8%/yr, e.g., minor surgery, hospitalization for acute illness, pregnancy/estrogen, long-haul flight, IBD, autoimmune disease, or no identifiable risk factor) and high (>8%/yr, active cancer, antiphospholipid syndrome). Harrison de-emphasizes the 'provoked vs unprovoked' dichotomy because many provoked VTEs recur at rates similar to unprovoked ones, and enduring risk factors (heart failure, chronic lung disease, IBD) raise recurrence risk. The Post-VTE Functional Status scale (grades 0-4) can track functional recovery (Harrison 22e p.2156-2157, 2163).

chunks.text: Wells clinical prediction rule for DVT (Harrison 22e p.2159): low likelihood if score <=0, moderate if 1-2, high if >=3. Points: active cancer +1; paralysis/paresis or recent cast +1; bedridden >3 days or major surgery <12 weeks +1; tenderness along distribution of deep veins +1; entire-leg swelling +1; unilateral calf swelling >3 cm +1; pitting edema +1; collateral superficial nonvaricose veins +1; alternative diagnosis at least as likely as DVT -2. Pretest-probability strategy: patients with low DVT likelihood undergo d-dimer first and need no imaging if it is normal, whereas high-likelihood patients should skip d-dimer and proceed straight to compression ultrasound imaging.
