chunks.text: GBS is an acute, often fulminant autoimmune polyradiculoneuropathy thought to arise from immune responses to non-self antigens (infections, vaccines) that cross-react with peripheral nerve via molecular mimicry, with gangliosides (glycosphingolipids concentrated at sites such as nodes of Ranvier) as likely targets. In AIDP, the demyelinating and most common form, both cellular and humoral mechanisms operate: complement deposits on the outer Schwann cell surface, triggering membrane-attack-complex formation, vesicular myelin disintegration, and macrophage-mediated removal of myelin. The resulting conduction block (with axons left intact) explains the flaccid paralysis and the potential for rapid recovery once remyelination occurs; secondary axonal degeneration in severe cases slows recovery and worsens residual deficit. In the axonal variants (AMAN/AMSAN), IgG and complement deposit at the nodes of Ranvier of motor axons, with anti-GD1a antibodies preferentially targeting motor over sensory roots; low CMAP amplitudes often reflect reversible nodal/paranodal conduction block rather than true axon loss, though severe cases show axonal degeneration (p.3617-3620).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.3617-3622 (Chapter 458)

chunks.text: About 70% of cases follow an acute infection (usually respiratory or GI) by 1-3 weeks; roughly 20-30% are preceded by Campylobacter jejuni, with a similar share after herpesvirus infection (often CMV or EBV) (p.3617).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.3617-3622 (Chapter 458)

chunks.text: Weakness usually evolves over hours to a few days and is classically ascending (legs more than arms), often first noticed as 'rubbery legs', with tingling dysesthesias in the extremities (p.3617).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.3617-3622 (Chapter 458)

chunks.text: Facial diparesis occurs in ~50% of patients and lower cranial nerve/bulbar involvement is common; bulbar weakness with difficulty handling secretions can initially be mistaken for brainstem ischemia (p.3617).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.3617-3622 (Chapter 458)

chunks.text: Pain (neck, shoulder, back, or diffuse spinal pain) is common early, in ~50% of patients, and deep aching muscle pain plus dysesthetic limb pain also occur (p.3617).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.3617-3622 (Chapter 458)

chunks.text: Large-fiber functions (deep tendon reflexes, proprioception) are affected more severely than cutaneous pain/temperature sensation (p.3617).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.3617-3622 (Chapter 458)

chunks.text: AMAN and AMSAN are axonal variants associated with anti-GD1a/anti-GM1 antibodies and preceding C. jejuni; AMAN can occur in seasonal outbreaks (e.g., rural China) and is prevalent in China and Mexico (p.3617-3619).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.3617-3622 (Chapter 458)

chunks.text: Miller Fisher syndrome (~5% of cases) presents with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia without limb weakness and carries anti-GQ1b antibodies in >90% (p.3617, p.3619).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.3617-3622 (Chapter 458)

chunks.text: About 85% of patients reach full functional recovery within several months to a year, though minor signs (e.g., persistent areflexia) and complaints such as fatigue may remain. Mortality is <5% in optimal settings, usually from secondary pulmonary complications. The outlook is worst with severe proximal motor and sensory axonal damage; other adverse factors are advanced age, a fulminant or severe attack, and delayed treatment. Elevated serum neurofilament light chains and high anti-GM1 titers both correlate with greater axonal involvement and poorer recovery. Between 5 and 10% of typical GBS patients have one or more late relapses, many later reclassified as CIDP (p.3621-3622).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.3617-3622 (Chapter 458)

chunks.text: Rapid tempo of progression and severe weakness on admission, plus facial and/or bulbar weakness in the first week, predict the need for mechanical ventilation (up to ~30% of patients require ventilatory support) (p.3617).

chunks.text: Presence of fever or constitutional symptoms at onset casts doubt on the diagnosis and should prompt reconsideration (p.3617).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.3617-3622 (Chapter 458)

chunks.text: Brighton Collaboration case definitions (2011) grade diagnostic certainty in three levels. Level 1 (highest certainty) requires bilateral flaccid limb weakness, decreased/absent reflexes in weak limbs, a monophasic course with onset-to-nadir of 12 h to 28 days followed by plateau, electrophysiology consistent with GBS, cytoalbuminologic dissociation (elevated CSF protein with CSF white cell count <50/microL), and no alternative diagnosis. Lower levels relax the laboratory/electrophysiologic requirements. Parallel criteria exist for Miller Fisher syndrome (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia without limb weakness) (p.3620-3621).

chunks.text: Pathologic reflux arises from anatomic and physiologic failure of the oesophagogastric junction valve - widening of the diaphragmatic hiatus with diminished crural diaphragm function, loss of the intra-abdominal oesophageal segment disabling the flap valve, axial (sliding) hiatus hernia causing LES hypotension, and increased junctional compliance allowing liquid to escape during transient LES relaxations (the belch reflex). Some reflux is physiologic and intertwined with belching, but esophagitis follows excessive reflux plus impaired acid clearance, which depends on peristalsis returning fluid to the stomach and bicarbonate in swallowed saliva neutralising residual acid; impaired peristalsis and reduced salivation therefore prolong acid contact. Mucosal injury is driven by a cytokine-mediated inflammatory pathway rather than purely direct caustic injury. Gastric acid hypersecretion is usually NOT the dominant factor (exceptions: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, severe esophagitis in ~50%); chronic H. pylori gastritis may even be protective by inducing hypoacidity. Pepsin, bile, and pancreatic enzymes also injure the epithelium, and bile persists in refluxate despite acid suppression and is implicated as a cofactor in Barrett's metaplasia and adenocarcinoma. Exacerbating factors include abdominal obesity, pregnancy, gastric hypersecretory states, delayed gastric emptying, disrupted peristalsis, and overeating. Esophageal chest pain itself reflects a shared nerve plexus with the heart and poor discriminative ability of oesophageal afferents (p.2503-2504, p.2509-2510).

chunks.text: GN reflects glomerular inflammation producing hypertension, volume expansion (edema, sometimes ascites), and an abnormal (nephritic) urinalysis; intense cellular proliferation reduces filtering surface area, causing oliguria/anuria, sodium and water retention, and concentrated low-sodium urine. Three mechanistic categories underlie RPGN (Fig.319-1): (1) ANCA-associated pauci-immune vasculitis (anti-proteinase-3/cANCA, anti-myeloperoxidase/pANCA) where autoantibodies recruit complement and drive inflammatory vasculitis of kidney and peripheral vessels; (2) anti-GBM disease, where circulating IgG directed at an epitope in the alpha-3 chain of the non-collagenous domain of type IV collagen binds in situ with C3; and (3) immune-complex disease with low circulating C3 from subendothelial deposits (post-infectious/PIGN, endocarditis, SLE, cryoglobulinemia, hepatitis B/C, syphilis). In PIGN, antibody-bacterial antigen complexes form ~10 days-3 weeks after pharyngeal or skin (impetigo) infection by nephritogenic group A strep, activate complement causing hypocomplementemia and subendothelial deposits, with later subepithelial 'humps'. Pathologically, RPGN shows parietal epithelial and inflammatory cell proliferation forming cellular crescents that compress capillaries; crescents progress to fibrosis and global glomerulosclerosis. IgA nephropathy results from mesangial deposition of C3 binding galactose-deficient IgA-1. (p.2354-2356)

chunks.text: HFrEF is a progressive disease in which an index injury (e.g. acute MI, chronic pressure/volume overload, genetic or congenital disease) triggers months-to-years of structural and functional cardiovascular remodelling; patients may stay asymptomatic for long periods because compensatory mechanisms are activated that ultimately drive further deterioration. Pressure overload produces concentric hypertrophy and volume overload produces eccentric (dilated) hypertrophy, accompanied by myocyte hypertrophy, interstitial fibrosis, apoptosis and re-expression of fetal genes. Sustained activation of the sympathetic nervous system and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system initially supports cardiac output but becomes maladaptive, causing excessive vasoconstriction, sodium/water retention, electrolyte and renal disturbance, direct myocardial toxicity and arrhythmias; counter-regulatory natriuretic peptides, prostaglandins, bradykinin and nitric oxide are upregulated but inadequate. Therapies that antagonise RAAS and the sympathetic system (RAAS inhibitors, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, beta blockers) attenuate or reverse remodelling and improve outcomes. Secondary mitral regurgitation arises from ventricular dilatation, sphericity and annular changes, perpetuating a vicious cycle. HFpEF reflects multiple mechanisms beyond diastolic dysfunction (impaired calcium reuptake, vascular stiffness, renal dysfunction, sodium avidity, inflammation related to adiposity, oxidative/nitrosative stress, insulin resistance). The cardiorenal syndrome is driven not only by low forward flow but importantly by systemic venous congestion and raised intra-abdominal/splanchnic pressure, so relief of congestion improves renal function (p.1977-1982).

chunks.text: Overall 5-year survival after a HF diagnosis is roughly 50%, and in severe HF 1-year mortality may reach 40%; one in eight U.S. deaths lists HF on the certificate, most dying of progressive HF or sudden cardiac death. After a HF admission, mortality runs from 8-14% at 30 days to 26-37% at 1 year and up to 75% at 5 years, with readmission of 20-25% at 60 days and nearly 50% at 6 months; risk of death rises with each subsequent admission. Independent predictors of adverse outcome include older age, male sex, diabetes, CKD, CAD, advanced NYHA class, a third heart sound or raised JVP, reduced LV (or RV) EF, secondary mitral/tricuspid regurgitation, raised wedge pressure, pulmonary hypertension, low peak VO2, hyponatraemia, hyperuricaemia, worsening renal function, raised troponin/natriuretic peptides and neurohormones, wide QRS/LBBB, atrial fibrillation and ventricular arrhythmia. HFrecEF (recovered EF) generally carries a better prognosis than HFrEF or HFpEF, but withdrawing therapy can cause relapse in up to half within 6 months (p.1976-1977).

chunks.text: HFrEF/HFmrEF/HFpEF phenotype by EF: reduced EF (HFrEF) <=40%, mildly reduced EF (HFmrEF) 41-49%, preserved EF (HFpEF) >=50%; LVEF >=50% is considered normal systolic function (p.1977-1978, p.1984). NYHA functional class I-IV grades symptoms by the activity that provokes them: class I none with ordinary activity, class II mild symptoms on ordinary exertion, class III symptoms on less-than-ordinary activity, class IV symptoms (or angina) at rest worsening with any activity (p.1982). ACC/AHA stages describe disease progression: stage B asymptomatic ventricular dysfunction, stage C symptomatic HF, stage D advanced/refractory HF with high mortality where transplant or mechanical circulatory support may be considered (p.1987). Killip classification (originally for acute MI) grades pump failure: class I no congestion; class II basal rales, S3 or right-heart congestion; class III pulmonary oedema; class IV cardiogenic shock (SBP <90 mmHg with peripheral vasoconstriction, cyanosis, confusion, oliguria) - historically rising mortality from class I to IV (p.2247).

chunks.text: Hepatic encephalopathy is an alteration of mental status and cognition resulting from liver failure, in which gut-derived neurotoxins are not cleared because of portosystemic vascular shunting and decreased functional hepatic mass and thus reach the brain. Ammonia is the principal candidate toxin: high ammonia concentrations are thought to drive increased synthesis of glutamine within astrocytes, causing osmotic astrocyte swelling, mitochondrial energy failure, and generation of reactive nitrogen and oxygen species, together with increased levels of the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA and synthesis of putative 'false' neurotransmitters. No single one of these mechanisms fully explains the confusion and stupor, and which is mainly responsible for hepatic coma is not known. Other contributing compounds include certain false neurotransmitters and mercaptans. Chronic HE is characteristically accompanied by diffuse astrocytosis. In acute liver failure (but not chronic liver disease) cerebral edema with gray-matter swelling can occur and carries a risk of cerebral herniation (Harrison 22e p.230-231, p.2716).

chunks.text: HHS arises from RELATIVE insulin deficiency combined with inadequate fluid intake. Insulin deficiency drives hepatic glucose overproduction (glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis) and impairs glucose uptake by skeletal muscle. The resulting hyperglycaemia causes an osmotic diuresis with intravascular volume depletion that is worsened by inadequate fluid replacement. The reason ketosis is absent is not fully understood; the insulin deficiency is presumed to be only relative and less severe than in DKA, and some studies show lower counterregulatory hormone and free-fatty-acid levels in HHS than in DKA, with possibly reduced hepatic ketone synthesis or an insulin/glucagon ratio that does not favour ketogenesis. Inflammatory markers (cytokines, C-reactive protein) are elevated in both HHS and DKA (p.3217-3219).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.416, p.3216-3219

chunks.text: Typical patient is an older adult with type 2 diabetes presenting after a several-week prodrome of polyuria, weight loss and falling oral intake, progressing to confusion, lethargy or coma (p.3219).

chunks.text: Examination reflects profound dehydration and hyperosmolality: hypotension, tachycardia and altered mental status (p.3219).

chunks.text: A debilitating condition (e.g. prior stroke, dementia) or a social situation that limits access to water frequently contributes to HHS by impairing water intake (p.3218-3219).

chunks.text: Severe, rapidly progressive BP elevation produces mechanical/pressure-related vascular injury that overwhelms protective vascular tone. In malignant hypertension the characteristic lesion is fibrinoid necrosis of small vessels — breakdown of the vessel wall with deposition of eosinophilic fibrin-containing material and a perivascular cellular infiltrate; larger interlobular arteries may show a hyperplastic 'onionskin' proliferative lesion. These changes can obliterate glomeruli and tubular structures, driving progressive kidney failure. Multiple pathways can generate this pressure injury, including activation of the renin-angiotensin system and intense vasospasm from catecholamine release; when endothelial injury is severe enough it triggers microangiopathic hemolysis. Cerebral involvement reflects failure of cerebral blood-flow autoregulation: at extreme pressures autoregulatory limits are exceeded, producing hyperperfusion, vasogenic edema and the encephalopathy/PRES picture — which is also why too-rapid lowering below the autoregulatory range can cause cerebral or optic ischemia (p.2153-2154, p.192, p.227).

chunks.text: Calcium balance is governed by PTH and the vitamin D metabolites 1,25(OH)2D and 25(OH)D acting across parathyroid, kidney, intestine and bone. Hypercalcaemia of malignancy arises mainly through three mechanisms. (1) PTHrP overproduction by solid tumours (squamous head/neck, lung, skin; breast; genitourinary; gastrointestinal) — PTHrP mimics PTH at the PTH receptor, raising bone resorption and renal calcium reabsorption. (2) Local osteolysis from skeletal metastases (breast, myeloma), where metastatic deposits secrete PTHrP and chemokines driving bone breakdown. (3) Excess 1,25(OH)2D production, notably by lymphomas (and granulomatous disease) via macrophage CYP27B1 converting 25(OH)D to active 1,25(OH)2D, enhancing intestinal calcium absorption. PTHrP induction is linked to PTHLH hypomethylation, hedgehog/Gli signalling, TGF-beta, oncogene activation (e.g. Ras) and p53 loss. In all these malignant mechanisms, the high serum calcium activates the parathyroid CaSR and appropriately suppresses endogenous PTH (p.363, 737).

[guideline] management

Hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism — common in diabetics, the elderly and renal insufficiency; classically suppressed renin and aldosterone, ~50% with associated acidosis (reduced urinary NH4+, positive urinary anion gap, urine pH <5.5) (p.402)
Primary adrenal insufficiency / Addison's disease (autoimmune or polyglandular endocrinopathy) (p.401-402)
Adrenal infiltration (amyloidosis, metastatic cancer) or adrenal haemorrhage/infarction (e.g. antiphospholipid syndrome) (p.402)
Pseudohypoaldosteronism type I (ENaC or mineralocorticoid receptor defects) and type II / hereditary hypertension with hyperkalaemia (WNK1/WNK4, KLHL3, CUL3 mutations) (p.402)
Hereditary hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis (SCN4A mutations) — weakness with K+ intake or rest after exercise (p.403)
Tubulointerstitial disease affecting the distal nephron (amyloidosis, sickle cell, interstitial nephritis, obstructive uropathy) causing hyperkalaemia out of proportion to GFR (p.402)
Tumour lysis syndrome and rhabdomyolysis — release of intracellular K+ from tissue necrosis (p.402)
Massive red-cell transfusion (p.402)

Adrenal insufficiency from infectious causes (HIV — important cause, usually subclinical and may be unmasked by stress, ketoconazole or steroid withdrawal; cytomegalovirus; tuberculosis; disseminated fungal infection) presenting with hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia (p.402)
Serum electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, serum osmolality, Mg2+ and Ca2+, complete blood count (p.403)
Urinary pH, osmolality, creatinine and electrolytes (urine Na+ <20 mM indicates distal Na+ delivery limits K+ excretion) (p.403)
Transtubular K+ gradient (TTKG) as a bedside index of urinary K+ excretion — expected >7-8 in hyperkalaemia; values <8 suggest tubular resistance/low aldosterone (interpret cautiously) (p.403)
Plasma renin activity and aldosterone, with 9-alpha-fludrocortisone response, to characterise hypoaldosteronism (p.403)

Pseudohyperkalaemia (factitious hyperkalaemia) — artefactual K+ release during/after venepuncture from fist clenching, marked thrombocytosis/leukocytosis/erythrocytosis with in vitro efflux, cold storage of the sample, or hereditary red-cell membrane transport defects (e.g. SLC4A1/AE1 mutations) (p.401-402)
Acute anxiety at venepuncture with respiratory alkalosis causing redistributive (true but transient) hyperkalaemia (p.402)

Plasma K+ rises when efflux of intracellular K+ outpaces clearance or when renal excretion falls. Acidaemia drives K+ out of cells via effective K+-H+ exchange to buffer extracellular pH — but this shift is seen mainly with non-anion-gap (mineral) and respiratory acidoses; it does NOT occur with the organic anion-gap acidoses (lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis). Hyperosmolality (mannitol, hypertonic saline, IVIG, hypertonic glucose without insulin in diabetics) shifts K+ out by solvent drag. Cationic amino acids (lysine, arginine, epsilon-aminocaproic acid) and Na+/K+-ATPase inhibitors (digoxin and related cardiac glycosides from yellow oleander, foxglove, cane-toad bufadienolide; fluoride) cause efflux. Succinylcholine depolarises muscle via upregulated acetylcholine receptors (contraindicated after burns, neuromuscular injury, disuse atrophy, prolonged immobilisation). Impaired excretion arises from blockade of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis, reduced distal Na+/flow delivery, hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism, mineralocorticoid resistance, and reduced functioning nephron mass. Cardiotoxicity reflects altered cardiac membrane excitability: mild rises alter repolarisation (T-wave changes), higher levels depress intracardiac conduction (PR/QRS prolongation, P-wave loss, QRS widening, sine wave). (p.401-403)
Hyperkalaemia (plasma K+ ≥5.5 mM) occurs in up to 10% of hospitalised patients; severe hyperkalaemia (>6.0 mM) in ~1% and carries significantly increased mortality (p.401).
Reduced renal K+ excretion is the single most common underlying cause; transcellular shift and reduced tissue uptake act mainly as acute contributors (p.401).

Excess dietary intake alone is a rare cause because the kidney can normally upregulate secretion — but small intake increments can provoke severe hyperkalaemia in susceptible patients (e.g. diabetics with hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism and CKD); occult sources include K+-containing salt substitutes (p.401-402).
The ECG changes of hyperkalaemia are notoriously INSENSITIVE, particularly in CKD/ESRD patients — a normal ECG does NOT exclude dangerous hyperkalaemia (p.403).

Hyperkalaemia per se impairs renal acid excretion (K+ competes with NH4+ for TALH reabsorption), so it can itself contribute to metabolic acidosis; restoring normokalaemia often corrects this hyperkalaemic acidosis (p.403).

Hyperkalaemia can produce a type I Brugada ECG pattern (pseudo-RBBB with coved ST elevation in precordial leads); the hyperkalaemic Brugada sign is distinguished from genetic Brugada syndrome by absent P waves, marked QRS widening and an abnormal QRS axis (p.403).
A urine Na+ concentration <20 mM signals that low distal Na+ delivery is limiting K+ excretion, suggesting volume repletion or a loop diuretic may help lower K+ (p.403).
Treating a falsely high K+: failing to exclude pseudohyperkalaemia before intervening (haemolysed sample, fist clenching, extreme thrombo/leuko/erythrocytosis, cold storage) (p.401-402).
Relying on a normal/near-normal ECG to exclude dangerous hyperkalaemia — ECG changes are notoriously insensitive, especially in CKD/ESRD (p.403).

Forgetting drug and dietary causes: ACEi/ARB/renin inhibitors and mineralocorticoid-receptor blockers (spironolactone, eplerenone, drospirenone) — additive in combination; K+-sparing diuretics and the structurally similar antibiotics trimethoprim and pentamidine block ENaC; NSAIDs/COX-2 inhibitors, calcineurin inhibitors and beta-blockers cause hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism; heparin/LMWH inhibit aldosterone synthesis (p.402).
Drugs blocking the RAA axis also blunt the adrenal aldosterone response to a rising K+, compounding the effect (p.402).

Anion-gap acidoses (lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis) do NOT shift K+ out by the acidosis mechanism, unlike non-anion-gap and respiratory acidoses — so attributing hyperkalaemia to acidosis in these settings can mislead (p.402).

Severe hyperkalaemia (>6.0 mM) is associated with a significantly increased risk of mortality. Cardiac toxicity can progress rapidly to fatal arrhythmia, but is reversible with prompt treatment; hyperkalaemic metabolic acidosis frequently corrects once normokalaemia is restored. (p.401, p.403)
Hyperkalaemia is a medical emergency because of its cardiac effects — arrhythmias include sinus bradycardia, sinus arrest, slow idioventricular rhythms, VT, VF and asystole (p.402-403).

ECG progression as a severity cue: tall peaked T waves (5.5-6.5 mM) -> loss of P waves (6.5-7.5 mM) -> widened QRS (7.0-8.0 mM) -> sine-wave pattern (>8.0 mM), heralding impending VF/asystole (p.403).
ECG manifestations mandate urgent treatment; but K+ ≥6.5 mM WITHOUT ECG changes should still be managed aggressively, because ECG findings are an unreliable predictor of cardiac toxicity (p.403-404).

Management principle (knowledge): a three-stage sequence — (1) immediately antagonise cardiac effects (IV calcium stabilises the myocardium by raising the action-potential threshold), (2) shift K+ into cells, (3) remove K+ from the body (p.403-404).
Secondary hyperkalaemic paralysis — ascending paralysis that can include diaphragmatic paralysis and respiratory failure (p.403).

By plasma K+: hyperkalaemia ≥5.5 mM; severe >6.0 mM (markedly increased mortality). ECG-correlated severity bands: peaked T waves 5.5-6.5 mM; loss of P waves 6.5-7.5 mM; widened QRS 7.0-8.0 mM; sine-wave pattern >8.0 mM. Emergency treatment is triggered by any ECG change or K+ ≥6.5 mM. (p.401, p.403-404)

Activating TSH-R mutation; activating GSalpha mutation (McCune-Albright) (p.3032)
Subclinical hyperthyroidism (low TSH, normal free T3/T4) (p.3034, 3041)
Toxic multinodular goitre (p.3032)
Toxic adenoma / hyperfunctioning solitary nodule (p.3032)
Destructive thyroiditis: subacute (de Quervain) or silent/postpartum thyroiditis - transient thyrotoxic phase from preformed hormone release (p.3037)
Iodine excess (Jod-Basedow phenomenon); amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis in up to 10% (p.3032, 3034)
Thyrotoxicosis factitia (exogenous thyroid hormone ingestion) (p.3032, 3037)

TRAb (TSH-receptor antibodies) - confirms Graves' when goitre/ophthalmopathy absent; useful for monitoring pregnant Graves' patients (high TSI crosses placenta -> neonatal thyrotoxicosis) (p.3033-3034)
Radionuclide (99mTc, 123I or 131I) scan and uptake - diffuse high uptake in Graves' vs LOW uptake in destructive thyroiditis, iodine excess, and factitious thyrotoxicosis (p.3034)
Color-flow Doppler ultrasonography - increased flow in hyperthyroidism vs destructive thyroiditis; avoids radioactivity (p.3034)
Unbound (free) T3 - to detect T3 toxicosis (2-5% of patients have only elevated T3) (p.3034)
TPO and thyroglobulin (Tg) antibodies; serum Tg increased in all thyrotoxicosis EXCEPT factitia (low in factitia, high in thyroiditis) (p.3033-3034, 3037)
Pituitary MRI/CT and alpha-subunit if TSH inappropriately non-suppressed (suspect TSH-secreting adenoma) (p.3034, 3037)
Panic / anxiety attacks (p.3034)
Mania (p.3034)
Phaeochromocytoma (p.3034)
Malignancy-associated weight loss (p.3034)
Depression (especially apathetic thyrotoxicosis in the elderly) (p.3033)

Graves' hyperthyroidism is caused by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSIs, detected as TSH-receptor antibodies/TRAb) that activate the TSH receptor. Susceptibility involves genetic (HLA-DR, CTLA-4, CD25, CD40, PTPN22, TSH-R gene) and environmental factors; concordance is 20-30% in monozygotic vs <5% in dizygotic twins. Triggers/risk factors include stress, smoking (moderate for Graves', major for ophthalmopathy), sudden iodine intake increases, the postpartum period (threefold rise), and immune reconstitution after HAART, alemtuzumab, or immune checkpoint inhibitors. Coexisting lymphocytic thyroiditis and TPO/Tg antibodies (up to 80%) mean there is no direct correlation between TSI level and hormone levels. Ophthalmopathy is driven by cytokine-mediated (IFN-gamma, TNF, IL-1) infiltration of extraocular muscles by activated T cells, fibroblast activation, glycosaminoglycan deposition trapping water, and aberrant IGF-1R signalling; the TSH-R is expressed in orbital tissue (p.3032-3033).

Thyrotoxicosis (state of thyroid hormone excess) is NOT synonymous with hyperthyroidism (excessive thyroid gland function); destructive thyroiditis and ingestion of exogenous hormone cause thyrotoxicosis without true hyperthyroidism (p.3032).

Graves' ophthalmopathy specific signs (proptosis, periorbital oedema, conjunctival injection, diplopia) occur in ~one-third of Graves' patients clinically; ~10% of ophthalmopathy is unilateral (p.3033-3034).
Graves' ophthalmopathy can occur in the absence of hyperthyroidism in ~10% (euthyroid ophthalmopathy); onset is within a year before/after thyrotoxicosis diagnosis in 75% (p.3034).
A diffuse, firm (non-nodular) goitre with a thrill or bruit at the inferolateral margins points to Graves' disease (p.3033).
Thyrotoxic hypokalaemic periodic paralysis is a recognised association, particularly common in Asian males (p.3033).

Mild hypercalcaemia occurs in up to 20% of patients (hypercalciuria more common) from thyroid-hormone-driven bone resorption; long-standing disease causes osteopenia and a small increased fracture rate (p.3033).
Graves' disease accounts for 60-80% of thyrotoxicosis; affects up to 2% of women, ~10x less common in men, typically ages 20-50 (p.3032).
In the elderly, features may be subtle or masked, presenting mainly with fatigue and weight loss ('apathetic thyrotoxicosis'), and may be mistaken for depression (p.3033).
Weight loss occurs despite increased appetite due to raised metabolic rate, but ~5% of patients GAIN weight due to increased food intake (p.3033).
Atrial fibrillation is more common in patients >50 years; treating the thyrotoxic state alone reverts AF to sinus rhythm in up to 75% of those without underlying cardiac disease (p.3033).

Symptoms in descending frequency: hyperactivity/irritability, heat intolerance/sweating, palpitations, fatigue/weakness, weight loss with increased appetite, diarrhoea, polyuria, oligomenorrhoea/loss of libido (p.3033 Table 396-2).
Signs: tachycardia (AF in elderly), fine tremor, goitre, warm moist skin, proximal myopathy, lid retraction/lag (p.3033 Table 396-2).
Fine tremor is best elicited by having the patient stretch out the fingers while feeling the fingertips with the palm (p.3033).
Lid retraction (staring appearance) results from sympathetic overactivity and occurs in ANY form of thyrotoxicosis; it is distinct from the specific eye signs of Graves' ophthalmopathy (p.3033).

Do NOT assume thyrotoxicosis means hyperthyroidism - low radionuclide uptake indicates destructive thyroiditis, iodine excess or factitia rather than gland overactivity, which changes management (p.3032, 3037).

T3 toxicosis: 2-5% have suppressed TSH with elevated T3 but normal T4, so a normal T4 does not exclude thyrotoxicosis; conversely iodine-induced T4 toxicosis can show elevated T4 with normal T3 (p.3034).
Diagnostic confusion: thyrotoxicosis can elevate bilirubin, liver enzymes and ferritin, and cause microcytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia (p.3034).

Antithyroid drug agranulocytosis (<1%) is idiosyncratic and abrupt - routine prospective blood-count monitoring is NOT useful; instead warn patients to stop the drug and obtain an urgent FBC for sore throat, fever or mouth ulcers (p.3036).

Suppressed TSH may persist for several months after starting antithyroid drugs, so TSH is not a reliable early index of response - titrate on unbound T4; euthyroidism is usually not reached until 6-8 weeks (p.3035).
Thyroid acropachy/clubbing without coincident dermopathy and ophthalmopathy in a Graves' patient should prompt a search for an alternative cause of clubbing (p.3034).
A normal TSH with normal unbound T4/T3 excludes thyrotoxicosis and excludes Graves' as the cause of a diffuse goitre (p.3034).

Untreated, clinical features generally worsen; historical mortality was 10-30% before effective therapy. Mild Graves' may show spontaneous relapses and remissions, and rarely fluctuates between hypo- and hyperthyroidism with changing TRAb activity. About 15% of treated patients in remission develop hypothyroidism 10-15 years later from the destructive autoimmune process. Ophthalmopathy runs an independent course: typically worsens over 3-6 months, plateaus over 12-18 months, then partially improves (soft-tissue changes especially); fulminant in up to 5% requiring acute intervention. Thyrotoxic crisis carries 4-17% mortality even with treatment (p.3034-3036).
Optic nerve compression at the orbital apex -> papilloedema, peripheral field defects and permanent vision loss; sight-threatening ophthalmopathy is an emergency (p.3034, 3036)
Corneal exposure/ulceration when lids fail to close during severe proptosis (p.3034)
Atrial fibrillation or worsening angina/heart failure, especially in elderly or pre-existing cardiac disease - high cardiac output can precipitate high-output failure (p.3033)
Features suggesting thyroid storm: fever, delirium, seizures, coma, vomiting, diarrhoea, jaundice (p.3036)

Subclinical hyperthyroidism = low TSH with normal free T3 and free T4; treatment is increasingly recommended in the elderly to reduce atrial fibrillation and bone-loss risk (p.3034, 3041). Graves' ophthalmopathy severity is graded by the NO SPECS mnemonic (0 no signs/symptoms; 1 only signs e.g. lid retraction/lag; 2 soft tissue involvement; 3 proptosis >22 mm; 4 extraocular muscle involvement/diplopia; 5 corneal involvement; 6 sight loss), though activity-based systems such as EUGOGO are preferred for monitoring/treatment decisions (p.3034).

Falling glucose triggers counterregulatory autonomic activation (catecholamines) producing adrenergic warning symptoms, while inadequate glucose supply to the brain produces neuroglycopenia. Endogenous hyperinsulinism (insulinoma) drives fasting hypoglycemia with elevated insulin, proinsulin, and C-peptide. Non-islet-cell tumors can cause hypoglycemia chiefly through secretion of incompletely processed IGF-II ('big' IGF-II), which weakly activates insulin receptors and more strongly IGF-I receptors; reduced IGFBP-3 and acid-labile subunit increase IGF-II bioavailability to target tissues, and large tumors may also impair hepatic gluconeogenesis or consume glucose. In severe malaria, hypoglycemia arises from failed hepatic gluconeogenesis combined with increased host (and to a lesser extent parasite) glucose consumption, and may be worsened by quinine-induced insulin secretion (p.204, p.635-636, p.721, p.782, p.1807).

Symptoms fall into two groups: autonomic/adrenergic features (tremor, palpitations, anxiety, sweating, hunger, paresthesias) driven by counterregulatory activation, and neuroglycopenic features (fatigue, weakness, dizziness, confusion, behavioral change, cognitive impairment) from impaired neuronal function (p.204).
Hypoglycemia can cause transient loss of consciousness and may mimic syncope or seizure; hunger as a premonitory symptom and absence of immediate reorientation help distinguish it (p.204).
Insulinoma may first be misattributed to psychiatric illness, with symptoms (confusion, irrational behavior, visual difficulty, coma) recognized as neuroglycopenic only in retrospect (p.721).

Distinguish endogenous insulin excess (insulinoma) from surreptitious exogenous insulin use: C-peptide and proinsulin are elevated with insulinoma but suppressed with exogenous insulin injection (p.721).

A non-islet-cell tumor cause is suggested by hypoglycemia with suppressed insulin and C-peptide plus an elevated IGF-II/IGF-I ratio (>10:1) and inappropriately low GH and beta-hydroxybutyrate (p.635-636, p.782).
Repeated hypoglycemia produces hypoglycemia unawareness by impairing the counterregulatory response, so the absence of adrenergic warning symptoms does not exclude dangerous hypoglycemia (p.204).

In severe malaria the clinical signs of hypoglycemia (sweating, gooseflesh, tachycardia) are typically absent and its neurologic effects mimic the underlying disease, so it is easily missed without glucose measurement (p.1807).
Failing to measure C-peptide/proinsulin can miss surreptitious exogenous insulin use, which mimics insulinoma (p.721).
Circulating IGF-II may not be overtly elevated in tumor-induced hypoglycemia, so a normal IGF-II level does not exclude it; the IGF-II/IGF-I ratio is more informative (p.635-636, p.782).
A markedly raised leukocyte count can cause artifactual low glucose (pseudohypoglycemia) if the sample is not processed promptly (p.635-636).
Hypoglycemia is rapidly reversible with glucose, but in severe malaria it independently signals a poor prognosis, particularly in children and pregnant women (p.1807).
Hypoglycemia complicating severe malaria carries a poor prognosis, especially in children and pregnant women, and the usual warning signs may be absent (p.1807)
Recurrent hypoglycemia blunts counterregulation, causing hypoglycemia unawareness — loss of the warning symptoms that normally prompt correction (p.204)
Coma or seizures from neuroglycopenia indicate severe, potentially irreversible CNS compromise (p.721, p.782)

[guideline] management
Hypovolaemic: GI losses (vomiting, diarrhoea, tube drainage) and insensible loss (sweating, burns) with inadequate replacement — urine Na+ typically <20 mM (p.390).
Hyperglycaemia-related ('true') hyponatraemia — plasma Na+ falls ~1.6-2.4 mM per 100 mg/dL rise in glucose; resolves after correcting hyperglycaemia (p.393).

Hypovolaemic renal: thiazide diuretics, mineralocorticoid/aldosterone deficiency (primary adrenal insufficiency, hypoaldosteronism), salt-losing nephropathies (reflux nephropathy, interstitial nephropathies, post-obstructive uropathy, medullary cystic disease, recovery phase of ATN) — urine Na+ typically >20 mM (p.390-391).
Osmotic/solute-driven hypovolaemic: glycosuria, ketonuria (starvation, diabetic or alcoholic ketoacidosis), bicarbonaturia (RTA, metabolic alkalosis) (p.391).
Cerebral salt wasting (subarachnoid haemorrhage, traumatic brain injury, craniotomy, encephalitis, meningitis) (p.391).
Hypervolaemic: congestive heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, and acute or chronic renal failure (the latter uniquely with raised urine Na+) (p.391).
Euvolaemic: SIAD, moderate-to-severe hypothyroidism, secondary adrenal insufficiency from pituitary disease (glucocorticoid deficiency) (p.391).
Low solute intake: beer potomania (alcoholics whose sole nutrient is beer) and nutrient-restricted/extreme vegetarian diets — urine osmolality <100-200 mOsm/kg, urine Na+ <10-20 mM (p.391-392).

SIAD causes (Table 56-1): malignancy (especially small-cell lung carcinoma — 75% of malignancy-associated SIAD; ~10% present with Na+ <130 mM), pulmonary disease (pneumonia, TB, abscess, pleural effusion), CNS disease (tumour, subarachnoid haemorrhage, meningitis, encephalitis, head trauma, hydrocephalus), drugs, and transient causes (pain, nausea, stress, endurance exercise, general anaesthesia) (p.391-392).
Pseudohyponatraemia — hyponatraemia coexisting with normal/increased plasma tonicity, from extreme hyperlipidaemia or hyperproteinaemia (p.393).

Serum osmolality, converted to effective osmolality/tonicity by subtracting urea (in mg/dL divided by 2.8) — true hyponatraemia has effective osmolality <275 mOsm/kg; this also excludes pseudohyponatraemia (p.393).
Imaging — chest CT in smokers/high-risk patients (screening CXR can miss small-cell lung carcinoma); CNS imaging where a central cause is suspected (p.393).
Serum glucose — to identify and correct hyperglycaemic (translocational) hyponatraemia (p.393).
Serum uric acid — low (<4 mg/dL) in SIAD physiology, often high in volume depletion (p.393).
Serum K+, BUN/creatinine — hyperkalaemia suggests adrenal insufficiency/hypoaldosteronism; raised urea/creatinine suggests renal cause (p.393).
Thyroid, adrenal and pituitary function testing, including a cosyntropin (ACTH) stimulation test to assess primary adrenal insufficiency, in the appropriate setting (p.393).
Urine osmolality — <100 mOsm/kg suggests primary polydipsia; >400 mOsm/kg indicates dominant AVP excess; intermediate values suggest multifactorial physiology (p.393).
Urine Na+ — <20-30 mM suggests hypovolaemia; >30 mM suggests SIAD, but values overlap, especially in the elderly (p.393).
Urine K+ — to calculate the urine-to-plasma electrolyte ratio, useful for predicting response to fluid restriction (p.393).
Demonstration that plasma Na+ corrects after isotonic saline hydration is the diagnostic gold standard for hypovolaemic hyponatraemia (p.393).
Pseudohyponatraemia from severe hyperlipidaemia/hyperproteinaemia: measured Na+ is low but plasma tonicity is normal or high; exclude by measuring serum osmolality (p.393).
Hyperglycaemic hyponatraemia: a translocational, true hyponatraemia driven by glucose-induced water efflux that corrects once glucose is lowered (p.393).

Hyponatraemia reflects a relative excess of body water to sodium, almost always from increased circulating AVP (or heightened renal AVP sensitivity) together with free-water intake. Volume status modulates AVP release: hypovolaemia raises AVP at any given osmolality, and 'hypervolaemic' arterial underfilling (heart failure, cirrhosis) triggers neurohumoral activation that likewise elevates AVP, causing water retention. In hypovolaemia, AVP-mediated V2-receptor water reabsorption plus free-water intake lowers Na+. In hypervolaemic oedematous states (CHF, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome), total-body Na+ rises but water rises proportionally more; reduced arterial filling drives the AVP response. In euvolaemic hyponatraemia, SIAD is the commonest cause: free-water intake persists at osmolalities below the normal thirst threshold, with patients subclinically volume-expanded (so-called 'AVP escape' limits distal tubular transport, preserving a modestly hypervolaemic steady state). Four AVP-secretion patterns occur in SIAD: erratic unregulated secretion (~1/3 of patients), failure to suppress at low osmolality, a 'reset osmostat', and a subset with undetectable AVP (gain-of-function V2-receptor mutations causing 'nephrogenic' SIAD). At the brain level, hyponatraemia causes water to move down the osmotic gradient from hypotonic ECF into cells, producing cellular swelling and cerebral oedema within the rigid skull; acute encephalopathy results when volume-regulatory mechanisms (CSF shunting, efflux of Na+/K+/Cl-) are overwhelmed. In chronic hyponatraemia, brain cells extrude organic osmolytes (creatine, betaine, glutamate, myoinositol, taurine), a process largely complete within 48 h, which mitigates but does not abolish symptoms (p.390-392).
Hyponatraemia (plasma Na+ <135 mM) is very common, affecting up to ~22% of hospitalised patients (p.390).
The absolute plasma Na+ concentration says nothing about a patient's volume status, which must be assessed separately for both diagnosis and management (p.390).

Hyponatraemia is almost always driven by excess circulating AVP and/or increased renal sensitivity to AVP combined with free-water intake; the main exception is hyponatraemia from low solute intake (p.390).
Diagnostically subdivide by ECF volume into hypovolaemic, euvolaemic, and hypervolaemic groups based on clinical history and volume status (p.390).
In hypovolaemic patients, a urine Na+ <20 mM predicts a brisk rise in plasma Na+ with isotonic saline, because AVP falls and a water diuresis ensues (p.391).
Serum uric acid helps discriminate: SIAD is typically associated with low uric acid (<4 mg/dL), whereas hypovolaemic hyponatraemia is often hyperuricaemic (p.391, p.393).
Thiazides can mimic SIAD and do not impair urinary concentrating ability, so AVP retains full effect; defer diagnosing SIAD until 1-2 weeks after stopping the thiazide (p.391, p.393).
The 48-hour mark distinguishes acute from chronic hyponatraemia and is decisive for how aggressively/cautiously sodium may be corrected (p.392).

Cerebral salt wasting (a rare hypovolaemic cause linked to intracranial disease) responds to aggressive salt-and-water repletion, so distinguishing it from SIAD is critical because their management diverges (p.391).
Hypovolaemic patients may appear clinically euvolaemic, with only a low urine Na+ to reveal the cause (p.390).
Hyponatraemia is frequently multifactorial, especially when severe — evaluate every source of excess AVP (volume status, drugs, nausea, pain) rather than settling on one (p.393).
Failing to exclude pseudohyponatraemia/hyperglycaemia before correcting; check serum osmolality and glucose first (p.393).
The 93%-water assumption used by ion-sensitive electrodes makes plasma Na+ falsely low in extreme hyperlipidaemia/hyperproteinaemia (p.393).
Urine Na+ values overlap substantially between SIAD and hypovolaemia (particularly in the elderly); the saline-challenge response is the definitive discriminator (p.393).
Diagnosing SIAD in a patient on thiazides — defer the SIAD label until 1-2 weeks after stopping the drug (p.393).
Distinguishing cerebral salt wasting from SIAD is critical because management differs (salt repletion vs fluid restriction) (p.391).

Acute symptomatic hyponatraemia carries high risk of severe neurological injury and death; encephalopathy is more severe in premenopausal women. The degree of hyponatraemia is an important prognostic indicator in hypervolaemic states, reflecting the intensity of neurohumoral activation. Chronic hyponatraemia, even when judged 'asymptomatic', is associated with subtle gait and cognitive deficits (reversible with correction), increased risk of falls, and an increased fracture risk due to neurological dysfunction and reduced bone density — so safe correction is warranted even without overt symptoms. Osmotic demyelination from overcorrection can produce permanent disabling neurological deficits (p.392-393).
Acute symptomatic hyponatraemia is a medical emergency: nausea/headache/vomiting can rapidly progress to seizures, brainstem herniation, coma and death (p.392).

Acute hyponatraemia can cause normocapnoeic or hypercapnoeic respiratory failure, typically from non-cardiogenic 'neurogenic' pulmonary oedema with normal wedge pressure; resulting hypoxia amplifies neurological injury (p.392).
Premenopausal women are far more likely than men to develop encephalopathy and severe neurological sequelae (p.392).

Overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia (>8-10 mM in 24 h or >18 mM in 48 h) risks osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS), classically central pontine myelinolysis — presenting days later with para-/quadriparesis, dysphagia, dysarthria, diplopia, 'locked-in' syndrome, or reduced consciousness (p.393).
ODS can occur even with appropriately slow correction in high-risk patients: alcoholism, malnutrition, hypokalaemia, and liver transplantation (p.393).
Plasma Na+ <125 mM is the threshold at which chronic hyponatraemia commonly becomes overtly symptomatic (nausea, vomiting, confusion, seizures) (p.392).

Iatrogenic settings for acute hyponatraemia: postoperative premenopausal women given hypotonic fluids, glycine irrigation (TURP/uterine surgery), colonoscopy prep, recent thiazide initiation (Table 56-2, p.392).
MDMA ('Ecstasy'/'Molly') causes potent thirst and AVP induction leading to severe acute hyponatraemia; exercise-associated (endurance/marathon) hyponatraemia is another acute setting (p.392).

By volume status: hypovolaemic (total body water down, total body Na+ down more), euvolaemic/no oedema (total body water up, Na+ near-normal), and hypervolaemic (total body water up markedly, Na+ up) — Fig. 56-5, p.391. By chronicity: acute hyponatraemia is <48 h (osmolyte extrusion incomplete, higher cerebral-oedema risk) and chronic is >48 h (osmolytes largely extruded, lower acute symptom risk but higher ODS risk on correction), p.392. By tonicity: true hypotonic hyponatraemia has effective osmolality <275 mOsm/kg, distinct from pseudohyponatraemia (normal/high tonicity) and hyperglycaemic translocational hyponatraemia, p.393. Symptomatic threshold for chronic disease is generally plasma Na+ <125 mM (p.392). SIAD diagnostic features include euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia, inappropriately concentrated urine (urine osmolality typically >400 mOsm/kg / not maximally dilute), urine Na+ >30 mM, low serum uric acid (<4 mg/dL), and absence of thyroid/adrenal dysfunction, diuretics, hypovolaemia or hypervolaemia (p.391, p.393).

chunks.text: Hypovolemic shock arises when a fall in intravascular volume reduces preload, lowering stroke volume and cardiac output and therefore systemic oxygen delivery; CVP and PCWP are low and systemic vascular resistance rises as a compensatory response (p.2311). Inadequate oxygen delivery forces cells into anaerobic metabolism, so pyruvate is converted to lactate with markedly less ATP generation; failure of ATP-dependent ion pumps disrupts ionic and pH homeostasis, and calcium influx activates phospholipases/proteases causing cell swelling and death, with leaked intracellular contents driving inflammation and microvascular injury (p.2310). In acute haemorrhage, hypovolaemia dominates first and threatens high-flow organs (brain, kidneys); the haemoglobin is initially normal and only falls over hours as fluid shifts from the extravascular to the intravascular space (haemodilution), so the haematocrit does not reflect the volume lost early on (pp.850-851).

chunks.text: IBD is a chronic idiopathic inflammatory disease of the GI tract regarded as a dysregulated, inappropriate immune response to the endogenous commensal microbiota (with or without an autoimmune component) in a genetically susceptible host. Homeostasis among the gut microbiota, intestinal epithelial cells, and mucosal immune system is normally maintained by regulatory pathways (e.g., FoxP3 T-regulatory cells); environmental factors (smoking, antibiotics, enteropathogens, diet) acting on genetic susceptibility (>240 GWAS loci, ~20% of risk explained; rare single-gene defects such as IL10/IL10R in very-early-onset disease) disrupt this balance and produce sustained inflammation. UC is a mucosal/superficial-submucosal disease, while Crohn's is transmural with fissuring and fistula/stricture formation (p.2551-2556).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.337 (Inflammatory Bowel Disease), p.2551-2564

chunks.text: UC inflammation is continuous from the rectum proximally without skip areas, whereas Crohn's is segmental with skip lesions and frequently spares the rectum; this distribution difference is a key way to separate the two (p.2555-2556).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.337 (Inflammatory Bowel Disease), p.2551-2564

chunks.text: Granulomas (noncaseating, in all bowel-wall layers) are characteristic of Crohn's but are found less often on mucosal biopsy than on surgical resection specimens, so their absence does not exclude Crohn's (p.2556).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.337 (Inflammatory Bowel Disease), p.2551-2564

chunks.text: On biopsy, distorted/branching crypt architecture and basal plasmacytosis/lymphoid aggregates indicate chronicity and help distinguish IBD from acute self-limited or infectious colitis (p.2556).

chunks.text: Toxic megacolon occurs rarely; about 50% of acute dilations resolve with conservative management, but those that do not require urgent colectomy. Perforation complicating toxic megacolon carries ~15% mortality. Risk of colorectal cancer rises with duration and extent of colitis (historically ~2% at 10 yr, 8% at 20 yr, 18% at 30 yr, though rates have fallen with better inflammation control and surveillance; still ~1.5-2x the general population). Extensive long-standing colitis carries the highest cancer risk. Strictures occur in ~5% of UC patients. Up to one-third of IBD patients develop at least one extraintestinal manifestation (p.2557-2563, p.2570).

chunks.text: Montreal classification of UC severity (Harrison Table 337-4, p.2557): S0 clinical remission (no symptoms); S1 mild = up to 4 stools/day +/- blood, no systemic illness, normal ESR; S2 moderate = 4 or more stools/day with minimal systemic toxicity; S3 severe = 6 or more bloody stools/day plus pulse >=90/min, temperature >=37.5 C, haemoglobin <10.5 g/dL, and ESR >=30 mm/h. (These severe-disease physiologic thresholds mirror the classic Truelove-Witts criteria for acute severe colitis.) Montreal extent: E1 proctitis, E2 left-sided (distal to splenic flexure), E3 extensive/pancolitis. Crohn's is categorised by the Vienna/Montreal classification (Table 337-5, p.2558) by age at diagnosis (A), location ileal/colonic/ileocolonic/upper (L), and behaviour nonstricturing-nonpenetrating/stricturing/penetrating (B) with a perianal modifier.

IBS is a multifactorial functional bowel disorder with no structural lesion. Proposed mechanisms include altered GI motor activity (e.g., exaggerated postprandial and distention-evoked colonic contractions, increased high-amplitude propagating contractions with rapid transit in IBS-D), visceral hypersensitivity (lower thresholds to rectal balloon distention with sparing of somatic pain pathways), and disordered brain-gut interaction with central neural dysregulation (greater activation of mid-cingulate and prefrontal cortices on functional imaging). Psychological factors (anxiety, depression, somatization, prior physical/sexual abuse) modulate pain thresholds, and genetic factors such as serotonin transporter (SERT) polymorphisms are implicated. Peripheral contributors include low-grade mucosal immune activation with mast cells, lymphocytes and proinflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-1beta, TNF), upregulated TRPV1 sensory channels, increased intestinal permeability ('leaky gut', chiefly in IBS-D and post-infectious IBS), gut dysbiosis (reduced microbial diversity, fewer Bifidobacterium/Faecalibacterium, more Enterobacteriaceae), abnormal serotonin pathways with increased enterochromaffin-cell serotonin in IBS-D, and bile acid malabsorption in up to ~25% of IBS-D.

Rome IV makes IBS a positive symptom-based diagnosis, not purely one of exclusion: recurrent abdominal pain on average at least 1 day/week over the prior 3 months plus at least two of being related to defecation, a change in stool frequency, or a change in stool form, with onset at least 6 months earlier.
Rome IV is stricter than Rome III: it requires pain at least weekly and dropped 'discomfort' as a qualifying symptom; painless diarrhoea or constipation alone does NOT meet criteria.
Abdominal pain is mandatory for the diagnosis; it is typically episodic and crampy, often worsened by eating or emotional stress and relieved by passing flatus or stool.

Subtype by predominant stool form: IBS-C (constipation), IBS-D (diarrhoea), and IBS-M (mixed) — but subtypes are unstable, with about three-quarters of patients changing subtype and ~29% switching between IBS-C and IBS-D over a year.
Onset is usually before age 45 and IBS is two to three times more common in women, who make up ~80% of severe cases.

Symptoms commonly overlap with other functional disorders (fibromyalgia, headache, backache, genitourinary symptoms) and with functional dyspepsia, suggesting a shared, more extensive digestive disorder.

Bloating and a subjective sense of excess gas are common, but most patients actually generate a normal volume of intestinal gas and instead have impaired gas transit/tolerance and proximal reflux of gas.
Malnutrition is exceedingly rare in IBS and the pain almost always occurs only during waking hours, so sleep disruption from pain is unusual.

Treating IBS as a diagnosis of exclusion only and over-investigating: few tests are needed when symptoms are typical and alarm features are absent, and unnecessary investigations may be costly and even harmful.

Missing organic disease in higher-risk patients: older age, rapidly progressive symptoms, or alarm features should prompt a thorough work-up to exclude IBD, coeliac disease and colorectal cancer rather than labelling as IBS.
Attributing bloating to excess gas when most patients produce a normal gas volume but have impaired gas transit.
Over-interpreting an abnormal hydrogen breath test, which can be positive simply from rapid small-bowel transit and does not reliably predict treatment response.

chunks.text: Hypertensive ICH usually results from spontaneous rupture of a small (~30-100 microns) penetrating artery deep in the brain, with chronic hypertension producing vascular injury preferentially at the basal ganglia (especially putamen), thalamus, cerebellum and pons. The clot may stay small or enlarge to compress adjacent tissue and cause herniation; dissection into the ventricles markedly increases morbidity and can produce hydrocephalus. Most hypertensive bleeds evolve over 30-90 minutes, whereas anticoagulant-related bleeds may keep expanding for 24-48 h. By ~48 h macrophages begin phagocytosing the haemorrhage at its surface, and over 1-6 months it resolves to a slit-like glial-scarred cavity with haemosiderin-laden macrophages. In cerebral amyloid angiopathy, arteriolar degeneration with amyloid deposition in cortical vessel walls causes single and recurrent lobar haemorrhages, the commonest cause of lobar bleeding in the elderly (p.3453-3454).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.439, p.3452-3456

chunks.text: ICH typically presents as abrupt-onset focal deficit; compared with ischaemic stroke, headache is more common, but imaging is still required to distinguish the two (p.3453).

chunks.text: Putaminal haemorrhage damages the adjacent internal capsule, so contralateral hemiparesis is the sentinel sign, often with the eyes deviated away from the side of the weakness (p.3454).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.439, p.3452-3456

chunks.text: Thalamic haemorrhage produces a prominent all-modality contralateral sensory deficit and characteristic ocular signs from inferior extension into the upper midbrain (e.g. eyes deviated down-and-in 'looking at the nose', poorly reactive unequal pupils, vertical-gaze palsy) (p.3454).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.439, p.3452-3456

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.439, p.3452-3456

chunks.text: Cerebellar haemorrhage classically gives occipital headache, repeated vomiting and gait ataxia; in mild cases gait ataxia may be the only sign (p.3454).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.439, p.3452-3456

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.439, p.3452-3456

chunks.text: Lumbar puncture is generally unnecessary and should usually be avoided in ICH because focal signs and raised ICP make it potentially herniation-inducing (p.3455).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.439, p.3452-3456

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.439, p.3452-3456

chunks.text: Cerebellar haemorrhage can deteriorate precipitously from brainstem compression or obstructive hydrocephalus; immediate surgical evacuation before severe brainstem compression may be lifesaving, and hydrocephalus from a cerebellar haematoma should generally be managed by definitive evacuation rather than ventricular drainage alone (p.3454).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.439, p.3452-3456

chunks.text: Haemorrhage outside the typical deep hypertensive sites, or in a non-hypertensive patient, should prompt a search for other causes (amyloid angiopathy, tumour, vascular malformation, vasculitis, coagulopathy) rather than being assumed hypertensive (p.3454).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.439, p.3452-3456

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.439, p.3452-3456

chunks.text: Overall, about 35-45% of patients die within the first month, and roughly 40% with a hypertensive ICH die, though survivors can achieve good to complete recovery because peri-haematoma tissue is displaced rather than infarcted and often regains function as the clot resorbs over months. The validated ICH Score stratifies mortality and outcome but should not be used to precisely prognosticate an individual, since withholding early aggressive care risks a self-fulfilling prophecy of poor outcome. Deep pontine haemorrhage with coma usually ends in death or a locked-in state, but small bleeds are compatible with survival; in cerebellar haemorrhage, full recovery is common if the deep cerebellar nuclei are spared (p.3453-3456).

chunks.text: ILDs are characterised by remodelling of the interstitium with variable degrees of inflammation and fibrosis, but alveolar epithelial and endothelial cell injury is also central to pathogenesis. The idiopathic interstitial pneumonias (IIPs) are the most common group. In IPF the histologic hallmark is a usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern: subpleural reticulation with honeycomb change and fibroblast foci (subepithelial collections of myofibroblasts and collagen) alternating with preserved normal alveolar architecture, producing temporal and spatial heterogeneity. NSIP shows more uniform interstitial inflammation and fibrosis with honeycombing usually absent and fibroblast foci rare. Genetic studies show that a substantial fraction of familial and even sporadic/idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis has a genetic basis: a MUC5B promoter variant (present in ~20% of Caucasians, 35-45% of IPF patients) confers an approximately sixfold risk, and variants in telomere-length genes (TERT, TERC, RTEL1) and surfactant protein genes (SFTPA2) are also implicated. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is an immune-mediated response to inhaled antigens small enough to reach distal airways and alveoli, driven by dysregulated TH1/TH17 responses with precipitating IgG and innate (Toll-like receptor/MyD88) signalling; chronic HP shares the MUC5B variant with IPF (pp.2259-2266; 2228-2229).

chunks.text: Prognosis varies widely by ILD subtype and disease extent. IPF carries a poor prognosis (~50% survival at 3-5 years; pre-antifibrotic-era life expectancy 3-5 years from diagnosis). Idiopathic NSIP is comparatively favourable (>80% 5-year survival), with cellular NSIP doing better than fibrosing NSIP. Reported subtype mortality includes RB-ILD ~25% at 7 years and systemic sclerosis-associated ILD ~20-30% at 10 years; sarcoidosis mortality is generally low but state-dependent. RB-ILD usually has prolonged survival with death from progressive ILD rare. AIP has >50% 6-month mortality with frequent recurrences, though survivors can recover substantial lung function. Acute exacerbations of fibrotic ILD carry very high mortality (>85%). In CTD-ILD, a UIP pattern and more extensive fibrosis (e.g. in RA) predict reduced survival. Chronic fibrotic HP can mirror IPF in radiology and prognosis (pp.2260, 2262-2266; 2229).

chunks.text: Harrison frames ILD pattern recognition rather than a single numeric severity score. ILDs are first split into known cause (occupational e.g. asbestosis/silicosis; drug-induced e.g. amiodarone, nitrofurantoin, methotrexate, bleomycin; systemic/CTD-associated; granulomatous including HP) versus unknown cause (idiopathic interstitial pneumonias, plus rarer entities such as LAM, PAP, PLCH, sarcoidosis). The idiopathic interstitial pneumonias are further classified (per the ATS/ERS consensus) into chronic fibrosing (IPF, idiopathic NSIP), smoking-related (RB-ILD, DIP), and acute/subacute (COP, acute interstitial pneumonia, lymphocytic interstitial pneumonia). The UIP pattern (subpleural, basal reticulation with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis) defines IPF, while NSIP shows more ground-glass and rare honeycombing. HP is now classified as nonfibrotic versus fibrotic (replacing the older acute/subacute/chronic terminology). Disease severity is gauged by extent of fibrosis/honeycombing on HRCT, degree of PFT (FVC/DLCO) impairment and its rate of decline, and presence of pulmonary hypertension/cor pulmonale (pp.2259-2266; 2229).

chunks.text: Acute occlusion of an intracranial artery reduces regional cerebral blood flow; the resulting deficit depends on collateral supply, occlusion site, and systemic pressure. Energy failure from loss of glucose and oxygen halts ATP-dependent ion pumps, causing depolarization, sodium and calcium influx, excess synaptic glutamate, and excitotoxicity with reactive oxygen species that damage membranes and DNA, followed by an innate inflammatory response. Fever and hyperglycaemia (glucose >200 mg/dL) worsen the injury. Mechanistically, ischemic stroke arises by three routes (the basis of TOAST-style classification): (1) embolic occlusion of a large intracranial vessel - either cardioembolic (e.g., atrial fibrillation, mural thrombus, valvular disease) or artery-to-artery from carotid/aortic-arch plaque; (2) in-situ thrombosis of small penetrating arteries from lipohyalinosis or microatheroma, producing lacunar (small-vessel) infarcts; and (3) hypoperfusion from flow-limiting stenosis of a major extracranial or intracranial vessel, producing watershed/border-zone ischemia. Cardioembolism causes ~20%, large-artery/carotid atherosclerosis ~10%, and small-vessel disease ~20% of ischemic strokes (p.3439, p.3443-3446).

chunks.text: Stroke is the second leading cause of death worldwide; outcome hinges on time to reperfusion ('time-is-brain'). For large-vessel occlusion, the chance of a good outcome falls steeply with delay - the odds of a good result exceed 3 if groin puncture for thrombectomy is within 2 h but fall to about 2 by 8 h, and over 80% do well if the vessel opens within 1 h of arrival versus about one-third at 6 h. In pooled thrombectomy trials ~46% achieved functional independence (modified Rankin 0-2) versus ~26.5% with medical care, with a mortality benefit. Small-vessel (lacunar) strokes generally recover more rapidly and completely than large-vessel strokes, though some stutter or leave severe disability. Without secondary prevention the annual risk of a further stroke after atherothrombotic stroke/TIA is about 8-10%; symptomatic intracranial atherosclerosis and untreated symptomatic carotid stenosis each carry ~15% per year. Care in a dedicated stroke unit followed by rehabilitation improves neurologic outcome and reduces mortality (p.3427, p.3441-3442, p.3445-3446).

chunks.text: Severity is graded clinically by the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS). A disabling deficit (NIHSS >5) flags potential eligibility for thrombolysis/endovascular therapy, whereas minor non-disabling stroke (NIHSS 0-5) may be managed with aspirin or short-term dual antiplatelet therapy. Mechanism-based (TOAST-style) classification - cardioembolic, large-artery atherosclerosis (carotid/intracranial), small-vessel/lacunar, other defined cause, and cryptogenic (~30%) - drives secondary prevention. Carotid disease is further classed as symptomatic vs asymptomatic and by degree of stenosis, with risk rising with stenosis severity except for near-occlusions, which carry lower risk (p.3440-3441, p.3443, p.3445).

chunks.text: ITP results from immune-mediated destruction of antibody-coated platelets by the reticuloendothelial system, and possibly impaired platelet release from megakaryocytes. Primary ITP has no identifiable cause; secondary ITP is associated with an underlying disorder such as autoimmune disease (notably SLE) or infection (HIV, hepatitis C). Childhood ITP commonly follows a viral infection through immune mechanisms and usually resolves spontaneously (Harrison 22e p.922, p.924).

chunks.text: Lung cancer arises from respiratory epithelium (bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli). Environmental carcinogens, chiefly tobacco smoke, drive transformation of bronchoepithelial cells, modulated by polymorphisms in carcinogen-metabolising genes (e.g. CYP1A1). Cancers accumulate gain-of-function oncogene mutations and loss-of-function tumour-suppressor mutations; allelic loss on chromosome 3p occurs very early, even in histologically normal smoke-damaged epithelium. NSCLC adenocarcinomas are frequently driven by targetable oncogenic alterations (EGFR ~10-35%, KRAS ~15-25%, ALK rearrangement 3-7%, plus BRAF, HER2, MET, RET, ROS1, NTRK), whereas nearly 90% of SCLCs carry TP53 and RB1 mutations. Clinical manifestations stem from the primary lesion, local/regional invasion, distant metastases, or paraneoplastic syndromes. Paraneoplastic endocrine effects reflect ectopic hormone secretion: PTH-related peptide (squamous cell) causing hypercalcaemia, ADH or atrial natriuretic peptide (SCLC) causing hyponatraemia, and ectopic ACTH (SCLC, pulmonary carcinoids) causing Cushing-type biochemistry. (p.615-619)

chunks.text: Outcome is closely tied to stage at diagnosis, but over half of patients present with locally advanced or metastatic disease. In NSCLC, about 15% have localised disease amenable to curative surgery or radiotherapy, roughly a quarter have local/regional disease that may or may not be curable, and about half have metastatic disease at diagnosis. SEER data (2022) show a 5-year survival of about 63% for localised disease. Extrathoracic metastases are found at autopsy in >50% of squamous, ~80% of adenocarcinoma/large-cell, and >95% of SCLC cases. SCLC is highly likely to present extensive-stage (60-70%). Adenocarcinoma pattern carries prognostic weight: lepidic-predominant is favourable, acinar/papillary intermediate, and solid or micropapillary poor; adenocarcinoma in situ and minimally invasive adenocarcinoma achieve essentially 100% 5-year disease-free survival after complete resection. Weight loss >10%, and thrombotic disease complicating cancer, are poor prognostic signs. (p.616, p.619, p.621-622)

chunks.text: NSCLC: TNM (8th edition, effective 2018; 9th edition expected 2024). T by size/invasion - T1 <=3cm (T1a <=1, T1b >1-2, T1c >2-3), T2 >3-5cm or visceral pleura/main bronchus/atelectasis (T2a >3-4, T2b >4-5), T3 >5-7cm or chest wall/pericardium/phrenic nerve invasion or same-lobe satellite nodule, T4 >7cm or invasion of mediastinum/heart/great vessels/trachea/oesophagus/spine/carina or different ipsilateral-lobe nodule. N: N0 none, N1 ipsilateral peribronchial/hilar/intrapulmonary, N2 ipsilateral mediastinal/subcarinal, N3 contralateral mediastinal/hilar or any scalene/supraclavicular. M: M1a contralateral-lobe nodule or pleural/pericardial nodule/malignant effusion, M1b single distant metastasis to one organ, M1c multiple metastases. SCLC: dual classification recommended - the Veterans Administration two-stage system (limited-stage = confined to ipsilateral hemithorax within a tolerable radiation port, including contralateral supraclavicular nodes, recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement and SVC obstruction; extensive-stage = overt metastatic disease, or cardiac tamponade/malignant effusion/bilateral parenchymal involvement) plus the TNM system, with TNM preferred for the rare apparent stage I SCLC. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma - nodal and extranodal disease; B symptoms part of staging (Harrison 22e p.860)
Acute or chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (can produce generalised adenopathy and constitutional symptoms) (Harrison 22e p.476)
Richter transformation of CLL - rapidly progressive focal adenopathy with night sweats, fever, weight loss and high LDH (Harrison 22e p.897)
Metastatic carcinoma to nodes (head/neck, lung, breast, thyroid, GI primaries) (Harrison 22e p.477)
Germ-cell tumour (retroperitoneal nodes in young men) (Harrison 22e p.477)
Occult solid tumours presenting with involuntary weight loss - GI/hepatobiliary, lung, breast, genitourinary, ovarian, prostate (Harrison 22e p.317)
Infectious mononucleosis (EBV or CMV) - generalised adenopathy with constitutional symptoms (Harrison 22e p.476)
Tuberculosis - can cause unilateral mediastinal adenopathy and mesenteric lymphadenitis mimicking lymphoma, with night sweats and weight loss (Harrison 22e p.477)
Histoplasmosis - unilateral paratracheal node involvement that can mimic lymphoma in endemic regions (Harrison 22e p.477)
Toxoplasmosis - generalised reactive adenopathy (Harrison 22e p.476)
HIV / AIDS - generalised lymphadenopathy and a recognised lymphoma risk factor (Harrison 22e p.476, p.903)

Excisional biopsy of the largest abnormal node is preferred; fine-needle aspiration should NOT be the first procedure as it usually yields insufficient tissue and delays diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.478)
Age/sex/risk-appropriate cancer screening (e.g. faecal occult blood, colonoscopy, mammography) and abdominal ultrasound in occult-malignancy weight-loss workup (Harrison 22e p.318)
Serum protein electrophoresis to detect a monoclonal paraprotein (Harrison 22e p.903)
Serum beta2-microglobulin and LDH - independent prognostic markers in NHL (Harrison 22e p.903)
CBC with differential, comprehensive metabolic/liver panel, uric acid and calcium (Harrison 22e p.317, p.904)
ESR and CRP as part of the constitutional-symptom / weight-loss workup (Harrison 22e p.316, p.869)
Contrast CT of chest/abdomen/pelvis for staging; FDG-PET/CT preferred for aggressive lymphomas and Hodgkin lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.904)
Bone marrow biopsy where indicated; lumbar puncture if CNS-risk histology or neurologic features (Harrison 22e p.903-904)
HIV and hepatitis B and C serology - risk factors for NHL and relevant to hepatitis B reactivation risk (Harrison 22e p.904)
Cervical node ultrasound long-to-short axis ratio (<2.0 favours malignancy) where head/neck cancer is suspected (Harrison 22e p.478)
Sarcoidosis - mediastinal/hilar adenopathy and constitutional symptoms (Harrison 22e p.477)
Systemic lupus erythematosus and mixed connective tissue disease - generalised adenopathy (Harrison 22e p.476)
Drug-induced (phenytoin/diphenylhydantoin and others) lymphadenopathy, including DRESS/DIHS with eosinophilia and extensive adenopathy (Harrison 22e p.193, p.476)
Castleman disease, Kikuchi histiocytic necrotizing lymphadenitis, Rosai-Dorfman disease, angioimmunoblastic lymphadenopathy, IgG4-related disease (Harrison 22e p.476)

B symptoms in lymphoma are cytokine-mediated systemic effects of the tumour rather than direct mass effects. In classical Hodgkin lymphoma the malignant Hodgkin/Reed-Sternberg cells are rare within a tumour mass that is largely a polyclonal inflammatory infiltrate reacting to tumour-derived cytokines; this inflammatory milieu drives constitutional symptoms and contributes to the generalised immune suppression seen in these patients. Involuntary weight loss in malignancy reflects a combination of anorexia, sarcopenia and a cytokine-driven cachexia syndrome. (Harrison 22e p.316, p.869)

B symptoms are formally defined for lymphoma staging (the Ann Arbor 'B' suffix) as unexplained fever (>38C), drenching night sweats, and/or unexplained weight loss exceeding 10% of body weight over the 6 months before diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.861, p.869).

Half of all cancer patients lose some weight and up to 20% of cancer deaths are attributable directly to cachexia; malignancy that declares itself through marked weight loss generally carries a poor prognosis (Harrison 22e p.317).
The tempo of symptoms helps separate aggressive from indolent lymphoma: rapid symptomatic progression and the presence of B symptoms suggest a more aggressive process (Harrison 22e p.903).
Among malignancies, lymphoma is by far the commonest cause of malignancy-related fever of unknown origin, and the fever can precede any palpable lymphadenopathy (Harrison 22e p.193).

About one-third of patients with classical Hodgkin lymphoma present with B symptoms; Hodgkin disease can even present as a fever of unknown origin, more often in older patients with abdominal mixed-cellularity disease (Harrison 22e p.869).
Pel-Ebstein fever (cyclical fever lasting days to weeks alternating with afebrile intervals) is a rare but classic Hodgkin lymphoma presentation (Harrison 22e p.869).

Node character matters: lymphomatous nodes tend to be large, firm, rubbery, mobile, symmetric and non-tender, whereas metastatic carcinoma nodes are typically hard, non-tender and fixed to surrounding tissue (Harrison 22e p.477).

Supraclavicular and scalene node enlargement is always abnormal and warrants prompt evaluation; a left supraclavicular node (Virchow node) classically reflects a gastrointestinal primary, but lung, breast, testis and ovarian cancers also seed these nodes (Harrison 22e p.477).

Examination in suspected lymphoma should systematically cover all peripheral nodal sites plus Waldeyer ring, liver and spleen size, effusions/ascites, and testicular, breast or skin involvement, since any of these can change staging and management (Harrison 22e p.903).

Enlarged intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal nodes are usually malignant (lymphoma, or germ-cell tumour in young men), in contrast to the largely benign causes of cervical adenopathy (Harrison 22e p.477).

Do NOT give glucocorticoids for undiagnosed lymphadenopathy - their lympholytic effect can obscure lymphoma, leukaemia and Castleman disease and delay/disrupt diagnosis (the rare exception is life-threatening pharyngeal obstruction from Waldeyer-ring tissue in mononucleosis) (Harrison 22e p.521).

Fine-needle aspiration is inadequate for an initial lymphoma diagnosis - obtain an excisional/core biopsy; FNA is reserved for thyroid nodules and confirming relapse of a known cancer (Harrison 22e p.478).
Antibiotics are NOT indicated for lymphadenopathy unless there is strong evidence of bacterial infection (Harrison 22e p.521).
Localized-versus-generalized adenopathy has limited discriminatory value because many causes produce either pattern; do not over-rely on it (Harrison 22e p.476).

In primary care most lymphadenopathy is benign (>two-thirds nonspecific/URI, <1% malignant) and needs only short-interval follow-up - but persistent or enlarging nodes must be re-evaluated and biopsied (Harrison 22e p.476, p.521).
If a head-and-neck primary is suspected behind a solitary cervical node, perform a careful ENT exam and biopsy any suspicious mucosal lesion first before excising the node (Harrison 22e p.478).

Lymphoma prognosis is stage- and biology-dependent. For NHL the International Prognostic Index uses five factors (age >=60, elevated LDH, ECOG performance status >=2, Ann Arbor stage III/IV, and >1 extranodal site); for DLBCL treated with R-CHOP, 0 factors gives ~94% 4-year survival versus ~53% with 3-5 factors. Across lymphomas, decreased outcome is associated with B symptoms, advanced stage, elevated LDH and bulky disease (e.g. lymph-node mass >7 cm). In occult solid malignancy, presentation through significant involuntary weight loss generally carries a very poor prognosis, whereas when no cause is found after thorough workup the prognosis is comparatively favourable. (Harrison 22e p.317, p.861, NHL prognosis section)
Supraclavicular or scalene adenopathy - always abnormal, biopsy promptly (Harrison 22e p.477-478)
Solitary hard non-tender cervical node in an older tobacco user - prompt biopsy after ENT mucosal assessment (Harrison 22e p.478)
Node size >2 cm with an abnormal chest x-ray in younger patients - predicts malignant/granulomatous biopsy yield (Harrison 22e p.521)
Hard fixed nodes, or firm mobile generalised adenopathy suggestive of lymphoma (Harrison 22e p.478)
Airway, oesophageal or SVC compression from thoracic adenopathy (cough/wheeze, hoarseness, dysphagia, facial/arm/neck swelling) (Harrison 22e p.520)
Enlarged intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal nodes (usually malignant) (Harrison 22e p.477)
Involuntary weight loss >=5% over 6 months prompting structured malignancy workup (Harrison 22e p.358)

Ann Arbor staging (stages I-IV) with suffix A (no systemic symptoms) or B (presence of B symptoms: fever >38C, drenching night sweats, or weight loss >10% body weight over preceding 6 months); suffix E for localized extralymphatic extension. B-symptom status (the A/B designation) and stage drive prognosis and therapy. (Harrison 22e p.861, p.869)
Imaging directed to site
Biopsy/histology
LDH, blood film
