chunks.text: Intestinal ischaemia occurs when splanchnic perfusion fails to meet the bowel's metabolic demand, producing ischaemic tissue injury. The gut is supplied by the celiac artery, SMA and IMA with extensive collateralisation between major trunks and mesenteric arcades; protective responses include this collateral network, autoregulation of flow and the ability to increase oxygen extraction. Watershed colonic zones with inherently lower flow are Griffiths' point (splenic flexure) and Sudeck's point (descending/sigmoid colon), the commonest sites of colonic ischaemia. The splanchnic bed can receive up to 30% of cardiac output. Occlusive ischaemia results from an embolus or progressive thrombosis in a major mesenteric artery (over 75% of emboli are cardiac in origin and lodge in the SMA distal to the middle colic artery). Chronic intestinal angina generally requires progressive stenosis of two of the three major vessels. Non-occlusive ischaemia is driven by disproportionate mesenteric arteriolar vasospasm in response to severe physiological stress such as shock; untreated, early mucosal stress ulceration progresses to full-thickness injury. Mesenteric venous thrombosis is usually precipitated by a hypercoagulable state. (p.2587-2588)

source.page: Harrison 22e p.2586-2589 (Chapter 340, Mesenteric Vascular Insufficiency)

chunks.text: Severe, acute, non-remitting abdominal pain that is strikingly out of proportion to physical findings is the most common complaint in arterial acute mesenteric ischaemia, present in about 95% of cases; pain precedes signs because ischaemia begins in the mucosa and progresses outward to the serosa (p.2588).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.2586-2589 (Chapter 340, Mesenteric Vascular Insufficiency)

chunks.text: About half of acute mesenteric ischaemia cases are embolic, lodging in the mid-to-distal SMA just past the middle colic artery origin; emboli commonly arise from atrial fibrillation, recent MI, soft atherosclerotic plaque, infective endocarditis, valvular heart disease, or recent cardiac/vascular catheterisation (p.2587).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.2586-2589 (Chapter 340, Mesenteric Vascular Insufficiency)

chunks.text: Acute-on-chronic thrombotic ischaemia (about 25-30% of cases) occurs at sites of severe atherosclerotic narrowing of the SMA or celiac artery, typically in patients with pre-existing mesenteric atherosclerosis who may have had prior chronic mesenteric ischaemia (p.2587, 2588).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.2586-2589 (Chapter 340, Mesenteric Vascular Insufficiency)

chunks.text: Embolic disease is suggested by older patients with a predisposing cardiac source (AF, prior embolic event, recent infective endocarditis), whereas thrombotic disease suggests underlying atherosclerosis with possible prior intestinal angina (p.2588).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.2586-2589 (Chapter 340, Mesenteric Vascular Insufficiency)

chunks.text: Chronic mesenteric ischaemia classically presents as recurrent dull, crampy, postprandial epigastric pain ('intestinal angina') with fear of eating and weight loss; chronic diarrhoea may occur and symptoms typically last 6-12 months before diagnosis (p.2587-2588).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.2586-2589 (Chapter 340, Mesenteric Vascular Insufficiency)

chunks.text: Mesenteric venous thrombosis tends to present more vaguely and subacutely with non-specific abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, distension, mild-to-moderate tenderness and dehydration, making it easy to under-recognise (p.2589).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.2586-2589 (Chapter 340, Mesenteric Vascular Insufficiency)

chunks.text: The decision to operate in suspected acute mesenteric ischaemia is often based on a high index of suspicion from history and examination despite normal laboratory results (p.2588).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.2586-2589 (Chapter 340, Mesenteric Vascular Insufficiency)

chunks.text: Treating pain out of proportion to examination as benign — early ischaemia produces severe pain with deceptively unremarkable abdominal signs because injury starts in the mucosa (p.2588).

source.page: Harrison 22e p.2586-2589 (Chapter 340, Mesenteric Vascular Insufficiency)

chunks.text: Waiting for abnormal labs before acting — lactate and acidosis are late and may be normal in reversible ischaemia or even necrosis; the operative decision is often made on clinical suspicion despite normal results (p.2588-2589).

chunks.text: Acute mesenteric ischaemia carries a high mortality, roughly 50-80% at presentation (with the acute arterial form quoted at over 50%); it is one of the most challenging diagnoses, and the single most important determinant of survival is the timeliness of diagnosis and treatment. Endovascular stenting for chronic mesenteric ischaemia has about an 80% long-term success rate. (p.2587-2588)

chunks.text: Harrison classifies intestinal ischaemia into chronic mesenteric ischaemia (CMI) and acute mesenteric ischaemia (AMI). Acute mesenteric vascular insufficiency is subdivided into (1) arterio-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia — further split into arterial embolus (~50%) and arterial thrombosis (~25-30%, often acute-on-chronic), (2) non-occlusive/vasospastic mesenteric ischaemia (~20%, vasospasm or hypoperfusion), and (3) mesenteric venous thrombosis (<10%). Ischaemic colitis mucosal injury is graded as mild (minimal erythema), moderate (pale ulceration extending into muscularis), or severe (black/green discoloration with full-thickness necrosis). (p.2587-2589)

chunks.text: Delirium reflects diffuse rather than focal brain dysfunction; the attentional deficit localizes broadly to brainstem, thalamus, prefrontal cortex and parietal lobes, and most cases arise from widespread cortical and subcortical disturbance rather than a single lesion. Acetylcholine deficiency is thought to be central (explaining the potency of anticholinergic drugs), with additional roles for excess dopamine, proinflammatory mediators and individual susceptibility. The concept is that of an insult acting on a vulnerable, low-reserve brain. For most metabolic causes (hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hyperosmolarity, hypercapnia, hypercalcaemia, hepatic and renal failure) the brain shows little or no structural damage and the effects are largely reversible, attributed to impaired energy supply, altered ion fluxes across neuronal membranes and neurotransmitter abnormalities. In hepatic encephalopathy, raised ammonia is proposed to drive astrocytic glutamine synthesis and osmotic swelling, mitochondrial energy failure, reactive nitrogen/oxygen species, increased inhibitory GABA tone and 'false' neurotransmitters, with chronic disease producing diffuse astrocytosis. Uraemic encephalopathy is multifactorial (urea itself is not the cause): accumulated neurotoxins, catecholamine depletion, altered glutamate/GABA tone, raised brain calcium and blood-brain-barrier disruption. Importantly, the degree of neurologic change in metabolic encephalopathies depends heavily on the rapidity with which the serum derangement develops, not just its absolute level. In sepsis-associated encephalopathy, circulating inflammatory mediators (TNF, IL-1, IL-2, IL-6) appear to cause diffuse cerebral dysfunction that is not simply explained by the metabolic derangements of organ failure (p.183, p.188-189, p.2348-2349).

chunks.text: Delirium is an acute, relatively rapid decline in cognition (hours to days) that characteristically fluctuates; the cardinal neuropsychological deficit is inattention, though memory, executive function, visuospatial skills and language are variably affected (p.181-182).

chunks.text: Once viewed as benign and transient, delirium is now recognized as a marker of serious illness with substantial morbidity and mortality: in-hospital mortality is roughly 25-33% (similar to sepsis), and delirious patients have about a fivefold higher mortality in the ensuing months versus matched non-delirious inpatients, plus longer stays, more nursing-home discharge, higher readmission and recurrent episodes. Most metabolic and toxic encephalopathies are reversible with no or minimal structural brain damage, and drug/toxin-induced coma typically resolves fully provided hypoxia or severe hypotension has not occurred. However, some episodes persist for weeks to months or longer, delirium can cause lasting cognitive decline, and lingering effects (ranging from amnesia for the episode to PTSD-like re-experiencing) are common. Sepsis-associated encephalopathy severe enough to cause coma carries a mortality approaching 50%, though this mainly reflects severity of the underlying critical illness rather than the encephalopathy itself (p.182, p.188-189, p.2349).

chunks.text: Migraine is understood as a brain disorder of sensory processing rather than a primary vascular disease. The characteristic sensory sensitivity is attributed to dysfunction of monoaminergic and other sensory-control systems in the brainstem and hypothalamus. The key nociceptive pathway is the trigeminovascular system: trigeminal innervation of large intracranial vessels and dura, with terminals that, when activated, release vasoactive neuropeptides - notably calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (PACAP) - at vascular terminals and within the trigeminal nucleus. Second-order neurons of the trigeminocervical complex (caudal trigeminal nucleus extending into the upper cervical dorsal horns, receiving C1-C2 input) decussate and project via the quintothalamic tract to ventrobasal and posterior thalamic nuclei, with additional projections to periaqueductal gray and hypothalamus that exert descending antinociceptive modulation; the dorsal raphe nucleus, locus coeruleus, parabrachial nucleus and rostroventromedial medulla are implicated in this modulation. Serotonin (5-HT) is involved - triptans are 5-HT1B/1D agonists (some also 5-HT1F) and ditans are selective 5-HT1F agonists - and dopamine contributes, with dopamine-receptor hypersensitivity in migraineurs. Functional imaging shows hypothalamic activation in the premonitory phase and persistent dorsolateral pontine (including locus coeruleus) activation during attacks and in chronic migraine, with lateralization correlating with the side of head pain. Genetic study of familial hemiplegic migraine implicates ion channels (CACNA1A/Cav2.1 P/Q calcium channel in FHM1 ~50%; ATP1A2 Na-K ATPase in FHM2 ~20%; SCN1A sodium channel in FHM3), suggesting altered membrane excitability predisposes to aura. The slowly advancing visual scotoma with luminous (fortification) edges is recognized as a marker of spreading cortical depression associated with migraine (p.3462-3464, p.3379).

chunks.text: Patients should understand that migraine is an inherited tendency to headache that can be modified and controlled by lifestyle measures and medication but not eradicated. Except on some occasions in women taking oral estrogens or contraceptives, migraine is not associated with serious or life-threatening illness (p.3464). Migraine is nonetheless the most common neurologic cause of disability worldwide (p.3462). Recognized complications (ICHD-3) include status migrainosus, persistent aura without infarction, migrainous infarction, and migraine aura-triggered seizure; migraine may also progress to chronic migraine (Table 441-1, p.3463). Overuse of acute analgesics can transform episodic migraine into refractory medication-overuse headache; many patients improve after withdrawal, though residual headache often persists reflecting the underlying primary disorder (p.115-116).

chunks.text: MS is an autoimmune CNS disease producing chronic inflammation, demyelination, gliosis (sclerotic plaques) and neuronal/axonal loss (p.3577). New lesions begin with perivenular cuffing by T cells and macrophages and blood-brain-barrier (BBB) disruption with a preserved vessel wall (unlike vasculitis); cytotoxic CD8 cells line the leading edge, B cells infiltrate, myelin-specific autoantibodies coat degenerating myelin, and complement is activated (p.3581). Sharply demarcated demyelination is the hallmark; axons are relatively spared early but can be destroyed in highly inflammatory lesions, and partial remyelination produces 'shadow plaques' (p.3581). Cumulative axonal/neuronal loss drives irreversible disability (up to ~70% of corticospinal axons lost in MS paraplegia) via demyelination-related loss of trophic support, ion-channel redistribution, and dying-back axonopathy (p.3581). Progressive MS features more diffuse microglial activation, chronic active (slowly expanding) plaques with microglia at a leading edge behind an intact BBB, cortical/subpial plaques poorly seen on MRI, and meningeal ectopic lymphoid follicles linked to subpial cortical demyelination (p.3581-3582). Physiologically, demyelination causes conduction block (hyperpolarization from exposed potassium channels) and conduction slowing; temperature and metabolic changes worsen block, explaining heat- and fever-related fluctuations (p.3582-3583). Susceptibility is polygenic with the strongest signal at HLA-DRB1*1501 (~10% of risk), and EBV seroconversion appears a near-universal prerequisite, plausibly via molecular mimicry between EBV peptides and myelin autoantigens (p.3580-3581).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: MS is defined by lesions disseminated in both time and space: plaques arise at different times and in anatomically separate CNS sites (p.3577).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Trigeminal neuralgia, hemifacial spasm, or glossopharyngeal neuralgia in a young patient, or with bilateral/atypical features or objective sensory loss, should raise suspicion of MS involving the cranial nerve root entry zone (p.3578).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Fatigue is experienced by most patients and is the leading cause of work-related disability in MS; depression affects about half of patients (p.3578).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: On MRI, MS plaques are oriented perpendicular to the ventricular surface (Dawson's fingers) reflecting perivenous demyelination; lesions >6 mm in the corpus callosum, periventricular white matter, brainstem, cerebellum, or cord are especially helpful diagnostically (p.3583).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: A central vein sign within plaques on susceptibility-weighted (T2*) imaging supports an MS diagnosis (p.3583).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Two or more discrete CSF oligoclonal bands not present in paired serum are found in >90% of MS patients; bands may be absent at onset and increase over time (p.3583).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Evoked potential abnormalities occur in 80-90% of MS patients; a marked latency delay (rather than reduced amplitude or distorted waveform) is what suggests demyelination, and EPs are most informative when testing a clinically uninvolved pathway (p.3583-3584).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Most MRI-visible lesions and most early disease activity in MS are clinically silent—bursts of focal inflammation on serial MRI far exceed the relapse rate (p.3583).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Even relapse-free RRMS patients undergo subtle 'silent progression,' and disability accumulation is now attributed mainly to progression independent of relapse activity (PIRA) rather than incomplete recovery from relapses (RAW), across RRMS, SPMS, and PPMS (p.3578-3580).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: A radiologically isolated syndrome (RIS) is incidental MRI evidence of MS in an asymptomatic person; clinically isolated syndrome (CIS) is a first demyelinating event at high risk for MS (p.3577-3580).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Typical onset is age 20-40 (slightly later in men); women are affected roughly three times as often as men (p.3577).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: The most common presenting symptoms are sensory loss (~37%) and optic neuritis (~36%), followed by limb weakness (~35%) and paresthesias (p.3577).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Optic neuritis usually causes monocular reduced acuity, dimness, and color desaturation, with periorbital pain worsened by eye movement and an afferent pupillary defect; uveitis is uncommon and should prompt thought of sarcoidosis or lymphoma (p.3577).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: A bilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia (impaired adduction with nystagmus of the abducting eye, from a medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion) is particularly suggestive of MS; related gaze findings include horizontal gaze palsy and the 'one-and-a-half' syndrome (p.3578).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Lhermitte's symptom is a neck-flexion-induced electric-shock sensation radiating down the spine/legs; it is not specific to MS and can occur with other cervical cord disease such as spondylosis (p.3578).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Uhthoff's symptom (heat sensitivity) is transient worsening of neurologic symptoms with elevated core temperature (hot shower, exercise, fever) and reflects temperature-dependent conduction block rather than a true new lesion (p.3578).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Exercise-induced weakness is characteristic; weakness is of upper-motor-neuron type with spasticity, hyperreflexia, and extensor plantar responses, though a tendon reflex can occasionally be lost if a plaque disrupts the afferent reflex arc (p.3578).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Paroxysmal symptoms (tonic spasms, paroxysmal dysarthria/ataxia, sensory bursts) are brief (10 s-2 min), frequent (5-40/day), without altered consciousness, and self-limited; they arise from spontaneous discharges at the edges of demyelinated plaques (p.3578).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Do not over-diagnose MS from a single isolated event or from MRI white-matter lesions alone - the diagnosis requires dissemination in space and time (clinical, MRI, or CSF evidence) per the McDonald criteria, and there is no single confirmatory test (p.3582-3583).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: A pseudoexacerbation from heat/fever/infection (Uhthoff phenomenon) can mimic a relapse but reflects transient conduction block, not a new lesion; treating it as a relapse with steroids is inappropriate (p.3578, 3585).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Failing to distinguish NMOSD, MOGAD, and GFAP autoimmunity from MS - clues are bilateral/severe optic neuritis, severe longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (>=3 vertebral segments), brain MRI lesions that are non-destructive/cloud-like and can fully resolve, and CSF pleocytosis greater than in MS with neutrophils/eosinophils and oligoclonal bands in <20% (p.3584, 3590).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: ADEM should be considered for hyperacute or postinfectious demyelinating presentations rather than assuming a first MS attack (p.3584).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: MS-associated genetic variants (including HLA-DRB1*1501) lack the sensitivity and specificity to be used for diagnosis (p.3581).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Highly restricted CNS oligoclonal antibodies are characteristic of MS but their specific antigenic targets differ between patients and their pathogenic role is uncertain - they aid diagnosis, not mechanistic certainty (p.3581).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Lhermitte's symptom and trigeminal neuralgia are not specific to MS and occur with other cervical cord/cranial nerve pathology (p.3578).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: The clinical course is highly variable. RRMS accounts for ~90% of cases with attacks evolving over days to weeks and substantial early recovery; PPMS (~10%) declines steadily from onset, begins later (mean ~40 years), has a more even sex ratio, and accrues disability faster (p.3578-3580). In the pretreatment era, by 15 years after onset only ~20% had no functional limitation and one-third to one-half of relapsing patients had progressed to SPMS needing ambulatory assistance, with ~80% reaching that level by 25 years; the prior RRMS-to-SPMS conversion rate of ~3%/year has fallen to <1%/year in the high-efficacy-therapy era (p.3579, 3588). Favorable prognostic features (pretreatment data): optic neuritis or sensory onset, fewer than two relapses in the first year, and minimal impairment at 5 years; adverse predictors: older onset age, male sex, greater disability, and motor signs in the first year. About <10% have a benign variant that never produces disability even untreated (p.3588). Pregnancy: fewer attacks during gestation (especially the third trimester) but more in the first 3 months postpartum, with the overall pregnancy-year course unchanged (p.3588).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Distinguish a true relapse from a pseudoexacerbation driven by raised ambient temperature, fever, or infection - glucocorticoids are inappropriate for a pseudoexacerbation (p.3585).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Features atypical for MS that should prompt an alternative diagnosis: symptoms confined to posterior fossa/craniocervical junction/spinal cord; onset <15 or >60 years; progressive course from onset; never any visual, sensory, or bladder symptoms; or atypical MRI/CSF/EP findings (p.3584).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Symptoms rare/uncommon in MS that favor another diagnosis: aphasia, parkinsonism, chorea, isolated dementia, severe muscle atrophy, peripheral neuropathy, episodic loss of consciousness, fever, headache, seizures, or coma (p.3584).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Bilateral and/or severe optic neuritis or severe transverse myelitis should raise NMOSD, MOGAD, or GFAP autoimmunity rather than MS (p.3584).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Uveitis is uncommon in MS and should suggest sarcoidosis or lymphoma (p.3577).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Intense inflammatory swelling can produce a mass lesion mimicking tumor (tumefactive MS), sometimes requiring brain biopsy (p.3584, 3589).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Ch. 455 (Multiple Sclerosis), p.3577-3589; Ch. 456 (Neuromyelitis Optica) p.3590

chunks.text: Course-based subtypes: relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS, ~90%), secondary progressive MS (SPMS, always evolves from RRMS), and primary progressive MS (PPMS, ~10%); 'relapsing MS (RMS)' covers all relapsing patients and 'active progressive MS' denotes SPMS/PPMS with ongoing relapses or new MRI lesions (p.3578-3579). Neurologic impairment is graded with the Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS), 0 (normal) to 10 (death), built from Functional Status (FS) subscores; EDSS <3.5 generally indicates normal walking and little disability, whereas EDSS >4.0 indicates gait-impaired progressive (SPMS/PPMS) disease. An EDSS >=4 plus a motor FS score >=2 supports an SPMS diagnosis (p.3579-3580, 3585). Fulminant clinical variants include Marburg's (acute fulminant) MS, tumefactive MS, and Balo's concentric sclerosis (p.3589).

chunks.text: MG is an autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder in which the number of available postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) is reduced and postsynaptic folds are flattened/simplified, decreasing the efficiency of neuromuscular transmission; ACh is released normally but produces small end-plate potentials that may fail to trigger muscle action potentials. The normal decline in ACh release on repeated activity (presynaptic rundown) combined with reduced transmission efficiency activates fewer fibers with successive impulses, producing fatigable weakness (myasthenic fatigue) and the decremental response to repetitive nerve stimulation. Anti-AChR antibodies (IgG, T-cell dependent) reduce receptors by three mechanisms: accelerated AChR turnover via cross-linking/endocytosis, complement-mediated damage to the postsynaptic membrane, and blockade of the ACh-binding site. Anti-MuSK antibodies (IgG4, non-complement-activating) impair MuSK-LRP4 binding and AChR clustering, so MuSK-positive MG does not respond to complement inhibition; anti-LRP4 antibodies (IgG1) cause complement-mediated destruction. Thymic abnormality (hyperplasia in ~65%, thymoma in ~10%) and dysfunction of regulatory T cells contribute to the autoimmune process (p.3624-3626).

chunks.text: Multiple myeloma is a malignant proliferation of a single plasma-cell clone. Myeloma cells adhere to bone marrow stromal cells and extracellular matrix, triggering cytokine loops (IL-6, IGF-1, VEGF) and signaling (Ras/Raf/MAPK, PI3K/Akt, PKC) that drive growth, survival, drug resistance, and migration. Osteoclast-activating factors (RANK ligand, MIP-1alpha, IL-1, lymphotoxin, TNF, VEGF) increase bone resorption while DKK-1 suppresses osteoblasts, producing purely lytic bone disease, hypercalcemia, fractures, and cord compression. The immune microenvironment is remodeled (expansion of MDSCs, plasmacytoid dendritic cells, TH17; suppression of effective antimyeloma T/B/NKT responses). Recurrent cytogenetic events include hyperdiploidy (trisomies) in ~half, and 14q32 IGH translocations [t(11;14), t(4;14), t(14;16)] in the rest, plus del13q, 1q amplification/1p deletion, and del17p; KRAS/NRAS are the most frequently mutated genes (~20% each), with TP53, DIS3, FAM46C, BRAF in 5-10%. No single unifying mutation exists; subclonal heterogeneity present at diagnosis drives genomic evolution. All myeloma is preceded by MGUS (p.883-885).

chunks.text: Serum beta-2-microglobulin is the single most powerful survival predictor; combined with albumin it defines the 3-stage International Staging System (ISS): Stage I (b2M <3.5 mg/L, albumin >=3.5 g/dL) median survival ~62 months; Stage II ~44 months; Stage III (b2M >5.5 mg/L) ~29 months. High LDH, circulating plasma cells, high labeling index, and poor performance status indicate worse outcome. Cytogenetic risk: high-risk = del(17p) (>=20% clonality)/TP53 mutation, t(4;14)/t(14;16)/t(14;20) with 1q gain or 1p deletion, biallelic/del1p with 1q gain, and high b2M with normal creatinine (~20-25% of patients, expected survival 3-4 years); standard-risk includes t(11;14), del(13), hyperdiploidy (~75-80%, survival 8-10+ years). del(13q) and t(11;14) are NOT high-risk markers. chunks.text: Long-standing thyroid hormone deficiency depresses the metabolic rate and thermogenesis, producing hypothermia, bradycardia, and reduced myocardial contractility. Dermal accumulation of glycosaminoglycans traps water, giving nonpitting myxedematous swelling. In myxedema coma, hypoventilation is central to pathogenesis: it leads to hypoxia and hypercapnia (CO2 retention). Dilutional hyponatremia (reduced renal perfusion with inappropriate vasopressin) and hypoglycemia further contribute. There is impaired adrenal reserve in profound hypothyroidism, and impaired peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion (p.3032; p.3768).

chunks.text: Nephrotic syndrome reflects increased glomerular permeability to plasma proteins. Minimal change disease causes diffuse fusion (effacement) of podocyte foot processes producing predominantly 'selective' albumin loss, whereas immune-complex disruption of the basement membrane and slit diaphragms yields 'nonselective' loss of albumin and larger proteins. Hypoalbuminaemia results from urinary loss plus increased proximal-tubule catabolism of filtered albumin, exceeding hepatic synthesis (a hypercatabolic, negative-nitrogen-balance state). Oedema arises from renal sodium retention and reduced plasma oncotic pressure; perceived reduction in effective intravascular volume activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, AVP and the sympathetic nervous system, and filtered proteases can directly activate the epithelial Na channel (ENaC) in principal cells, promoting further salt/water retention. Hyperlipidaemia/hypercholesterolaemia reflect increased hepatic lipoprotein synthesis. Notably, hypertension is uncommon in primary kidney diseases causing nephrotic syndrome (p.385). Hereditary nephrotic syndrome can result from podocyte slit-diaphragm gene mutations (nephrin NPHS1, podocin NPHS2); APOL1 risk variants predispose to FSGS, with disease expression triggered by a 'second hit' of infection/inflammation damaging podocytes and glomerular endothelium (p.2357-2358).

[guideline] management
Cholinergic (muscarinic/nicotinic) poisoning — also causes miosis plus a depressed physiologic state (p.3748)
Sedative-hypnotic / GABAergic poisoning (alcohols, barbiturates, benzodiazepines, GHB) — depressed state, distinguished as naloxone-unresponsive (p.3748)
Sympatholytic poisoning (alpha-2 agonists e.g. clonidine, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, cardiac glycosides) (p.3747)
Other causes of coma including hypoglycemia (reversed by dextrose) (p.3748)
Blood/urine toxicology can confirm a suspected diagnosis but must not delay clinical management (p.3690)
ECG to detect QT prolongation (e.g. methadone), which can cause sudden death (p.3733)
Chest imaging for noncardiogenic pulmonary edema / ARDS, a recognized complication of opioid poisoning (p.3749)
In IV users, screen for blood-borne infection (hepatitis B, HIV) and bacterial complications (meningitis, osteomyelitis, abscesses, endocarditis) (p.3733)
Hypoglycemia (responds to dextrose, mimics opioid coma) (p.3748)
Benzodiazepine intoxication (responds to flumazenil) (p.3748)

Opioids act mainly through the mu receptor (also kappa, delta, nociceptin/orphanin), all G protein-coupled, inhibiting the cAMP system and opening GIRK potassium channels to hyperpolarize and silence neurons. Life-threatening respiratory depression results from opioid-induced insensitivity of brainstem (medullary) respiratory neurons to rising carbon dioxide; analgesia and respiratory depression are mediated by receptors in the periaqueductal grey and medulla oblongata. Untreated, progression goes to respiratory and then cardiovascular collapse and death (p.3733, p.3690).
The classic overdose picture is shallow/slow respirations, miosis, bradycardia, hypothermia, and stupor or coma; toxicology can confirm but immediate management is clinical (p.3690).

Pinpoint pupils are characteristic, BUT mydriasis (dilated pupils) appears once significant cerebral anoxia supervenes — dilated pupils do not exclude opioid toxicity in a deteriorating patient (p.3690).

Hypoxia, not the drug itself, is what kills: in opioid and sedative-hypnotic poisoning, vital-sign changes are secondary to CNS depression or consequent hypoxemia and do not appear until consciousness is markedly reduced (grade 3-4 depression) (p.3748).
Aspiration pneumonia is common in overdose because of loss of the gag reflex (p.3733).
Opioids generally do NOT cause seizures, except in polydrug use, with meperidine, with high-dose tramadol, or in the newborn (p.3690).

Fentanyl and its derivatives may require severalfold higher reversal doses than other opioids, and adulteration of illicit fentanyl with xylazine markedly worsens respiratory suppression (p.3689, p.3733).

Prompt reversal of altered mental status and vital signs within minutes of IV naloxone is virtually diagnostic of opioid poisoning (alongside dextrose for hypoglycemia and flumazenil for benzodiazepine intoxication) (p.3748).
Fluoroquinolones commonly cause false-positive opiate urine screens; rapid urine drug screens are screening-only, prone to false results, and miss agents such as kratom (p.3748).
When naloxone has only a limited effect, suspect a co-ingested sedative — most commonly a benzodiazepine, which has caused fatal overdoses in combination with buprenorphine (p.3691).
Do not assume normal-sized or dilated pupils exclude opioids — mydriasis does NOT occur until significant brain anoxia supervenes (p.3690).
Significant vital-sign abnormalities do NOT occur in opioid poisoning until there is a marked decrease in level of consciousness, so early near-normal vitals are falsely reassuring (p.3748).

A negative urine drug screen does NOT rule out opioid toxicity (concentration too low, or agent such as kratom not detected); opiate screens also give false positives (e.g. fluoroquinolones) (p.3748).

Primary buprenorphine overdose is nearly impossible because it is a partial agonist with increasing antagonist activity at higher doses; failure to respond to naloxone should prompt search for a co-ingested sedative (p.3690-3691).
Be sure a patient is not also withdrawing from alcohol or sedatives, which may be more dangerous to manage than opioid withdrawal (p.3733).

Potentially lethal but rapidly reversible if respiratory depression is recognized and supported; untreated overdose progresses to respiratory and cardiovascular collapse and death. Opioid use disorder is chronic and relapsing, and most patients relapse during or after detoxification (p.3690, p.3691). Some opioid intoxications can leave delayed diffuse white-matter injury producing a persistent coma syndrome (p.232).
Dilated pupils in a suspected opioid overdose suggest cerebral anoxia has already occurred (p.3690)
Re-sedation: naloxone lasts only a few hours while most opioids (especially methadone, sustained-release/'toxic time-bomb' formulations) last far longer (p.3691, p.3747)
Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema / ARDS (p.3749)

Harrison frames poisoning severity by physiologic state (Tables 470-1/470-2): opioids produce a 'depressed' physiologic state (decreased pulse, BP, respiratory rate, temperature, neuromuscular activity, with miosis). Severity is graded by depth of CNS/physiologic depression (grades 1-4); marked vital-sign abnormalities indicate grade 3-4 depression (p.3747-3748). Note: opioid WITHDRAWAL is a separate 'stimulated' syndrome — onset 8-10 h after the last dose with lacrimation, rhinorrhea, yawning and sweating, progressing to gooseflesh, nausea/vomiting, myalgia, hyperpnea, hyperthermia, hypertension, mydriasis over a 7-10 day acute course (p.3690).

[guideline] management
Carbamate insecticide poisoning (aldicarb, carbaryl, propoxur) — same cholinergic mechanism (p.3712)
Other acetylcholinesterase inhibitors: medicinal agents neostigmine, physostigmine, tacrine (p.3712)
Muscarinic agonists: bethanechol, pilocarpine, and muscarine-containing mushrooms (Boletus, Clitocybe, Inocybe spp.) (p.3712)
Nicotine / tobacco and lobeline (nicotinic agonists) (p.3712)
Opioid poisoning (also causes miosis and physiologic depression) (p.3705)
Cholinesterase activity in plasma and red cells is <50% of normal in acetylcholinesterase-inhibitor poisoning (p.3712)
ECG — may show bradycardia and atrioventricular block (p.3706)
EMG/nerve conduction studies in delayed neuropathy — early repetitive firing of CMAPs and decrement on repetitive nerve stimulation; later, axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy (p.3610)
Guillain-Barré syndrome / acute flaccid paralysis — organophosphate, thallium and arsenic poisonings are listed in the GBS differential (p.3620)
Botulism and myasthenia gravis (neuromuscular junction disorders in the acute paralysis differential) (p.3620)
Paralytic shellfish poisoning, ciguatera, type E botulism and tetrodotoxin poisoning — organophosphate poisoning is in their shared differential (ciguatera chapter)

Organophosphate (and carbamate) insecticides, and nerve agents such as sarin, soman, tabun and VX, inhibit acetylcholinesterase, leading to accumulation of synaptic acetylcholine at both muscarinic and nicotinic cholinergic receptor sites; the resulting overstimulation produces the combined muscarinic, nicotinic and CNS toxidrome. Organophosphates are 'toxic time-bombs' in that they may require metabolic activation, so onset of toxicity can be delayed. Separately, organophosphates bind and inhibit neuropathy target esterase, with axonal degeneration of the gracile fasciculus and corticospinal tracts producing a delayed sensorimotor polyneuropathy. (p.3610, p.3712, p.3704)

Belongs to the depressed physiologic state / cholinergic toxidrome; miosis is common and is most pronounced in opioid and cholinergic poisoning, distinguished from other depressant syndromes by muscarinic and nicotinic signs (p.3705).

Muscarinic features: seizures, excessive secretions (lacrimation, salivation, bronchorrhoea and wheezing, diaphoresis), and increased bowel/bladder activity with nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal cramps, and incontinence of faeces and urine (p.3712).
Nicotinic features: hypertension, tachycardia, muscle cramps, fasciculations, weakness, and paralysis — note these oppose the muscarinic picture, so vital signs can be mixed (p.3712).
Death is usually due to respiratory failure (p.3712).
Organophosphates and carbamates can produce bradycardia and atrioventricular block on ECG (p.3706).
Organophosphate (and amanita/mushroom) poisoning can present as acute, often systemic-compromising diarrhoea (p.46/Acute Diarrhea chapter).
Organophosphates can cause a delayed organophosphate-induced neuropathy: early generalised weakness from neuromuscular blockade, then an axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy ensues (p.3610).

Vital signs may be discordant: muscarinic effects cause bradycardia while nicotinic stimulation can cause hypertension and tachycardia, so a 'normal' or mixed heart rate does not exclude poisoning (p.3712).
Organophosphates are 'toxic time-bombs' requiring metabolic activation, so a patient may be initially well or minimally symptomatic and deteriorate later (p.3704).
Cholinesterase activity is <50% of normal in acetylcholinesterase-inhibitor poisoning — a key confirmatory threshold not to overlook (p.3712).

Death is usually due to respiratory failure (p.3712). Outcome and reversibility of any poisoning depend on the functional reserve of the individual or target organ, influenced by age and preexisting disease (p.3704).
Bronchorrhoea, wheezing and excessive secretions with progression to respiratory failure — the usual cause of death (p.3712)
Nicotinic weakness, fasciculations and paralysis (p.3712)
Seizures (p.3712)
Bradycardia / atrioventricular block (p.3706)

Harrison grades poisoning by degree of physiologic depression rather than by a disease-specific scale (Table 470-2): grade 1 — arousable by voice/touch, can converse and follow commands; grade 2 — responds to pain but not voice, brainstem reflexes intact; grade 3 — unresponsive to pain, brainstem reflexes depressed, decreased respirations and temperature; grade 4 — flaccid paralysis with absent brainstem reflexes and respirations and decreased cardiovascular vital signs (p.3705).

Perforated viscus, especially peptic ulcer

Serum lipase (>3x ULN) - preferred enzyme; more specific than amylase; remains elevated 7-14 days (Harrison 22e p.2740, p.2745)
Contrast-enhanced CT - to assess necrosis and local complications when not improving, ideally at 3-5 days (Harrison 22e p.2745-2746)
C-reactive protein - severity marker during hospitalization (thresholds >100 mg/L reported) (Harrison 22e p.2748)
Liver profile incl. ALT - ALT >3x ULN supports gallstone aetiology (Harrison 22e p.2745)
Serum triglycerides - to detect hypertriglyceridaemic cause (levels usually >1000 mg/dL) (Harrison 22e p.2744, p.2748)
Serum calcium - to detect hypercalcaemic cause and to monitor for hypocalcaemia (~25% of patients) (Harrison 22e p.2744-2745)
Hematocrit - hemoconcentration >44% is a severity marker (Harrison 22e p.2745-2746)
Blood urea nitrogen (BUN) at admission and 48 h - rising BUN predicts mortality (Harrison 22e p.2745, p.2748)
White cell count - leukocytosis 15,000-20,000/uL is common (Harrison 22e p.2745)
MRI/MRCP - more sensitive than CT for mild pancreatitis, necrosis, choledocholithiasis and ductal abnormalities (Harrison 22e p.2739)
EUS - useful for occult microlithiasis/biliary cause and choledocholithiasis; best performed ~4 weeks after resolution to find predisposing lesions (Harrison 22e p.2741)
Diabetic ketoacidosis - abdominal pain with raised TOTAL amylase mimics pancreatitis, but lipase is often NOT elevated and pancreatic imaging is normal (Harrison 22e p.2745-2746)
Perforated peptic ulcer - can raise serum/ascitic amylase (Harrison 22e p.2739, p.2745)
Acute cholecystitis / biliary colic - amylase may be raised; pain is more right-sided/epigastric and ileus is usually absent (Harrison 22e p.2745)
Mesenteric ischemia/infarction - can raise ascitic-fluid amylase (Harrison 22e p.2739, p.2745)
Intestinal obstruction - can raise ascitic-fluid amylase; differentiated by crescendo-decrescendo pain and obstruction pattern on CT (Harrison 22e p.2739, p.2745)

Acute pancreatitis is thought to begin with autodigestion: intracellular premature activation of trypsin (via lysosomal cathepsin B colocalising with digestive zymogens) within acinar cells, which then activates other proteolytic and lipolytic enzymes (chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, phospholipase A2). A second phase recruits and sequesters leukocytes/macrophages, amplifying intrapancreatic inflammation, and a third phase results from activated enzymes and cytokines acting on distant organs, producing edema, hemorrhage, vascular damage, fat necrosis and coagulation/cellular necrosis. Release of bradykinin, vasoactive substances and histamine drives vasodilation, increased vascular permeability and edema, and can culminate in SIRS, ARDS and multiorgan failure. Pathologically the spectrum runs from interstitial (perfusion preserved, self-limited) to necrotizing pancreatitis (perfusion interrupted). Genetic susceptibility/modifier variants include PRSS1 (cationic trypsinogen), SPINK1, CFTR, CTRC, CASR and CLDN2, all converging on control of intrapancreatic trypsin activity (Harrison 22e p.2744-2745).
Diagnosis requires 2 of 3: typical epigastric pain radiating to the back, serum lipase/amylase >=3x ULN, or characteristic findings on cross-sectional imaging (Harrison 22e p.2745).

Lipase is more pancreas-specific than amylase and is the single best enzyme to measure; it stays elevated longer (7-14 days) whereas amylase often normalises by 3-7 days (Harrison 22e p.2740, p.2745).
Gallstones and alcohol together account for ~80-90% of cases; gallstones are the single most common cause (30-60%), alcohol the second (15-30%) (Harrison 22e p.2744).
ALT >3x ULN strongly points to a gallstone aetiology in acute pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2745).

Abdominal ultrasound is the recommended initial imaging study, chiefly to assess for gallstones and bile-duct dilation; contrast CT is best deferred to ~3-5 days if the patient is not improving and is usually not needed in the first 48-72 h (Harrison 22e p.2745-2746).
Persistent organ failure (>48 h) is the most important determinant of severity; if SIRS has resolved by 24 h, organ failure or necrosis is unlikely to develop (Harrison 22e p.2746, p.2748).
Hemoconcentration (hematocrit >44%) and a rising BUN are early warning signs of more severe disease and higher mortality (Harrison 22e p.2745-2748).
Cullen's sign (periumbilical bruising) and Grey Turner's sign (flank discoloration) are rare but signal severe necrotizing/hemorrhagic disease (Harrison 22e p.2745).
Enzyme magnitude does NOT track severity - degree or serial trend of lipase/amylase does not correlate with how severe the pancreatitis is (Harrison 22e p.2745).
Serum amylase can be falsely normal or low in hypertriglyceridaemic pancreatitis, masking the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2739, p.2745).

Amylase is non-specific - raised in salivary, tubo-ovarian, pulmonary, malignant and other conditions, and spuriously high in acidemia/DKA (arterial pH <=7.32) without true pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2740, p.2745).

Lipase can be mildly elevated in renal failure, and >3x ULN can occur in hepatobiliary/GI malignancy, sepsis, cirrhosis, SLE, head injury, chronic alcoholism, diabetes and post-ERCP without pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2740).
Routine/early CT (within 72 h) is overused and usually unnecessary, especially in mild disease; necrosis may not be visible until several days in (Harrison 22e p.2746-2747).
Prophylactic antibiotics are NOT recommended, even in severe or necrotizing pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2746, p.2749).
Enzyme levels may be normal if blood is drawn 2-5 days after onset or if the underlying problem is chronic rather than acute pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2740).

Overall mortality is low (~1%) and median hospital stay ~4 days; most cases are mild and self-limited within 3-7 days. Interstitial pancreatitis (90-95% of admissions) carries low mortality, whereas necrotizing pancreatitis (5-10%) drives most deaths. In necrotizing disease the median prevalence of organ failure exceeds 50% (slightly higher with infected vs sterile necrosis); mortality is 3-10% with single-organ failure but approaches 50% with multiorgan failure. Patients with only extrapancreatic necrosis fare better than those with pancreatic parenchymal necrosis. About 25% of patients have a recurrence, most commonly from alcohol or gallstones (Harrison 22e p.2747, p.2749).
Persistent organ failure >48 h (respiratory, cardiovascular or renal) - hallmark of severe disease (Harrison 22e p.2746)
Ascending cholangitis (sepsis + biliary obstruction) complicating gallstone pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2748)
Modified Marshall organ-failure signs: systolic BP <90 mmHg, HR >130/min, PaO2 <60 mmHg, or creatinine >2.0 mg/dL (Harrison 22e p.2748)
BISAP score >=3 - increased in-hospital mortality (Harrison 22e p.2748)

Persistent SIRS at 24 h - predisposes to organ failure and necrosis (Harrison 22e p.2746, p.2748)
Pancreatic necrosis on CT - greatest mortality risk (3-10% with single-organ failure, ~50% with multiorgan failure) (Harrison 22e p.2747)
Hypoxemia (PaO2 <=60 mmHg) - may herald ARDS (Harrison 22e p.2745)
Cullen's sign / Grey Turner's sign - severe necrotizing/hemorrhagic pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2745)

Revised Atlanta classification (Banks et al., Gut 2013). PHASES: early (<2 weeks; severity judged clinically, not by morphology) and late (>2 weeks; imaging for local complications). SEVERITY: (1) Mild - no local complications and no organ failure (most interstitial cases; self-limited 3-7 days); (2) Moderately severe - transient organ failure (resolves <48 h) and/or local or systemic complications without persistent organ failure; (3) Severe - persistent organ failure >48 h in >=1 organ system (respiratory, cardiovascular, renal; defined by modified Marshall score >=2). MORPHOLOGY (Table 359-2): two types - interstitial (parenchymal enhancement, no necrosis) vs necrotizing (lack of parenchymal enhancement and/or peripancreatic necrosis); local collections - acute pancreatic fluid collection and pseudocyst (interstitial, pseudocyst usually >4 wk) vs acute necrotic collection (ANC) and walled-off necrosis (WON, usually >4 wk, encapsulated). SEVERITY SCORES/MARKERS (Table 359-3): BISAP >=3 (BUN >25 mg/dL, Impaired mental status/GCS<15, SIRS >=2/4, Age >60, Pleural effusion); APACHE II >=8 at 24 h; SIRS >=2 of 4 (temp <36 or >38C, HR >90, RR >20 or PCO2 <32, WCC >12,000 or <4000 or >10% bands); hematocrit >44%; admission BUN >20 mg/dL; persistent organ failure >=48 h, and pancreatic/extrapancreatic necrosis as in-hospital markers. Ranson criteria are a traditional severity index (referenced contextually).

chunks.text: Virchow's triad of venous stasis, hypercoagulability, and endothelial injury, typically with an inflammatory trigger, recruits activated platelets that release microparticles and drive neutrophil extracellular trap formation, promoting thrombin generation; venous thrombi flourish in stasis, low oxygen tension, and proinflammatory gene upregulation. Detached lower-limb thrombi embolize through the vena cava and right heart to lodge in the pulmonary arteries (rarely paradoxically to the arterial circulation via a patent foramen ovale or atrial septal defect). The dominant gas-exchange defects are arterial hypoxemia and a widened alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient with increased dead space; additional mechanisms include raised pulmonary vascular resistance from obstruction and vasoconstrictors (e.g., serotonin), ventilation-perfusion mismatch remote from the embolus, reflex hyperventilation, increased airway resistance, and reduced compliance. Pulmonary-artery obstruction plus neurohumoral mediators raise pulmonary pressure and resistance; rising RV wall tension produces RV dilation, stretch and dysfunction (releasing BNP), septal bowing that impairs LV filling, and compression of the right coronary artery causing RV ischemia/microinfarction (releasing troponin), ultimately reducing LV output and systemic pressure, leading to circulatory collapse and death. Prothrombotic states include factor V Leiden, the prothrombin gene mutation, and deficiencies of antithrombin/protein C/protein S (rare); antiphospholipid syndrome is an acquired thrombophilia predisposing to both venous and arterial thrombosis. (p.2156-2158)

chunks.text: Low-risk PE (about 65-75% of cases) with normal blood pressure and normal RV carries an excellent prognosis; submassive (intermediate-risk) PE (~20-25%) has RV dysfunction despite normal pressure with raised cardiac biomarkers and a high risk of deterioration; massive (high-risk) PE (5-10%) presents with hypotension/shock and can lead to multisystem organ failure and death. A high-probability V/Q scan confers ~90% diagnostic certainty for PE. Roughly half of survivors report persistent dyspnea, fatigue, and reduced exercise capacity, and about one-quarter have persistent RV dysfunction on echo ('post-PE syndrome'); CTEPH is a less frequent late complication. Risk of recurrent VTE after stopping anticoagulation ranges from low (<3%/yr, e.g., major surgery/trauma) to intermediate (3-8%/yr) to high (>8%/yr, e.g., active cancer, antiphospholipid syndrome) (ESC 2019). (p.2154-2155, 2158, 2161, 2163-2164)

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic ulcer disease / upper GI bleed
chunks.text: Peptic ulcers are mucosal breaks >5 mm extending into the submucosa, occurring in the stomach (gastric ulcer, GU) or duodenum (duodenal ulcer, DU); >95% of DUs lie in the first part of the duodenum, within about 3 cm of the pylorus. The disease reflects an imbalance between aggressive factors (acid, pepsin) and mucosal defence. H. pylori and NSAIDs cause the majority of ulcers but act differently: H. pylori-associated benign GUs show antral gastritis, whereas NSAID-related GUs typically lack chronic active gastritis and instead show a chemical gastropathy (foveolar hyperplasia, lamina propria oedema). Duodenal ulcer patients tend to have increased basal and nocturnal acid secretion (with substantial overlap with controls) and reduced duodenal bicarbonate, both potentially influenced by H. pylori; gastric acid output in GU patients is usually normal or reduced, implying impaired mucosal defence. H. pylori is a gram-negative microaerophilic urease-producing rod living in the gastric mucous layer; virulence factors such as the cag pathogenicity island (delivering CagA), VacA, and urease determine the clinical outcome among colonisation, PUD, MALT lymphoma, and gastric adenocarcinoma (pp.2518-2520).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.335, pp.2514-2536 (peptic ulcer disease and related disorders)

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic ulcer disease / upper GI bleed
chunks.text: Around two-thirds of patients with peptic ulcer disease have no abdominal pain, and up to ~87% of those with NSAID-related mucosal injury first present with a complication (bleeding, perforation, or obstruction) without any preceding symptoms (p.2522).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.335, pp.2514-2536 (peptic ulcer disease and related disorders)

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic ulcer disease / upper GI bleed
chunks.text: Classic duodenal ulcer pain comes on roughly 90 minutes to 3 hours after eating and is typically eased by food or antacids; pain that wakes the patient between midnight and 3 a.m. is the most discriminating symptom and is reported by about two-thirds of duodenal ulcer patients (p.2522).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.335, pp.2514-2536 (peptic ulcer disease and related disorders)

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic ulcer disease / upper GI bleed
chunks.text: Gastric ulcer pain can instead be provoked by eating, and nausea and weight loss are commoner with gastric than duodenal ulcers (p.2522).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.335, pp.2514-2536 (peptic ulcer disease and related disorders)

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic ulcer disease / upper GI bleed
chunks.text: Elderly and immunosuppressed patients are less likely to have typical pain and may present directly with bleeding or perforation (pp.2522-2523).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.335, pp.2514-2536 (peptic ulcer disease and related disorders)

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic ulcer disease / upper GI bleed
chunks.text: H. pylori and NSAIDs are the dominant risk factors (US odds ratios ~3.7 and ~3.3); NSAIDs are now described as the most common cause of PUD, with only ~one-quarter of duodenal and ~one-sixth of gastric ulcers now attributable to H. pylori (pp.2518, 2520).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.335, pp.2514-2536 (peptic ulcer disease and related disorders)

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic ulcer disease / upper GI bleed
chunks.text: More than half of patients with ulcer-related haemorrhage bleed without any preceding warning signs or symptoms (p.2522).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.335, pp.2514-2536 (peptic ulcer disease and related disorders)

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic ulcer disease / upper GI bleed
chunks.text: Endoscopy detects an ulcer in fewer than 30% of patients investigated for dyspepsia, reflecting how poorly symptoms predict an actual ulcer (p.2522).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.335, pp.2514-2536 (peptic ulcer disease and related disorders)

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic ulcer disease / upper GI bleed
chunks.text: Every gastric ulcer must be biopsied (multiple samples) at discovery because a GU may be malignant, and healing on therapy does not exclude cancer - about 70% of GUs ultimately found malignant show significant (usually incomplete) healing; repeat endoscopy with biopsy at 8-12 weeks is needed if the ulcer persists (pp.2519, 2531-2532).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.335, pp.2514-2536 (peptic ulcer disease and related disorders)

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic ulcer disease / upper GI bleed
chunks.text: Abdominal pain has poor predictive value for an ulcer, and a normal exam or absent pain does not exclude PUD - many patients, especially the elderly or those on NSAIDs, present first with a complication (pp.2522-2523).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.335, pp.2514-2536 (peptic ulcer disease and related disorders)

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic ulcer disease / upper GI bleed
chunks.text: Right-sided epigastric tenderness in about 20% of patients can mislead the examiner; epigastric tenderness overall has low predictive value (p.2522).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.335, pp.2514-2536 (peptic ulcer disease and related disorders)

chunks.text: Widespread PPI use can mask and delay the diagnosis of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome and increase false-positive gastrin results (p.2534).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.335, pp.2514-2536 (peptic ulcer disease and related disorders)

chunks.text: Consider gastrinoma/ZES when ulcers occur in unusual locations (second part of duodenum or beyond), are multiple, are refractory, recur after acid-reducing surgery, present with frank complications, or arise without H. pylori or NSAID use (p.2535).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch.335, pp.2514-2536 (peptic ulcer disease and related disorders)

chunks.diseaseName: Peptic ulcer disease / upper GI bleed
chunks.text: More than 90% of both gastric and duodenal ulcers heal with conventional therapy; a GU not healed by 12 weeks or a DU not healed by 8 weeks is considered refractory. Eradicating H. pylori has cut duodenal ulcer recurrence by >80%. GI bleeding complicates roughly 15% of PUD with a 30-day mortality of about 2.5-10% (most deaths from non-bleeding causes such as multiorgan failure, pulmonary complications, and malignancy). Perforation occurs in ~6-7% of patients with 30-day mortality >20%, and penetration carries comparable mortality; gastric outlet obstruction is least common (~1-2%). Complications and mortality rise in patients over 60, partly reflecting greater NSAID use (pp.2522-2523, 2532).

chunks.text: Inflammation of the pericardium from infectious or noninfectious causes. Because the visceral and most of the parietal pericardium are insensitive to pain, the discomfort is attributed mainly to associated pleural inflammation, producing pleuritic, position-dependent pain that, via overlapping phrenic and C3-C5 somatic innervation, may be referred to the shoulder, neck, and trapezius ridge (p.147, p.149).

chunks.text: Excess production of catecholamines, usually by a benign neuroendocrine tumour of chromaffin cells in the adrenal medulla (80-85%) or in extra-adrenal paraganglion tissue (paraganglioma). The catecholamine surge drives paroxysmal hypertension, headache, sweating and cardiac arrhythmias, and produces a hyperdynamic catecholaminergic state. Chronic/episodic catecholamine exposure can cause microvascular myocardial ischaemia (microinfarcts similar to those seen with stimulant toxicity) and a catecholamine-mediated cardiomyopathy; the same mechanism of sudden catecholamine release underlies stress (takotsubo / apical ballooning) cardiomyopathy (hypertension, cardiomyopathy and cardiac-tumour chapters).

Phaeochromocytoma crisis (non-infective) — Endocrine
Episodic headache, palpitations and sweating with paroxysmal hypertension suggests a catecholamine-secreting tumour.
Red flags: Paroxysmal severe hypertension — alpha-blockade before beta
[guideline] management
Congestive heart failure (typically bilateral transudative effusions) (Harrison 22e p.314)
Cirrhosis / hepatic hydrothorax (often right-sided) (Harrison 22e p.366, p.373)
Nephrotic syndrome and other hypoalbuminemic states (Harrison 22e p.422)
Parapneumonic effusion / empyema complicating pneumonia (Harrison 22e p.1235)
Malignant effusion (e.g., lung cancer, metastatic disease) (Harrison 22e p.662)
Tuberculous pleurisy (Harrison 22e p.1430)
Pulmonary embolism (Harrison 22e p.314)
Tuberculous pleural effusion — straw-colored (sometimes hemorrhagic) lymphocyte-predominant exudate that can mimic a parapneumonic or malignant effusion (Harrison 22e p.1430).
Tuberculous empyema, usually from rupture of a cavity into the pleural space, sometimes with a bronchopleural fistula and air in the pleural space (Harrison 22e p.1431).
Spontaneous bacterial empyema complicating hepatic hydrothorax in cirrhosis (Harrison 22e p.373).
Diagnostic thoracentesis to determine whether the fluid is a transudate or an exudate and to identify the underlying cause (Harrison 22e p.1430).
Pleural fluid pH — a value of ≤7.1 in a parapneumonic setting indicates empyema requiring drainage (Harrison 22e p.1235).

Pleural fluid protein, glucose, and cell count/differential; in TB the fluid is an exudate with protein >50% of serum (often ~4-6 g/dL), normal-to-low glucose, pH ~7.3 (occasionally <7.2), and 500-6000 WBC/uL, with neutrophils early and lymphocyte predominance later (Harrison 22e p.1430).
Pleural fluid adenosine deaminase (ADA) — an elevated level is consistent with TB and a very low level helps exclude it (Harrison 22e p.1430).
Pleural fluid IFN-gamma and lysozyme as adjuncts for suspected tuberculous effusion (Harrison 22e p.1430).
Pleural fluid cytology for malignancy, with repeat thoracentesis if the first sample is negative (Harrison 22e p.663).
Needle (closed) pleural biopsy for suspected TB, which reveals granulomas and/or yields positive culture in up to ~80% of cases and is favored over fluid analysis (Harrison 22e p.1430).
Xpert MTB/RIF on pleural biopsy tissue (positive in ~75%); testing pleural fluid itself with this assay is not recommended owing to low sensitivity (Harrison 22e p.1430).
Serum-to-pleural-fluid albumin gradient — a value >=1.1 g/dL suggests hepatic hydrothorax (Harrison 22e p.373).
Heart-failure transudate, which can be unilateral and be mistaken for a localized pathologic effusion (Harrison 22e p.314).
Hepatic hydrothorax from cirrhosis, mimicking other right-sided effusions (Harrison 22e p.366, p.373).
Malignant effusion, which may be exudative or bloody and can coexist with or be confused for a parapneumonic effusion (Harrison 22e p.663).

Fluid abnormally accumulates in the pleural space when the balance of hydrostatic and oncotic forces, lymphatic drainage, or capillary permeability is disturbed. Transudates arise from systemic forces (raised hydrostatic pressure or low plasma oncotic pressure) as in the sodium-avid edematous states of heart failure, cirrhosis, and nephrotic syndrome (Harrison 22e p.422). Exudates result from local pleural or capillary processes such as infection, malignancy, or inflammation. In hepatic hydrothorax, ascitic fluid migrates through diaphragmatic fenestrae into the pleural space (Harrison 22e p.373). Tuberculous effusion typically reflects a hypersensitivity reaction to mycobacterial antigens after recent primary infection, or contiguous spread from parenchymal disease (Harrison 22e p.1430). Malignant effusions arise from pleural involvement or from lymphatic obstruction by tumor (Harrison 22e p.662).

On examination an effusion gives dullness to percussion, reduced or absent breath sounds, and decreased tactile fremitus over the fluid; this contrasts with consolidation, where fremitus is increased (Harrison 22e p.2243).
Percussion helps separate the two causes of a quiet hemithorax: an effusion is dull, whereas a pneumothorax is hyper-resonant (Harrison 22e p.2243).
Skodaic resonance, a band of hyper-resonance just above the dull effusion, is a classic percussion sign (Harrison 22e p.89).

Bilateral effusions are characteristic of congestive heart failure (and some collagen-vascular disorders), whereas a unilateral effusion should raise suspicion of malignancy or pulmonary embolism, though heart failure and parapneumonic effusion can also be unilateral (Harrison 22e p.314).
A right-sided pleural effusion can occur in advanced cirrhosis even when no ascites is clinically detectable (Harrison 22e p.366).
In a malignant effusion an initially negative thoracentesis does not exclude cancer; repeating the tap is essential because cytologic yield improves with repeat sampling (Harrison 22e p.663).
Avoid attributing every quiet, dull hemithorax to effusion — confirm with percussion and fremitus, since pneumothorax and consolidation differ (Harrison 22e p.2243).
A negative initial pleural cytology does not rule out malignancy; failing to repeat the tap is a diagnostic pitfall (Harrison 22e p.663).
Do not assume a unilateral effusion is benign heart failure — it may be malignant or embolic (Harrison 22e p.314).
Testing pleural fluid (rather than biopsy tissue) with Xpert MTB/RIF is unreliable for TB because of low sensitivity (Harrison 22e p.1430).
AFB smears are rarely positive and cultures are often falsely negative in tuberculous effusions, so a negative smear/culture does not exclude pleural TB (Harrison 22e p.1430).
In hepatic hydrothorax, chest-tube placement should be avoided (Harrison 22e p.373).

Tuberculous pleural effusion responds rapidly to antituberculous chemotherapy and may even resolve spontaneously; concurrent glucocorticoids may shorten fever and chest pain but are of unproven benefit (Harrison 22e p.1430). Parapneumonic effusions are usually a self-limited inflammatory response, whereas a true empyema requires drainage and carries a worse course if undrained (Harrison 22e p.1235).

Frank pus, organisms on microscopy, or pleural fluid pH <=7.1 in a parapneumonic effusion — diagnostic of empyema and mandates aggressive complete drainage, usually via chest tube (Harrison 22e p.1235).
New or persistent fever and leukocytosis after 4-5 days of appropriate antibiotics for pneumonia — suspect empyema (Harrison 22e p.1235).
Exudative or bloody effusion — raises concern for malignancy (Harrison 22e p.663).
Unilateral effusion without an obvious cause — investigate for malignancy or pulmonary embolism (Harrison 22e p.314).

Parapneumonic effusions are distinguished from empyema by their character: an uncomplicated parapneumonic effusion is a self-limited reaction to adjacent pneumonia, whereas frank pus, visible organisms, or a pleural fluid pH <=7.1 defines empyema (a complicated/infected collection) that requires complete drainage (Harrison 22e p.1235).

chunks.text: PMR sits on the same disease spectrum as giant cell arteritis, an antigen-driven panarteritis of medium- and large-sized vessels with mononuclear infiltrates and frequent giant cell formation. Activated CD4+ T lymphocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells are central; restricted clonal T-cell receptor expansion suggests an antigen residing in the arterial wall. Two CD4 T-cell lineages (IFN-gamma-producing TH1 and IL-17-producing TH17) participate in vascular inflammation, with IL-6 signaling driving hepatic acute-phase protein (CRP, and effects on ESR) production. Familial aggregation and HLA-DR4 / HLA-DRB1*04 associations have been reported for the GCA end of the spectrum (p.2945).

chunks.text: Pneumothorax is the accumulation of gas in the pleural space. In primary spontaneous pneumothorax, apical subpleural blebs rupture, allowing air to enter the pleural space without preceding trauma and in the absence of underlying lung disease. Secondary pneumothorax occurs when the same process complicates established lung disease, where loss of pulmonary reserve makes the event more dangerous. Traumatic pneumothorax results from penetrating or non-penetrating chest injury, and iatrogenic pneumothorax (a traumatic subtype) follows procedures such as transthoracic needle aspiration, thoracentesis, or central venous catheter insertion. In a tension pneumothorax, a one-way valve effect produces pleural pressure that remains positive across the whole respiratory cycle; this both severely compromises ventilation and transmits positive pressure to the mediastinum, reducing venous return to the heart and thereby cardiac output (Harrison 22e p.2313, p.2314).

Ruptured/impending-rupture abdominal aortic aneurysm — abdominal pain radiating to the flank, sacral region, or genitalia should always raise suspicion of a leaking AAA; pain may precede rupture by days (p.154).
Acute mesenteric ischemia (pain out of proportion to exam in a vascular patient) (p.154).

Other causes of acute lower abdominal pain such as appendicitis, salpingitis, ectopic pregnancy, inguinal hernia, inflammatory bowel disease, and bowel obstruction (p.18 abdominal pain differential table).
Ureteric obstruction due to extrinsic malignancy (pelvic/prostatic/gynecologic tumors, retroperitoneal nodes) or post-radiation ureteric fibrosis, which can mimic stone-related obstruction (p.631).
Acute pyelonephritis (flank pain, fever, pyuria) (p.1118).

Perinephric or renal abscess — flank/abdominal pain, fever in at least half; suspect when pyelonephritis remains febrile after 4-5 days, when urine culture is polymicrobial, when stones are known, or when fever and pyuria coexist with a sterile urine culture (p.1118).

Renal ultrasonography — useful to identify hydronephrosis/ureteric and pelvic dilation, though it may be falsely negative early or when ureteric dilation is prevented (e.g., retroperitoneal fibrosis or tumor encasement) (p.383, p.631).
Abdominal CT and renal ultrasound are the most useful modalities when perinephric/renal abscess is suspected (p.1118).

Urinalysis showing alkaline urine plus a urease-producing organism (e.g., Proteus) may prompt evaluation for urolithiasis, though Harrison notes clinical support for routine action on this finding is lacking (p.1334).
Serum calcium / PTH and metabolic workup when an underlying stone-promoting metabolic disorder (e.g., primary hyperparathyroidism) is suspected (p.406).
Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm with flank/genital radiation, especially in older patients (p.154).
Ureteric obstruction from malignancy or retroperitoneal fibrosis presenting with flank pain (p.631).

Colicky flank pain arises from acute distention of the renal collecting system and ureter when a stone obstructs urinary outflow, producing visceral cramping pain (p.551). Obstruction proximal to the bladder produces hydroureter and renal pelvic dilation (hydronephrosis); if unrelieved this impairs glomerular filtration and causes postrenal azotemia (p.383). In urease-producing infection (e.g., Proteus), hydrolysis of urea to ammonia raises urinary pH; the resulting alkaline environment precipitates struvite and carbonate-apatite, building staghorn calculi that perpetuate infection and obstruction (p.1118, p.1334). Stones also serve as a chronic nidus that promotes recurrent and recalcitrant urinary infection (p.1118).
Renal colic is classic visceral pain from distention of a hollow viscus (the obstructed collecting system/ureter): cramping and intermittent rather than constant (p.551).
Stones obstructing urinary flow are the single most important risk factor for perinephric/renal abscess; 20-60% of patients with perinephric abscess have renal stones (p.1118).

Urea-splitting organisms (notably Proteus, also other urease producers) alkalinize the urine, favoring precipitation of struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) and carbonate-apatite, which can form staghorn calculi in the renal pelvis (p.1118, p.1334).
Struvite stones act as a persistent nidus for recurrent UTI and typically cannot be eradicated by antibiotics alone without removal of the stone (p.1118, p.1334).

Stone-associated obstruction is a recognized cause of postrenal azotemia/AKI; because one functioning kidney clears adequately, obstructive renal failure from stones generally requires bilateral ureteric obstruction or unilateral obstruction in a solitary/single functioning kidney (p.383).
Nephrolithiasis can be the presenting feature of an underlying metabolic disorder such as primary hyperparathyroidism/hypercalcemia (p.406).
Imaging of the upper tracts is advised in any patient with hematuria, a history of calculi, or prior urinary tract problems (p.747).
Assuming flank pain radiating to the groin is always a stone — in older patients a ruptured/leaking AAA can present identically and is rapidly fatal if missed (p.154).
Relying on a negative ultrasound to exclude obstruction; dilation may be absent early or when the ureter cannot distend (p.383).
Failing to recognize an infected obstructed system / perinephric abscess in a patient with known stones who stays febrile or has polymicrobial or sterile-but-pyuric urine (p.1118).
Overlooking an underlying metabolic cause (e.g., hyperparathyroidism) in a stone former (p.406).

Stone-related obstruction is usually reversible if relieved promptly; urinary tract obstruction accounts for under 5% of acute renal failure and must be excluded early because it is correctable (p.383). When obstruction is complicated by infection (abscess), diagnosis is frequently delayed and mortality is appreciable, though lower than historically (p.1118). Struvite/staghorn stones tend to recur and perpetuate infection unless the stone is removed (p.1118, p.1334).
Pain radiating to flank, sacral region, or genitalia in an older patient — exclude a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm (p.154).
Rising serum creatinine, oliguria, or anuria — suggests obstruction of a solitary kidney or bilateral obstruction and warrants immediate evaluation (p.383, p.631).

Persistent fever after several days of treatment for presumed pyelonephritis, polymicrobial urine, or fever/pyuria with sterile culture — suspect perinephric/renal abscess complicating an obstructing stone (p.1118).

Clostridial myositis/myonecrosis — predictably precipitates acute rhabdomyolysis (Harrison 22e p.1096).
Streptococcal (group A) myositis — also predictably causes acute rhabdomyolysis (Harrison 22e p.1096).
Viral myositis — influenza, echovirus, coxsackievirus and Epstein-Barr virus infections may be associated with rhabdomyolysis (Harrison 22e p.1096).
Legionella infection — reported association with rhabdomyolysis (Harrison 22e p.1096).
Urine dipstick for blood with microscopy — dipstick blood-positive but RBC-negative supports myoglobinuria rather than true haematuria (Harrison 22e p.343).
Urine sediment / microscopy for muddy-brown (pigmented) granular casts and tubular epithelial cells, indicating accompanying acute tubular necrosis (Harrison 22e p.343).
Serum phosphate and calcium — hyperphosphataemia and hypocalcaemia accompany acute muscle injury (Harrison 22e p.359, p.363).
Fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) — may be <1% in early rhabdomyolysis-associated ATN, limiting its discriminatory value (Harrison 22e p.343).

Massive skeletal muscle breakdown releases intracellular contents — including myoglobin, potassium, phosphate and creatine kinase — into the circulation. Filtered myoglobin (a heme protein) is nephrotoxic and contributes to pigment-induced acute tubular necrosis; the released heme pigment also causes a false-positive dipstick reaction for blood. Concurrent volume sequestration into injured muscle produces a prerenal/hypovolaemic insult that compounds the tubular injury (Harrison 22e p.343).

Myoglobinuria characteristically produces a positive urine dipstick for blood while urine microscopy shows no (or few) red cells — a key clue distinguishing pigment nephropathy from true haematuria (Harrison 22e p.343).

In rhabdomyolysis-associated acute tubular necrosis the fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) may be paradoxically low (<1%), unlike the classic >1% of established ATN, because the injury is often early/non-oliguric (Harrison 22e p.343).
Rhabdomyolysis is listed among the 'don't-miss' metabolic emergencies whose urgency can be underappreciated, alongside malignant hyperthermia and tumour lysis syndrome (Harrison 22e p.102).

Heat-related exertional rhabdomyolysis is a recognised, albeit rare, cause of sudden death in sickle cell trait carriers during strenuous exercise — a reason to counsel carriers before sports participation (Harrison 22e p.818).
Interpreting a dipstick-positive 'haematuria' as bleeding from the urinary tract when no RBCs are seen on microscopy — this pattern reflects myoglobinuria in rhabdomyolysis (Harrison 22e p.343).
Relying on a low FENa to exclude ATN: rhabdomyolysis-related ATN can present with FENa <1% (Harrison 22e p.343).

Acute rhabdomyolysis typically causes hypocalcaemia, but the recovery phase (with renal failure) can produce rebound hypercalcaemia — calcium should not be over-corrected early (Harrison 22e p.362, p.363).

Rhabdomyolysis-associated acute kidney injury is frequently of the milder, non-oliguric ATN type and is potentially reversible with adequate perfusion; the recovery phase may be complicated by rebound hypercalcaemia (Harrison 22e p.343, p.362).
Hyperkalaemia from release of intracellular potassium during muscle necrosis — predictable and potentially life-threatening (Harrison 22e p.359).
Rising creatinine with pigmented granular casts signalling evolving pigment-induced acute tubular necrosis (Harrison 22e p.343).
