chunks.text: RA is a chronic, systemic, symmetric erosive polyarthritis driven by an interaction of genetic predisposition (e.g., the HLA shared epitope) and environmental triggers such as cigarette smoking. Antigen-presenting cells activate synovial CD4+ T cells (via TCR-MHC class II and CD28-CD80/86 co-stimulation), which differentiate into TH1 and TH17 subsets. These activate B cells that mature into plasma cells producing autoantibodies (RF and anti-CCP/ACPA); immune complexes form within the joint and activate complement, amplifying inflammation. T effector cells stimulate synovial macrophages and fibroblasts to release pro-inflammatory cytokines, with TNF-alpha playing a central role by upregulating endothelial adhesion molecules and driving IL-1, IL-6 and GM-CSF production. TNF-alpha also disrupts the bone balance: it raises DKK-1 (inhibiting Wnt-driven osteoblastic bone formation) and promotes osteoclastogenesis through M-CSF and RANKL signalling, with osteoprotegerin acting as a decoy that limits bone loss. The net result is pannus formation, cartilage and bone erosion, and generalised inflammatory bone loss (Harrison 22e p.2845).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chapter 370 (Rheumatoid Arthritis), pp. 2839-2849

chunks.text: Early-morning joint stiffness lasting more than 1 hour that improves with activity is characteristic; the earliest joints involved are typically the small joints of the hands and feet (Harrison 22e p.2839).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chapter 370 (Rheumatoid Arthritis), pp. 2839-2849

chunks.text: Wrists, MCP and PIP joints are most often affected; isolated DIP involvement usually reflects coexistent osteoarthritis rather than RA itself (Harrison 22e p.2839).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chapter 370 (Rheumatoid Arthritis), pp. 2839-2849

chunks.text: Flexor tendon tenosynovitis is a frequent hallmark, producing reduced range of motion, weakened grip and trigger fingers, and can lead to tendon rupture (most commonly flexor pollicis longus) (Harrison 22e p.2839-2840).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chapter 370 (Rheumatoid Arthritis), pp. 2839-2849

chunks.text: Anti-CCP (ACPA) and RF are useful both diagnostically and as prognostic biomarkers; anti-CCP carries the most value for predicting worse outcomes (Harrison 22e p.2839, p.2847).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chapter 370 (Rheumatoid Arthritis), pp. 2839-2849

chunks.text: Anti-CCP has sensitivity similar to RF but much higher specificity (approaching 95%), so a positive anti-CCP in early inflammatory arthritis helps distinguish RA from other arthritides; testing both RF and anti-CCP adds incremental yield because some patients are positive for only one (Harrison 22e p.2847).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chapter 370 (Rheumatoid Arthritis), pp. 2839-2849

chunks.text: About three-quarters of RA patients are seropositive (RF and/or ACPA) and one-quarter are seronegative; seronegative RA is a clinical diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2847).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chapter 370 (Rheumatoid Arthritis), pp. 2839-2849

chunks.text: A fever above 38.3C (101F) at any point in the course should raise suspicion of systemic vasculitis or superimposed infection rather than being attributed to RA activity alone (Harrison 22e p.2840).

chunks.text: Approximately 30% of RA patients are ANA-positive and some have p-ANCA, but anti-MPO and anti-PR3 are not expected and their presence points to an ANCA-associated vasculitis instead (Harrison 22e p.2847).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chapter 370 (Rheumatoid Arthritis), pp. 2839-2849

chunks.text: Synovial fluid in RA is inflammatory (typically 5,000-50,000 WBC/uL, neutrophil-predominant) versus under 2,000 WBC/uL in osteoarthritis; aspiration is most useful to confirm inflammation and to exclude infection or crystal arthritis (Harrison 22e p.2847).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chapter 370 (Rheumatoid Arthritis), pp. 2839-2849

chunks.text: The 2010 ACR-EULAR criteria are classification (not diagnostic) criteria intended to identify early patients likely to progress; a positive RF or anti-CCP alone does not establish the diagnosis without supporting clinical features (Harrison 22e p.2847).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chapter 370 (Rheumatoid Arthritis), pp. 2839-2849

chunks.text: A negative RF does not exclude RA - IgM RF is found in only ~75% of patients, and RF also occurs in other connective tissue diseases, chronic infections and 1-5% of healthy people (Harrison 22e p.2847).

chunks.text: Accelerated growth of subcutaneous nodules can occur in up to 10% of patients on long-term methotrexate and should not automatically be read as worsening disease (Harrison 22e p.2840).

chunks.text: Periarticular osteopenia, the classic earliest x-ray finding, is difficult to appreciate on plain (especially digitised) films, so early radiographs may appear normal (Harrison 22e p.2848).

chunks.text: Most patients show persistent, waxing-and-waning progressive disease; about 10% (particularly seronegative) remit spontaneously within 6 months, while a minority follow either a relapsing explosive course or an aggressively erosive course (now less common with modern therapy). Early disability is driven mainly by joint inflammation (potentially reversible) and later by cumulative irreversible joint damage. Overall mortality is roughly twice that of the general population, with excess deaths from respiratory illness, cardiovascular disease and infection; median life expectancy is shortened by about 7 years in men and 3 years in women. Worse survival is associated with systemic extraarticular involvement, low functional capacity, low socioeconomic status, low education and chronic prednisone use. Cardiovascular disease is the most common cause of death (Harrison 22e p.2848). Seropositivity for RF and especially anti-CCP predicts worse outcomes (Harrison 22e p.2847).

source.page: Harrison 22e Chapter 370 (Rheumatoid Arthritis), pp. 2839-2849

chunks.text: Fever above 38.3C (101F) during the course should prompt evaluation for systemic vasculitis or infection rather than being ascribed to RA activity (Harrison 22e p.2840).

chunks.text: RA patients have the highest incidence of septic (most often S. aureus) arthritis due to chronically inflamed joints, glucocorticoid therapy and breakdown of nodules/vasculitic ulcers; TNF inhibitors add risk of mycobacterial and other infections (Harrison 22e Chap. 124, p.~).

chunks.text: Atlantoaxial (C1-C2) subluxation can cause compressive myelopathy; neurologic signs may evolve slowly with progressive instability (now seen in under 10% of patients) (Harrison 22e p.2840).

chunks.text: Diagnosis is supported by the 2010 ACR-EULAR classification criteria (for patients with at least one joint of definite clinical synovitis not better explained by another disease), scored 0-10 across four domains - joint involvement (0-5), serology (RF/ACPA, 0-3), acute-phase reactants (CRP/ESR, 0-1), and symptom duration (0-1); a score of 6 or more fulfils requirements for definite RA. Disease activity (the main driver of treatment decisions) is tracked with composite indices: ACR 20/50/70 improvement criteria (mainly for trials) and continuous measures including DAS, SDAI, CDAI and RAPID3 used in practice. Functional disability is measured with the Health Assessment Questionnaire (HAQ) (Harrison 22e p.2847-2848).

chunks.text: Excluding trauma, the commonest cause is rupture of a saccular ('berry') aneurysm, which forms at bifurcations of large- to medium-sized intracranial arteries (about 89% in the anterior circulation, mostly on the circle of Willis). Aneurysm walls show loss of the internal elastic lamina at the neck base with medial thinning and replacement of smooth muscle by connective tissue; rupture is usually at the thin-walled dome through a tear often <=0.5 mm. Rupture deposits blood in the subarachnoid space of the basal cisterns (and sometimes adjacent parenchyma), abruptly raising ICP. Other causes include vascular malformations (AVM, dural arteriovenous fistula) and subarachnoid extension of a primary intracerebral haemorrhage. Roughly 2% of adults harbour intracranial aneurysms and about 20% of affected patients have multiple aneurysms (frequently mirror-image bilateral). Delayed cerebral ischaemia is thought to arise from clot breakdown products acting on basal arteries to cause vasospasm and vessel-wall thickening, but also from vasospasm-independent mechanisms (microthrombosis, inflammation, microvascular dysregulation, cortical spreading depolarisation). Hyponatraemia results from natriuresis with volume depletion ('cerebral salt wasting'), mediated by atrial and brain natriuretic peptides (p.3457-3461).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch. 440, p.3457-3461

chunks.text: The single most important feature of aneurysmal SAH headache is its sudden (abrupt) onset, even more than its severity; ruptures may occasionally present as only moderate headache or as a change in the patient's usual headache pattern (p.3458).

source.page: Harrison 22e Ch. 440, p.3457-3461

chunks.text: Transient loss of consciousness occurs in nearly half of patients at the moment of rupture, reflecting an abrupt rise in intracranial pressure; many patients only report the headache after regaining consciousness (p.3458).

chunks.text: Overall mortality of aneurysmal SAH is about 35%, with roughly a third dying before reaching hospital; over half of survivors are left with significant neurologic deficits from the initial bleed, delayed cerebral ischaemia, or hydrocephalus. Outcome worsens with increasing presentation grade: grade 1 (Hunt-Hess) patients rarely die if treated, whereas mortality for grades 4-5 may reach about 60%. In an untreated aneurysm, rebleeding risk is about 20% in the first 2 weeks, 30% in the first month, then about 3% per year; rerupture (~30% in the first month, peaking in the first 7 days) carries about 50% mortality. Delayed cerebral ischaemia occurs in about 30% and is the leading cause of delayed morbidity and death among initial survivors. Unruptured aneurysms <7 mm had ~0% 5-year rupture risk in a large study (though many ruptured aneurysms are <6 mm); giant aneurysms (>25 mm) carry ~8-10% annual rupture risk (p.3458-3460).

chunks.text: Two presentation-based clinical grading scales are used (Table 440-1): the Hunt-Hess scale (1 = asymptomatic/minimal headache and slight nuchal rigidity through 5 = coma with reflex posturing or flaccidity) and the World Federation of Neurosurgical Societies (WFNS) scale based on Glasgow Coma Scale score and motor deficits (1 = GCS 15 no motor deficit through 5 = GCS 3-6). Higher grade predicts worse outcome. The modified Fisher CT grading system (Table 440-2) predicts symptomatic vasospasm by the amount and distribution of subarachnoid/intraventricular blood ('thin' <1 mm vs 'thick' >=1 mm), with risk rising from 0% (grade 0) to ~40% (grade 4, thick blood with intraventricular blood) (p.3459-3460).

Other causes of drug-induced respiratory alkalosis: theophylline/aminophylline; also sepsis, hepatic failure, pregnancy/progesterone (p.376)

Salicylate increases sensitivity of the CNS respiratory center and directly stimulates the medullary chemoreceptor, driving hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis. It also uncouples oxidative phosphorylation, inhibits Krebs cycle enzymes, and stimulates carbohydrate and lipid metabolism, generating unmeasured endogenous anions (and increased lactate) that produce a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (p.376, p.3714).

Classic course: early nausea/vomiting and hyperventilation with respiratory alkalosis and alkaline urine, evolving to a mixed respiratory alkalosis plus high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with paradoxical aciduria; late stages show acidemia with CNS and respiratory depression (p.3714).
Salicylates are the most common cause of drug-induced respiratory alkalosis, acting by direct stimulation of the medullary respiratory chemoreceptor (p.376).
Only part of the elevated anion gap is attributable to salicylate itself; concurrent lactic acid production and other endogenous unmeasured anions also contribute (p.370, p.3714).
Cerebral and pulmonary edema can develop in severe poisoning; non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema (ARDS) is a recognized complication (p.3705, p.3714).
Hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia, hypokalemia, and seizures can occur in salicylate toxicity (p.3714).
Ketosis can accompany salicylate poisoning and may mimic other causes of ketoacidosis (p.3705).
Salicylate is detected on quantitative serum assay; serum levels guide management and are usually available within an hour (p.3706).

Enteric-coated and sustained-release salicylate preparations cause delayed/slow absorption and can form gastric concretions (bezoars), acting as a 'toxic time-bomb' with continued rising levels (p.3705, p.3752).
Vigorous gastric lavage, if used, should be with isotonic saline, NOT NaHCO3 (p.370).
Only a portion of the anion gap is due to salicylate itself; do not assume the whole gap reflects drug level (p.370).
Acid (acidic) diuresis is never indicated and is potentially harmful (p.3752).
Acetazolamide can cause systemic metabolic acidosis if excreted bicarbonate is not replaced, which markedly reduces salicylate clearance (p.370).
Delayed/slow absorption from enteric-coated, sustained-release, or concretion-forming salicylate means a single early level can underestimate toxicity; repeat levels (p.3705, p.3752).
Coma, seizures, cerebral edema (p.3714)
Pulmonary edema / ARDS (p.3705, p.3714)
Renal failure (impairs clearance) (p.376)
Progressive acid-base disturbance / late acidemia with CNS and respiratory depression (p.3714)
Salicylate level >7 mmol/L (100 mg/dL) after acute overdose (p.3714)

Stages by clinical/acid-base course: (1) early respiratory alkalosis with alkalemia, alkaluria, nausea/vomiting and hyperventilation; (2) mixed respiratory alkalosis plus high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with paradoxical aciduria; (3) late acidemia with CNS and respiratory depression, cerebral and pulmonary edema in severe cases. Severe-toxicity markers include coma, cerebral edema, seizures, pulmonary edema, renal failure, progressive acid-base disturbance, and salicylate level >7 mmol/L (100 mg/dL) after acute overdose (p.3714).

chunks.text: Sarcoidosis is thought to arise from a heightened, antigen-driven host immune response to an undetermined (likely inhaled bioaerosol or inorganic) environmental antigen in a genetically susceptible person; the inciting antigen may differ between individuals/populations. A poorly degradable material is presented to lymphocytes by dendritic cells/macrophages via MHC, triggering an innate cytokine/chemokine cascade and recruitment of adaptive immune cells. The immunopathologic hallmark is highly polarized CD4+ TH1 lymphocytes (less so CD8+) producing IFN-gamma, with upregulation of TH1-promoting cytokines/chemokines (IL-1, IL-2, IL-15, IL-18, CXCR3) that activate macrophages and drive formation of tightly organized nonnecrotizing (noncaseating) granulomas. Altered regulatory T-cell and TH17 responses are implicated in failure to resolve and in progression to fibrosis. Granulomas comprise macrophages, epithelioid cells, and multinucleated giant cells rimmed by lymphocytes/fibroblasts (CD4+ central, CD8+ and B cells peripheral). Mycobacterial proteins (mKatG, ESAT-6, superoxide dismutase A, antigen 85A, heat-shock proteins) and Cutibacterium acnes have been disproportionately implicated; the transmissibility seen with the Kveim-Siltzbach reagent and via organ transplantation supports an antigenic trigger (p.2922-2923).

chunks.text: Sarcoidosis is a systemic granulomatous disease of unknown cause; the lung is involved in over 90% of cases, but roughly half of patients have extrapulmonary disease and almost any organ can be affected (p.2921, p.2924).

chunks.text: Disease resolves spontaneously in just over half of patients, but 30-40% develop chronic disease threatening vital organs or causing debilitating symptoms. Most patients show radiographic or spirometric improvement by 2 years (treated or untreated). Death attributable to sarcoidosis occurs in roughly 1-5%, most often from progressive respiratory insufficiency/pulmonary fibrosis (leading cause in the US/Northern Europe) or cardiac involvement (predominant cause of death in Japan). A robust acute initial immune response predicts a better outcome: Löfgren and Heerfordt syndromes remit spontaneously in up to ~80%, and immunosuppression is rarely needed. Adverse prognostic factors include lupus pernio, chronic uveitis, older age, chronic hypercalcemia, nephrocalcinosis, African ancestry, pulmonary hypertension, fibrotic pulmonary disease, sinus involvement, cystic bone lesions, neurosarcoidosis, and cardiac involvement. Relapses are common and associated with shorter treatment duration (p.2928-2929).

chunks.text: A seizure reflects a shift in the normal balance between excitation and inhibition in the CNS. At the cellular level the hallmark of focal seizure activity is the electrographic spike, generated by near-simultaneous bursting (the 'paroxysmal depolarization shift') of local excitatory neurons - a prolonged membrane depolarization driven by calcium influx that opens voltage-gated sodium channels, followed by a GABA- or potassium-mediated hyperpolarizing afterpotential. Surrounding inhibition normally limits spread; when recruitment overwhelms it (via rising extracellular potassium, presynaptic calcium accumulation with enhanced transmitter release, NMDA-receptor activation, and ephaptic effects), activity propagates through local cortical and long commissural pathways (e.g., corpus callosum). Generalized 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges of absence seizures arise from thalamocortical oscillatory circuits involving GABA-B receptors, T-type calcium channels, and potassium channels. Many causes converge on three interacting factor classes: endogenous (genetic/developmental seizure-threshold) factors, epileptogenic factors (CNS injury such as severe penetrating head trauma, stroke, infection, or neurodegeneration that, over months to years, transforms a normal network into a chronically hyperexcitable one - 'epileptogenesis'), and precipitating factors (sleep deprivation, stress, hormonal change, toxins, certain drugs, photic stimulation). Many inherited epilepsies are channelopathies due to ion-channel mutations (p.3411-3415).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Chapter 436 (Seizures and Epilepsy), p.3408-3428

chunks.text: A seizure is a transient event from abnormal excessive or synchronous neuronal activity; epilepsy is the distinct condition of recurrent unprovoked seizures from a chronic underlying process. A single seizure, or seizures due to a correctable/avoidable cause, is not by itself epilepsy (p.3408).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Chapter 436 (Seizures and Epilepsy), p.3408-3428

chunks.text: If the sole cause of a seizure is a correctable metabolic disturbance (e.g., electrolyte or glucose abnormality), or a precipitant drug/illicit substance, treatment targets the underlying problem and chronic antiseizure drugs are usually unnecessary (p.3419).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Chapter 436 (Seizures and Epilepsy), p.3408-3428

chunks.text: An apparently unprovoked first seizure carries a recurrence risk estimated at roughly 31-71% in the first 12 months; accepted risk factors favoring treatment are prior brain insult (stroke/trauma), epileptiform EEG, a significant imaging abnormality, or a nocturnal seizure (p.3420).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Chapter 436 (Seizures and Epilepsy), p.3408-3428

chunks.text: A serum prolactin rise in the 30 min after most generalized and some focal seizures can support an epileptic cause, but it is unreliable because baseline levels are rarely available and some drugs elevate prolactin (p.3419).

chunks.text: The clinical range of focal seizure behaviors is extremely broad, so caution is advised before dismissing paroxysmal stereotypic bizarre episodes as non-epileptic (p.3409).

chunks.text: The age of the patient strongly informs the likely etiology of new seizures - e.g., febrile seizures and genetic/developmental causes in young children versus cerebrovascular disease, tumor, metabolic disturbance and degenerative disease in older adults (p.3411-3414).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Chapter 436 (Seizures and Epilepsy), p.3408-3428

chunks.text: Operationally, epilepsy is defined as two or more unprovoked seizures, though a single seizure with clinical or EEG features portending high recurrence risk can establish the diagnosis (p.3408-3409).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Chapter 436 (Seizures and Epilepsy), p.3408-3428

chunks.text: Seizures are fundamentally classified as focal (network limited to one hemisphere; often structural) versus generalized (rapidly engaging both hemispheres) versus unknown onset; the older terms 'partial', 'simple/complex partial' are no longer used (p.3409).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Chapter 436 (Seizures and Epilepsy), p.3408-3428

chunks.text: Focal seizures are subclassified by awareness (intact vs impaired) and onset (motor vs nonmotor); a focal seizure can evolve to a bilateral tonic-clonic seizure (formerly 'secondary generalization') (p.3409).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Chapter 436 (Seizures and Epilepsy), p.3408-3428

chunks.text: Distinguishing a focal seizure that evolves to generalized from a primary generalized tonic-clonic seizure is critical but difficult, because bystanders emphasize the dramatic convulsive phase and overlook the subtle focal onset; a careful history for a preceding aura or focal features, and EEG, are needed because evaluation and treatment differ substantially (p.3410).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Chapter 436 (Seizures and Epilepsy), p.3408-3428

chunks.text: Status epilepticus is continuous seizures, or repetitive discrete seizures with impaired consciousness between them; for generalized convulsive status epilepticus the practical operational threshold is seizures lasting beyond 5 minutes (older definitions used 15-30 min) (p.3425).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Chapter 436 (Seizures and Epilepsy), p.3408-3428

chunks.text: Generalized convulsive status epilepticus (GCSE) is a medical emergency: prolonged seizures cause cardiorespiratory dysfunction, hyperthermia, and metabolic derangements that can produce irreversible CNS injury (p.3425-3426).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Chapter 436 (Seizures and Epilepsy), p.3408-3428

chunks.text: Treatment principle for status epilepticus is an escalating sequence beginning with a benzodiazepine, followed by an IV antiseizure drug, with anesthetic agents for refractory cases - alongside attention to airway, oxygenation, glucose, and reversible metabolic causes (no doses given here) (p.3426).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Chapter 436 (Seizures and Epilepsy), p.3408-3428

chunks.text: After 30-45 min of uninterrupted GCSE the motor signs can become very subtle (only fine finger twitching or rapid eye movements); if a patient stops overt convulsions yet remains comatose, an EEG is required to exclude ongoing (nonconvulsive) status epilepticus (p.3426).

chunks.text: Failing to exclude a treatable provoking cause (metabolic, toxic, structural, or infective) before labeling a patient as having epilepsy - many such seizures need only correction of the underlying problem, not chronic antiseizure drugs (p.3408, p.3419, p.3416-3417).

chunks.text: About half of people respond to the first antiseizure drug; roughly 30% have ongoing seizures despite drug combinations (refractory epilepsy). People with epilepsy have a 2-3 times higher mortality than matched controls, mostly driven by the underlying etiology (e.g., tumor, stroke); excess deaths also arise from accidents, status epilepticus, and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP), which typically affects young patients with convulsive seizures and tends to occur at night, possibly via brainstem-mediated cardiorespiratory/arousal effects. Simple febrile seizures do not raise the risk of later epilepsy, whereas complex febrile seizures carry a 2-5% risk. Severe penetrating head trauma carries up to a ~45% (penetrating/depressed fracture/hemorrhage/prolonged coma: 30-50%) risk of subsequent epilepsy, closed head injury with contusion 5-25%, and mild concussion only slightly increased risk. Favorable factors for staying seizure-free after planned drug withdrawal include 1-5 years of control, a single seizure type, normal exam/intelligence, normal EEG, and no family history (p.3411, p.3414, p.3420, p.3424, p.3426-3427).

chunks.text: Seizures are classified (ILAE 2017) by onset: (1) Focal onset (with intact or impaired awareness; motor or nonmotor onset; may evolve to bilateral tonic-clonic); (2) Generalized onset - motor (tonic-clonic, or other such as atonic/myoclonic) or nonmotor (absence); (3) Unknown onset. Status epilepticus is staged by duration/refractoriness in management terms: impending/early (5-30 min), established and early-refractory (30 min to 48 h), and late refractory (>48 h), with subtypes generalized convulsive (GCSE) versus nonconvulsive (NCSE) (p.3409, p.3425-3426).

chunks.text: Serotonin syndrome results from excess CNS and peripheral serotonergic activity — promotion of serotonin release, inhibition of its reuptake, or direct stimulation of serotonin receptors (chiefly 5-HT1A and 5-HT2), occurring alone or when serotonergic drugs are combined. NMS, in contrast, is linked to dopamine-antagonist (neuroleptic) exposure or abrupt loss of dopaminergic tone, producing central hyperthermia, rigidity and autonomic dysfunction; central dopamine depletion impairs hypothalamic (preoptic/anterior) thermoregulation. Both are classified among the hypothalamic disorders of autonomic/temperature regulation (Harrison 22e p.3541, p.3517, p.3715).

chunks.text: A delayed, T-cell-mediated (type IVa, cytotoxic) severe cutaneous adverse reaction. A drug or metabolite-altered antigen is presented in association with a risk HLA class I allele by keratinocytes or other antigen-presenting cells; a restricted T-cell receptor on skin-enriched CD8+ T cells recognizes this drug-HLA complex, triggering activation and release of cytolytic mediators (notably granulysin) that cause full-thickness epidermal keratinocyte death and detachment. Proposed antigen-presentation models include hapten/prohapten covalent binding, the pharmacologic-interaction (p-i) noncovalent model, and the altered-peptide-repertoire model (as proven for abacavir-HLA-B*57:01). Carbamazepine SJS/TEN shows a highly restricted V-alpha/V-beta TCR repertoire shared among HLA-B*15:02 patients. A risk HLA allele alone is insufficient; non-MHC factors such as drug metabolism (e.g., CYP2C9*3 slow metabolism with phenytoin) contribute. (Harrison 22e p.417-420)

chunks.text: SLE arises from overactive innate and adaptive immunity with autoantibodies directed at nuclear components (nucleic acids, nucleosomes, RNA-binding proteins). Impaired clearance of cellular debris — driven by high neutrophil turnover/NETosis and defective complement-mediated phagocytosis — overwhelms macrophages and dendritic cells. Accumulated nucleic acids engage toll-like receptors and nucleic-acid sensors in plasmacytoid dendritic cells, driving type 1 interferon production that primes the immune response. Autoreactive B cells (including expanded age-associated B cells) lose tolerance and, with help from T follicular/T peripheral helper cells, mature into autoantibody-secreting plasma cells, while regulatory T-cell function is defective. Resulting immune complexes deposit in tissues and cause inflammation, repair, and eventual fibrosis after recurrent flares. Strong genetic component (monozygotic twin concordance 24% vs 2% dizygotic; >150 GWAS loci, with the MHC the strongest and nearly half of loci linked to type 1 interferon; monogenic complement-pathway deficiencies — C1q, C1r/s, C2, C4 — cause severe SLE). Environmental triggers include UV light, smoking, crystalline silica, mercury/toxins, sex hormones, EBV, and gut microbiome/permeability changes (p.2827-2829).

Bleeding occurs beneath the dura (subdural space). The bleeding producing larger subdural haematomas is primarily venous in origin, classically from torn bridging veins, although arterial bleeding sites are occasionally found at operation and a few large haematomas are purely arterial. Chronic subdural haematomas develop days to weeks after (often trivial) injury, favoured by age-related cerebral atrophy that stretches bridging veins; they organise into a vascular fibrous capsule, and weeks-old collections often contain a mixture of blood and serous fluid. Anticoagulant-related intracranial haemorrhages are often subdural and may continue to evolve over 24-48 h if coagulopathy is insufficiently reversed (pp.3572-3573, 3498).

Direct cranial trauma may be minor and is not always required for an acute subdural bleed, particularly in the elderly and those on anticoagulants; acceleration forces alone (e.g. whiplash) can suffice (p.3572).
Up to one-third of patients with acute subdural haematoma have a lucid interval of minutes to hours before coma supervenes, but most are drowsy or comatose from the moment of injury (p.3572).
A unilateral headache with a slightly enlarged pupil on the side of the haematoma is frequently, though not invariably, present (p.3572).
Small subdural haematomas may be asymptomatic and usually do not require evacuation unless they enlarge (p.3572).
In chronic subdural haematoma, drowsiness, inattentiveness and incoherent thinking are generally more prominent than focal signs such as hemiparesis (p.3573).
Chronic subdural haematoma headache typically fluctuates in severity, sometimes with changes in head position (p.3573).
A history of trauma may be absent in chronic subdural haematoma; the injury may have been trivial and forgotten, especially in the elderly and those with clotting disorders (p.3572).
Recurrent falls in older adults place them at risk for subdural haematoma; brain imaging is warranted when neurologic signs are present (pp.222-223, 3927, 3929).
Trauma should be considered in any patient with an unexplained acute neurologic deficit (hemiparesis, stupor, confusion), particularly after a fall (p.3498).
Subacute pitfall: between roughly 2 and 6 weeks after the initial bleed the clot becomes isodense relative to adjacent brain on non-contrast CT and may be inapparent/missed (p.3573).

Acute subdural produces more horizontal displacement (mass effect) than expected from its thickness because of its large rostral-caudal extent, so mass effect can be underestimated from clot thickness alone (p.3572).
Absence of a trauma history does not exclude chronic subdural haematoma in the elderly or anticoagulated (p.3572).
Skull fractures are markers of injury site/severity, not the haematoma itself, and may be absent (p.3572).

In contrast to epidural haematomas, acute subdural haematomas requiring surgery carry significant morbidity and mortality, partly reflecting frequently associated underlying cortical brain damage. Chronic subdural collections evacuated through burr holes are usually treated successfully when a postoperative cranial drain is used; encapsulating fibrous membranes may require craniotomy to prevent recurrent fluid accumulation (pp.3572-3573).
Stupor or coma, hemiparesis, and unilateral pupillary enlargement indicate a larger acute haematoma (p.3572)
Acutely deteriorating patient requiring emergency craniotomy (p.3572)
Repetitive vomiting, nystagmus, drowsiness and unsteadiness may signal a posterior fossa subdural haematoma (p.3619)
Large bleed after only minor trauma should raise concern for coagulopathy or anticoagulant therapy (p.3573)

chunks.text: SVC syndrome results from obstruction of the superior vena cava causing a severe reduction in venous return from the head, neck, and upper extremities. Obstruction may be due to external compression, direct tumour invasion, intraluminal thrombosis (often device-related), or fibrosis. Venous congestion produces facial/upper-body swelling, distended neck veins, and development of collateral venous channels over the chest wall. The 'hot quadrate' focal hepatic hotspot on CT reflects portosystemic shunting between the SVC and portal vein. Chronic SVCS can produce 'downhill' oesophageal varices (cephalad-to-caudad flow, opposite to portal-hypertension 'uphill' varices), which may bleed late.

Pericardial fluid accumulates between the visceral (epicardial) and parietal pericardial layers. Tamponade develops when intrapericardial pressure rises enough to exceed the filling pressures of the cardiac chambers, generally the right ventricle, impairing diastolic filling. Because the relatively non-distensible pericardial sac determines tolerance, the rate of fluid accumulation is more important than absolute volume: slow accumulation allows large effusions without compromise, while rapid accumulation (trauma, cardiac rupture, procedural perforation, aortic dissection into the pericardium) causes tamponade at small volumes. Inspiratory augmentation of right-heart filling at the expense of the left, mediated by exaggerated interventricular dependence within the fixed pericardial space, produces pulsus paradoxus (p.1906, p.1938).

Tamponade is fundamentally a clinical diagnosis in an unstable patient; the textbook triad is hypotension, raised jugular venous pressure with neck-vein distention, and quiet/muffled heart sounds (p.630).
It is the balance between intrapericardial pressure and ventricular (especially right ventricular) filling pressure that drives compression, not the absolute volume of fluid (p.1938).

Rate of accumulation matters more than total volume: slowly forming effusions (e.g. malignant) can become large without classic tamponade physiology, whereas rapid accumulation (e.g. cardiac rupture, perforation, aortic dissection into the pericardium) can cause tamponade with only a small effusion (p.1938).
Pulsus paradoxus is an inspiratory fall in systolic pressure of more than 10 mmHg and represents an exaggerated form of normal interventricular dependence (p.1906).

Measure pulsus paradoxus by deflating the cuff slowly and noting the gap between the pressure where Korotkoff sounds are first heard (only in expiration) and the pressure where they are heard with every beat regardless of respiration; a difference >15 mmHg may even be palpable at the brachial or femoral pulse (p.1906).
A pulsus paradoxus exceeding 12 mmHg in a patient with a large pericardial effusion is highly predictive of tamponade (reported sensitivity ~98%, specificity ~83%) (p.1910).

The ECG triad of sinus tachycardia, low QRS voltage, and total electrical alternans (beat-to-beat P-QRS-T alternation) strongly suggests pericardial effusion with tamponade physiology, though it is insensitive (p.1917).

Total electrical alternans (whole-complex) is relatively specific for effusion/tamponade; in contrast, pure repolarization (ST-T/U-wave) alternans signals electrical instability and risk of ventricular arrhythmia, not tamponade (p.1917).
Echocardiography is the initial test of choice for suspected effusion/tamponade and can usually be done rapidly at the bedside (p.1938).

Do not delay decompression in a hemodynamically unstable patient waiting for confirmatory tests; tamponade is a clinical/emergency diagnosis and instability requires immediate drainage (p.147, p.630).
Failing to appreciate the urgency of the situation is a recognized diagnostic error for tamponade (listed among can't-miss time-critical diagnoses) (p.102).
Pulsus paradoxus can be hard to measure or unreliable in tachycardia, atrial fibrillation, or tachypnea (p.1906).

A large slowly-accumulating effusion may lack classic tamponade signs, while a small rapidly-accumulating effusion may already be causing tamponade; judging severity by volume alone is misleading (p.1938).

In malignant tamponade, relatively specific signs (paradoxical pulse, diminished heart sounds, pulsus alternans, friction rub) are LESS common than in nonmalignant disease, so their absence does not exclude tamponade (p.630).
ECG and chest radiograph are abnormal in ~90% of malignant pericardial cases but about half of those abnormalities are nonspecific (p.630).

Outcome depends heavily on cause and timeliness of drainage. Untreated tuberculous pericarditis is usually fatal and even treated TB pericarditis carries case-fatality rates up to ~40% in some series, with risk of progression to constrictive pericarditis. Cancer patients whose pericardial fluid contains malignant cells on cytology have very poor survival. After percutaneous catheter drainage of malignant effusions the recurrence rate is ~20%, and a subset develop paradoxical hemodynamic worsening after drainage (post-drainage low cardiac output syndrome) (p.630, p.1432).
Hypotension with tachycardia in a chest-pain patient mandates rapid evaluation for tamponade as one of the immediately life-threatening causes (p.147)
Life-threatening hemodynamic instability with acute tamponade requires immediate fluid drainage (p.630)
Hemorrhagic tamponade from cardiac rupture, procedural perforation, or aortic dissection into the pericardium can be catastrophic at small effusion volumes (p.1938)

chunks.text: A panarteritis of medium- and large-sized arteries, classically branches of the carotid (especially the temporal artery) but systemically involving the aorta and its branches. Histology shows mononuclear inflammatory infiltrate within the vessel wall with frequent giant cell formation, intimal proliferation, and fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina; organ damage results from ischemia of involved vessels. It is considered an antigen-driven process: CD4+ T cells enter via the adventitial vasa vasorum, become activated, and drive macrophage differentiation, with restricted clonal T-cell expansion suggesting an arterial-wall antigen. Lesional T cells produce mainly IL-2 and IFN-gamma; both IFN-gamma-producing TH1 and IL-17-producing TH17 lineages contribute and may differ in glucocorticoid responsiveness. [guideline] management

Other causes of thyrotoxicosis besides Graves' disease must be considered (e.g. toxic adenoma, toxic multinodular goitre, destructive thyroiditis, ectopic thyroid tissue, factitious thyrotoxicosis); radionuclide scan/uptake or color-flow Doppler ultrasonography helps distinguish hyperthyroidism from destructive thyroiditis (Harrison 22e p.3078).
Suppressed TSH with elevated total and unbound (free) T4 and T3 (Harrison 22e p.3078).

T3 toxicosis (only T3 raised) in 2-5% of patients, more in areas of borderline iodine intake; T4 toxicosis (raised T4, normal T3) is occasionally seen when hyperthyroidism is iodine-induced (Harrison 22e p.3078).
TRAb (TSH receptor antibody) measurement to support a diagnosis of Graves' disease (Harrison 22e p.3078).
Watch for confounding biochemistry: elevated bilirubin, liver enzymes and ferritin, plus microcytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia, may accompany thyrotoxicosis (Harrison 22e p.3078).

Thyroid storm represents a severe, decompensated form of thyroid hormone excess (thyrotoxicosis), typically arising when an acute stressor is superimposed on partially treated or untreated hyperthyroidism. Excess circulating thyroid hormone drives a hypermetabolic, hyperadrenergic state; high cardiac output produces a bounding pulse, widened pulse pressure and may precipitate or worsen heart failure or angina, particularly in the elderly or those with pre-existing heart disease (Harrison 22e p.3077, p.3080).
Thyrotoxic crisis (thyroid storm) is a rare, life-threatening exacerbation of hyperthyroidism (Harrison 22e p.3080).
Characteristic features include fever, delirium, seizures, coma, vomiting, diarrhoea and jaundice (Harrison 22e p.3080).

Often precipitated by an acute intercurrent illness (e.g. stroke, infection, trauma, diabetic ketoacidosis), by surgery (especially thyroid surgery), or by radioiodine treatment given to a patient whose hyperthyroidism is only partially treated or untreated (Harrison 22e p.3080).
Apathetic thyrotoxicosis: in the elderly, features may be subtle or masked, presenting mainly with fatigue and weight loss, and can be mistaken for depression (Harrison 22e p.3076).
Thyrotoxicosis may be complicated by a form of hypokalaemic periodic paralysis, particularly common in Asian males (Harrison 22e p.3076).
Treatment of the thyrotoxic state alone restores sinus rhythm in up to 75% of patients with thyrotoxicosis-associated atrial fibrillation who have no underlying cardiac disease (Harrison 22e p.3077).
Radioiodine therapy in a patient with partially treated or untreated hyperthyroidism can itself precipitate thyrotoxic crisis (Harrison 22e p.3080).
In the elderly, thyrotoxicosis may be masked (apathetic thyrotoxicosis), delaying recognition (Harrison 22e p.3076).
Mortality remains high (4-17%) even with treatment, usually from cardiac failure, arrhythmia or hyperthermia (Harrison 22e p.3080).
Fever, delirium, seizures or coma in a thyrotoxic patient indicate thyroid storm (Harrison 22e p.3080).
Death is most often due to cardiac failure, arrhythmia or hyperthermia (Harrison 22e p.3080).

A TIA results from transient focal cerebral ischaemia when blood flow falls for longer than several seconds; neurons lack glycogen so deficits appear within seconds, but because the occluded vessel reopens and flow is restored before infarction occurs, symptoms resolve completely. Mechanisms mirror ischaemic stroke: emboli to the brain (cardiac or proximal arterial source) or in-situ thrombosis of an intracranial vessel. Small-vessel (lacunar) TIAs may recur several times a day and last only minutes (Harrison 22e p.3428, 3448, 3447).
TIA classically produces 'negative' symptoms (transient loss of function); positive sensory symptoms or involuntary movements point instead to seizure (p.3378).
Most TIAs last under 1 hour, well within the historical 24-hour window (p.3448).

About 25% of symptomatic internal carotid disease is heralded by recurrent transient monocular blindness (amaurosis fugax), typically described as a horizontal shade sweeping down or up across one eye, lasting a few minutes (p.3430).
A high-pitched carotid bruit fading into diastole suggests a tight stenosis; paradoxically the bruit may fade or vanish as occlusion becomes imminent and flow drops (p.3430).
Causes of TIA and ischaemic stroke are identical, so the diagnostic evaluation of a TIA should parallel that of a completed stroke (p.3448).
A TIA is a clinical diagnosis: a normal brain imaging study does NOT rule it out (p.3448).

If a relevant infarction is seen on imaging, the event is reclassified as a stroke regardless of how briefly symptoms lasted — the modern definition is tissue-based, not purely time-based (p.3428, p.3448).
Patients with carotid/vertebrobasilar TIA may report symptoms 'in one eye' when the deficit is actually a homonymous hemifield loss affecting both eyes (p.3430-equivalent / cortical visual TIA).
Acephalgic migraine can mimic TIA even with no prior migraine history and even after age 65 (p.3428).

Stroke risk after a TIA is approximately 10-15% within the first 3 months, with most events occurring in the first 2 days; this early risk is well predicted by the ABCD2 score, so urgent evaluation and treatment are justified (Harrison 22e p.3448).
Most strokes after a TIA occur within the first 2 days — the early window is the highest-risk period and warrants urgent (not deferred) workup (p.3448)
Stuttering or crescendo course of small-vessel TIAs heralding lacunar infarct can progress to severe permanent disability (p.3447)
Amaurosis fugax indicates a symptomatic internal carotid source needing prompt carotid evaluation (p.3430)

ABCD2 score (Harrison 22e p.3448) stratifies early stroke risk after TIA: 1 point each for Age >=60, BP (SBP >140 or DBP >90 mmHg), and Diabetes; for Clinical features 2 points for unilateral weakness or 1 for speech disturbance without weakness; for Duration 2 points for >=60 min or 1 for 10-59 min. The 3-month stroke rate rises with the total: ~0% at score 0-1, ~3% at 2-3, ~8% at 4, ~12% at 5, ~17% at 6, and ~22% at 7.

chunks.text: Liver injury can follow ingestion of essentially any xenobiotic (industrial toxins, drugs, herbal/dietary supplements). Most drugs are lipophilic and undergo phase I oxidation/methylation by cytochrome P450 enzymes followed by phase II conjugation (glucuronidation, sulfation) or glutathione inactivation to a water-soluble form for renal/biliary excretion; most hepatotoxicity arises from a reactive phase I metabolite, and glutathione depletion compounds the injury. Damage occurs through several overlapping routes: direct hepatocyte injury via free radicals/reactive intermediates causing membrane lipid peroxidation; activation of innate or adaptive immune responses (HLA-haplotype-dependent hapten binding, cytotoxic lymphocytes, antibody-mediated cytotoxicity); triggering of apoptosis via TNF-alpha/Fas pathways; disruption of bile canalicular transport pumps (e.g., MRP3) leading to toxic bile-acid accumulation and cholestasis; and inhibition of mitochondrial beta-oxidation/respiration producing lactic acidosis and microvesicular steatosis. Nuclear receptors such as CAR and PXR can also induce hepatotoxicity. For acetaminophen specifically, a minor fraction is converted by CYP2E1 to the reactive metabolite NAPQI, normally detoxified by conjugation with hepatoprotective glutathione; when NAPQI overwhelms or glutathione is depleted, NAPQI binds covalently to hepatocyte macromolecules forming protein adducts that drive centrilobular necrosis.

chunks.text: Most DILI is self-limited and resolves after the offending agent is withdrawn. However, acute liver failure develops in about 10% of DILI cases; once that threshold (coagulopathy plus hepatic encephalopathy) is reached, spontaneous recovery occurs in fewer than 30%, and liver transplantation is undertaken in more than 40% of these patients (p.2668). For acetaminophen, up to 72% of poisoned patients in some Scandinavian series progress to encephalopathy and coagulopathy (lower in the UK/US); a single dose of 10-15 g can cause clinical injury and fulminant fatal disease is usually associated with >=25 g; the N-acetylcysteine antidote markedly reduces severity and is most effective given early (within ~8-12 h), though it retains some benefit up to 24-36 h. Survivors of acetaminophen overdose rarely have ongoing liver injury (p.2668, p.2670). Several agents cause chronic injury or progression to cirrhosis (methotrexate, tamoxifen, amiodarone), and the autoimmune-pattern agents (nitrofurantoin, minocycline, hydralazine, methyldopa) can lead to cirrhosis if not recognised early (p.2668-2670).

chunks.text: Injury pattern is classified by the R value (ALT/ALP as multiples of ULN): R >5.0 hepatocellular, R <2.0 cholestatic, R 2.0-5.0 mixed (p.2667). Hy's Law serves as a severity/prognostic marker: jaundice (significant bilirubin rise) accompanying hepatocellular DILI predicts a markedly higher risk of acute liver failure (about a 10:1 jaundice-to-failure ratio) (p.2667). The aminotransferase threshold of >5x ULN (or >3x ULN with symptoms) marks the point at which the offending agent should be withdrawn (p.2668). Causality (not severity) is graded on a five-point likelihood scale by DILIN (definite, highly likely, probable, possible, unlikely) (p.2668). The clinical endpoint of severity is acute liver failure, defined by coagulopathy plus hepatic encephalopathy (p.2668).

chunks.text: TTP arises from deficient or antibody-inhibited ADAMTS13, the metalloprotease that cleaves von Willebrand factor (VWF). VWF is secreted by endothelium as ultra-large multimers; when these are not cleaved they persist and drive pathological platelet adhesion and aggregation, producing microvascular thrombi. ADAMTS13 deficiency alone is not sufficient — congenitally ADAMTS13-deficient individuals develop TTP only episodically, implying a second trigger. In HUS the dominant lesion is endothelial injury with deposition of fibrin in capillary/arteriolar walls, predominantly in the kidney; typical (diarrhoea-associated) HUS is driven by Shiga toxin from E. coli O157:H7, while atypical HUS results from dysregulated activation of the complement alternative pathway with consequent endothelial damage. The shared downstream picture is microvascular platelet/fibrin thrombi causing red-cell fragmentation (MAHA), consumption thrombocytopenia and end-organ ischaemia (Harrison 22e pp.967-968, 800-801).

chunks.text: Plasma exchange transformed TTP outcomes, reducing mortality from roughly 85-100% to about 10-30%. Relapse is common: 25-45% of plasma-exchange-treated patients relapse within 30 days of apparent remission and 12-40% relapse late, with relapse more frequent in those with severe ADAMTS13 deficiency at presentation. In diarrhoea-associated HUS roughly 40% of children need some dialysis but overall mortality is <5%; non-diarrhoeal HUS carries higher mortality (~26%). Untreated atypical HUS had acute-phase mortality up to ~15% with up to 50% progressing to end-stage renal disease, though spontaneous remission occurs and relapse is likely with re-exposure to a trigger. Cancer-/chemotherapy-associated HUS has a high case-fatality rate, with most patients dying within months (Harrison 22e pp.968, 800-801, 638).

Thrombotic microangiopathy (TTP/HUS) (non-infective) — Hematology
Microangiopathic haemolysis with thrombocytopenia and neurological signs suggests TTP — do not transfuse platelets reflexively.
Red flags: Haematological emergency — urgent plasma exchange
[guideline] management
Peptic ulcer disease — the most common cause of upper GI bleeding (~50% of UGIB hospitalisations) (p.360)
Mallory-Weiss tear — ~2-10% of UGIB, classically preceded by vomiting/retching/coughing, usually on the gastric side of the gastro-oesophageal junction; stops spontaneously in ~80-90% (p.360)
Bleeding gastric varices, intestinal varices, and portal hypertensive gastropathy/enterocolopathy — other portal-hypertension-related sources distinct from oesophageal varices (p.361, p.2714)
Erosive disease — erosive oesophagitis, gastritis, duodenitis (up to ~30% of UGIB), commonly NSAID-related (p.361)
Stress-related gastric mucosal injury in the critically ill (p.361)

Less common: neoplasm, vascular ectasias (including hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, gastric antral vascular ectasia), Dieulafoy's lesion, aortoenteric fistula, haemobilia/haemosuccus pancreaticus (p.361)

Upper endoscopy within 24 h is first-line both to diagnose the bleeding source and to treat acutely; more urgent endoscopy (6-12 h) does not improve outcomes and may worsen them in high-risk patients (p.362, p.2714)

Endoscopic surveillance for varices: recommended at diagnosis of compensated cirrhosis, then every 2 years (active liver disease) or every 3 years (inactive); also at the time of hepatic decompensation (p.2714)
Liver stiffness by transient elastography — if <20 kPa and no thrombocytopenia, high-risk varices are rare and screening endoscopy may be deferred (p.2714)
HVPG measurement by interventional radiology (hepatic vein cannulation) in selected cases to confirm/quantify portal hypertension (p.371, p.2714)

Complete blood count (thrombocytopenia from hypersplenism is often the first marker of portal hypertension), liver biochemistry, albumin, and prothrombin time/INR to assess hepatic function and severity (p.371, p.2714)

Endoscopic stigmata predicting bleeding risk: red wale signs, hematocystic spots, diffuse erythema, bluish colour, cherry-red spots, white-nipple spots; larger varices and worse Child-Pugh/MELD also predict bleeding (p.2713)

Portal hypertensive gastropathy — snakeskin-like mosaic mucosal pattern on endoscopy; can cause acute or chronic (iron-deficiency) GI bleeding and mimics variceal bleeding as a cause of haematemesis/melaena in the same cirrhotic patient (p.2714)
Gastric varices — also driven by portal hypertension but managed differently from oesophageal varices (p.361, p.2714)

Oesophageal varices are a consequence of portal hypertension, defined as an HVPG >5 mmHg. Portal hypertension arises from two simultaneous haemodynamic processes: (1) increased intrahepatic resistance to portal blood flow (from cirrhosis, regenerative nodules and microthrombi) and (2) increased splanchnic blood flow secondary to splanchnic vasodilation. Cirrhosis is associated with decreased intrahepatic endothelial nitric oxide synthase and nitric oxide, causing intrahepatic vasoconstriction, while systemically nitric oxide, VEGF and TNF rise, driving splanchnic vasodilation. In advanced stages, neurohumoral and vasoconstrictor activation causes sodium/water retention, increased blood volume and a hyperdynamic circulation that further raises portal pressure. Intrahepatic causes (mainly cirrhosis) account for >95% of portal hypertension; pre-hepatic (portal/splenic vein thrombosis) and post-hepatic (Budd-Chiari, right-heart congestion) causes also occur. Elevated portal pressure decompresses into portosystemic collaterals, producing gastro-oesophageal varices that can rupture and bleed. (p.2713-2714)

Portal hypertension is defined as a hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) >5 mmHg; compensated cirrhosis typically has an HVPG of 5-10 mmHg, while clinically significant portal hypertension (CSPH), defined as HVPG ≥10 mmHg, carries substantial risk of decompensation (variceal bleeding, ascites, encephalopathy). Patients with a gradient >12 mmHg are at risk for variceal haemorrhage (p.2713-2714).
Each episode of variceal haemorrhage carries a 20-30% mortality rate, making it an immediate life-threatening complication of portal hypertension (p.2713).

In cirrhotic patients presenting with upper GI bleeding, prophylactic antibiotics (typically ceftriaxone) started before endoscopy reduce bacterial infections, recurrent bleeding AND mortality — this is a mortality-altering intervention, not merely supportive (p.362, p.2714).

A vasoactive/vasoconstricting agent (somatostatin, octreotide, terlipressin, vapreotide) improves initial bleeding control, reduces transfusion needs and reduces all-cause mortality; combined endoscopic plus pharmacologic therapy is superior to either alone (p.360, p.2714).

A restrictive transfusion strategy (transfuse when haemoglobin <7 g/dL, target 7-9 g/dL) reduced early rebleeding and mortality compared with a liberal threshold in randomised trial; haemoglobin may be normal at initial presentation because plasma and red-cell volumes fall proportionately ("people bleed whole blood") and may take up to 72 h to fall (p.362, p.2714).

Roughly one-third of patients with histologically confirmed cirrhosis have varices; about 5-15% of cirrhotics develop varices per year, and roughly one-third of patients with varices will bleed (p.2713).
IV erythromycin given shortly before endoscopy is suggested as a promotility agent to improve endoscopic visualisation in UGI bleeding, reducing the need for repeat endoscopy (p.362, p.2713).

Routine correction of an elevated prothrombin time with fresh frozen plasma is NOT recommended in acute variceal bleeding unless there is evidence of coagulopathy such as bleeding at other sites (e.g. IV-line sites) (p.2714).

Bleeding gastric varices, especially when entirely within the stomach or extending into the proximal stomach, are often not amenable to band ligation; tissue-adhesive injection (e.g. cyanoacrylate), TIPS, or balloon-occluded retrograde transvenous obliteration (BRTO) are alternative principles (p.361, p.2714).

Assuming a normal initial haemoglobin excludes severe bleeding — haemoglobin may be normal or only minimally reduced at presentation and can take up to 72 h to fall as extravascular fluid re-equilibrates (p.362)

Reflexively correcting a prolonged prothrombin time with FFP — not recommended in variceal bleeding without evidence of true coagulopathy, and FFP can raise portal pressure and cause volume overload (p.2714)
Over-liberal transfusion — a liberal threshold (Hb 9 g/dL) increased early rebleeding and mortality versus a restrictive (<7 g/dL) threshold (p.362, p.2714)
Omitting antibiotics in a cirrhotic UGI bleed — prophylactic antibiotics reduce infection, rebleeding and mortality and are a core, not optional, intervention (p.362, p.2714)
Attempting band ligation on gastric or proximal-stomach varices, where it is often unsuccessful — consider tissue adhesive, TIPS or BRTO (p.2714)
Forgetting that TIPS causes new or worsened hepatic encephalopathy in as many as 20% of patients, especially the elderly and those with pre-existing encephalopathy (p.2714)

Variceal haemorrhage carries a 20-30% mortality rate with each bleeding episode and patients with variceal haemorrhage have poorer outcomes than those with other UGIB sources. Control of acute bleeding is achievable in the vast majority of cases, but bleeding recurs in the majority of patients unless definitive endoscopic therapy is instituted; oesophageal varices reflect clinically significant portal hypertension (HVPG ≥10 mmHg), and once cirrhosis decompensates the median survival is <2 years. Prophylactic antibiotics, vasoactive drugs and a restrictive transfusion strategy each independently reduce mortality. (p.360, p.2713-2714)
Variceal haemorrhage is immediately life-threatening with 20-30% mortality per bleeding episode — treat as a major haemorrhage with airway/haemodynamic priority (p.2713)
Hemodynamic compromise (tachycardia, hypotension), increasing age and comorbidities predict rebleeding and death (p.362)
Increased frequency of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) in patients with variceal haemorrhage — SBP prophylaxis is recommended at presentation with upper GI bleeding (p.2715)

Persistent or recurrent bleeding despite endoscopic and medical therapy, and advanced liver disease (Child-Pugh B score 8-9 with active bleeding, or Child-Pugh C score 10-13), mark patients who benefit from early/salvage TIPS (p.360-361)

Bleeding/decompensation risk is stratified by Child-Pugh class and MELD score, by HVPG/wedged-hepatic-vein pressure (CSPH ≥10 mmHg; variceal bleeding risk at >12 mmHg), by varix size and location, and by endoscopic high-risk stigmata (red wale signs, cherry-red spots, etc.). For triage of UGIB generally, the Glasgow-Blatchford score (0-23) identifies very-low-risk patients (score 0-1) suitable for outpatient management. Advanced-disease thresholds favouring early TIPS: Child-Pugh B 8-9 with active bleeding at endoscopy, or Child-Pugh C 10-13. (p.362, p.2713-2714)

Crossmatch, coagulation
Vasoactive (terlipressin) + antibiotic prophylaxis
Variceal bleeding (non-infective) — Hepatology / GI
Haematemesis/melaena in a patient with chronic liver disease suggests variceal bleeding.

chunks.text: Vasculitis is inflammation of and damage to blood vessel walls, usually compromising the lumen and causing ischaemia of supplied tissues; any size, type, or location of vessel may be affected, and disease may be primary/single-organ or secondary to another illness. Most syndromes are at least partly immune-mediated through three broad mechanisms (Harrison 22e p.2936): (1) Immune-complex formation/deposition (e.g., IgA vasculitis, lupus vasculitis, serum sickness, hepatitis-B-associated vasculitis, hepatitis-C cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis) - resembling serum sickness, complexes deposit in vessel walls, activate complement (notably C5a, chemotactic for neutrophils), and neutrophils infiltrate and release enzymes that damage the wall. (2) ANCA production (GPA, MPA, EGPA) - when neutrophils/monocytes are primed by TNF-alpha, IL-1, or alternative-complement activation, PR3 and MPO translocate to the cell membrane where ANCA can engage them, triggering degranulation, reactive oxygen species, endothelial injury, and release of IL-1/IL-8. (3) Pathogenic T-lymphocyte responses and granuloma formation (GCA, Takayasu, GPA, EGPA) - cytokine (IFN-gamma) activated endothelium expresses HLA class II and interacts with CD4+ T cells, with IL-1/TNF-alpha inducing adhesion molecules (ELAM-1, VCAM-1). The 1992/2012 Chapel Hill Consensus nomenclature underpins the classification of these syndromes by predominant vessel size (Harrison 22e p.2936, p.2942).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Chapter 375 (The Vasculitis Syndromes), pp. 2893-2948

chunks.text: Untreated GPA was historically fatal within months; with cyclophosphamide-based therapy >90% improve, ~75% achieve complete remission, and 5-year survival exceeds 80%, but 50-70% of remissions later relapse and many accrue irreversible damage (renal insufficiency, hearing loss, subglottic stenosis, saddle-nose deformity, chronic sinus dysfunction) (Harrison 22e p.2941). Treated MPA has a ~74% 5-year survival, with deaths from alveolar haemorrhage or GI/cardiac/renal disease, and relapse in at least ~34% (Harrison 22e p.2942). Untreated EGPA has a ~25% 5-year survival; treated, prognosis is favourable (~72% at 78 months), but myocardial involvement causes ~39% of deaths (Harrison 22e p.2944). Untreated PAN has a poor 5-year survival of 10-20% (deaths from GI and cardiovascular causes); prednisone plus cyclophosphamide markedly improves survival, with relapse in ~10-20% (Harrison 22e p.2944-2945). In GCA acute death is uncommon, but patients face late mortality from aortic aneurysm rupture/dissection (18x more likely to develop thoracic aortic aneurysm than the general population) (Harrison 22e p.2946). Takayasu outcomes vary widely (overall survival >=94% in some North American series; 5-year mortality 0-35% elsewhere), and the disease is usually chronic and relapsing (Harrison 22e p.2947). IgA vasculitis has an excellent prognosis with rare mortality and only 1-5% of children progressing to end-stage renal disease (Harrison 22e p.2948).

chunks.text: Vasculitides are classified by predominant vessel size per the Chapel Hill Consensus nomenclature (Harrison 22e p.2936, p.2942): LARGE-VESSEL (giant cell/temporal arteritis, Takayasu arteritis); MEDIUM-VESSEL (polyarteritis nodosa, Kawasaki disease); SMALL-VESSEL, which splits into ANCA-associated (GPA, MPA, EGPA) and immune-complex (IgA vasculitis/Henoch-Schonlein, cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis). The chapter also separates PRIMARY syndromes from SECONDARY vasculitis (associated with probable etiology e.g. drug-induced, hepatitis-B/C-related, cancer-associated; or with systemic disease e.g. lupus, rheumatoid, sarcoid vasculitis), and single-organ vasculitis (cutaneous leukocytoclastic angiitis, cutaneous arteritis, primary CNS vasculitis, isolated aortitis) (Harrison 22e p.2936). For management stratification, ANCA-associated vasculitis is divided into SEVERE (life- or organ-threatening; e.g., alveolar haemorrhage, and active glomerulonephritis is severe even with normal renal function) versus NONSEVERE/limited disease - severity depends on both extent and the specific organ involved (e.g., nodular pulmonary disease without respiratory compromise is nonsevere, whereas alveolar haemorrhage is severe) (Harrison 22e p.2941).

chunks.text: Standing pools 500-1000 mL of blood in the lower extremities, buttocks, and splanchnic circulation, reducing venous return, ventricular filling, cardiac output, and blood pressure. Normally baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch trigger a compensatory reflex that raises sympathetic outflow and lowers vagal activity, increasing peripheral resistance, venous return, and cardiac output. In neurally mediated (reflex/vasovagal) syncope this reflex transiently fails: there is a paroxysmal shift in autonomic efferent activity with increased parasympathetic outflow plus sympathoinhibition, producing bradycardia, vasodilation/loss of vasoconstrictor tone (vasodepressor response), and reduced cardiac output. The resulting fall in systemic blood pressure drops cerebral blood flow below the limits of autoregulation, causing transient global cerebral hypoperfusion and loss of consciousness. Multiple afferent triggers (orthostatic stress, carotid sinus, gastrointestinal tract, bladder) converge on the central autonomic network in the medulla. Hyperventilation-induced hypocarbia (cerebral vasoconstriction) and raised intrathoracic pressure (impaired venous return) contribute to many situational reflex syncopes. By contrast, orthostatic hypotension reflects chronic impairment of these homeostatic reflexes (autonomic failure), and cardiac syncope results from arrhythmias or structural disease reducing cardiac output.

source.page: Harrison 22e, Chapter 23 (Syncope), pp.155-162

chunks.text: Syncope is a transient, self-limited loss of consciousness from acute global cerebral hypoperfusion, with rapid onset, brief duration, and spontaneous complete recovery; reorientation is almost immediate after a syncopal event.

source.page: Harrison 22e, Chapter 23 (Syncope), pp.155-162

chunks.text: A clinically meaningful syncope usually corresponds to a fall in systolic BP to roughly 50 mmHg or lower; cessation of cerebral blood flow for 6-8 s produces loss of consciousness.

source.page: Harrison 22e, Chapter 23 (Syncope), pp.155-162

chunks.text: Causes fall into three categories: neurally mediated (reflex/vasovagal) syncope, orthostatic hypotension, and cardiac syncope; clinical features, mechanisms, and prognosis differ markedly among them.

source.page: Harrison 22e, Chapter 23 (Syncope), pp.155-162

chunks.text: Neurally mediated syncope is the most common cause overall in population-based studies and accounts for the vast majority of syncope in the young (peak incidence ~age 15); incidence is higher in women, and a first-degree family history is common in young patients.

source.page: Harrison 22e, Chapter 23 (Syncope), pp.155-162

chunks.text: Vasovagal syncope (the common faint) is provoked by intense emotion, pain, the sight of blood, venipuncture, and/or orthostatic stress; situational reflex syncopes have specific localized triggers (cough, micturition, swallow, defecation, carotid sinus pressure).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Chapter 23 (Syncope), pp.155-162

chunks.text: Premonitory (prodromal) features of autonomic activation in neurally mediated syncope include diaphoresis, pallor, palpitations, nausea, lightheadedness, hyperventilation, and yawning.

source.page: Harrison 22e, Chapter 23 (Syncope), pp.155-162

chunks.text: A functioning autonomic nervous system is required to develop neurally mediated syncope, in contrast to syncope from autonomic failure (orthostatic hypotension).

source.page: Harrison 22e, Chapter 23 (Syncope), pp.155-162

chunks.text: Neurally mediated syncope can be subdivided by efferent pathway: vasodepressor (sympathetic vasoconstrictor failure), cardioinhibitory (bradycardia/asystole from vagal outflow), or mixed.

source.page: Harrison 22e, Chapter 23 (Syncope), pp.155-162

chunks.text: Orthostatic hypotension is defined as a fall in systolic BP of at least 20 mmHg or diastolic BP of at least 10 mmHg within 3 min of standing or head-up tilt; supine and standing BP/HR at 3 min should be measured in every initial evaluation.

source.page: Harrison 22e, Chapter 23 (Syncope), pp.155-162

chunks.text: Convulsive syncope mimics seizure: myoclonic and other movements occur in up to ~90% of syncopal episodes, but syncope-related jerks are typically arrhythmic, multifocal/generalized, and brief (<30 s), with mild flexor/extensor posturing; EEG seizure discharges are absent during syncope.

source.page: Harrison 22e, Chapter 23 (Syncope), pp.155-162

chunks.text: Distinguishing features from seizure: seizure loss of consciousness usually lasts >5 min with prolonged postictal drowsiness/disorientation, whereas reorientation after syncope is almost immediate; muscle aches are longer and more severe after seizures; seizures are rarely provoked by emotion or pain.

source.page: Harrison 22e, Chapter 23 (Syncope), pp.155-162

chunks.text: Urinary incontinence can occur in both syncope and seizure and does not distinguish them; fecal incontinence is very rare in syncope and postictal confusion is rare after syncope.

source.page: Harrison 22e, Chapter 23 (Syncope), pp.155-162

chunks.text: During neurally mediated syncope the eyes typically remain open and deviate upward with dilated pupils, and grunting/moaning/stertorous breathing may occur, which can be mistaken for a seizure.

source.page: Harrison 22e, Chapter 23 (Syncope), pp.155-162

chunks.text: Syncope of noncardiac and unexplained origin in younger individuals carries an excellent prognosis with unaffected life expectancy. In contrast, cardiac syncope (structural heart disease or primary arrhythmia) is associated with an increased risk of sudden cardiac death and overall mortality, and mortality is also increased with orthostatic hypotension related to age and comorbidities. Hospitalization and mortality risk are higher in older adults.

chunks.text: Harrison categorizes syncope by mechanism rather than a graded severity score: (1) neurally mediated (reflex/vasovagal) syncope, (2) orthostatic hypotension, and (3) cardiac syncope. For risk stratification, Table 23-1 lists high-risk features indicating hospitalization or intensive evaluation (e.g., ischemic chest pain, heart failure, significant valvular/structural disease, ECG ischemia, ventricular arrhythmia history, QT >500 ms, SA block/sinus pauses, persistent sinus bradycardia, bi-/trifascicular block or QRS >=120 ms, atrial fibrillation, nonsustained VT, family history of sudden death, preexcitation, Brugada pattern, palpitations at syncope, syncope at rest or during exercise). Neurally mediated efferent subtypes are vasodepressor, cardioinhibitory, and mixed.

chunks.text: Wernicke disease results from thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency. Thiamine is a cofactor for several enzymes including transketolase, pyruvate dehydrogenase, and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase. Deficiency causes a diffuse fall in cerebral glucose utilization and mitochondrial damage; impaired alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase leads to glutamate accumulation, which together with the energy deficit may produce excitotoxic neuronal injury. Lesions are periventricular, surrounding the third ventricle, aqueduct, and fourth ventricle, with predilection for midline structures (dorsomedial thalamus, mammillary bodies, midline cerebellum, periaqueductal gray, and trochlear/abducens nuclei). Acute cases may show petechial hemorrhages; chronic cases show mammillary body atrophy.

chunks.text: Outcome depends on early thiamine administration. Ocular palsies improve within hours of thiamine; horizontal nystagmus may persist. Ataxia improves more slowly than ocular signs, and roughly half of patients recover incompletely, left with a slow, wide-based, shuffling gait and inability to tandem walk. Apathy, drowsiness, and confusion resolve gradually. Korsakoff psychosis is frequently persistent, with permanent gaps in memory, confabulation, and disordered temporal sequencing; prolonged untreated deficiency can cause an irreversible profound amnestic syndrome or death. Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome is underdiagnosed despite a typical history and picture.
